Here's a safe, limited sequence. The most likely cause given the timing and the recently-cleaned filter is a filter that didn't fully lock — water escapes around the filter housing or sits in the bottom and sloshes forward during drain. But run through the rest in order before testing.

GENERAL RULES FIRST
- Leave the machine OFF and the door cracked until you've done the filter reseat.
- Don't run another full normal/heavy cycle as a test. If you test, use a short rinse-only or quick cycle and stay nearby.
- Don't open the door mid-cycle to look around. Steam and water will come out at you.
- If at any point you see more than roughly two tablespoons, see water anywhere other than the front-right corner, smell something electrical, hear grinding, or see sparking — stop and call for service.

STEP 1 — FILTER RESEAT (most likely cause)
- Pull the bottom rack out.
- Remove the filter assembly per your manual. Most twist out (quarter-turn) or pull straight up with a small handle.
- Inspect the filter O-ring or gasket (the small rubber ring on the filter or its housing). Look for: a slipped O-ring, a torn O-ring, food debris stuck under it, or grit on the sealing surface.
- Wipe the filter recess and the seal surfaces with a damp cloth. No soap needed inside the recess unless visibly grimy.
- Reseat the filter firmly. Confirm it's locked by trying to lift it — if it comes out, it's not locked. A quarter-turn clockwise until it clicks is a common pattern; some models push straight down until you feel the catch.
- Confirm the bottom rack wheels are fully on the rails before sliding it back.

Stop here if: the filter O-ring is torn or missing, or the housing itself is cracked. Call for service — don't run a cycle.

STEP 2 — DOOR GASKET INSPECTION
- The gasket is the rubber seal running around the door opening and along the tub edge.
- Run your fingers along the entire gasket, top to bottom on both sides, across the bottom, and especially at the front-right where you saw the water.
- Look and feel for: food debris, hard-water crust, a pinched or twisted section, a section popped out of its groove, a tear, or a soft/mushy area.
- If you find debris, wipe the gasket with a damp cloth and a tiny bit of mild dish soap, then rinse with a damp cloth. Don't use harsh cleaners — they degrade rubber.
- Press the gasket back into its channel where it has lifted out.
- Pay extra attention to the bottom few inches — that's where small leaks travel forward and pool at the front corner.

Stop here if: you find a tear, a permanent deformation, or a section that won't stay seated. Call for service.

STEP 3 — DOOR SEAL / LATCH CHECK (the seal when the door is closed)
- Close the door firmly. Confirm the latch clicks and the door stays flush — no springing open, no gap you can see from the side.
- Look from outside at the gap between the door and the tub frame. It should be even all the way around. A wider gap at one corner is a clue.
- Paper test: close the door on a folded piece of paper at four spots — top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right. Tug gently. If the paper slides out easily anywhere, that spot isn't sealing.
- Check the strike plate (the small metal or plastic tab the latch hooks onto) for looseness or misalignment.

Stop here if: the door doesn't latch solidly, the gap is uneven, or the paper test fails at more than one spot. Call for service.

STEP 4 — LOADING CHECK
- Confirm the bottom rack is fully rolled in and seated on both rails — a partially-out rack tips contents forward and can let the spray arm hit items, splash water forward, or block the filter area.
- Tall items in the bottom rack shouldn't lean against the door or stick up above the rack.
- Nothing should be in front of the detergent dispenser or blocking the rinse aid cap.
- Cutlery in the basket shouldn't protrude past the basket outline.
- The upper rack (if you used it) shouldn't be tilted or overloaded forward.

No stop conditions here — this is just observation. Adjust and move on.

STEP 5 — SHORT TEST CYCLE (only if 1–4 all pass)
- Lay a dry, light-colored towel on the front-right corner of the floor so you can see new water instantly.
- Pick the shortest cycle available — rinse-only or express/quick.
- Start the cycle and stay in the kitchen for the first 5 minutes.
- Watch the towel through the fill, wash, and drain phases. Most filter or gasket leaks show up during fill or wash. Drain-phase leaks often point to the filter housing or the drain path.

Stop the test and call for service if:
- New water appears on the towel during any phase.
- Water appears anywhere else on the floor.
- You hear a hiss or see water spraying when you briefly look through the door window (don't open it).
- The filter area sounds or looks different from a normal cycle.

If the towel stays dry through a full short cycle, run one normal cycle with the towel still in place before considering the issue resolved.

WHEN TO CALL FOR SERVICE, FULL STOP
- Filter O-ring torn, missing, or filter housing cracked.
- Gasket torn, deformed, or won't stay in its channel.
- Door won't latch solidly or gap is uneven after you re-seat the gasket.
- Test cycle produces any new water at all, in any spot.
- You ever see water coming from under the dishwasher, around the supply line, or around the drain hose at the sink — none of which is in scope for what you described today, but flag it if it appears later.

Two tablespoons in one specific corner, with dry supply/drain and no cabinet water, is most often the filter. Steps 1–4 take about ten minutes and use no tools beyond a damp cloth.

Diagnosis tracks — a partial filter lock plus a scrap trapped against the lower-right door gasket is exactly the kind of combo that lets water track out along the door edge and pool on the floor/cabinet while leaving the supply and drain connections dry. Good catch on the filter quarter-turn; that's an easy one to miss because the filter often feels seated before the detent clicks.

A few small things worth keeping an eye on, without turning this into a project:

- Run the next 2–3 cycles with normal loads, not just empty rinses. The gasket where the scrap sat may have a slight crease or imprint from being compressed unevenly — that can hold under an empty cycle and weep under a loaded one. A quick visual check of the door edge and the cabinet floor after each cycle is enough.
- Inspect the lower-right gasket corner closely. If the rubber looks pinched, deformed, or no longer flush where the scrap was, that's worth knowing — paper gaskets sometimes don't fully recover after being held out of shape, and a corner replacement is cheaper than finding out during a load at 11 p.m.
- The cabinet wood will have absorbed some moisture even if it looks dry now. Worth re-checking the underside of the counter and the cabinet floor in 24–48 hours — slow wicking can show up later.
- On the filter itself: was this a "hadn't fully clicked into place this load" situation, or does the detent feel worn? If the filter has been seating loosely for a while, it's worth paying closer attention to that step for the next few runs.

Nothing here suggests an appliance problem — the supervised empty rinse coming back dry, supply and drain connections dry, and the cause being identifiable and removable is a good closeout. Treating it as resolved is reasonable.

The egg and zest are the two that don't scale linearly, so here are the practical moves:

  Egg. Crack 1 large egg into a small bowl, beat it loose with a fork, then weigh out 26 g. A large egg runs ~43 g without shell, and 0.6 × 43 ≈ 26. Whisk first so yolk and white are evenly distributed before you weigh. The leftover ~17 g is yours for breakfast — don't try to "eyeball half an egg" into dough, the binder ratio will be off.

  Orange zest. Zest isn't a weight ingredient, it's "zest of 1 orange." Easiest move: zest 1 medium orange, then lightly pack roughly 3/4 of that into the dough — about 4–5 g. Don't pack hard or you'll pull in the white pith, which goes bitter. If weighing feels like overkill here, just zest 1 small orange and use all of it; at this batch size, a touch more zest reads as "more orange," not "weird."

Everything else is straight ×0.6 off the card.

Type me the ingredient lines (butter, sugar, flour, salt, vanilla, etc. with whatever amounts the card shows) and I'll give you the gram numbers in one clean block — direct numbers to set your scale to, no percentages.

Logged: orange butter cookies, Dec 23, 2023, ~3:30 PM CT. Yields 30, dough ~528 g total, so each cookie is small (~17 g) — appropriate for delicate tea-style orange butter cookies.

Recipe looks balanced: butter-to-flour ratio (~170:300) is on the rich/shortbread side and sugar-to-butter (~150:170) keeps them from being cloying, which lets the orange zest carry the flavor. The 30-minute chill is right for this fat content — long enough to prevent spreading, short enough that the dough stays scoopable.

One small gap: the original didn't include bake time. For ~17 g scoops at 350°F, expect about 11–14 minutes — pull when the rims are pale gold and the centers still look slightly underdone; they'll finish on the sheet. If the cookies are larger (say, 25–30 g scoops), plan 14–17 minutes instead.

60% scale of a 30-cookie recipe lands at 18 cleanly, and most ingredients just multiply straight through.

Straight 60% (multiply each by 0.6):
  Butter, softened:  ~135g (about 1 stick + 1 Tbsp)
  Sugar:             ~65g  (about 1/3 cup)
  Flour:             ~185g (about 1 1/2 cups, spooned)
  Salt, baking powder, vanilla: scale 60% too. Vanilla is fine to round
    to a flat 1 tsp rather than try to measure 0.6 tsp.

The egg — beat the whole egg first, then portion:
  A large egg out of shell is about 50g; 60% is 30g, which is roughly
  2 level tablespoons. Crack the egg into a small bowl, beat with a
  fork until yolk and white are completely homogeneous — this is the
  step that matters. If the egg isn't beaten smooth, a yolk-heavy
  scoop behaves differently from a white-heavy one and the dough ends
  up uneven in spots. Once it's smooth, measure out 30g. A kitchen
  scale is the most accurate; 2 level tablespoons is the spoon
  equivalent.

  The reason for beating-then-measuring instead of trying to "remove"
  40% after the egg is already in the dough: once the egg is
  emulsified into the butter and sugar, you can't cleanly subtract
  any of it. The portioning has to happen before it goes in.
  Whatever's left over (about 20g) is perfect for tomorrow's toast
  or a quick scramble.

  To keep the dough from going wet: add the 30g gradually while
  mixing, just until it disappears. If your kitchen is humid or the
  butter ran a bit soft, backing off to 28g won't be noticeable in
  the final cookie.

The zest — round up to a whole orange:
  "60% of an orange" isn't something you can do at the zester
  without under-extracting one half and wasting fruit. Round to the
  zest of 1 whole medium orange, which comes out to about 6-7g
  packed. For 18 cookies this actually gives a slightly more
  concentrated citrus note per bite than the original 30-cookie
  batch, which is welcome in a smaller tray — flavor matters more
  when there are fewer cookies to share it around. If the recipe
  called for zest of 2 oranges originally, round to 2; the rule is
  whole oranges only.

Quick practical 18-cookie batch, in grams:
  Butter, softened:              135g
  Sugar:                          65g
  Salt:                            2g  (a generous 1/4 tsp)
  Vanilla:                         4g  (1 tsp — round to the spoon)
  Beaten egg, portioned:          30g
  Orange zest:                    6-7g (zest of 1 medium orange)
  Flour:                         185g
  Baking powder:                  ~1g (about 1/4 tsp — adjust if your
                                          recipe uses a different amount)

Method is the same as the original: cream butter, sugar, salt, and
zest until fluffy; beat in the 30g egg portion and vanilla; add flour
(and baking powder if using) just until combined; chill 30-60
minutes; scoop and bake at whatever temperature the recipe card
gives. If the actual recipe has slightly different flour or butter
ratios, scale those specific lines by 0.6 from the card itself
rather than from my defaults above.

**Tonight, before bed (ideally before midnight so it’s done before the sub-freezing window opens around 1 AM)**

1. Disconnect the garden hose from the bib it’s still attached to. Drain the hose and put it somewhere it won’t freeze — bathtub, inside the front door, garage. This is the single highest-leverage action of the night. A hose full of water against an outdoor faucet is the most common pipe-burst pattern in Texas freezes, because the hose keeps water trapped in the short exposed stem instead of letting it drain back out.

2. The second exposed bib (no hose):
   - If your house has an interior shutoff for outdoor faucets (usually laundry room, under a sink, or a closet near the exterior wall — common but not universal in East Austin), close it, then go outside and open the bib to drain. Leave the outside bib open overnight.
   - If there’s no interior shutoff, cover the bib: a foam hose-bib cover (Walmart/Hardware is open Christmas Eve day, any $2 cover works), or improvise with a towel wrapped in a plastic bag and a rubber band. The goal is just to keep wind and direct cold off the metal stem.

3. Exterior-wall plumbing (kitchen + guest bath):
   - Open the cabinet doors under both sinks before you go to bed. Warm interior air reaching the supply and drain lines is the main mitigation for pipes in exterior walls.
   - Run a slow pencil-thin drip from the cold side of both faucets. Cold side is enough — hot-side lines sit deeper in the wall and aren’t the first to freeze. Movement plus open doors covers a 27°F / ~6-hour event for pipes inside an insulated wall.
   - Close the garage door overnight if any supply lines run through it (most East Austin homes have at least the water-heater inlet in the garage).

4. Confirm you know where the main shutoff is. Not because you’ll use it — just so if anything does drip tomorrow morning, you can act in 30 seconds instead of searching.

**Skip for one night — these would be over-engineering for 27°F:**
- Foam pipe wrap on accessible pipes (open cabinets is more effective per minute spent)
- Draining the water heater
- PEX vs copper worry (mitigation is the same either way)
- Sprinkler system (you don’t have one)

**Tomorrow morning, after temps are above freezing (so roughly 9–10 AM at the earliest)**

1. Walk outside with a flashlight and look at both bibs. You’re checking for:
   - A steady drip or stream from the spout when nothing inside is turned on (sign the body cracked)
   - Water staining or wetness on the exterior wall around where the pipe enters
   - Ice still hanging off the bib (normal, ignore)

2. If you closed an interior shutoff for a bib, reopen it slowly, then look at the supply line under the sink or in the laundry for any new moisture before the bib starts running again.

3. Run both sinks for 30–60 seconds, hot and cold:
   - A momentary hiss or sputter as a partial ice plug clears is fine.
   - Then look under both cabinets with a flashlight for new wetness — shutoff valves, supply-line connections, and the P-trap especially.
   - Feel the wall behind each sink from inside; any new cold/damp spot?

4. Quick whole-house sweep:
   - Ceilings (if two-story): any new stains?
   - Around the water heater: any new drip, especially at the T&P valve?
   - Toilets: refill normally?
   - Washing machine connections (laundry or garage): dry at the hoses?

5. If everything is dry, close the cabinet doors, shut off the dripping faucets, and reconnect the hose bib whenever you’re confident — usually by midday is fine. The disconnected hose can go back on then too.

**Call a plumber if:**
- A bib is running continuously when nothing inside is on
- Water appears on a wall, ceiling, or in a cabinet that wasn’t wet last night
- A faucet won’t run at all, or runs at noticeably lower pressure than the others after a minute of running (could be a partial split leaking behind the wall)

That’s it for one night at 27°F. The hose disconnect plus open cabinets plus two pencil-drips covers the actual risk profile; everything else is habit you don’t need tonight.

Two parts. First the decision rule, then the smallest breakdown. I don't have the actual unsub rate, sample size, or which send produced the signal in front of me, so I can't place this specific signal on the scale — the rule below is what I'd apply to it.

PART 1 — Is the signal strong enough to cancel or pause?

A single-send unsub signal is "strong enough to act on" when ALL of:

  (a) Rate vs. baseline. From prior retained-account admin digest
      reads: baseline ~0.10–0.20%; 0.42% (2x+) was investigation
      territory, not incident; 0.12–0.18% post-fix is normal.

  (b) n is large enough. A 2x elevation on <500 recipients is noise.
      Want n≥500 in the relevant cell before treating it as real.

  (c) Not the first send of refreshed copy or a new audience
      definition. First-send variance is expected — wait for send #2.

  (d) Supporting signals align. Elevated unsubs AND elevated spam
      complaints AND/OR reply tone ("not relevant", "wrong person").

Decision:

  - All four hold       → pause, fix root cause, retest before next send.
  - Only (a), <2x       → don't pause; flag for next-send review.
  - Only (a), 2–3x on   → pause the NEXT send, treat this one as
    adequate n            diagnostic, dig into the breakdown first.
  - (a) on small n      → wait. Do not pause on noise.

Common false-positive triggers that look strong but aren't:

  - First send of refreshed copy
  - First send after a Helio-Start eligibility change
  - Digest into a long-dormant segment
  - Reminder queued before a suppression refresh

None of those alone should trigger cancel. They should trigger a check
on whether the segment was clean at send time.

For the reminder specifically: unless the reminder IS the elevated
send, do not let an unrelated digest's unsub rate cancel it. Each lane
has its own signal. Conflating lanes is how you either over-pause or
under-fix.

You actually need to separate three things, not two:

  1. Broad channel fatigue (uniform across role × engagement)
  2. Role-selection problem (concentrated in one role)
  3. Stale-role contacts (segment hygiene — separate from both)

Steps, lowest risk first — stop wherever it reads as "good enough":

1. Hands off until it dries.
   140-lb cold-press that's still slightly damp can take 12–24 hours depending on room humidity and how wet the wash was. Don't rush it with a hair dryer or by hanging it near a heater — uneven drying is what creates the hard lines and buckles you've hit before. Flat, face-up, out of direct sun, normal room air. If it wants to curl, weight the corners with a clean sheet of glass or a couple of books while it dries.

2. Read it before you touch it.
   When it's dry, look at it the way you'd read a number: once at arm's length in good north light, once squinted, once with the painting upside down or rotated. The muddy area is usually less uniform than it feels in the moment. You're looking for where it's actually too dark, where it's just too gray-cool, and where a small dark accent would do the work without re-painting anything.

3. First move: a single thin glaze.
   Mix a clean yellow-leaning green — sap green with a touch of aureolin or lemon yellow, plus enough water that it flows like weak tea. Soft synthetic round (size 8 or 10), loaded but not dripping. Quick, light strokes across the muddy zone, wet-on-dry, letting the brush just deposit pigment without scrubbing. This won't "fix" the muddiness so much as shift the value balance back toward grass. One pass. Let it dry before judging.

4. Negative shapes, not more wash.
   If the glaze isn't enough, the real rescue is dark accents painted around what grass would be: shadow seams between clumps, the edge where grass meets path or a bare patch, a couple of darker blade groups near the figures' feet. This adds structure without touching the wash that's already there. Small pointed brush (size 2 or 4), slightly stronger mix than the glaze, still wet-on-dry. The muddiness recedes because the eye now has shapes to read.

5. If you're tempted to lift, don't.
   Cold-press will pill before it gives up pigment. Anything that requires rewetting the area, scrubbing, or scraping is a higher cost than leaving a slightly muddy patch.

6. Optional, last: a controlled spatter.
   Tap — don't flick — a nearly-dry brush loaded with the same green mix over the area, one quick pass, then stop. Adds texture without reworking.

Same discipline as the other rescues: smallest possible intervention, stop as soon as it reads, don't trade a muddy area for a pilled one.

Single grass vomit with the reassuring picture you've already laid out — pink gums, soft belly, alert, interested in water, no repeat retching, no diarrhea, no known exposure — is the typical benign pattern for a dog who ate grass and brought it back up. Kibo has cleared several small incidents on home monitoring before. Here's a conservative plan for the next several hours, with explicit escalation rules so you don't have to re-decide in the moment.

Water — withhold briefly, then re-offer in small amounts:

  - Skip water until roughly 11:45 to 12:00 so the stomach settles.
  - First re-offer: a few laps only (roughly 1/4 cup for a medium dog), then wait 15-20 minutes.
  - If it stays down, another small amount. Repeat every 15-20 minutes for about an hour.
  - If that all stays down, normal water access is fine by early afternoon.
  - Ice cubes or a few licks of ice water are often tolerated better than a full bowl right away. Don't let him gulp a big bowl — that's the most common way to trigger a second vomit.

Food — wait, then reintroduce bland and small:

  - Hold food for about 2-3 hours after the last vomit, so roughly 1:30-2:00 pm if nothing else happens.
  - First meal: small and bland. Plain boiled skinless chicken (no salt/oil) with plain white rice, OR a couple of plain scrambled eggs, OR a few tablespoons of plain canned pumpkin (NOT pie filling). Or his regular food at about 1/4 of his normal portion.
  - If that stays down 1-2 hours, offer a slightly larger portion.
  - Resume his normal next scheduled meal (dinner or tomorrow's breakfast) if all goes well.

Monitoring schedule for today:

  - 11:15-12:00 (now): rest, no food/water, watch for repeat retching or behavior change.
  - 12:00: small water trial. Recheck the same three things you already checked — gums still pink, energy still alert, belly still soft.
  - 1:00-2:00: if water is staying down, bland meal trial.
  - 3:00 and again before bed: repeat the three checks (gum color, energy, belly feel) and note stool when he goes out.
  - Overnight: one quick check before you sleep; normal wake-up recheck in the morning.

Call the emergency vet NOW — don't wait, don't email, go or call on the way:

  - Repeated unproductive retching — 3 or more attempts in an hour with little or nothing coming up. This is the classic obstruction pattern.
  - Any blood in the vomit (red, or brown/coffee-ground).
  - Belly becomes hard, swollen, or he pulls away when you touch it.
  - Gums go pale, white, blue, yellow, or feel sticky/tacky.
  - Collapse, sudden weakness, can't stand, or sudden confusion.
  - You realize after the fact he could have gotten into something — xylitol, chocolate, grapes/raisins, human medication, antifreeze, rat poison, a swallowed toy/sock/corn cob/rock. If any of those is possible, call ASPCA Poison Control (888-426-4435, fee applies) or the e-vet now, not after symptoms.
  - Deep-chested dog with a swollen belly, restlessness, and unproductive retching = possible bloat/GDV. That is a minutes-count situation.

Call your regular vet today — same day, doesn't have to be the e-vet:

  - A second or third vomit episode, even if he otherwise seems OK.
  - Diarrhea, especially bloody, black, or tarry.
  - Refuses water for more than a couple of hours, or keeps small amounts down but won't take more.
  - Lethargy that persists past mid-afternoon.
  - Won't eat by his next normal meal.
  - Anything that's just off for Kibo — unusual pacing, panting at rest, hiding, won't settle. You know his baseline better than anyone.

Keep watching — this is the expected-good path:

  - One vomit, then back to normal.
  - Water stays down on the small-and-gradual plan.
  - Bland meal stays down.
  - Energy, gums, belly, and stool all stay normal through the evening and overnight.

One last thing. I'm not a vet, and your gut is part of the data here. If something about how he's acting just doesn't sit right with you before any of the lines above get crossed, that itself is reason to call. Vets say "if the owner is worried, the dog should be seen" and they mean it; that's not overreaction, it's the system working.

Six hours clean — held water, held a small bland meal, normal stool, normal walk, normal energy, pink gums, soft belly, no retching, no diarrhea. That's a picture consistent with a one-time grass-and-foam event, not the start of something. Ordinary observation is the right posture from here.

For the loop, only repeated or bloody vomiting, refusing water for more than a few hours, an energy drop or pale/tacky gums, belly tightening or pain, or persistent or bloody diarrhea would warrant re-engagement. None of that's on the table right now.

Quiet NYE at home with Kibo. Happy New Year in advance.

Top-line: this conclusion is wrong on at least seven independent grounds, and the slide is built in the wrong order. The conclusion ("ship to all trial admins") precedes the data and is contradicted by several pieces of the data the slide actually shows. Here is what is wrong with it, in the order a good readout would surface them.

1. Denominator is conditional, not the operating one. The slide shows 28% and 31% only among the 1,105 of 1,920 randomized users who reached the eligible setup state by the cutoff. That is a "denominator of the already-engaged." The rate a ship-to-all decision actually moves is the unconditional rate (treatment vs control among all 1,920), and the slide never shows it. If treatment slowed users on the path to eligibility, the conditional lift could coexist with a zero or negative unconditional lift. The slide hands you a number that doesn't answer the question the conclusion asks.

2. First significance, not stabilization. Eight of fourteen planned observation days are complete, and p=.04 is exactly the first-significance threshold. The stabilization rule the framework teaches is: first significance alone is not the read. A held-out or maturation cohort is required. The worked example from earlier this quarter is the point — first cohort at +0.7pp / p=.04 did not hold in the second cohort at +0.2pp / p=.31. Calling +3pp shippable on a half-mature window repeats that mistake at a larger scale.

3. No confidence interval. With n≈1,105 and p=.04, the 95% CI is wide enough that the true effect could plausibly be near zero. A point estimate without a CI cannot distinguish "real lift" from "noise we happened to call." Effect size without interval is incomplete.

4. The arms are imbalanced on a covariate that almost certainly matters. Secondary admins are 42% of treatment and 27% of control — a 15-point gap. From the December 19 Customer.io work, secondary admins engage very differently from primary admins (click-through 7.2% vs 22.1%; unsubscribe 8.74% vs 0.75% in that audit). Whether this is a randomization failure or an assignment confound, the treatment and control are not comparable on a known behavioral driver, and the difference cannot be interpreted causally.

5. Downside metrics are missing. No support contact rate. No unsubscribe rate. The frame is "we lifted setup 3pp, ship it." A 3pp setup lift is not free if it doubles support tickets or pushes an already-elevated unsubscribe rate higher. The slide does not let you evaluate cost.

6. The action is broader than the evidence. "Ship to all trial admins" reaches users — including secondary admins and not-yet-eligible users — that the readouts never measured. The data speaks to one subset; the decision applies to a larger and different population. That is the missing-population jump.

7. No segmentation check, and segmentation is the obvious next cut. The right move before any ship call is to break the +3pp by primary vs secondary admin. Given the arm imbalance, the lift is likely concentrated in (or entirely in) one subgroup. If the primary-admin lift is real and the secondary-admin effect is zero or negative, shipping to all trial admins is net-zero at best and harmful at worst.

8. Conclusion-before-evidence structure. The slide title is the conclusion. A readout that leads with "ship to all" and ends with the numbers is inverted. The discipline the framework teaches is denominator, then effect size, then conclusion. Here, if you put the numbers first, the conclusion falls out as "do not ship yet," not "ship to all trial admins."

The rewrite, in three lines: setup completion among the 1,105 eligible users was 28% control vs 31% treatment, +3.0pp, p=.04, 95% CI roughly (something, something), with secondary admins imbalanced across arms by 15 points; the read is first-significant on a half-mature window, downside metrics are not yet captured, and the effect has not been segmented by admin role. Recommendation: hold the ship decision, run the held-out cohort to day 14, reweight or stratify by admin role, capture support and unsubscribe outcomes, and re-read.

CRITIQUE OF THE INES DRAFT

The draft is directionally useful and lands the right shape. The risk is that a fast reader can answer "p=.018, ship it" and exit. Five specific gaps:

1. Denominator stays implicit. Without surfacing the four-cell breakdown (active-admin x CS-intervention), learners can mark "denominator ok" without seeing that intervention was 6x more concentrated in active-admin accounts (41.8% vs 7.1%). The exercise either needs to include the four-cell table or require learners to ask for it.

2. Effect size is the unadjusted headline. If learners see "7.3pp, p=.018" and nothing else, they will argue about whether 7.3pp is "big enough" rather than recognizing the unadjusted figure is the wrong number to ship on. The exercise should either give the adjusted figure or require learners to ask for it.

3. Stabilization is not a hard gate. First significance is not ship-ready. The draft needs to make stabilization-after-first-significance a non-negotiable step before any action, not a sentence buried in the conclusion.

4. Audience risk is missing. Even if the read were valid, a renewal-risk trigger that fires on accounts with open CS plans, recent support contacts, Expansion Assist exposure, or pricing-page overlap creates churn-of-attention and confused ownership. Ines's lane is the right place for this, but the exercise needs to ask for it explicitly, not as a footnote.

5. Approval-queue drift. The framing should reinforce that this is a default practice for Growth and CS readouts, not a companywide approval queue. Every readout doesn't need Owen and Ines to sign off; teams internalize the shape and apply it themselves.

THE BAD READOUT (what learners see)

Title: Recent Active-Admin Absence Increases Renewal Risk — A 7.3 Point Drop

Body: A year-end analysis of 384 mid-segment accounts found that accounts without a recent active admin renewed at a significantly lower rate than those with one. Of 238 accounts without a recent active admin, 196 renewed (82.4%), compared to 131 of 146 accounts with a recent active admin (89.7%). This 7.3 percentage-point difference is statistically significant (p = .018).

Recommendation: Add "no recent active admin" as a renewal-risk trigger in lifecycle messaging. CS should reach out to these accounts with proactive renewal support. This represents an actionable retention signal that could meaningfully reduce Q1 churn.


ANSWER KEY (back of the half-page)

1. Denominator. The 7.3pp headline is a raw gap. CS intervention was 6x more concentrated in active-admin accounts (61/146 = 41.8% vs 17/238 = 7.1%). Without the four-cell (active-admin x CS-intervention) breakdown, the denominator is silently confounded. Ask for the four-cell table before trusting the gap.

2. Effect size. Raw 7.3pp collapses to 2.4pp (95% CI: -1.8 to +6.6, p=.26) once intervention status and account age are accounted for. The "statistically significant" headline is the unadjusted figure; the adjusted effect is not significant. Effect size lives in the adjusted model, not the raw headline.

3. Conclusion order. Recommendation appears before the adjusted effect, before the stabilization status, and before the audience qualification. The conclusion is in the headline. Move it to the end, after the evidence supports it.

4. Stabilization. No stabilization or held-out cohort is used. This is a single-cohort snapshot. First significance is not ship-ready; the action comes after a stabilization window, not before.

5. Audience risk. A trigger here would fire on accounts with open CS plans, recent support contacts, Expansion Assist exposure, and pricing-page overlap. Treating this as a customer-facing renewal trigger risks duplicating CS coverage and confusing ownership. At most this is a CS coverage watchlist input or an exclusion signal, not a customer-facing trigger.


THE BETTER READOUT (one-paragraph shape learners should reach)

Denominator: 384 closed-Q4 mid-segment accounts (146 with active admin, 238 without).
Effect size: raw 7.3pp (p=.018); adjusted for intervention status and account age, 2.4pp (95% CI: -1.8 to +6.6, p=.26). The raw signal was confounded by CS selection.
Conclusion status: first-significant read, not confirmed in a stabilization or held-out cohort.
Audience risk: would fire on accounts with open CS plans, recent support, and Expansion Assist exposure. Use as a CS coverage watchlist input or exclusion signal at most, not as a customer-facing trigger.


TAKEAWAY (facilitator reads at 3:30)

First-significant is not ship-ready. Stabilization, adjusted effect size, and audience qualification come before the action. This is the default shape Growth and CS use on their own readouts — not an approval queue.

**Classification: query-side event-window scoping bug, not a CS miss, not a missing source event.**

The source events are there. CS routed them. Entitlement populated cleanly on all 22. The bug is that the support-state lookup is bounded below by `workspace_created`, and routed-before-setup events by definition precede workspace creation for any workspace that was eventually created after CS help. The window drops exactly the events that should populate that field.

The structural reason it happened: support state lives on the invite/accept chain, not the workspace lifecycle. Activation lives on the workspace lifecycle. Using the same timestamp anchor for both is the conflation. Fixing the window is the symptom fix; the structural fix is a different join key for support state.

**Smallest query correction**

Keep the support-state field on its own join, anchored to the invite/admin chain rather than the workspace-created timestamp.

- For support-state only: look up the routed-before-setup event by `invite_id` (or the admin/accept chain), with no lower timestamp bound, taking the most recent routed event on that chain before workspace creation; null/`not_routed` if none.
- Do not change the entitlement join (stays anchored at `workspace_created`).
- Do not change the activation join (stays post-`workspace_created`).
- Concretely: if the current support-state subquery has a `WHERE event_timestamp >= workspace_created` predicate, that predicate is the bug. Remove it for that field only.

If the export stacks the three lookups in one query and shares a window, split them. Don't widen a shared window — that risks pulling unrelated historical events into entitlement or activation. Three fields, three joins, three windows.

**Acceptance tests Daniela should run before rerunning**

1. **Re-run the dry run on the same 22 Q4 workspace rows.** Expect 22 rows, every row with a non-null `support_state`. Expect exactly the 3 previously-blank rows to flip to `routed_before_setup` (or the canonical label). Expect the other 19 unchanged.

2. **Manual walk-through of the 3 corrected rows.** For each: confirm invite → unsure → CS routed → CS worked → `workspace_created` → first integration. Confirm the routed-before-setup event exists in source. Confirm it now appears in the export. Proof the join fixed, not coincidence.

3. **Negative test — no false positives.** Pick any of the 19 workspaces with no routed-before-setup event. Confirm its `support_state` is still null/`not_routed`, not accidentally populated. The fix should fill blanks, not invent values.

4. **Boundary test — the 13 routed-but-never-created invites.** Of the 16 Q4 routed-before-setup invites, 3 created workspaces; the other 13 should NOT appear in this workspace export (no workspace row exists). Confirm they're absent. They belong in the pre-setup-routing-per-accepted-invite readout, not here. Confirms the window wasn't widened into non-workspace rows.

5. **Reconciliation against Q4 closeout denominators.** Pre-setup CS routing = 16 across Q4. Workspace-level support_state in the export = 3 routed + 19 not_routed = 22. The two denominators stay separately reportable. Don't merge.

6. **Entitlement and activation unchanged.** Rerun should produce the same 22/22 entitlement-filled and the same activation values as the original dry run. If anything moved in those columns, the join change leaked — split the subqueries further.

7. **Staging-vs-production parity.** If a staging copy exists, rerun the corrected query there and diff against the production dry-run. Expect exactly 3 cells to flip from null to `routed_before_setup`; nothing else moves.

8. **Future-window test.** Pick a workspace created in, say, late November with a routed-before-setup event in October. Confirm it picks up correctly. The lookup should reach back as far as the invite chain exists, not be accidentally bounded to a short lookback.

9. **Document the three joins in the export definition.** `support_state` joins on `invite_id` (admin chain), no lower timestamp bound. `entitlement` joins on `workspace_id` at `workspace_created`. `activation` joins on `workspace_id` post-`workspace_created`. That's the structural fix, written down so the next export doesn't re-conflate them.

**Support state stays separate from activation**

Yes — the 3 fixes should never have shown up in the activation column, and the corrected export should keep them in three separate columns with three separate joins. Activation is "did this workspace reach a defined activation event by day X." Support state is "what was the support posture of this invite chain — routed before setup, not routed, escalated post-setup, etc." Different fields, different join keys, different denominators, different audiences. The readout reports them as separate numbers — pre-setup CS routing per accepted invite stays its own line; post-workspace support questions per created workspace stays its own line. Don't blend.

Quick read: stripped plastic anchor on one side, sound wall, shelf itself OK. That's a single-bracket remount problem, not a shelf replacement. Three viable paths; the choice turns on (a) whether a stud is reachable at a bracket position and (b) whether you're comfortable enlarging the existing hole for a toggle. Both can be DIY. Calling a handyman is also a proportionate answer if any of the stop conditions below trip.

DECISION TREE

Step 0 - One safety check before any drilling:
  - Any electrical outlet, switch, or plumbing fixture on either side of this wall?
    - Yes, and you don't know where the wires/pipes run -> call a handyman (or at minimum use a stud finder with AC wire detection before drilling).
    - No / clearly interior partition -> proceed.

Step 1 - Locate the stud situation:
  - Use a magnetic or electronic stud finder on the wall around the bracket. Standard interior studs are 16" on center, sometimes 24".
  - Three sub-cases:
    (a) A stud edge or face is within ~1-2" of the current bracket position -> REMOUNT INTO STUD.
        - Pull or push the old plastic anchor out of the wall.
        - Drive a #10 or #12 wood screw, ~2.5" long, straight through the bracket into the stud. No anchor needed.
        - Holds 80-100+ lbs in shear. Massive margin for linens.
    (b) A stud is reachable by shifting the bracket horizontally 1-3" -> REMOUNT INTO STUD at the new position.
        - Same as (a). Shelf may overhang slightly; usually fine in a linen closet.
    (c) No stud within reasonable reach of either bracket position -> go to Step 2 (toggle) or Step 3 (handyman).

Step 2 - Toggle path (only if Step 1 lands in (c)):
  All of these must be true:
    - Drywall is sound (you said yes - dry, no cracking beyond the hole).
    - You can enlarge the existing hole cleanly to the diameter the toggle requires (typically 1/2" for a standard snap-toggle or spring toggle).
    - You can confirm the cavity behind the wall is empty at that spot (no loose insulation, no plumbing, no wire).
  Procedure:
    - Drill out the hole to the toggle's specified diameter.
    - Use a snap-toggle or spring toggle rated for at least 50 lbs in 1/2" drywall. (Avoid plastic threaded anchors - same class as what just failed.)
    - Install per package directions; the wings must deploy flat behind the drywall.
    - Snug the machine screw, don't over-torque.
  Stop and call a handyman instead if:
    - Drywall crumbles when you drill the larger hole.
    - You hit something solid behind the wall that isn't a stud (firestop, pipe, conduit).
    - The toggle doesn't deploy flat / it spins instead of catching.
    - You're not confident in any step. This is the legitimate "don't want to deal with this" branch.

Step 3 - Call a handyman. Sensible triggers (any one):
    - Stud finder gives a confusing reading you can't resolve.
    - Wall shows any sign of past water damage, softness, or prior patching you can't read.
    - You're behind plumbing/wiring and don't want to drill blind.
    - You'd rather pay roughly $100 and have it done in 20 minutes. Fine answer for a one-off shelf.

CONSERVATIVE TEST BEFORE RELOADING LINENS

Goal: catch a failed repair under controlled load, before linens are back and the shelf is in daily use.

Phase 1 - Static hand-load (5 minutes, shelf still empty):
    - Push down firmly on the bracket with your hand at the wall side. Then pull the bracket outward from the wall.
    - Pass: no movement, no creak, no new gap between bracket and drywall.
    - Fail: any movement, dust falling, or the bracket shifting -> don't load. Re-evaluate (probably handyman).

Phase 2 - Weighted dwell test (24 hours):
    - Load the shelf with the heaviest convenient items you have, equal to or exceeding the planned linen load. Good options: a case of water bottles, a stack of hardcover books, a few cans of paint.
    - Rule of thumb: at least ~1.5x what you expect linens to weigh. For a normal linen shelf, 30-40 lbs across the shelf is a reasonable test load.
    - Leave it 24 hours.
    - Pass criteria at 24 hours:
        - Bracket still flush to wall, no new gap.
        - No drywall dust or crumbs on the shelf or floor below.
        - No creak when you bump the shelf lightly.
        - Shelf still visually level (no sag on the repaired side).
    - Fail: any of the above -> unload, treat as not fixed, call a handyman.

Phase 3 - Light live use (1 week):
    - After passing the 24-hour dwell, put the linens back and use the shelf normally.
    - One quick visual check at one week: bracket still flush, no gap, no debris.
    - If clean at one week, treat as resolved.

OPTIONAL - OLD HOLE PATCH
  If you went the stud-remount path, the old anchor hole is a small cosmetic blemish. A pea-sized dab of spackle, sanded flush after drying and touched up with wall paint, prevents the hole from collecting dust. Five minutes, low stakes. Skip it if you went the toggle path - the toggle fills the enlarged hole.

A couple of notes:
  - The firm left bracket is a useful control. If it stays firm through your test load, that confirms the load is reasonable and the test is meaningful. If the left bracket also moves under test load, you're overloading the whole shelf, not just one side.
  - Plastic drywall anchors are the weak link. Whatever path you pick (wood screw into stud, or properly rated toggle), the replacement will be several times stronger than the original.
  - The shelf being straight is a good sign - no racking force on the brackets from a twisted shelf, so you're just remounting, not realigning.

That sounds like a clean resolution. The asymmetry of the fix is the right call: stud-backed on the left where you found one, properly rated toggle on the right after confirming fastener length and drywall integrity — and the staged load test with a 30-minute observation window before declaring it done is proportionate confirmation without overengineering.

Keeping heavy bottles off that shelf is the right call given the right side is now toggle-supported rather than stud-supported. Light observation over the next week or two is plenty; if there's any drift or hairline crack at the toggle, you'd catch it early.

Here's a tight workflow for 36 photos where half have back annotations. The whole thing should fit in one session of about 90 minutes, with minimal handling and a clean front/back pairing that survives an interruption.

SETUP (5 min)
- Pick a table near a window with indirect daylight. No flash, no direct sun.
- Lay down a dark cloth or sheet (solid dark gray or black gives the cleanest edge contrast against old photo paper).
- Prop your phone against a stack of books so it's stable, lens angled down at the table, photo area centered in frame. Lock focus/exposure if your camera app allows.
- Prepare 36 small sticky notes or index cards. Number them 1 to 36 in big clear digits. Test one capture before starting the run.

CAPTURE LOOP (one photo at a time, ~2 min each)
  1. Lay the photo face-up on the cloth.
  2. Put the matching numbered card next to it, in frame, clearly readable.
  3. Snap the front. Quick check on screen: full photo, in focus, even light, no finger, no glare.
  4. Don't slide the photo. Pick it up and flip it face-down in the same spot.
  5. Put the same numbered card next to it again so the number stays visible.
  6. Snap the back. Check: handwriting legible, full frame, no shadow on the writing.
  7. Move the photo to a "done" pile.

Doing one pair at a time keeps front and back attached even if you get interrupted, and avoids the whole-batch shift problem when flipping. Two handlings per photo (set down, pick up to flip) is the floor for a paired capture — there's no real shortcut that preserves the relationship.

NAMING (do this on import or right after)
Use a single scheme so each front is permanently tied to its back:

  2024-01-06_mom_shoebox_001_front.jpg
  2024-01-06_mom_shoebox_001_back.jpg
  2024-01-06_mom_shoebox_002_front.jpg
  2024-01-06_mom_shoebox_002_back.jpg
  ... and so on through 036.

Date prefix keeps the batch identifiable later. Sequential number is the front-to-back key. Sort by capture order, rename in batch.

QUICK QUALITY CHECK (10 min, after all 72 files exist)
- Scroll through the 36 fronts: any blurry, finger-in-frame, off-center, or glare? Recapture now while originals are still out.
- Open each front next to its matching back: confirm the annotation belongs to that front. The numbered card on the back tells you which original to reshoot if anything is mismatched.
- Confirm 36 pairs total (72 files).

A LITTLE EXTRA FOR HARD-TO-READ BACKS
If a back has faint pencil or smudged ink, recapture once with the photo held at a slight angle to a window (backlit). Pencil often shows up better that way than under top-down light. Don't try to fix anything else.

ONE BACKUP COPY
Pick a destination that's not the same device as your master:
- Easiest: a shared iCloud / Google Photos album, since Mom's Photos are already syncing. Drop the folder in and let it upload.
- Alternative: copy the folder to an external SSD or USB drive.

Verify the backup: open three or four files from the backup location and confirm they read correctly. Don't return the originals to Mom until you've seen the backup open cleanly.

WHEN YOU'RE DONE
Return the originals. Keep the master and the backup separate (one at home, one in cloud — or one on laptop, one on drive). Don't delete anything off the phone until the backup is verified. There's no need to do anything else with the files right now — they can sit in the folder until you or Mom want to organize them later.

The signs here are textbook package smishing: small-dollar fee, shortened link, no carrier/retailer name, unfamiliar sender. Your mom has already done the most important thing by not clicking. Here's a tight sequence.

PART 1 — No-click case (her current situation)

With the text itself:
- Do not tap the link.
- Do not reply. Replying confirms the number is live and invites more.
- Do not delete yet. Screenshot it first (sender number, timestamp, full message, link preview if visible). This is useful if she wants to report it.
- After screenshotting, block the number in her phone and delete the thread.
- Report it: forward the text to 7726 (SPAM) — that's the US carrier shortcode that lets AT&T/Verizon/T-Mobile investigate. Then file at reportfraud.ftc.gov and, if a carrier name is being impersonated, also at the carrier's own fraud-report address (USPS: spam@uspis.gov, UPS: fraud@ups.com, FedEx: abuse@fedex.com, Amazon: stop-spoofing@amazon.com).

Verify the package from the official channel (this is the only thing that should drive a real action):
- Identify which retailer or carrier is actually shipping the package she expects. Don't use the text to figure that out — use what she already knows: where she ordered it, what app she used, the order confirmation email in her inbox.
- For the retailer (Amazon, Target, Etsy, etc.): open the app directly or type the retailer's full URL into the browser. Check "Your Orders" / order history. Real address or delivery issues will appear there, not as an out-of-band $0.30 charge.
- For the carrier (USPS, UPS, FedEx, DHL):
  - USPS: type usps.com and use Informed Delivery, or call 1-800-ASK-USPS. USPS does NOT charge small address-correction fees via text; any legitimate attempted-delivery notice will be a physical slip in the mailbox.
  - UPS: type ups.com and use UPS My Choice, or call 1-800-PICK-UPS.
  - FedEx: type fedex.com and use FedEx Delivery Manager, or call 1-800-GO-FEDEX.
  - DHL: type dhl.com and check tracking directly.
- If tracking shows the package already delivered or in transit with no address problem, the text is a scam by elimination. If tracking shows a real delivery problem, the carrier's page will say so and will never route payment through a shortened SMS link.

Rule of thumb: the legitimate version of "pay a fee" is always on the carrier or retailer's own site, requires a real account login, and is for amounts like a postage due or customs fee — not a 30-cent address correction pushed through a bit.ly-style link.

PART 2 — Only if she had already tapped the link or entered information

If she only opened the link but did not type anything:
- Same as the no-click case for now: don't enter anything, close it, clear browser, run a basic check. Treat as still-low-risk and watch for the next 24–48 hours.

If she entered information, the steps escalate depending on what she entered:

If she entered payment info (card number, etc.):
- Call the card issuer's number on the back of the card, not a number from the text or the suspicious site. Ask to flag the card, issue a new one, and reverse the $0.30 charge if it posted. That tiny charge is actually the dangerous part — it's a card-validity test.
- Watch the card for the next 30 days for small test charges followed by larger ones.

If she entered login credentials for any account (email, retailer, etc.):
- Change that password immediately, from a known-clean device.
- Turn on two-factor authentication on the account if it isn't already on.
- If the same password is used anywhere else (especially email), change those too. Email is the most important one to reset because it's usually the password-recovery vector for other accounts.

If she entered personal data (name, address, SSN, DOB):
- File a report at reportfraud.ftc.gov and ic3.gov.
- Place a free fraud alert with one of the three credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, or TransUnion) — by law the one you contact must notify the other two.
- Consider a credit freeze, which is stronger and free. A freeze prevents new credit accounts from being opened in her name.
- Monitor her credit reports at AnnualCreditReport.com (free weekly).

If she downloaded anything from the link:
- Don't open it. On iPhone, deleting the message and the downloaded profile/shortcut is usually enough; on Android, go to Settings → Apps and uninstall anything unfamiliar.
- Run a mobile antivirus scan if she has one installed.
- If the device starts behaving oddly (unexpected pop-ups, battery drain, unknown apps), back up important data and consider a factory reset.

One universal extra step in the entered-information case: forward the original screenshot to the impersonated company's real fraud inbox so they can warn other customers.

The short version she can keep: don't tap, screenshot and forward to 7726, then go to the retailer's app or type the carrier's URL directly. If a real fee exists, it'll show up there — never in a shortened text.

Clean containment, and the verification path Mom used is exactly right. She went to the source she already trusted — the saved order-confirmation email — not the inbound link, and the source confirmed the package is real, in transit for Tuesday, no address problem, no fee. That habit generalizes well: for any future delivery, billing, or account text, the saved email or the retailer's site reached directly beats any link in an inbound message.

Nothing here requires follow-up. No link opened, nothing entered, nothing downloaded, so no account, payment, or device remediation is warranted. Reporting the text as junk and blocking the sender is the appropriate close. Treating it as resolved is correct.

If another similar text comes in over the next few weeks, the same rule applies: don't tap, verify through the saved order email.

Front brake plus pulsing through the lever is the part that pushes me toward conservative. The single-point rotor-to-pad contact you described is most consistent with a slightly bent or warped rotor, which is usually rideable to a shop, but a few of those are not. Here is how to tell which one you have.

Two-minute check you can do right where you stopped:

1. Spin the wheel slowly with the bike off the ground and look at the rotor edge-on (squat down so you see the edge against a clean background). A true rotor shows a uniform edge as it turns. A bent one shows a single visible hop or step where one spot reaches toward the pad.
2. Run a finger carefully behind the rotor's edge as it spins. It should feel even. Any sharp step or catch means do not ride.
3. Squeeze the lever while stationary. It should feel firm and stop well before the bar. Spongy, weak bite, pulls to one side, or bottoms out — do not ride.
4. Look at the pads. Clean surface, normal thickness above the wear line, no glazing, no oil sheen.

Walk it in (or get a ride / call the shop) if any of these is true:

  - Visible hop, bend, or step in the rotor edge.
  - Lever pulses under braking — you already felt this, so do not paper over it.
  - Lever feel has changed from before: spongy, weak, or pulls to the bar.
  - A slow squeeze-test stop from walking pace does not feel crisp.
  - Pads look glazed, oily, or below the wear line.
  - Any hot-brake smell, blue discoloration on the rotor, or deep grooves.
  - The ride to the shop involves a descent, wet roads, or fast traffic.

Probably safe to ride carefully to a nearby shop if all of these are true:

  - Rotor edge looks uniform when spun, no visible hop.
  - Lever feels normal and firm, no pulsing under a real squeeze.
  - Pads look clean with material left.
  - A slow test stop works cleanly.
  - The route is short, flat, low-traffic, and the shop is close.

Front-brake specific note: since this is the front, I would rather walk a ten-minute errand than ride a five-minute one. A front-brake failure on a descent is the worst mechanical failure a bike can give you. The cost of being conservative here is small; the cost of being wrong is not.

If it were my bike: do the edge-on check now. If you see a hop, walk it. If the rotor looks uniform but the lever still pulses under a real squeeze, walk it. If both the edge and the lever feel normal apart from a quiet constant rub, ride slowly and directly to the shop.

One more thing worth doing while you have the wheel off the ground: confirm the wheel is actually seated straight in the dropouts (axle ends flush, skewer or thru-axle fully closed) and that the rotor sits centered between the pads with roughly even gap on both sides. A wheel that has shifted a couple of millimeters in the dropouts will produce exactly the symptoms you described and is a five-minute fix at home.

Plan: don't recapture until you've tried the cheapest fixes first, and keep the existing files exactly where they are. Treat the existing 12 front and 12 back captures as your archival color masters; new files are tagged alternates that sit beside them, never on top of them.

A. Try the existing files first (5–10 minutes, no extra handling)

For the 5 pale-pencil backs:
  - Convert to grayscale
  - Push levels so the midtone darkens and the highlights stay clipped (graphite responds to contrast more than to brightness)
  - If the pencil is still nearly invisible, try inverting — pale graphite often reads better as dark marks on light
  - Try a light unsharp mask at the end
  - Mark which ones software recovered and which still need a recapture

For the 2 glossy fronts with glare near faces:
  - Try shadow/highlight recovery first
  - If the glare is a small hot spot, a basic spot-heal pass often clears it without recapture
  - If glare covers a face, plan a recapture — software can't reliably recover that

You're likely to still need recaptures for most of the 5 backs and both fronts, but this step tells you how many.

B. Capture sequence (do one photo end-to-end before batching)

Keep the originals in their numbered sleeves throughout. Pull a sleeve, capture, verify pairing, slide it back.

For the pencil backs (raking light):
  - One lamp, almost flat to the surface — about 10–20 degrees above the plane, off to one side
  - Camera straight down, not at the same angle as the light
  - Camera in grayscale if it has the option; otherwise shoot color and convert
  - Lock exposure so the lamp angle doesn't shift brightness between shots
  - One capture per back; check legibility on screen before returning the sleeve

For the glossy fronts with glare (reposition the light, not the photo):
  - Turn off any overhead light
  - Use one diffused source from one side, well off-axis from the lens
  - If the glare still falls on a face, tilt the photo a few degrees in the sleeve so the reflection walks off the face, not across it
  - One capture per front; check the face is clear before returning the sleeve

C. Naming (keep the existing convention, add an explicit suffix)

Whatever your current scheme is (e.g. 01_front.jpg / 01_back.jpg), keep the number prefix identical so the front/back pairing is preserved by the filename itself, and use a descriptive suffix on alternates:

  - 01_front.jpg          (existing color master — never renamed or overwritten)
  - 01_back.jpg           (existing color master — never renamed or overwritten)
  - 01_back_pencil.jpg    (alternate back, only for the 5 with illegible pencil)
  - 07_front_noglare.jpg  (alternate front, only for the 2 with face glare)

Avoid generic _alt or _v2 — if you or Mom ever look at these in a year, "pencil" and "noglare" tell you what the file is for without opening it. The shared number prefix is what keeps the front/back pair intact across both files for that photo.

D. Quick pairing check after each recapture

  - Open the new file next to its existing partner (the color master front or back)
  - Confirm the sleeve number, the face/scene on the front, and any writing on the back all match
  - Originals back in sleeves immediately

That gives you 7 likely recaptures total (5 backs, 2 fronts), leaves the 24 unstarted photos on your existing workflow, and keeps your color masters and your front/back pairs both intact.

What the $38 is actually buying

The single named difference is $5,000 of water-backup coverage. By industry pricing, a $5K water-backup endorsement on a renters policy typically runs $30-$60 as a standalone rider. The $38 sits right in that range, which strongly suggests the $38 is just the cost of the endorsement — not a sign the current carrier's base policy is more expensive. The competitor's lower price is consistent with dropping that one rider.

So the honest reframe: you're not choosing between two $30K/$300K/RC/$1K policies. You're choosing whether to pay $38/year for $5K of water-backup coverage.

What water-backup actually pays

  - Sewer or drain backup into the unit
  - Sump-pump discharge overflow (where applicable)
  - Property damage plus additional living expenses if the unit is uninhabitable, both up to the $5K limit
  - Subject to the same $1,000 deductible, so net indemnity is capped at $4,000

Quantifying the tradeoff for your specific unit

The expected value of this endorsement depends almost entirely on your floor, because backups manifest in lower units:

  Upper floor (2nd+):
    Annual claim probability is roughly 0.3-0.5%. Expected indemnity around $15-20/year. You're paying roughly 2x fair value for a low-probability event. But a $4-5K hit is annoying, not catastrophic — most households could absorb it without much pain.

  Ground floor:
    Annual claim probability rises to 1.5-3%. Expected indemnity around $70-130/year. The $38 is a bargain. Skipping this coverage is real risk you don't want to self-insure against.

  Below grade / basement with floor drains:
    Highest risk category. At $38/year this endorsement is essentially mandatory; refusing it on price would be the wrong trade.

So the deciding question is: what floor are you on?

Shortest useful questions for the current carrier

Before deciding, push on these to make sure the $248 quote isn't hiding a downgrade the headline limits don't show. Roughly in priority order:

  1. "Send me the full declarations page and the endorsements/exclusions page for both quotes side by side." This is the single highest-leverage ask. If both carriers produce a one-page dec sheet, you can scan them yourself in five minutes. Most hidden differences surface here.

  2. "On the competitor's quote, does replacement cost apply to all personal property, or only some categories (with actual cash value for the rest)?" The most common silent downgrade — headlines say "replacement cost" while fine print limits which items qualify.

  3. "What sub-limits sit inside the $30K personal-property limit on each quote — jewelry, electronics, bikes, collectibles, business property, watercraft?" Standard HO-4 forms cap most categories at $1,500-$2,500. The cheaper quote may have lower caps on categories you actually own.

  4. "What is the loss-of-use / additional-living-expenses limit on each policy?" Typically 20-30% of personal property, so $6K-$9K — but cheaper quotes sometimes bundle only $3K. For a sewer backup that makes the unit uninhabitable for a week, this matters.

  5. "Are the discounts applied the same on both quotes?" Often the cheaper carrier simply applied fewer discounts (bundling, claims-free, alarm, etc.) that you actually qualify for. Worth confirming it's like-with-like.

If all five come back clean and the only real difference is the $5K water-backup endorsement, the decision reduces to the floor question above. If any of them surfaces a real downgrade on the $248 quote, the comparison shifts and $38 may not be the real delta.

A March-2019 battery in January is by far the most likely root cause; that framing is what makes the post-start checks useful rather than just a hopeful restart. Conservative sequence with explicit stop conditions, then the smallest set of checks that separates "old battery" from "charging-system problem".

PRE-CONNECT (before any clamp touches metal)
- Confirm the pack is actually charged right now (indicator LEDs), not just "I charged it last week". A low pack on a dead battery gets you nowhere.
- Identify POSITIVE (+) and NEGATIVE (-) on the battery. Red cover or marking = +. Black = -. If there's white/green corrosion, brush off loose material so the clamp can bite metal. Don't pry or scrub hard.
- Confirm 12V system (almost all passenger cars). If the badge or manual says 24V or hybrid high-voltage, the jump-pack rules are different — call service.
- Skim YOUR pack's manual once: any engine-size selector (gas/diesel), any "boost/override" mode, any reverse-polarity alarm. Different packs want the pack powered on at different points.

CONNECTION ORDER (pack OFF until step 5)
1. RED clamp to POSITIVE (+) terminal. Solid metal contact, not on paint or plastic.
2. BLACK clamp to a CHASSIS GROUND away from the battery — a clean unpainted engine bracket, alternator bracket, or designated ground stud. NOT the negative battery post. This is the spark-control rule: a battery can off-gas hydrogen, and a spark at the post can ignite it.
3. Confirm clamps are nowhere near a belt, fan, or hot exhaust manifold, and the cables are clear of the radiator fan.
4. Confirm the two clamps are not touching each other.
5. Turn the jump pack ON. If your pack has a "boost" or "override" mode for deeply discharged batteries, use it only if the manual tells you to.
6. Wait 30–60 seconds so some surface charge transfers.

CRANK — LIMITED, NOT HAMMERED
- Turn the key for 3–5 seconds max. Release fully.
- If the engine starts: go straight to POST-START CHECKS.
- If it cranks but doesn't fire in that window: stop. Wait 30 seconds. One more attempt of the same length. If it still doesn't fire, stop and don't keep trying.
- If you get the same rapid clicking and the dash still dies hard: stop. Re-check clamp bite and pack charge, then one more try. After that, stop — further cranking on a deeply discharged or shorted battery can overheat the pack and the cables.

STOP CONDITIONS — STOP AND DISCONNECT IF YOU SEE ANY OF THESE
- Smoke or hissing from the battery
- Swelling, bulge, or cracked case on the battery
- Rotten-egg smell (sulfur)
- Battery or cable getting noticeably hot
- Sparking at the clamps after the initial connection
- Jump-pack warning light, buzzer, or reverse-polarity alarm

If you have to stop, disconnect in REVERSE order: pack OFF, BLACK clamp from chassis, RED clamp from positive. Keep the pack and clamps away from the battery while you reassess.

POST-START — SMALLEST USEFUL SET
The single question you want answered: is the alternator actually charging the battery, or is the battery the only problem? You don't need a multimeter for the first pass; the car tells you.

Immediately after the engine starts and is idling:
  A. BATTERY/CHARGING WARNING LIGHT. The red battery-shaped icon (or ALT) should be OFF within a few seconds of running. If it stays on, the alternator or its wiring is the problem — don't plan a long drive; go straight to a shop or call for diagnosis.
  B. HEADLIGHTS. Turn them on. At idle they should be steady and roughly normal-brightness. Raise RPM gently to ~1500 and watch: slight brightening at higher RPM is normal; big flicker, dimming, or pulsing is not.

Then drive 15–20 minutes (don't just idle; the alternator needs load and RPM to actually put charge back):
  C. PARK, ENGINE OFF, WAIT 5 MINUTES. Try to restart cold.
     - Starts cleanly and cranks strong → alternator is charging. The battery is the problem. Replace the battery (5 years old, due anyway). The 15–20 min drive was enough to top it up; the cold-soak restart is the proof.
     - Won't restart or very weak crank → either the battery won't hold charge (dead cell) or the alternator wasn't actually charging it. Either way, that's a shop, not a driveway, problem. Don't keep cycling the pack — you'll just flatten it and lose the diagnostic signal.

INTERPRETATION
- Warning light off + headlights normal + clean restart after drive → just an old battery. Replace within the next week or two; don't trust it yet for a long trip.
- Warning light on at idle → charging-system problem. Don't drive far.
- Headlights dim/flickering at idle, no warning light → weak alternator output or a slipping belt. Shop, soon.
- Restart fails after the drive → battery won't hold charge or alternator didn't charge it. Shop.

WHY THIS BOUNDED CHECK IS ENOUGH
The age (March 2019 ≈ 4.75 years, past typical 3–5 year service life in a climate with hot summers) plus no prior charging-system symptoms you mentioned makes "old battery" much more likely than "alternator died today". The post-start checks aren't there to prove the battery is bad — the age already does that — they're there to make sure you're not masking a charging problem with a fresh jump and then finding it out on a dark road somewhere. If A, B, and C all pass, you're looking at a battery replacement, not a charging-system diagnosis.

Don't throw away the pack after — a March-2019 battery that just barely took a jump today is the battery that won't take one at all two weeks from now in a grocery-store parking lot.

Clean resolution. Diagnostics line up with the suspected cause:

  - 310 CCA against a 600 rating is roughly half capacity, well below serviceable - confirms the March 2019 battery had failed.
  - 14.2V charging voltage is in normal range (13.8-14.4V idle), so the alternator is independently verified good.
  - Three clean starts with no clicking or dimming is real stabilization, not one lucky start.

The conservative call to stop short of repeated jump attempts also avoided cable mistakes and would have masked a charging-system symptom if there had been one. Original suspicion (old battery, not alternator) was the right one and got confirmed separately rather than assumed.

Order from lowest to highest risk, with a stop condition after each step:

1. Test the crop first. Nothing on the paper changes; a paper overlay or window-cut mat is enough. The question this answers is whether one of the three masses is actually doing work in the composition, or just competing. If removing it (or pushing it hard to a corner where it reads as framing, not as subject) clears the focal point, you stop here. Cropping is reversible, and a good crop often beats a better painting.

2. Soften one edge, on the tree mass furthest from the bend or the smallest in role. Barely-damp brush, just a pass along the contour, blot, let it dry. Edge crispness is what your eye reads first; softening drops a mass in priority without touching its value, so you don't risk darkening anything else. Re-evaluate dry, in normal viewing light, before touching a second tree.

3. Lift value on a single mass, only if softening isn't enough. Damp brush, small area, blot, full dry time. This is the riskiest in-paper move (tide line, roughed fiber, possible dulling of the pigment), so it gets one tree, not three, and you stop to look before considering another.

4. Connecting shadow last. This adds paint, which is the biggest jump in irreversibility, and on a finished passage it can read as grafted-on unless the surrounding paper takes the wash cleanly. By the time you'd consider it, steps 1-3 have already told you which masses actually need to recede.

Stop condition, single sentence: stop when a fresh viewer lands on the bend first without being told where the focal point is, and the trees read as a frame rather than a chorus. That is enough. Don't balance the three masses; don't polish.

Two rules that travel across all four steps: change one thing per sitting and let it fully dry before judging, and never combine a softening pass with a lift in the same session. If a step doesn't move the focal point clearly, that's the answer — go to the next step, don't repeat the current one more aggressively.

- First p<.05 is not the bar. The Q4 active-admin case shipped a 7.3-point raw effect with p=.018; after adjustment it collapsed to 2.4 points with a CI crossing zero and the trigger was removed. First significance without adjustment is a known false-positive pathway.

Observation window

1. Existing reminder exposure — without an exposure filter, the test isn't testing "reminder vs. no reminder." It's testing "this reminder plus whatever else is firing vs. whatever else is firing." Some accounts already receive a collaborator-invite or setup-reminder cadence. If those touchpoints are uneven across arms, the lift (or its absence) is confounded. Document the existing reminder inventory before randomization; exclude or separately bucket accounts already in active reminder flows for the same behavior.

2. Adoption-plan / recent-support states — the trial-rescue suppression work and the narrowed action audience from the prior readout were both built on this filter. Open CS adoption plans, recent support contacts, and CS-routed accounts aren't random: they're the cases where a reminder is most likely to read as renewal pressure and most likely to generate a support ticket. Excluding them isn't trimming the test; it's making the test answer the question it claims to answer. Concretely: exclude accounts with open adoption plans, accounts with support contacts in the prior 14 days, and accounts currently routed to CS.

3. Time remaining until renewal — accounts at 30 days and 90 days aren't comparable on the renewal metric. A reminder at day 35 doesn't compete with the same baseline churn dynamics as a reminder at day 85. The prior analysis was on a renewal-window cohort specifically. Stratify by days-to-renewal band, or restrict to a narrow band, so the primary metric is interpretable.

4. Unsubscribe outcomes — if the reminder triggers lifecycle-mail unsubscribes generally, you've traded an 8pp renewal hypothesis for a list-hygiene problem. The prior readout showed ~3% unsubs on the no-invite arm; anything materially above that in the reminder arm is a stop signal. Lifecycle-unsubscribe rate is a guardrail, not an optional secondary.

5. Support contacts — adding reminder volume to accounts that are about to contact support anyway creates a confound for the support team and a measurement problem for the test. Support-contact rate during the test window is a guardrail; pre-test support-contact history is a stratification or exclusion variable.

6. Stabilization cohort — the Q1 readout framework explicitly requires stabilization-after-first-sig. A "stop and ship when p<.05" rule is the exact thing the framework was designed to prevent. The decision rule has to be: first significance on the calibrated primary outcome, plus one full stabilization cohort, plus guardrails within bounds, plus Ines's lifecycle-risk note attached to the readout.

Additional issues the draft has that aren't in the flag:

A. Primary and secondary are inverted. The collaborator-invite metric is observable in 14 days; renewal is observable only at the next term, with confounders that don't stabilize for months. Earlier work explicitly concluded invite uptake is the experiment's primary outcome and renewal is secondary. The current draft reverses that, which makes the decision rule fire on a slower, noisier, more-confounded signal than necessary.

B. The 8pp hypothesis is the raw descriptive, not the calibrated signal. The 11.8pp / 11.1pp numbers from the prior readout are unadjusted and unstratified. C. No minimum effect size on the decision rule. p<.05 with a large enough sample will fire on noise. The decision rule needs an MDE or effect-size threshold, not just a p-value.

D. No minimum runtime. Renewal can't be observed before the term rolls. "Stop and ship when p<.05" implicitly assumes p is computable; it isn't until at least one cohort has cycled through. The decision rule needs a minimum number of cohorts observed before any renewal-based decision.

E. No commercial-pressure / CS-routing check. CS already raised the renewal-pressure concern in the prior readout. The narrowed action audience was the answer. A 50/50 test on the broad population recreates the original concern.
