Plan: Cherrywood workroom Wi-Fi — diagnose, fix, decide on AP

Background. Front-room stability plus the doorway-proximity effect means this is a coverage/signal-strength problem, not upstream bandwidth. The interior wall is the attenuator. Every test runs with the door closed — that's how the room will actually be used. None of these steps factory-reset the modem or router; the prior home-internet pattern that bit you on Jan 28 is a useful reminder to keep the diagnostic reversible and observable.

0. Baseline, before any change
   Door closed, same laptop, same charger state.
   - Three measurement points: workroom at the desk (the real position), workroom at the doorway, front room (control).
   - At each: Wi-Fi signal in dBm (macOS: Option-click the Wi-Fi icon; Windows: `netsh wlan show interfaces`); ping to the router; one speedtest.
   - Run a 15-minute video call from the desk and load the large dashboard. Note timing and exact behavior of each drop — full disconnect, or stutter/re-buffer? That distinction matters for the fix.
   - Repeat the desk measurement on at least one more morning at the same hour. Single-day reads lie; Wi-Fi behavior varies with neighbor congestion, time-of-day, even weather.
   Without these numbers you can't prove any fix worked, and you can't tell coverage from band choice from interference.

1. No-cost tweaks, today, 10–20 minutes
   - Identify which band the desk actually connects on. If only 2.4 GHz reaches the desk, the router may already be giving you what signal it can on the more wall-friendly band — note that.
   - If your router uses a single SSID with band steering, split into two SSIDs temporarily so you can force the laptop onto 5 GHz or 2.4 GHz and measure each at the desk with the door closed. A clean 2.4 GHz result might already be enough; a clean 5 GHz result is a fast win.
   - Elevate the router off the floor and away from metal, TV, microwave. Same room, just position.
   - Quick firmware check.
   Re-measure at the desk after each change.

2. Modem/router placement test, today
   Try 2–3 candidate positions: closer to the workroom-side wall, elevated, away from metal. Re-run the three-point measurement set at each.
   Pass criteria for declaring step 2 done:
   - Workroom-at-desk signal improves ≥10 dBm versus baseline.
   - Front-room measurement unchanged or only trivially worse.
   - A 15-minute call and a dashboard load both complete without drops.
   Partial pass (better but not stable under load, or kills front room) means go to step 3.

3. Decision: install the wired AP this weekend?
   Install if any of these are true after step 2:
   - Desk signal still worse than about −70 dBm. Rough rule of thumb: −60 to −65 is reliable, −70 to −80 is marginal, below −80 is unusable for sustained calls.
   - Desk throughput is materially below front-room throughput.
   - A call or dashboard load still drops with the door closed.
   - The doorway is the only stable spot — meaning the wall between front room and workroom is doing real attenuation and relocation alone can't put signal at the desk.
   Don't install just because the signal could theoretically be stronger. If the room works reliably under your real workload, leave it.

4. AP deployment, weekend, only if step 3 says yes
   - Run one ethernet drop from the main router to a hallway or doorway-adjacent location, not inside the workroom. The AP belongs at the threshold of the room; the wall is doing acoustic work you want kept (quiet, Kibo, separation).
   - Use the same SSID and password so devices roam.
   - Validate roaming: walk from front room to workroom with a call active; the laptop should hand off cleanly. If it sticks to the far router, lower the AP's transmit power or set a minimum-RSSI handoff threshold so devices release cleanly.

5. Validation, one week after any change
   - Re-run the three-point measurement set.
   - Three consecutive work-from-home mornings, door closed, normal call + dashboard pattern, no drops.
   - Keep the baseline numbers in a note so any future regression is comparable.

Out of scope
   - Upstream/ISP changes. Front room is fine; the link isn't the problem.
   - Opening the door as a workaround. Door stays closed — it's part of how the room works.
   - Wireless-backhaul mesh. You said wired, and wired is strictly the right call here.

Short version: don't ride it Monday. Get it to a shop this weekend if you can.

Why this call, not a softer one:

The pattern is informative. Skip on only the two smallest cogs, crisp shifting everywhere else, no visible damage, and a fresh clean/lube didn't change anything. That combination points to mechanical wear, not contamination or stiffness — lubrication is exactly the intervention that should have helped if it were just grit or a dry link, and it didn't. The most common cause is a worn cassette on the smallest cogs (they wear fastest because they carry the most direct load and have the fewest teeth engaging the chain at once). A stretched chain alone usually shows across more of the cassette, but a chain near the end of its life combined with marginal cassette wear will produce exactly this "only the hardest gear" symptom.

Why I wouldn't ride it even though it isn't a sudden brake-style hazard:

- "Moderate pedal pressure" is the force range you'd use for normal commuting — accelerating from a stop, climbing a short ramp, pulling out of an intersection. You're not stomping on it; you're commuting on it.
- A skip under load can drop the chain off the inside of the cassette into the spoke gap. That locks the rear wheel instantly. That's the failure mode, not the skip itself.
- The skip is on the gears you'd actually use on a commute (the small cogs are the cruising/higher-speed gears on a typical drivetrain), so you can't just "avoid" the problem by shifting differently.

What to ask the shop to check (concrete list, in priority order):

1. Cassette wear on the smallest two cogs — visually look for hooked/shark-fin tooth profile. If present, replace the cassette. This is the most likely finding.
2. Chain wear — measure with a chain-check tool at 0.5% and 0.75% stretch. At or past 0.75%, replace. At 0.5%–0.75%, the result depends on cassette condition.
3. Replacement rule: chain and cassette almost always replace as a pair. A new chain on a worn cassette will skip worse than what you have now, because the new, unworn chain no longer matches the worn tooth profile. If the shop quotes just a chain, ask them to confirm the cassette is within wear spec first, and have them show you the measurement.
4. Stiff links — flex every link by hand and watch for one that doesn't articulate fully. If a single stiff link survived the clean/lube, it'll still skip under load and can masquerade as cassette wear.
5. B-tension and derailleur hanger — verify the upper jockey wheel sits the correct distance from the cassette and the hanger isn't bent. Worth checking while it's on the stand; less likely given crisp shifting, but cheap to confirm.
6. Rear derailleur pulley wheels — check for tooth wear on the jockey wheels. Worn pulleys can mimic cassette skip on the small cogs because the chain meshes differently there.

Recommended setup: rotate the table 90°, add one white foam board, defer the curtain.

The glare is specular reflection — light from the window hitting the wet paper and bouncing straight back into your eyes. The fix is to change the angle of incidence so the reflection goes off to the side, not back at you.

1. Rotate the table 90° now. Put the window on your side (non-dominant-hand side if you can — opposite your brush hand, so your working hand doesn't cast a shadow on the wet area). Light now rakes across the paper instead of bouncing off it. This is a one-time physical move, not a project. As a bonus it removes the eye strain of painting while looking toward a bright window.

2. Add a single white foam board (or white mat board) propped vertically on the shadow side of the painting. Two jobs at once:
   - Bounces ambient light into the shadow side of the work, so you can read values accurately when the directional light is strong.
   - Gives you a continuous neutral white reference for judging color temperature and value, which the wall and tabletop almost certainly don't provide.

   A 16×20 or 18×24 board is plenty. Tuck it behind the table or lean it against the wall when not painting. If you don't already own one, this is the only new purchase (a few dollars) and it stays out of the room's circulation.

3. Defer the sheer curtain. It's the right idea for occasional peak-glare hours, but it's a project — curtain, rod or clips, possibly measuring, and it dims the whole corner. Keep it as the fallback if 1 + 2 doesn't fully solve the problem during the worst afternoon hours.

What this preserves: natural light stays the primary light source; the corner stays a corner, not a project; the setup is fully reversible (rotate back, remove the board). Color accuracy comes from side-lit diffuse light + a neutral white reference, not from filtering the window.

Two small notes that don't expand the project:
  - Worst-glare hours are the ones when direct sun actually falls on the paper surface. Shifting the session earlier in the day, or by an hour, is free.
  - If you already have a clipboard or small rigid board, propping the paper at a 5–10° tilt reduces glare further and is easier on your wrist. Only if it's already in your kit.

BIKE: CHAIN/CASSETTE DIAGNOSIS — OPTION COMPARISON

  Diagnosis recap (one sentence):
    Stretched chain (~0.75% wear) plus visible wear on the two smallest
    cassette cogs = the classic worn drivetrain pattern, and skipping under
    load on exactly those cogs is the symptom that confirms it.

  Option A — chain only ($68):
    - Replaces the worn chain.
    - Mechanic's warning is not generic: a fresh chain's shorter pitch will
      not seat cleanly on shark-finned cassette teeth, so skipping under load
      on those cogs usually persists (and can even feel worse until the new
      chain beds in unevenly).
    - Likely outcome: skip continues on the smaller cogs; shifting may feel
      crisper on the larger cogs; the small-cog problem is not solved.

  Option B — chain + cassette + adjustment + loaded test ($214):
    - Replaces both worn parts as a matched set, sets shifting, then verifies
      under real pedaling force.
    - The loaded test is the right verification — confirms the skip is
      actually gone before you ride it home.
    - Cost delta vs A: $146 more today.

  Is chain-only false economy here?
    Yes, on these facts:
      1. Skip is on the exact cogs with visible wear — chain-only fixes
         half the problem at best.
      2. You rely on those cogs in the faster part of the commute, so a
         "skip still happens when I push" outcome is unacceptable for how
         you actually ride.
      3. If chain-only fails, you pay $68 now and then $214 (probably the
         same quote) for a second shop visit — same end state, more money,
         more time without the bike.
      4. Option B includes the loaded test; Option A has no equivalent
         verification, so you can't tell whether the $68 worked until
         you're back on the road.
    Edge case where chain-only is NOT false economy: cassette wear is
    barely measurable, skip is mild, you can avoid the small cogs by
    riding mid-range on the fast portion, and cassette replacement is on
    a known near-term schedule anyway. None of those fit what you
    described.

  Can you ride before the work is done?
    No. Walk, transit, or drive.
      - Skip-under-load is exactly the failure mode that drops your foot at
        the wrong moment (accelerating from a light, short rise, clearing
        an intersection) and tends to cause low-speed falls or knee/ankle
        twists.
      - Worn drivetrains are also more prone to a thrown chain under load.
      - Same class of mechanical failure that triggered the walk-in on
        January 14 (rotor/pads): predictable degradation, stop riding,
        repair, then resume.
    If you must move it before repair: walk it (you've done this before)
    or carry it in/on a vehicle.

  Recommendation:
    - Authorize the $214 chain-and-cassette replacement with adjustment
      and loaded test.
    - Treat the bike as not rideable until the loaded test confirms the
      fix on the smallest cogs.
    - Keep the $68 quote as a reference for price structure, not as a
      live option.

Primary recommendation — one coherent rule

Every Helio Start readout carries two timestamps in its header, and the table exposes one more in its data:

  - state_as_of: the most recent hourly refresh the current-state table reflects. Example value: 2024-05-07 09:00:00 -05:00.
  - exported_at: when Owen (or anyone) actually pulled the snapshot. Example value: 2024-05-07 09:05:00 -05:00.
  - table-level state_as_of on the current-state view itself, so anyone querying the table directly sees the freshness boundary without reading the readout header.

The header line under the title reads, in narrow language:

  "Snapshot reflects the 09:00 hourly refresh; exported at 09:05. Rows shown as 'pending' are pending at the time of that refresh. Cases whose final routes landed between 09:00 and the next refresh will appear as 'pending' here and as their final state in the next readout. No case was admitted in error."

That sentence is the labeling rule. It is short, it is self-describing, and it removes the only thing that would let a reader mistake a refresh lag for a routing discrepancy: ambiguity about what the snapshot is a snapshot of.

Cutoff and export discipline (small, reversible)

  - Cutoff stays at the top of the hour (09:00). That is when the case-state is captured by the hourly refresh.
  - Export moves to five past the hour (09:05). That is when the post-refresh snapshot is read.
  - Decision work that needs a stable picture happens between 09:10 and 09:55, never on a snapshot pulled before 09:05.

The five-minute gap is bounded on purpose. It is short enough that no one's working clock is disrupted, and long enough that the export is unambiguously reading a refreshed table. The same rule applies to every subsequent readout (10:00 refresh, 10:05 export, 10:10+ decision work; 11:00 / 11:05 / 11:10+; etc.). Owen stops pulling mid-hour, period.

The key supporting signal — pending-cohort post-state_as_of activity

This is the one addition that turns the labeling rule from "trust the header" into "the data tells you itself." For any row showing a 'pending' state, surface a flag computed at export time from the existing event log:

  - post_state_as_of_event_count: integer, default 0.
  - post_state_as_of_last_event_type: nullable, e.g., 'connector_authentication_final' or 'admin_proof_attested'.

Computed meaning: for this submission, how many raw events landed after the state_as_of timestamp, and what was the most recent type. In Daniela's situation, the 9:05am export would show 12 pending rows, and 7 of them would carry post_state_as_of_event_count >= 1 with post_state_as_of_last_event_type pointing at the final-routing event. A reader sees that signal in the snapshot itself and immediately knows: the 9:00am refresh didn't catch these finalizations; the 10:00am refresh will. No raw-log chase, no Owen reconciliation.

This is a derived column, not a schema migration. It is computed at export time by joining the current-state view against the append-only provisional-and-final event log on submission_id with event_timestamp > state_as_of. Daniela's reporting helper can produce it from the same tables the readout already uses.

What this preserves (explicit)

  - No case was admitted in error. Nothing about routing, eligibility, or the connector-access cue changes.
  - No historical event is rewritten. The append-only event log stays append-only. The provisional-and-final event preservation from the 2024-05-07 working session is unchanged.
  - Owen's manual reconciliation is not reintroduced. The post_state_as_of_event_count is computed automatically from the event log; the reader does not need to traverse it by hand.
  - The hourly refresh cadence is unchanged. Whether hourly is the right cadence is a separate conversation with Daniela about moving to a shorter refresh window or an event-driven refresh on the relevant event types. That is a real engineering change, not a labeling rule, and should not be smuggled into this fix.

What this does NOT do (and you should know before adopting)

  - It does not eliminate the lag; it makes the lag visible and bounded.
  - It does not help if someone exports at, say, 9:47 and reads the snapshot without checking state_as_of. The five-past export discipline and the table-level state_as_of column together make that mistake harder, but the header line is still the primary defense.
  - It does not promise the next refresh will be the "real" one. The 10:00 refresh is just as honest a snapshot as the 9:00; cases can still finalize between 10:00 and 10:35. The labeling rule applies to every readout, not just the ones where the lag is obvious.

Where this lives

This is a reporting-infrastructure fix, not a routing or eligibility change. It does not belong in BRIEF-2024-04-helio-start-connector-access-gap, and it does not need a new growth brief. The natural home is a short operational note attached to the Helio Start reporting helper — the same place Daniela's 2023-10-31 same-session event-ordering annotation lives. If you want it discoverable in the Monday readout discussion, one paragraph in the working-session doc covering "preservation of provisional and final routing events, the derived current state per submission, and the exceptions Owen currently reconciles manually" is enough.

If you want, the next step is a one-line ask to Daniela: add state_as_of, exported_at, post_state_as_of_event_count, and post_state_as_of_last_event_type to the readout export, with the header sentence above. Owen can stop doing manual reconciliation as soon as that ships, and the 9:05 / 10:05 / 11:05 export convention goes in the same note.

TRUCK-MORNING PLAN

A few low-effort pieces:

1. Learn the schedule. Recycling trucks at Cherrywood almost certainly run on a fixed weekday morning. Confirm with management or watch for 2-3 weeks. Predictability is the cheapest stress reducer.

2. Pre-position, don't react. About 10-15 minutes before the expected window, calmly move Kibo to the workroom with blanket, water, and white noise already set up. Don't wait for the barking — by then he's already aroused. The closed room + familiar items worked: 8 min of arousal, 5 min to settle.

3. Cut the visual trigger. Close blinds on the workroom's north window and on any front-facing windows in the rest of the unit. He can't react to what he can't see.

4. Keep your energy flat. Calm voice, normal routine, no reassurance that signals "something is wrong." Treat it like a normal morning.

5. Hold the recovery window. After the truck passes, give him 5-10 minutes of quiet before opening the workroom door. Don't release him back into a still-charged environment.

6. Track briefly. For the next 2-3 weeks, note day, time, duration, intensity (1-5), and recovery time. Habituation to a predictable environmental sound at a new home typically shows within that window.

7. Don't rush graduation. Once he's consistently calm in the workroom, over weeks not days, test whether he handles it with just blinds closed + white noise in his normal spot. Change one variable at a time.

WHEN TO CALL A VET OR BEHAVIORIST

This event doesn't warrant either. He settled with a working protocol, no residual signs, and intact self-regulation — he accepted the move to the workroom.

Same-day vet if you see:
  - Self-injury: broken nails, broken skin, damage to nose or paws from pawing doors/windows
  - Refusal of food or water for more than 24 hours, or a meaningful drop in normal intake over 2-3 days
  - Vomiting or diarrhea tied to episodes
  - Panting or shaking that doesn't resolve within 30-60 minutes after the trigger ends
  - Any physical injury — limping, favoring a paw, swelling
  - New aggression toward you, Sam, or other pets

Behaviorist referral (non-urgent) if a pattern develops over 2-6 weeks:
  - Episodes getting longer, more frequent, or more intense despite the protocol
  - Generalization — Kibo starts reacting to similar sounds (garbage trucks, leaf blowers, lawn equipment, other large vehicles) when he didn't before
  - Recovery time growing longer (5 min → 15-20 min)
  - Anxiety showing up in other contexts — separation distress when you leave, restlessness at night, change in baseline temperament
  - No meaningful improvement after 4-6 weeks of consistent protocol at the new home

Context: Kibo is 8 days into a new home. Mild environmental over-reactivity is normal for the first 4-6 weeks after a move. A single event with a working response is not a clinical signal; an escalating pattern is. The workroom + blanket + water + white noise protocol already in place is the right shape — consistency matters more than escalation.

Let me draft this carefully. The passage: "A measure begins as a window and ends as a target; once people are rewarded for moving it, the organization sees the number more clearly than the work."

Three angles:
1. Incentives — what changes when the measure becomes a target
2. What numbers hide — the work that disappears behind a rounded figure
3. How to use a metric without letting it replace judgment

Connection to Helio: the intake-vs-outcome split, raw vs operating panel, first significance vs stabilization — but framed as a discussion lens, not a launch deck.

---

**1. Incentives — what "moving the number" does to the work**

The window-target shift isn't about the metric getting worse. It's about the *direction of effort* bending toward whatever the metric rewards. Once "79% activation" or "11-point invite-renewal gap" is the thing being moved, time and attention flow toward producing the number, and away from the work that produced the number originally — the credential-readiness screening, the connector-specific authority check, the separate intake and downstream denominators. The passage names the moment: when people are *rewarded* for moving it. Before that, a measure is descriptive — it tells you something about the system. After, it's prescriptive — it tells the system what to do. The same integer can describe the work or replace it, depending on which side of the reward line you're on.

**2. What numbers hide — the rounded figure as vanishing point**

A rounded figure makes the underlying composition harder to see. "79% activated" is true and useful at one level, and invisible at another: 116/147 raw and 116/129 operating panel describe different cohorts, and the 18 credential-readiness cases that pass Helio admin proof but can't authenticate their chosen connector aren't a footnote — they're the design gap. The number doesn't lie. It just stops carrying the shape. Discussion angle: ask what gets *made invisible* when a metric stabilizes into a headline. Not "is the number wrong" but "what work does the rounding erase." The composition lives in the gap between raw and operating panels, between intake denominator and downstream denominator, between the assisted-routing panel kept separate and the self-serve panel promoted to headline.

**3. Using a metric without letting it replace judgment — the discipline is procedural, not rhetorical**

The Helio practice that fits this is small and specific, not a manifesto: keep the raw count next to the operating count; keep the first-significance read next to the stabilization-cohort rule; keep the descriptive gap next to the missing causal claim. None of those moves are expensive individually. The reason they hold is that they put denominators and effect sizes *before* the conclusion in the writeup order, which forces the conclusion to negotiate with the number rather than inherit it. The angle for discussion: a metric serves judgment when the workflow around it forces the human to look at composition, denominator, and effect size before the headline. When the workflow skips that step — when the slide is built around the conclusion and the number is the justification — the metric has stopped being a window and started being the verdict.

**Helio connection, kept as lens not lecture**

The thread between the passage and Helio Start is the same thread that runs through the 116/147 vs. 116/129 split, the connector-access intake descriptive read, and the Expansion Assist shadow-learning framing: the metric stays useful only as long as the workflow around it preserves the composition the metric would otherwise hide. The 12-readout audit (10 with denominator and effect size before conclusion; 2 corrected) isn't a process document — it's the procedural expression of "see the work more clearly than the number." A measure that replaces its own work is a measure whose team has stopped looking at it.

Lateral ankle pain that creeps in during the last mile, without trauma, swelling, or bruising, and that only registers as ~2/10 on stairs is most consistent with a low-grade peroneal tendon irritation or mild lateral-ankle soft-tissue strain. Both behave the same way under early self-care, which is convenient because the early plan is the same either way: relative rest, gentle mobility, and a controlled return test before resuming normal running.

Plan for the next 3-5 days

- Rest from running. Walking is fine as long as it stays at 0-1/10. Today and tomorrow are walking-only days, with normal daily activity otherwise.
- Ice is optional. If the area feels warm or "annoyed" after the run, 10-15 minutes on, 45 minutes off, 2-3 times today and tomorrow is reasonable. If it just feels quiet, you can skip it.
- Skip NSAIDs unless you actually need them for comfort. For a low-grade tendon irritation, anti-inflammatories can blunt the tissue's adaptation response and aren't clearly helpful.
- A simple compression sleeve or light ankle sleeve can reduce the sense of "awareness" on stairs and is fine to wear during the day. Don't use it as a substitute for the rest test below.
- Gentle mobility, twice daily, only within comfort:
  - Ankle alphabet: trace the letters A-Z in the air with the big toe, slow and pain-free
  - Calf stretch against a wall with the heel down, 2 x 30 seconds each side, only to the point of stretch, not pain
  - Single-leg balance on the right leg near a counter, 3 x 20-30 seconds. If this reproduces the ache, that's a useful data point.
- Avoid for now: hill running, lateral cuts, uneven trail, jumping, plyometrics, prolonged stair descent, and any running.

Yes, skip the next run

Skip at least the next scheduled run, and possibly the one after that. The decision to try a return run should be made on Day 3 (Monday), based on these four checks all being true:

1. Walking is 0/10, including on stairs
2. No swelling, bruising, or warmth has appeared
3. A single-leg calf raise on the right is pain-free and feels as strong as the left
4. The single-leg balance test (above) doesn't reproduce the ache

If any of those fail, hold another day and recheck. None of these are medical diagnostic tests, just gate criteria.

Return-to-run protocol (assuming Day 3 checks pass)

- Day 3 (Monday): first return test. 20 minutes easy, flat sidewalk or path, familiar shoes, conversational pace. Stop early if the ache shows up.
- Day 4 (Tuesday): rest or walk only, regardless of how Day 3 felt. Note any delayed soreness 12-24 hours later.
- Day 5 (Wednesday): if Day 3 was clean and there's no delayed soreness, second test, 25-30 minutes easy, same surface and shoes.
- Day 6-7: rest day after, then a normal 3-mile easy run if everything is clean.
- Build back at roughly +1 mile or +10 minutes per session over the next 2-3 weeks. Don't re-add hill work or speed until you've held a normal easy distance for a week without symptoms.

A useful framing: the same symptom appearing at the same point in the run, or earlier, on two consecutive return runs means it isn't ready, not that you need to push through. Pushing through lateral ankle irritation is the most common way a 2/10 becomes a 6/10.

Signs that justify prompt medical evaluation (not "wait and see")

Call or seek same-day evaluation if any of these appear, even if the ankle still "feels okay":

- A pop, snap, or sudden sharp pain at any point, including during a return test
- Visible swelling, bruising, or deformity that wasn't there before
- Inability to bear weight, or a strong feeling of the ankle giving way
- Pain at rest or at night that wakes you or is unrelated to movement
- Pain ≥3-4/10 during normal walking, or pain that is trending worse over 48-72 hours rather than better
- Locking, catching, or a block to motion when pointing the foot up or down
- Numbness, tingling, color change, or coldness in the foot
- Calf swelling, calf tenderness, or warmth behind the knee or in the calf (different concern, unrelated to the ankle but worth knowing)
- Fever, red streaking, or any sign of skin infection over the area

For context on the pattern: your prior right-calf tightness (March 9, 2024) followed almost exactly the same shape — gradual onset, no trauma, mild pain, resolved with one rest day. That's reassuring about your general injury response, but the ankle is a different structure with a different recovery profile, so treat the gate above, not the prior precedent, as the trigger.

One small thing worth noting in a log: today's run, the location (outside of right ankle, lateral), the stair pain (2/10), and the absence of swelling. If you ever do see someone for this ankle, those four facts are the most useful 30 seconds of history you can give them.

Safe internal temperature
  - 165 F is the safety floor for all poultry (USDA/FSIS).
  - Mom's recipe says "Cook until done, turning once" without a number — treat 165 F as "done." If you prefer a more tender thigh, holding to roughly 175 F is common because dark meat has more connective tissue, but 165 F is the line you must clear. Going higher is texture, not safety.

Where to put the thermometer in chicken thighs
  - Insert into the thickest part of the thigh.
  - Stay in meat, not in fat or gristle.
  - Do not let the tip touch bone. Bone conducts heat and runs hotter than the meat around it, so a bone-touching reading can look done while the meat next to it is still under. For bone-in thighs this matters; if these are boneless, the thickest part of the largest piece is the spot.
  - Check more than one thigh. Cold spots in a crowded pan are real; the smallest piece, not the largest, is often the one that tells you whether the batch is safe.

Avoiding raw-marinade contamination of the cooked chicken
  - The 2 Tbsp you set aside BEFORE the chicken went in is the clean portion. It never touched raw meat. That is the sauce Mom intends you to brush on during the last few minutes. Use it as-is with a clean spoon or a fresh brush.
  - The marinade the raw chicken sat in is now contaminated. Do not brush it on the cooking chicken raw and do not serve it as a sauce raw. Two acceptable paths if you want to use it at all: discard it, or bring it to a full rolling boil for at least 1 minute in a separate small saucepan and use that as sauce instead. Easiest is to just discard it and rely on the reserved 2 Tbsp — Mom's recipe already provides exactly that.
  - Use a clean utensil for the reserved sauce. Don't double-dip a brush between the raw marinade container and the chicken in the pan.
  - Don't return cooked chicken to the bowl or bag that held raw marinade.
  - Anything that touched raw chicken or raw marinade — hands, board, tongs, the bowl — should be washed with hot soapy water before it touches the cooked chicken or the serving plate. A quick rinse is not enough; soap and a scrub, or a run through the dishwasher, is the bar.

Quick order of operations that keeps it clean
  1. Mix marinade, pull 2 Tbsp into a small separate bowl, set aside.
  2. Add chicken to the remaining marinade, refrigerate 2 hours.
  3. Cook in a clean pan, turning once, until the thickest thigh reads 165 F away from bone.
  4. During the last few minutes, brush the reserved 2 Tbsp on with a clean brush or spoon.
  5. Discard the used raw marinade (or boil it in a separate pan if you really want a sauce beyond the reserved portion). Wash hands, board, tongs, and the raw-marinade bowl before plating.

Nothing in the above changes Mom's quantities, timing, or seasoning — it's just where the thermometer goes and which sauce gets used.

A clean, symptom-free 24-minute test — during and across the eight hours after, with no swelling, focal tenderness, limp, or instability — is real progress, but it isn't yet evidence the ankle tolerates continuous running. The right move is one small, reversible step, not a jump back to four continuous miles.

WEEK OF MAY 27 — RECOMMENDED PROGRESSION

Two sessions, three to four days apart:

  - Tuesday May 28 (or Wednesday if Tuesday feels too soon): repeat today's 24-minute session exactly — 2W:1J for the first 12 minutes, then 1W:1J for the last 12. Roughly 10 minutes of jogging.
  - Saturday June 1: 26 minutes total, with the 2W:1J block shortened to the first 8–10 minutes and the 1W:1J block filling the rest. Same pattern, slightly more time in the harder ratio, ~10–11 minutes of jogging total.

Memorial Day Monday is a rest day or pain-free walking/cycling only. No pace work, no hills, no continuous running, no target distance — interval pattern and total minutes only.

If Tuesday/Wednesday feels premature, do today's 24-minute session on both days and treat Saturday as a third repeat. There's no urgency to advance.

REPEAT THE LEVEL (DON'T PROGRESS) IF ANY OF THESE ARE TRUE

  - The ankle isn't cleanly back to baseline the next morning.
  - A repeat of the same session reproduces any sensation at all — ache, tightness, awareness.
  - Two consecutive sessions at the same level reproduce the same feeling.
  - You simply feel under-recovered or uncertain. Repeating a clean level costs little; progressing on a shaky one can cost a lot.

STOP THE SESSION MID-RUN IF

  - Any ache crosses roughly 2/10, worsens through the session, or changes your gait.
  - Sharp or pinching pain, a pop, or a feeling of giving way.
  - Pain or tightness that doesn't settle within about a minute of switching to walking.
  - Anything that produces a limp, favoring, or a shortened stride.

If any of those happen: walk home cool-down only. Don't push through, and don't "test" it again later in the same session.

STEP BACK OVER THE NEXT 24–48 HOURS IF

  - The ankle is still aware, stiff, or sore the next morning.
  - Mild symptoms appear with ordinary walking or stairs.
  - Swelling, focal tenderness, or a limp shows up after the session.
  - Two rest days don't return you to a clean baseline.

If any of those happen, drop back to pain-free walking or cycling only for several days and resume the ladder from the previous clean level (or one notch below).

SEEK EVALUATION FOR ANY OF THESE

  - Swelling, bruising, or warmth around the ankle or lower leg.
  - Focal bony tenderness — especially over the lateral malleolus, medial malleolus, or sinus tarsi.
  - A limp, inability to bear weight normally, or any sense of instability or giving way.
  - Pain at rest, or pain that wakes you.
  - Numbness, tingling, or color change in the foot.
  - Calf pain, swelling, or tenderness — that's a separate pathway, not part of an ankle-return program.

WHAT MAKES THIS WEEK "SUCCESSFUL"

Both sessions at the chosen level, pain-free during, immediately after, the next morning, and through ordinary walking and stairs, with no swelling, focal tenderness, limp, or instability at any check. If those conditions hold, a reasonable next move is to lengthen one or two of the jog intervals to two minutes (introducing a small 2J:1W block) while keeping total time near 26–28 minutes. Continuous running and any four-mile target are still several weeks away and shouldn't be reintroduced on the strength of one clean week.

Sam — here's a conservative prep and service sequence for the one sesame-allergy meal on June 1. I've kept the scope tight: what cannot be guaranteed by just dropping the garnish, what to reconfirm with the guest and chef-owner before the event, and the prep/service sequence I'd run.

THE CORE PROBLEM WITH "JUST LEAVE OFF THE GARNISH"

The garnish is the smallest part of the sesame exposure. The bigger issues are:

  - Sesame oil is in the glaze itself. It is incorporated into the sauce and cooked onto/with the chicken. Sesame protein does not cook off. "No garnish" does not remove sesame from the entrée.
  - Shared equipment is the next concern: the same pan, tongs, basting brush, squeeze bottle, tasting spoon, and plating area used for the soy-ginger version become a cross-contact path even if the final plate has no seeds on it.
  - Kitchen airborne sesame from earlier toasting/seeding in the day can settle on nearby surfaces or uncovered food.
  - Guest sensitivity is unknown. Some allergic guests react to trace amounts; some react to airborne residue. "No visible sesame" does not equate to "no sesame protein."

So "leave off the garnish" only addresses the most visible sesame. It does not, by itself, make the standard entrée safe for a sesame-allergic guest.

WHAT STILL NEEDS TO BE RECONFIRMED WITH THE GUEST (do this by ~May 30)

  - Severity: any history of anaphylaxis, EpiPen or other auto-injector carried, asthma, recent reaction.
  - Sesame forms they react to: seeds only, oil only, tahini/paste, all forms. (Sesame oil refined to high heat can have reduced protein but is not universally tolerated.)
  - Trace sensitivity: are they comfortable with shared-kitchen prep, or do they need a fully segregated cook and a different protein/flavor profile?
  - What they actually want: a modified version of the same entrée, or a different dish prepared from scratch with segregated equipment.
  - Medication: are they bringing their own? Where will it be during service? Who at the table knows how to use it?
  - Comfort steps: would they like to speak briefly with you or the chef-owner before service, see the label on the sauce ingredients, or have the plate brought out and shown before being set down?
  - Their arrival time and seating — relevant for plating timing and to confirm the kitchen knows which cover is theirs.

If the guest describes anaphylaxis, auto-injector use, or "any sesame at all," the plan below is the right shape. If they say "seeds are fine, just pick them off," that is a different conversation and you should not assume — clarify in writing.

WHAT STILL NEEDS TO BE RECONFIRMED WITH THE CHEF-OWNER (before prep starts)

  - Approval of the chosen approach: a fully separate allergen entrée prepared on segregated equipment, not a modified version of the soy-ginger chicken.
  - Equipment segregation: dedicated pan, tongs, basting brush, tasting spoon, small saucepan for sauce, cutting board if any prep is done that day. None of these may have touched the sesame glaze earlier that day.
  - Work area: a sanitized and visibly clear section, with sesame-containing items (oil bottle, seed container, glaze pot, tasting spoons) physically removed or kept well outside that zone.
  - Oil dispensers: a fresh, sealed bottle of neutral oil for the allergen cook — not the same bottle that has had sesame oil poured from it.
  - Ingredient labels: confirm the substitute sauce contains no sesame, no "natural flavoring" or "spice" that could conceal it, and no shared-vat soy sauce. Pull and keep the labels.
  - Timing of the day's sesame prep: when does toasting/seeding/glazing happen relative to the allergen cook? Allergen meal should be cooked after the work area has been cleaned and ideally after the sesame prep is done and put away — not in parallel.
  - Plating and pass: separate plating area or fully sanitized station; the allergen plate labeled clearly so it cannot be confused with the regular plates; no sesame-containing garnish anywhere near the pass.
  - Service flow: who carries it out, who announces it (or doesn't), and what to do if the guest has any reaction at the table — including calling 911 immediately and not waiting.
  - Tasting: the chef should not taste the allergen version with a spoon that has touched the sesame glaze, even between bites.

RECOMMENDED PREP SEQUENCE (allergen entrée)

  1. Confirm the guest's wishes and the chef-owner's approval before any shopping or prep.
  2. Build a written ingredient list for the allergen entrée — a different protein or a different flavor profile (e.g., a simple pan sauce with butter, lemon, herbs; or a separately sourced non-sesame soy-ginger variation made with a neutral oil and verified sesame-free soy sauce). Keep the ingredient labels.
  3. Pull dedicated equipment before service: a clean pan, tongs, basting brush, small saucepan, tasting spoon, plating spoon. Set them on a clean towel at a sanitized station.
  4. Stage a sealed neutral-oil bottle and verified sesame-free sauce components at that station.
  5. Do all sesame prep (toasting, seeding, glazing) first, put those items away, then clean the work area, then cook the allergen entrée. Do not cook them in parallel.
  6. Cook the allergen entrée. Plate it on a distinct plate/liner if possible. Label the plate cover or pick it up directly so it is unmistakable.
  7. Hold it covered and warm until service.

RECOMMENDED SERVICE SEQUENCE

  - Confirm with the guest (or their table) which cover is theirs before the plate goes out.
  - The allergen plate goes out first, separately carried, identified by the server by sight and by label. It is not placed on the pass next to the other plates.
  - The server (or you) confirms visually with the guest that it is the correct plate before setting it down.
  - Keep the ingredient label list on hand in case the guest asks.
  - Know where the guest's medication is and who at the table would administer it. If anyone shows any sign of reaction — itching, swelling, throat tightness, hives, GI symptoms — call 911 immediately and do not wait. State "suspected allergic reaction" to dispatch.

WHAT THIS PLAN DOES NOT DO (explicit boundaries)

  - It does not guarantee the entrée is safe for the guest. Only the guest, with full information, can decide whether to eat it.
  - It does not replace an in-person conversation with the guest before the event. That conversation is the most important control.
  - It does not assume the standard entrée is safe with the garnish omitted. Sesame oil in the glaze makes that approach inadequate.
  - It does not promise a sterile kitchen, only a segregated cook and plating path. If the guest requires a fully allergen-free kitchen, that needs to be raised with the chef-owner and may not be feasible in a working restaurant.
  - It does not cover other potential allergens (soy, wheat, etc.) that may also be in the standard entrée. Confirm the full allergy profile with the guest and read every label.

The 11 applications are UNPAID REFERRAL. They are not paid acquisition, and they are not excluded. They stay in the Helio Start application cohort with their source properly attributed.

Why Marcus's binary is wrong

  Paid acquisition has an operational meaning: Helio pays a third party for placement, lead, or click; Helio runs paid media; or a Helio sales rep makes outbound contact that produces the application. None of those hold here:

    - Directory listing is free.
    - Helio has no commercial relationship with the directory.
    - No ad, no spend, no sales contact before the application.
    - utm_medium=referral is the canonical label for organic inbound and is distinct from paid-media values (cpc, paid, paid_search, display, etc.).

  Excluding them is the other wrong move. These are real prospects who met the intake criteria and submitted valid applications. The Helio Start intake is reachable from the public pricing page (the connector-authentication cue has been live there since 2024-04-23), and an organic visitor following a directory link to the pricing page and into the intake is legitimate inbound — not contamination. Source-based exclusion would create a selection effect and bias the application denominator, and it would make Q3 non-comparable to prior periods.

Correct classification

  Source channel:        referral (unpaid)
  utm_medium:            referral (keep as-is)
  utm_source:            directory name (preserved for analysis)
  Attribution class:     organic inbound — neither paid nor direct
  Cohort treatment:      full Helio Start application, eligibility-checked, routed per normal rules
  Paid-acquisition flag: NO
  Exclude flag:          NO

Q3 reporting approach

  1. Keep the 11 in the Q3 application denominator. They are real applications.
  2. Surface referral as a descriptive channel tag (utm_source, or a referral-source label) so the 11 are visible by channel without changing cohort status. The breakdown is observational, not causal.
  3. Do not create a paid-acquisition line. There is no spend, no campaign, no design — nothing to attribute.
  4. Do not create an exclude line. Source-based exclusion is retroactive cherry-picking.
  5. If Q3 reporting shows a source mix, list referral alongside any other channels actually present (direct, organic search, etc.). The point is observation, not verdict.
  6. If anyone asks whether this validates the directory as a paid-acq channel, the answer is no. Organic inbound from a free directory is one observation of an unpaid channel. No cost was incurred; no ROI is computable; extrapolation to paid placement is unauthorized.

How to preserve the referral source without treating it as a paid-acq test

    - Track utm_source for the directory so the channel is observable going forward. Descriptive tagging, not paid-acq measurement.
    - Keep intake, eligibility, connector cue, and downstream routing rules unchanged. The 11 go through the same gate as every other application — admin proof, eligibility boundaries, routing logic.
    - Do not interpret the 11 as a designed test. There is no control, no random assignment, no pre-registered hypothesis, no spend. Calling this a "test" of any kind is a category error.
    - If the directory keeps sending volume, treat it as ongoing observational data about an organic channel. It does not authorize paid placement with the directory, paid acquisition generally, pricing-page positioning change, GA framing, launch framing, pipeline attribution, forecast, or revenue credit.
    - Connector-authentication cue stays unchanged; routing stays unchanged; eligibility stays unchanged.

Boundary statement for the Q3 write-up

  The 11 applications are unpaid referral traffic and remain part of the Helio Start application cohort. Their presence reflects an organic inbound path — third-party directory → public pricing page → Helio Start intake — and does not represent a paid-acquisition signal, a designed test, or a change to Helio Start's exposure, eligibility, lifecycle, or support posture.

Diagnosis

Owen's mock is reading the raw eligibility event log as if each row were an independent current-state record, instead of deriving one current state per submission from the terminal event. That is why A-117 and A-219 each appear in two state buckets:

  A-117: provisional_pending at 08:03 was an interim state while review was in flight. It was superseded 19 minutes later by final_assisted at 08:22. Terminal state is assisted, not pending.

  A-219: provisional_admitted at 10:01 was an interim optimistic state. It was superseded 18 minutes later by final_ineligible at 10:19. Terminal state is ineligible, not admitted.

  A-204: a single final_admitted at 09:14 with no provisional precursor. Terminal state is admitted; this row is correctly placed.

Provisional events are intermediate, not terminal. They do not belong in the current-state aggregation. They belong in the exception view, with their original timestamps, so the order is auditable. The current-state view must be derived.

Corrected current-state view (one row per submission, mutually exclusive buckets)

Aggregation logic:

  1. Group all eligibility events by submission_id.
  2. Within each submission, select the terminal event. The robust precedence is: any event with a "final_" prefix outranks any "provisional_" prefix; event timestamp is the secondary ordering key on top of that prefix precedence. The expected pattern is provisional first, final later, but the rule should not break if a record arrives out of order.
  3. Map the selected terminal event to exactly one bucket:
       final_admitted     -> admitted
       final_assisted     -> assisted
       final_ineligible   -> ineligible
  4. Emit one row per submission. Admitted / assisted / ineligible counts are mutually exclusive by construction. No submission appears in more than one bucket.

Result on the mock's five rows:

  A-117 -> assisted    (terminal: final_assisted at 08:22)
  A-204 -> admitted    (terminal: final_admitted at 09:14)
  A-219 -> ineligible  (terminal: final_ineligible at 10:19)

Counts: 1 admitted, 1 assisted, 1 ineligible. No double-count.

Corrected exception view (provisional, in-flight, and contradictory)

Aggregation logic: surface any submission that should not appear in the current-state view because its terminal state has not been established or its transitions are off-pattern. The view preserves raw event rows intact (timestamps and event order visible); it does not delete or rewrite history.

Surface conditions:

  - Latest event for the submission carries a "provisional_" prefix and no final event has arrived yet -> still in flight. On this mock: none. Both A-117 and A-219 have a final event after their provisional one.
  - Out-of-order or contradictory transitions: a final event preceded by an inconsistent provisional, or a sequence that does not match the expected provisional -> final flow.
  - Missing terminal event beyond a defined staleness threshold: surface separately from in-flight so the dashboard can distinguish "review still in progress" from "stuck or dropped."
  - Duplicate submission_id, or a submission whose events reference an unknown prior state.

On this mock, the exception view would carry A-117's provisional_pending (08:03) and A-219's provisional_admitted (10:01) as preserved historical rows with their original timestamps, paired with their terminal final events for audit. Neither submission is flagged as in-flight because each has a terminal final event after the provisional one.

What this preserves

  - Raw event log: untouched, all five rows present, ordered. No deletion, no rewriting of provisional events.
  - Provisional events: visible in the exception view with their timestamps and the final events that superseded them.
  - Current-state aggregation: one derived row per submission, mutually exclusive buckets, driven by the terminal event.
  - Provisional overlap or in-flight cases: explicit and countable, not silently absorbed into a final-state bucket.

This matches the pattern already used elsewhere in the Q3 panel: raw events stay in the underlying table; the automated current-state table derives one row per submission; the exception view carries provisionals and any submission whose terminal event has not arrived or whose transitions are off-pattern.

     it will be identified at service (plate pattern, mark, or pick).


PREP AND LABELING ORDER

The rule throughout: STANDARD contains sesame (sesame oil in the glaze AND toasted
sesame garnish); SESAME-FREE contains no sesame in any form. They travel through
every stage in separate, labeled vessels with separate utensils. When in doubt,
do not combine, reuse, or guess.

A. STAGE AND LABEL (before opening any packages)

  - Two zones on the prep counter (or two separate times with full wipe-down
    between). The sesame-free zone is set up first so standard-zone traffic does
    not pass through it.
  - Apply labels NOW, before ingredients move:
        STANDARD — CONTAINS SESAME   (on the 22-serving vessel)
        SESAME-FREE — NO SESAME      (on the 2-serving vessel)
  - Dedicated, labeled containers for each batch: marinating vessels, sheet pans,
    finishing bowls, holding lids, transport vessels, plating dishes.
  - Shared stock items (soy sauce, brown sugar, rice vinegar) may come from one
    source IF measured into separate, labeled prep cups before the sesame oil
    bottle is uncapped in the kitchen. The sesame oil bottle stays in the
    standard zone only. Canola oil stays in the sesame-free zone only.
  - Ginger: portion 0.55 cup into the standard prep cup; portion 2 tsp into the
    sesame-free prep cup, from the same ginger source is fine, separate utensils.
  - Raw chicken: keep the 1.5 lb sesame-free package SEALED until the standard
    13.2 lb is portioned and put away in its labeled zone.

B. MARINADE

  - Mix STANDARD marinade in its labeled vessel, add 13.2 lb chicken, cover,
    mark start time.
  - Mix SESAME-FREE marinade in its labeled vessel (canola oil, not sesame oil,
    no garnish), add the 1.5 lb chicken from its sealed package, cover, mark
    start time.
  - Both batches marinate per recipe. Lids stay on. Zones stay distinct. Do not
    move a vessel from one zone to the other.

C. COOK

  - Cook SESAME-FREE first, on its labeled sheet pan/pan, with utensils that
    have not touched sesame. Cover and set aside in its labeled holding vessel.
  - Wipe down the cooking surface (or swap to a clean sheet pan) before the
    standard batch goes on.
  - Cook STANDARD on its labeled pan with its own utensils. These utensils do
    not return to the sesame-free side without a wash.
  - Toasted sesame garnish goes on the STANDARD batch ONLY, applied at the end,
    with a dedicated garnish utensil that has not touched the sesame-free
    batch. Garnish work happens away from the sesame-free plating zone so
    seeds cannot scatter onto the wrong plate.

D. HOLD AND TRANSPORT

  - Both batches held covered in their labeled vessels.
  - Transport containers labeled: STANDARD — CONTAINS SESAME and SESAME-FREE.
  - If both travel together, the sesame-free vessel is fully sealed inside a
    second container so a spill or scatter cannot reach it.

E. PLATE AND SERVICE

  - Sesame-free meal on a plate that is visually distinct from the standard
    pattern, or marked with a discrete identifier (colored pick, sticker,
    marked plate rim) so the server and the guest can confirm at handoff.
  - Standard plates receive the toasted sesame garnish; sesame-free plates do
    not, and the garnish station stays away from the sesame-free plating area.
  - The server confirms verbally with the guest that the marked plate is
    theirs before it is set down.


DEFAULTS IF ANY STAGE IS UNCERTAIN

  - If a utensil, surface, or vessel that touched sesame is needed and a clean
    alternative is not immediately available: stop, wash, then proceed. Do not
    reuse.
  - If the sesame-free plate is dropped, contaminated at the pass, or its mark
    is lost: pull it, prepare a fresh sesame-free portion from the held batch
    (or re-batch the small sesame-free recipe), re-mark, re-serve. Do not
    guess.
  - If the guest's allergy severity turns out to be anaphylactic and any of the
    separation steps could not be confirmed: do not serve the held sesame-free
    batch; prepare a fresh portion from scratch in a cleaned zone and confirm
    before plating.

For the corner, judgment first; only act if it still reads from normal viewing distance:

1. Look before you do anything. 1/8 inch at a corner is often invisible at arm's length, especially against the value transition a wash edge usually has. Photograph the corner in even light and look at the image rather than the painting; eyes relax and small damage disappears more easily in a photo.

2. Do not press the lifted fibers back down. On cold-press this usually creates shiny flat spots or pulls more fibers loose. Same instinct with water: residual moisture can reactivate sizing and cause swelling that makes the roughened strip read worse.

3. Do not glaze the roughened strip. The lifted tooth grabs pigment harder than the surrounding wash, so a local color match tends to read as a thin darker line exactly where you do not want one.

If it still reads after step 1, escalate in this order:

4. Crop it. Since the mat opening is already planned at 8x10, shifting the opening half an inch or rotating it slightly can bury a 1/8 inch intrusion entirely. This is the lowest-risk fix because it changes nothing on the paper.

5. Last resort only: a single very dilute wash (more water than pigment, near the value of the surrounding paint) tested on scrap of the same paper first, applied in one light pass with a barely-damp brush. Accept the result before any second pass.

For future sheets, fiber lifting when pulling low-tack tape is almost always one of three things:

   - Pull angle. Tape should be pulled back on itself at a low angle, folding the tape back along its own length close to the paper, not lifted up at 90 degrees. Lifting at 90 puts shear force across the paper's surface grain and is the single most common cause of lifted fibers on cold-press.

   - Adhesive cure time. Even true low-tack tape cures over hours and days; pulling within roughly 24 hours of application is gentler than pulling a week later.

   - Residual paper moisture at application. Even slight dampness under the tape creates a stronger bond with the surface fibers. If you have stretched, washed, or recently glazed the sheet, let it fully equilibrate before taping.

Two small changes that help most: pull the tape back along its own length rather than up, and do a quick corner test of that specific tape roll on a scrap of the same paper before committing a full sheet. If the scrap test lifts fibers, switch tape or use masking fluid for the edge instead.

Owen's combined layout compresses four things that should stay apart and then draws a funnel that does not exist. The fix is structural, not cosmetic: four lateral panels with explicit cohort definitions, no funnel between them, and a top-of-dashboard scope statement that says what this readout is and is not.

Top-of-dashboard scope statement (one paragraph, not a headline, not a target):

  Q3 Helio Start readout. Day-7 activation is on admitted workspaces with
  complete day-7 windows. First-paid is an interim day-30 cash-collection
  measure on a separate admitted-workspace cohort with complete day-30
  windows. The connector-check observation is intake-design evidence from
  a separate cohort. None of these four panels overlap by construction,
  and no funnel connects them. This dashboard is not a continuation
  decision, an expansion proposal, a launch readiness read, a pricing
  signal, a paid-acquisition channel, a forecast, or a Q4 revenue
  attribution.

Panel 1 — Final routing (application intake)

  Denominator: applications received in the Q3 reporting window.
  Splits:
    - final_admitted
    - final_assisted (pre-setup routing)
    - final_ineligible (with reason class: stale-profile, alias-merged,
      explicit unsubscribe, support/adoption open, other)
    - provisional_pending (held; not yet final)
  Each application counted once at its final state, with the audit
  trail preserved. The A-117 / A-219 deduplication logic from the
  current-state and exception views stays in this panel — that was a
  separate fix Owen already owns.
  This panel is intake only. It does not imply activation, payment,
  retention, or pipeline.

Panel 2 — Day-7 activation (mature admitted-workspace outcome)

  Denominator: admitted workspaces with complete day-7 windows, in
  non-overlapping mature weekly cohorts. Three non-overlapping cohorts
  totaling at least 150 admitted accounts with complete day-7 windows
  is the Q3 continuation gate; the dashboard shows the running total
  against that gate, not against a sales or forecast target.
  Numerator: completed a supported first integration.
  Composition splits (API / CSV / warehouse) are descriptive only.
  Credential-readiness cases stay visible as a separate sub-line; they
  are not removed from the headline denominator, and the 18-of-31
  intake-design finding is referenced here as evidence, not as a
  correction to the headline rate.
  Provisional operating read (116/129 = 89.9% on the credential-clean
  subset) is shown only as a footnote, never as a headline or trend.

Panel 3 — Connector-check observation (separate cohort, side panel)

  This panel sits beside Panel 1, not above Panel 4. It carries:
    - 92 applications reviewed for connector authority
    - 68 admitted from that review
    - 59 of 68 day-7 first integration (86.8% on that cohort's denom)
  Header line on the panel itself: "Separate cohort. Intake-design
  finding. Not a continuation signal. No overlap established with
  Panel 4's first-paid cohort."
  Owen should also note the date window this cohort covers so a
  reader cannot assume it is the same population as Panel 1 or
  Panel 4.

Panel 4 — First-paid evidence (interim day-30)

  Denominator: 52 admitted workspaces with complete day-30 windows
  in the interim Helio Start first-paid measurement.
  Numerator: 41 settled first cash payments by day 30 (non-zero cash
  collected, no same-day full refund, one workspace-level record per
  invoice).
  Header line: "Interim first-paid measure. Not retention. Not
  forecastable revenue. Not a continuation input."
  The dashboard-vs-billing reconciliation (41 vs 48, resolved as a
  classification cleanup, not customer behavior) is a footnote on
  this panel, not a headline. The same-day full-refund and
  zero-cash-credit exclusions are stated in the methodology line.

Cross-panel rules (these are the structural guardrails)

  1. No arrows, gradients, sankey-style ribbons, or stacked bars
     connecting Panel 1 → Panel 3 → Panel 4. A funnel implies an
     overlap we have not established and a pipeline we have not
     authorized. The only visual relationship between panels is
     lateral placement.
  2. No composite "conversion" rate that divides anything in Panel
     1 or Panel 3 by anything in Panel 4.
  3. No "of the 92 applications, X% went on to pay" sentence
     anywhere on the dashboard. That sentence requires the overlap
     claim and is exactly what the funnel was implying.
  4. Panel order on the page is by decision relevance, not by
     implied pipeline. Recommended order: Panel 1 (routing) →
     Panel 2 (activation, the Q3 gate input) → Panel 3
     (connector-check observation, side panel) → Panel 4
     (first-paid, interim). Panel 3 should not appear above Panel 4
     unless a reader would mistake it for a lead finding, in which
     case the header note does the work.
  5. Each panel carries its own cohort definition, its own window
     dates, and its own "what this is not" line. The cohort registry
     (definitions and dates) lives in a small footer block, not as a
     tooltip — it has to be visible at the same time as the numbers.
  6. No Q3 target, no forecast, no pipeline channel, no pricing-page
     reference, no paid-acquisition attribution, no GA framing. If a
     field would only make sense under one of those framings, it
     does not belong on this dashboard.

What stays out of the dashboard entirely

  - Day-90 retention (we don't have it; Panel 4 is day-30).
  - Forecastable revenue (Panel 4 is interim by definition).
  - Connector causality (Panel 2's composition splits are
    descriptive).
  - Expansion or continuation decisions (the gate is the gate; the
    dashboard reports against it, not toward it).
  - Pre-admission vs post-admission contact counts as headline
    numbers (they belong in the support-load panel, not here).

Owen's two structural mistakes were (a) a visual hierarchy that put
the 92-observation above the first-paid result, which made a side
finding read like a lead finding, and (b) the 92 → 68 → 41 funnel,
which implies an overlap we have not established. The lateral
four-panel structure with no connecting arrows fixes both without
losing any of the underlying evidence, and it leaves the Q3
continuation gate, the interim first-paid status, and the
connector-check intake-design finding each visible on their own
terms.

NEAR MISS AT JUNE 1 EXPO — STANDING PROTOCOL FOR DINNERS 2-8

The kitchen allergen protocol itself — sanitized work area, separate tools and containers, sealed package, chef-owner approval of the two-serving batch — is unchanged.

For the remaining seven dinners (June 8 through August 18).

1. PLATE PLACEMENT AT EXPO

  - Allergy-safe plates go on a dedicated side station — lower pass shelf, north end — with a taped boundary line that runners are told not to cross. Not on the main pass among standard plates.
  - Each allergy-safe plate is covered (cloche or labeled dome) for the entire time it sits at expo, so a runner walking by cannot mistake it for a plate awaiting garnish.
  - The sesame-garnish tray stays at the plating line. It does not enter the expo zone for any service that includes allergy plates. Standard plates are garnished at the plating line, not at the pass.

2. LABELS

  - Each allergy-safe plate carries a printed allergy pick flag, bright color (red), taped to the plate rim, visible from the server's approach angle — not only from Sam's side of the pass.
  - Where chef-owner agrees, allergy plates are built on a different colored service plate (red band) for the run of eight dinners, so the cue survives even if the flag is missed.
  - The printed chit for each allergy seat is taped to the dome or cover, not just rested on the pass.
  - Fixed wording on the flag and on the chit: "SESAME-FREE — Cover [#] — Do not garnish. Standard sesame garnish does not go on this plate."
  - The approved two-serving sealed-batch label stays on the package until build. Sam (or the designated alternate briefed at the start of that dinner) breaks the seal at build, not earlier.

3. WHO MAY GARNISH

  - Only Sam, or the designated alternate briefed at the start of that dinner, may place garnish on standard plates when allergy plates are also in service.
  - Runners do not garnish allergy plates. Runners also do not place garnish trays near allergy plates at any point.
  - If timing forces overlap at the pass — standard plates going out while allergy plates are still at expo — allergy plates move first to the side station and stay covered until servers arrive. Standard plates do not pass through the allergy zone.

4. FINAL VERBAL HANDOFF TO SERVERS

Let me compute the watts and watt-hours directly.

Modem: 12 V × 1.5 A = 18 W
Access point (PoE injector): 48 V × 0.32 A = 15.36 W

Combined nameplate: 18 + 15.36 = 33.36 W

Realistic operating draw is usually 70–85% of nameplate for these small wall-warts/injectors, so call it ~25–28 W steady. But for UPS sizing you size on the nameplate as the worst case.

UPS sizing — common rule of thumb is to load the UPS to no more than ~70–80% of its rated capacity so the inverter isn't running at the edge. So you want the UPS rated wattage to be roughly 1.25–1.5× the load.

Load ≈ 33 W → UPS rating ≈ 45–50 W minimum, comfortably 60–80 W. A 100 W unit is the most common sense sweet spot — small, cheap, and gives headroom.

Runtime math — UPS batteries are rated in VA·h or W·h, and the inverter is maybe ~90% efficient at this tiny load. For 90 minutes = 1.5 h at ~33 W:

  Energy at the device ≈ 33 W × 1.5 h = ~50 Wh
  Battery energy needed  ≈ 50 Wh / 0.9 ≈ ~55 Wh

A 12 V 5 Ah sealed lead-acid battery holds 12 × 5 = 60 Wh of nameplate capacity, but you really only get about 50% of that before the voltage sags badly, so ~30 Wh usable — not enough for 90 minutes.

A 12 V 7 Ah battery (common in small UPS units) holds ~84 Wh nameplate, ~40–45 Wh usable — still a bit short of 90 minutes for the 33 W load.

A 12 V 9 Ah battery: ~108 Wh nameplate, ~50–55 Wh usable — right at the edge for 90 minutes.

Lithium-based small UPS units are more efficient and can use 80–90% of capacity, so the same runtime requires a much smaller nameplate. A 50–60 Wh lithium UPS would handle it; a 70–80 Wh lithium UPS would do it comfortably.

Recommendation summary:

- Load: ~33 W nameplate (modem 18 W + PoE injector 15.4 W)
- Recommended UPS rating: 80–150 W (a 100 W class "mini" or "desktop" UPS is the practical sweet spot; size up to 150 W if you want extra headroom for a small switch or future device)
- Battery capacity for ~90 min runtime:
  - Lead-acid UPS: 12 V 9 Ah battery or larger (about 100 Wh nameplate)
  - Lithium UPS: about 60–80 Wh
  - Equivalent: roughly 50–55 Wh usable at the load

A practical off-the-shelf match would be something like a "150 VA / 90 W" line-interactive UPS with a 12 V 7–9 Ah internal battery — at a 33 W load these typically deliver 45–90 minutes depending on the exact unit and battery age, so check the manufacturer's runtime chart for your specific model rather than trusting the marketing. For a comfortable margin on a 33 W load for 90 minutes, target a UPS spec sheet that lists at least ~60 minutes at 50 W (which implies roughly 75–90 minutes at 33 W, given the flatter discharge curve).

Boundary callouts:

- This is nameplate math only; PoE injectors in particular often run 10–20% below label
- UPS runtime degrades with battery age — derate 20–30% for a 2–3 year old battery
- If you ever add a small switch or a phone charger to the UPS, recalculate

Direct answer: one labor-compliant test is not enough to commit to another sale run. It is enough to justify a small repeatability test, not to skip one.

What the 6/5 test establishes
- Labor ceiling met: 58 min ≤ the chef-owner's 60-min cap on a single run.
- Yield direction is close: 19.1 lb cooked vs. the prior 19.6 lb — about a 0.5 lb drop, or one 7-oz portion.
- Net per-plate economics actually look better on paper, even with one fewer plate:
  - Raw: $93 case / 43 = $2.163 vs. $2.114 prior (+$0.05/plate).
  - Labor at ~$28/hr loaded: 58 min ≈ $27 vs. $84 prior. Per plate: $0.63 vs. $1.91 (-$1.28/plate).
  - Net: roughly +$1.23/plate to contribution if the labor number holds.
- The prior sale run had 6 of 44 unsold (sent to staff meal). The yield loss matters less than the demand question does.

What one test cannot establish
- Whether 58 min is the new mean or a favorable outlier. A single observation in a quiet kitchen on a Tuesday cannot bound variance; it can be flattered by timing, staffing, or attention.
- Whether 19.1 lb is the new normal or a low outcome. Chicken cook-yield can easily swing ±1–2% on a 30-lb batch from water retention, raw temperature, or trim differences. One point can't tell you where you sit in that range.
- Whether the revised method is reproducible by the line cooks who will actually run it on a service night, not just by the chef-owner under test conditions.
- Whether sell-through supports prepping 43 plates, or whether the prior 6-plate staff-meal drag will repeat.
- Whether the new per-plate math holds when other variable costs (sides, plating labor, waste) are layered in.

Evidence Sam should require before proposing another sale run
1. At least 2 more kitchen trials of the revised batch plan (3 total minimum), each capturing:
   - Incremental labor in minutes, by the cook who will run it on a sale night.
   - Raw weight in, cooked weight out, complete 7-oz portions, leftover ounces.
   - Any deviations (e.g., bird temp, trim differences, oven load).
   The mean and rough range of those three numbers — not just the best one.
2. A demand-side decision before the next sale night: how many plates to prep, based on realistic sell-through, with an explicit fallback for leftovers (smaller prep count, staff-meal plan, or price drop late in service). The prior run's 14% gap is the relevant base rate.
3. Updated per-plate margin using the mean labor and mean yield from the repeatability set, not the best single observation. Decide against a fixed threshold (e.g., contribution per plate after food + labor) before booking the night.
4. A simple go/no-go rule stated in advance: e.g., "proceed if mean incremental labor ≤ 60 min AND mean cooked yield ≥ 19.0 lb across 3 trials AND prep count ≤ expected sell-through."

What to tell the chef-owner
- The labor problem is plausibly solved; one run is not a confirmation.
- The yield loss is small and probably absorbable; do not optimize away the labor win chasing one extra plate.
- A 2- or 3-run repeatability test is kitchen-only, takes one prep cycle each, and does not require a service night. It is the cheapest way to turn one good run into a decision.
- Until those numbers are in, the right posture is "the approach is promising, the special is not yet cleared to run." That is consistent with the prior rule (≤1 incremental staff-hour) and does not commit to a sale night the kitchen cannot yet staff or price with confidence.

Bottom line for Sam: require the repeatability test. One labor-compliant run with a one-portion yield loss clears the "worth testing" bar; it does not clear the "ready to sell" bar. The repeatability test is small, fast, and proportionate to the decision it protects.

Bottom line: this text has multiple strong scam indicators. Mom did the right thing by not clicking or replying. Because nothing was entered, opened, or downloaded, no account or payment remediation is needed — treat it as a closed non-incident once verification and reporting are done.

SCAM INDICATORS

1. Unsolicited, not initiated by Mom, and she was not expecting a refund.
2. The $185 figure matches the exact balance the provider recently removed after reviewing the EOB. That congruence is the most concerning signal — either the recent billing activity leaked somewhere, or the sender is fishing with a plausible-looking number. Either way, the link is not safe regardless of how the figure was chosen.
3. Asks Mom to "confirm bank details" via a link. Legitimate refunds route to the payment method already on file in the portal — they do not ask the patient to re-enter or confirm bank info by SMS.
4. Bit.ly short link. Real provider communications do not route patients through a link shortener to a credential or bank-detail page; they direct you to log into your existing portal.
5. Urgency: "today." Pressure to act before verification is a standard phishing tactic.
6. Generic sender label "Provider Billing," not the actual provider's name.
7. STOP opt-out language. Common in legitimate marketing but also used by scammers to look legitimate. Replying STOP also confirms the number is live and monitored.

What is NOT a red flag here, for completeness: receiving any text at all from an unknown short code, and the existence of a corrected $0 statement. Those are neutral.

SAFE VERIFICATION SEQUENCE — official channels only

Use the provider's known portal and the phone number from the statement/paper bill/insurance card. Do not use any phone number, URL, or reply path from the text.

Step 1. Screenshot the text now, including the sender number and the bit.ly preview if visible. Keep the original message intact on the phone for reporting; do not delete yet.

Step 2. Independently retrieve the provider's billing contact:
   - From the corrected paper statement already in Mom's files
   - From the patient portal Riley has logged into before (typed URL or bookmark, not anything from the text)
   - From the insurer's explanation of benefits or provider directory

Step 3. Through that official channel, ask the billing office three narrow questions:
   - Is any refund currently owed to Mom's account?
   - Did the provider send an SMS about a $185 refund, and if so, through what short code or vendor?
   - Has any change been made to Mom's bank details, payment method, or contact preferences since the balance was removed?

The expected answer is no refund is owed and no such SMS was sent, which confirms the text is fraudulent. If the provider says a refund was sent, ask for the method and destination already on file and reconcile through the portal, not through the text link.

Step 4. While you have the billing office on the line, flag that the $185 amount matches the recently removed balance and ask whether patient billing data has had any exposure incident. That is worth raising regardless of how the text is resolved.

REPORTING SEQUENCE

Step 5. Report the text:
   - Forward the message to 7726 (SPAM). This is the carrier reporting shortcode used by all major US carriers and routes the report into carrier anti-abuse systems.
   - File at reportfraud.ftc.gov under "Impostor scams / unsolicited text." Include the screenshot and the bit.ly link.
   - Report to the provider's billing office or compliance contact so they can warn other patients and check for any matching campaign.
   - Optional: report to the state attorney general's consumer protection office. Useful if a pattern emerges; not required for a single message.

Step 6. Block the sender number on Mom's phone after the screenshot and 7726 forward are done.

Step 7. Only after the above, delete the message from the phone.

WHAT NOT TO DO

- Do not click the link, even to "see what's there." Bit.ly redirects can fingerprint the device and confirm the number is active.
- Do not reply STOP, HELP, or anything else. Any reply confirms the number is live and may increase follow-up scam volume.
- Do not call any number in the text or visit any URL in the text.
- Do not enter bank details, card numbers, SSN, or portal passwords anywhere reachable from the text.
- Do not treat the $0 corrected statement as invalidated by the text. The text is unrelated to the actual ledger; the corrected statement stands on its own from the provider.

NO-REMEDIATION CONFIRMATION

Because Mom has not opened the link, not replied, not entered any card number, bank detail, password, address, SSN, or other information, and has not downloaded anything, there is nothing to clean up:

- No bank or card password rotation needed
- No card replacement needed
- No portal password change needed
- No antivirus scan needed
- No fraud alert or credit freeze needed for this incident alone

WATCH-ONLY ITEMS, LOW RISK

- Glance at the provider portal once after verification to confirm no new refund, payment-method change, or address change has appeared.
- Glance at the bank/card statement over the next two cycles. This is general hygiene, not because anything was exposed.
- If a second suspicious text arrives referencing Mom's provider, billing, or a refund, treat it as the same scam pattern and repeat from Step 1. Two near-simultaneous sends targeting the same person would meaningfully raise the possibility of a data exposure and would justify a more pointed question to the provider.
