The "pasted on" reading on scrap is almost always pigment load, not color choice — you probably had 2–3× too little water. The mud risk is real though: burnt sienna sits close to ultramarine's complement, so dropping it directly onto the blue-gray is exactly the recipe for a flat gray smear. The fix is a bridge color that the blue can coexist with.

Sequence:

1. Confirm the blue-gray is bone dry — back of hand to the paper, no cool spot. If there's any tackiness, wait.

2. Mix a rose glaze: roughly 80% quinacridone rose, 20% burnt sienna, thinned to weak-tea consistency. This is your transition color, not your rim color.

3. Pre-wet a narrow band, about 5–8 mm wide, just inside the planned rim line. Damp, not flooded — the surface should hold a sheen without beads. This is where the rose glaze will feather its inner edge.

4. Drop the rose glaze along the rim, letting the inner edge settle into the pre-wet band. If a hard edge starts to form, touch it with a clean damp brush and pull it outward into the shadow by a hair. Don't push the rose back into the dry blue zone — let it stop at the damp boundary.

5. Let dry fully.

6. Mix a slightly warmer glaze: about 50/50 rose + burnt sienna, still weak-tea dilute. Apply a narrower band — only the brightest rim line — sitting on top of (not overlapping) the rose zone. The rose is now the buffer between blue and orange.

7. If the rim still reads weak after drying, one more pass of pure dilute burnt sienna at the very hottest point, and stop there.

Why this avoids mud:

- Quinacridone rose and ultramarine are related hues, not complements. Rose over blue makes luminous violet, not gray.
- The orange-leaning mix never physically touches the blue-gray. Rose is the chemical bridge on the paper, sitting between cool and warm the way it sits between them on the color wheel.
- Glazes stay thin, so the paper keeps glowing through and the cool shadow doesn't get buried.

Edge softening lives in steps 3 and 4 — the pre-wet band does most of the work. If the orange-rose band in step 6 dries with any hard inner edge, mist very lightly and blot with a soft tissue, or lift with a damp brush, before adding another pass.

For the scrap test: redo it at the dilution you'll actually use on the painting, not at mixture strength. The pasted-on feeling is pigment load. Once you see the same mix at weak-tea strength you'll know whether the color is right or the strength is the whole problem.

One thing not to fold into this session: don't try to also lift value, fix the shadow, or rework the rim's shape. The rim sitting softly is the one change. Judge it dry before deciding whether it needs another pass.

Quick load check first, then the side-by-side.

Combined load at the labels in memory: modem 12 V × 1.5 A = 18 W, PoE injector 48 V × 0.32 A = 15.36 W → 33.36 W. Call it ~35 W with reasonable overhead. Both UPS options are wildly over-sized for that load in pure wattage terms; the binding question is runtime, not capacity.

Sizing
- Option A (225 W max): load ratio ~15%. Plenty of wattage headroom, but published 50 min at 30 W is already below your 90-min target. At the actual ~33–35 W load and with any inverter loss, realistic runtime is closer to 40–48 min, not 90.
- Option B (450 W max): load ratio ~7%. Even more wattage headroom. Published 100 min at 30 W leaves a thin but real margin; at ~33–35 W the realistic runtime is ~85–95 min before aging is considered.

So on published numbers alone, Option A does not meet your stated 90-min goal, and Option B plausibly does.

Confidence in published runtime
Treat the manufacturer's number as a best-case ceiling, not a guarantee. Real-world factors that compress it:
- Inverter/conversion loss: typical 85–95% efficient at moderate load, but small loads on a large UPS waste more energy to fixed inverter overhead. A 33 W load on a 450 W box is in the lowest-efficiency operating band; you pay a few minutes of "overhead tax" per outage.
- Battery aging: SLA cells in a typical UPS lose noticeable capacity by year 2 and a lot by year 3–4. At end-of-service-life you might see 50–70% of new-battery runtime.
- Temperature: cooler than the 25 °C test = less capacity; warmer = faster aging.
- Initial state-of-charge and recent cycle history matter at the margin.

Practical framing: a fresh, room-temperature Option B likely delivers ~80–95 min on your load. A 3-year-old Option B might be down to ~50–65 min. Option A starts below target when new and degrades from there.

Recommendation
Option B is the only one that plausibly supports a 90-min outage with reasonable margin on day one. Option A fails the runtime requirement on its own published spec, regardless of aging.

The user-replaceable battery on Option B also matters for a multi-year deployment: when the cell ages you can swap it and recover published-class runtime, instead of replacing the whole unit (which is what Option A's sealed, non-replaceable battery forces). That's a real lifecycle advantage on top of the runtime win.

If you want a wider margin against aging — say, target 90 min at year 3 rather than at purchase — you'd want a unit rated closer to 130–150 min at 30 W, or accept that 90 min is a "new-battery, mild conditions" figure and plan around it degrading over time. Option B as specified is the right pick between these two; the only honest caveat is that "90 minutes" should be read as approximately, not contractually, and will shorten as the battery ages.

That is not yet alarming, but it is the second data point at the same threshold, so the cautious read is: do not progress again from where you are.

Next conservative running step

    Step back to the 24-minute flat walk-jog from May 25 and June 8: walking warm-up, three rounds of about two minutes easy jogging / one minute walking (or a similar 2:1 mix you used there), then two more rounds at roughly 1:1, walking cooldown. Total easy-jog time should sit at or just under ten minutes, on the same flat route, same shoes, same surface. Do not add speed, distance, hills, or a fourth interval.

    Treat the next session as a confirmation, not a progression. The decision point is the next-morning response plus the evening and stair behavior over the following 48 hours. The bar for moving forward is a fully clean session and a fully clean 48-hour response: no delayed ache, no morning awareness, no stair sharpness, no swelling, no focal tenderness.

    Plan for at least two, preferably three, completely uneventful repeats of this 24-minute level before any re-attempt at three five-minute intervals. The first repeat establishes that the load is tolerated again; the second repeat starts to look like stability rather than a lucky day. Only after those should a cautious re-attempt at the prior step be considered, and even then the previous step should be reached by small additions (for example, two 5-minute intervals first, or three 4-minute intervals) rather than jumping straight back to three 5-minute intervals.

Step-back-further thresholds (before another progression attempt)

    If the 24-minute level now produces the same delayed outer-ankle ache, that is a third recurrence at the same general load family and is enough pattern to warrant clinical evaluation even without red-flag symptoms, because the body is telling you the current total easy-jog volume is at or above its tolerance for now.

    If the 24-minute level is fully clean but the next small addition (for example, a fourth round at 2:1 or extending one interval to six minutes) reproduces the ache, treat that the same way: hold at the last fully clean level, repeat it again, and consider evaluation if it recurs at any sub-step.

    Shorten or skip jogging entirely (pain-free walking and easy cycling only) for a session if the ankle feels any different from baseline on the morning of a planned run, even without pain: stiffness, awareness on stairs, mild tightness, or a sense that it is "still there."

Clinical evaluation thresholds (arrange before another progression attempt)

    Any of the following, regardless of how the next session goes, is a reason to be evaluated rather than progress:

        Visible or palpable swelling around the lateral ankle or any of the peroneal tendons.
        Bruising, including faint discoloration behind or below the lateral malleolus.
        Focal bony tenderness over the lateral malleolus, the fifth metatarsal base, the talus, or the calcaneus, or focal tendon tenderness along the peroneal line, the Achilles insertion, or the anterior talofibular region.
        A limp, a feeling of giving way, or true mechanical instability on uneven ground or single-leg balance.
        Inability to bear weight normally, or pain that is reproduced by a single-leg hop or calf raise.
        Escalating pain, meaning the next episode is clearly worse than 2/10, lasts longer than four hours, or begins to appear at rest, at night, or with ordinary walking rather than only stairs.
        Pain or awareness that persists beyond 48 to 72 hours after a session, or that does not fully return to baseline between sessions.
        A new mechanical event: a twist, a pop, a snap, a fall, or pain that begins at a specific instant rather than building over the run.
        Neurologic changes: numbness, tingling, burning, or weakness distal to the ankle.
        Vascular changes: persistent color or temperature difference between the two feet, or swelling that does not resolve overnight.

    Outside those, two recurrences at progressively higher loads, with a clean repeat at the lower load in between, is on its own a reasonable reason to ask a clinician to look at the ankle before the next progression attempt. The point of evaluation in that case is not to declare an injury but to make sure there is nothing specific being masked by a soft-tissue pattern, and to get a load tolerance you can trust rather than guess at.

What to track, briefly, so the next decision is clean

    For the next session, note only: total minutes, total easy-jog minutes, interval pattern, surface, shoes, any warmth or awareness during the run, and the timing, location, intensity, and duration of any post-session sensation. The single rule that matters for progression is whether the ankle is fully back to baseline by the next morning and stays there through 48 hours of normal stairs and walking. Anything short of that means hold or step back; anything more concerning from the lists above means evaluate.

One quiet note that is not a recommendation to change anything: the recurrence has now happened on flat ground, in the same shoes, with an easy effort, at increasing easy-jog volume. That is consistent with a load-tolerance issue rather than a structural one, which is the more reassuring interpretation, but it is also exactly the pattern that benefits from a professional eyeball if it persists one more cycle. You are still well within conservative self-management, and the appropriate response right now is to step back to the last clean level, repeat it, and not let a third recurrence happen by accident.

Before touching the painting, look at it from normal viewing distance (an arm's length or further) and ideally in the same light you'll view it in later. Hard backruns read much harsher up close than at viewing distance — the dark line and concentrated shape that look prominent a foot away often fade into the wash at two or three feet. If it reads as a soft tone variation rather than a defined mark at viewing distance, leave it alone. This is the cheapest possible fix.

If it still reads as a hard mark at viewing distance, work in this order, with a scrap test before each step on matching cold-press:

  1. Edge-soften only. Load a clean soft brush (sable or synthetic round, size 6–8) with clear water, tap most of it out so the brush is barely damp, and touch just the dark edge — not the body of the mark. Immediately lift with a dry tissue or paper towel pressed flat, not rubbed. Goal: break the hard outline without disturbing the paper tooth. Dry fully, then judge at viewing distance. Do this once; one pass only.

  2. If the body is still too dark but the edge is no longer defined, glaze locally. Mix a very dilute wash of the same ultramarine + quinacridone rose you used for the sky — dilute enough that a test stroke on scrap dries noticeably lighter than the mark but matches the surrounding sky value. With the painting dry and flat, lay this only over the backrun and a small feathered margin, not over the whole sky. Work wet-into-dry, controlled, and stop short of the roof line. Dry fully, judge at viewing distance.

  3. If glazing unifies the value but the shape still reads as a flat darker patch, accept it as a soft cloud-form variation. A diffuse low-value shape in a sky is a natural read; a hard dark shape is not. You've moved from "mark" to "form," which is integration, not removal.

  4. If after step 2 the area still reads as a discrete dark shape, stop. Do not glaze again, do not try to lift pigment (the quinacridone rose is staining and the ultramarine will leave a ghost even after lifting; both will roughen the cold-press tooth and create a patch that catches pigment darker than its surroundings in every future wash). At this point the restrained options are: leave it as is and let the study teach you something about wash consistency, or crop — if the mark sits within a half inch of the lower edge, a tighter crop can place it below the new edge entirely.

Constraints worth holding:
  - One change per session. Soften the edge, dry fully, judge. Next session, glaze if needed. Don't combine steps.
  - Never scrub the body. Cold-press tooth roughens fast and roughened tooth darkens in unpredictable ways later.
  - Never re-wet the whole sky. The bead dried into a backrun once because of a wet-edge interaction; you do not want to recreate the conditions that made it.
  - Match the glaze pigment load to the surrounding sky, not to your memory of the original wash — original washes dry lighter than they go on, so your reference is the dry sky next to the mark, not the wet mix.

The mark crosses an airy area, which means your tolerance for residual darkness is low. If step 1 alone gets you to "reads as a soft tone variation at viewing distance," stop there. Step 2 is only worth doing if step 1 fails and you're willing to accept a slightly lower local value in exchange for losing the hard shape.

Here is the rule. Plain text, plain language, no headers. Paste it into the design-review doc as-is or trim to taste.

---

RULE (one sentence): For Expansion Assist eligibility evaluation, every behavior signal and the CS suppression check must be a current-state read at evaluation time; if any read is stale beyond its window, the query is unavailable, or two sources conflict, the affected signal is treated as MISSING and the account is excluded from the candidate set — never included on the strength of an outdated or unverified read.

FRESHNESS WINDOWS (measured at evaluation time, not at QA-export time):

  - Usage ceiling: snapshot dated within the last 48 hours.
    Rationale: usage ceiling is volatile — seat counts, API volume, storage can shift in a single business day. A 9-day-old read (acct_014) is not "probably still true"; it is the absence of evidence. 48 hours catches a missed daily refresh on the first cycle after it breaks.

  - Active-admin behavior: snapshot dated within the last 7 days.
    Rationale: login cadence and admin activity move on a weekly rhythm; a 7-day window matches the typical aggregation bucket without letting month-old activity stand in for current state.

  - Integration depth: snapshot dated within the last 7 days.
    Rationale: integrations change on a multi-week cadence, but a 7-day ceiling keeps a recently removed integration from quietly still counting as "pass."

CS SUPPRESSION — SOURCE OF TRUTH AND CONFLICT RESOLUTION:

  The CS suppression check is NOT the nightly warehouse field. It is a LIVE query against the CS system of record, executed within 15 minutes of the eligibility evaluation.

  The nightly suppression field is a CACHE and is resolved as follows:

    - Cache says suppressed, live query confirms open CS adoption or renewal work → suppressed. (No change.)
    - Cache says suppressed, live query finds no open CS work → NOT suppressed. (Work closed; cache lagged.) Live query wins.
    - Cache says not suppressed, live query confirms open CS work → SUPPRESSED. (acct_027 case.) Live query wins; the cache-vs-timeline disagreement is the expected lag pattern, not an exception.
    - Cache says not suppressed, live query finds no open CS work → not suppressed. (No change.)

  If the live CS query fails, times out, or returns an error → treated as SUPPRESSED (fail closed). Account is excluded. Failure is logged so the integration can be chased.

FAIL-CLOSED SEMANTICS:

  The eligibility query is the AND of four conditions:
    1. Integration depth = pass AND snapshot within its window
    2. Active-admin behavior = pass AND snapshot within its window
    3. Usage ceiling = pass AND snapshot within its window
    4. CS suppression = false on the live query

  If any condition fails for any reason — stale snapshot, missing field, source conflict, query error, null result — that condition is FALSE and the account is excluded. There is no "default to pass" branch. The candidate set only contains accounts where all four conditions hold on a verified current read.

HOW THE TWO QA EXAMPLES RESOLVE UNDER THE RULE:

  acct_014: usage-ceiling snapshot dated 2024-06-08, evaluation 2024-06-17 → 9 days old → exceeds the 48-hour window → usage-ceiling condition fails → account excluded. Integration depth and admin behavior being fresh and pass does not rescue it; the AND drops the account. This is exactly the case the rule is built for: a stale read that looks like "pass" but is actually "unknown."

  acct_027: nightly cache says false; CS timeline shows renewal work opened 2024-06-16 15:42 Central (≈18 hours before QA) → live query returns open CS work → suppression condition is true → account excluded. The cache disagreement is not an edge case to investigate; it is the cache doing what stale caches do, and it never overrides a confirmed live read.

AUDIT TRAIL:

  For every account excluded by the freshness or conflict rule (rather than by a clean fail of one of the three signals), the evaluation logs:
    - account_id
    - evaluation timestamp (UTC and local)
    - which condition(s) triggered exclusion
    - for behavior signals: snapshot date and age in hours
    - for CS suppression: cache value, live-query result, query timestamp, and (if applicable) error code

  This lets you tell "the signal truly says no" apart from "we don't know and excluded on that basis" — the distinction you want at the design review and in any later audit of why an account wasn't exposed.

WHAT THIS RULE DOES NOT DO:

  - It does not auto-refresh stale snapshots. If the upstream refresh job is broken, accounts stay excluded until the refresh is restored. That is the intended fail-closed behavior; an auto-refresh would silently mask the data-pipeline bug that produced acct_014.
  - It does not treat the nightly cache as ground truth under any circumstance. The cache is a hint; the live query is the read.
  - It does not redefine pass/fail for any of the three signals — only the freshness and conflict resolution around the read.
  - It does not authorize sending a prompt. The 2024-07-08 earliest-live boundary and the 5-account weekly cap remain intact and are downstream of this rule, not part of it.

---

Two things worth flagging before Tuesday, not as part of the rule itself but as adjacent decisions you'll likely be asked:

1. Who owns the "live CS query within 15 minutes" requirement operationally — CS ops or data eng — and what the on-call path is when that query is degraded for more than a short window. Fail-closed under query failure is correct, but a sustained failure should page someone, not silently shrink the candidate pool for a week.

2. Whether the 48-hour usage-ceiling window should tighten to 24 hours once you know the actual refresh cadence. 48 hours tolerates one missed daily run; 24 hours would not. I went with 48 because it matches the failure shape Owen found (one missed refresh compounded), but if the refresh is meant to be intraday, 24 is safer.

I don't have a code-exec tool in this session, so I did the runtime math inline and present the protocol with the numbers shown.

Quick math sanity-check (rounded):
  * Published 100 min @ 30 W is at a *lower* load than your real 33.36 W.
  * Load-scaled alone: 100 × (30 / 33.36) ≈ 90 min.
  * Real-world at low load: inverter is ~85-90% efficient, battery usually delivers ~80-90% of nameplate (less as it ages), and the manufacturer's chart usually assumes a fresh cell at 25 °C.
  * Realistic expectation at your 33.36 W: somewhere in the 65-80 min range on a fresh unit, falling into the 55-70 min range after a year.
  * So plan around ~60-75 min of *usable* runtime, not the published 100.

That gap matters because it changes your stop rule (below).

---

SAFE SETUP

1. First-charge window before any test
  * New SLA UPSs ship partially discharged. With the unit plugged into the wall and *nothing* on its outlets, charge for at least 8 hours, overnight is fine.
  * While charging, confirm: no error LED, fan not constantly running at high speed, unit does not click. If it beeps on battery while wall power is on, do not proceed — return/exchange.
  * Full-charge indicator: most units stop flashing the battery LED and show a steady green. Don't trust a "charged" light that arrives in under 4 hours — that's almost always only an 80% state.

2. Placement
  * Hard, flat, ventilated surface. Not on carpet, not inside a closed cabinet, not draped.
  * Where you can see and hear it (audible low-battery alarm matters).
  * Within reach of the modem, the PoE injector, and the wall outlet — but the outlet side should not be where a foot, chair wheel, or pet will snag it.
  * Label the UPS-side outlets with a small piece of tape: "MODEM + AP ONLY." That label is your main defense against the laptop ever landing on it.

3. Visible "not this" boundaries (write these on a sticky note next to the unit before the test)
  * Laptop charger is NOT plugged into this UPS. Ever, for this test.
  * Monitor is NOT plugged into this UPS.
  * Phone charger, Kibo's fountain, speakers, etc. are NOT plugged into this UPS.
  * If a work call starts during the test window, the test stops and wall power is restored. The test is reversible.

4. Pre-test inventory (do this with wall power still on)
  * Modem (12 V / 1.5 A = 18 W) → UPS.
  * PoE injector (48 V / 0.32 A = 15.36 W) → UPS.
  * Confirm both devices have lit status indicators after moving their plugs.
  * Confirm wired AP is actually online from your laptop (still on wall power) — speed test or just load a page.
  * Record the time you finished moving the plugs.

---

WHAT TO RECORD (one line per row in a notes file or paper)

  * Date / time UPS first plugged in for initial charge.
  * Date / time charge indicator first read "full."
  * Date / time you moved the modem and AP plugs onto UPS (still on wall).
  * Wall-power draw while on UPS-pass-through, if your UPS has a meter readout (most 900 VA units do). Note it.
  * Date / time of the transfer test below.
  * Date / time of the runtime test start (wall unplug).
  * Any device drop, beep, LED change, or anomaly — with the elapsed minute.
  * Date / time of safe stop.
  * UPS display readings at safe stop (load %, battery %, runtime estimate if shown).
  * Date / time wall power restored.
  * Date / time both devices back to normal indicators.

If something goes wrong, the row that matters is the anomaly row with the elapsed minute. That's how you compare against the manufacturer chart later.

---

CONTROLLED RUNTIME-TEST SEQUENCE

Step A — Transfer test (60-90 seconds, do this first, separate day is fine)
  * Pick a window with no work calls for at least the next two hours.
  * With the modem and AP running happily on UPS-pass-through, pull the UPS's wall plug.
  * Wait 90 seconds. Modem and AP indicators should stay solid, no reboot, no link drop.
  * Plug wall power back in.
  * If anything rebooted in those 90 seconds, the UPS is undersized for that inrush, or the battery isn't actually charged — stop, re-check, do not proceed to step B.

Step B — The runtime test (separate day, call-free block)
  * Pick a 3-hour block where you will not take a work call and will not be tempted to plug a laptop into the UPS.
  * Silence notifications on the laptop so an incoming call ping doesn't tempt you.
  * Put the laptop on its own wall charger, not the UPS.
  * T+0: Unplug the UPS from the wall. Start a stopwatch. Note the time.
  * Every 10 minutes, glance at the UPS display and write down load %, battery %, and any estimated-runtime readout. Do not interact with the modem or AP.
  * If you hear the low-battery alarm at any point → stop, that is the alarm trigger, go to wall power immediately.
  * Otherwise continue to the safe-stop rule below.

---

WHEN TO STOP INSTEAD OF FULLY EXHAUSTING

Pick one of these three, whichever fires first:

  1. Conservative safe-stop: at 60 minutes elapsed. Rationale: realistic runtime is in the 65-80 min range, so 60 min is roughly the 75% depth-of-discharge point on a fresh unit and the 85-90% point on a year-old unit. Stopping here preserves battery life and keeps the UPS ready for a *real* outage that might happen later in the week.
  2. UPS low-battery alarm (continuous beep, distinct from the brief "on battery" chirp). Whatever minute that fires on, that's the stop.
  3. Any device dropout, reboot, link flap, or AP client disconnect. Whatever minute that fires on, that's the stop.

Do *not* run until the UPS dies on its own. Three reasons:
  * SLA cells last many more cycles if you stop at ~75% DOD rather than 100%.
  * A truly dead UPS right before an actual outage is exactly the failure mode you're trying to avoid.
  * You don't learn anything more useful past the 60-minute mark — the published chart already told you what the upper bound looks like.

After the stop, plug the wall back in, confirm the UPS returns to "charging" / "full" state, then let it recharge for at least 8 hours before relying on it as your actual outage backup.

---

WHAT THIS TEST DOES AND DOES NOT ESTABLISH

Does establish:
  * That the UPS holds the modem and AP through a clean transfer.
  * A real, recorded runtime at your actual 33.36 W load on *this* unit, not the manufacturer's chart.
  * That no laptop, monitor, or other device snuck onto the UPS by accident.
  * That the unit is healthy enough to use as an outage backup.

Does not establish:
  * Runtime under reduced battery capacity a year from now — re-test then.
  * Runtime with anything else added to the UPS — if you ever add a device, treat it as a new test.
  * That the UPS will start a work call's video meeting cleanly during a real outage — the test is wall-unplug, which is gentler than a true brownout or surge.

Treat the recorded minute as the operating number, not the published 100. Use that recorded number — minus a 15-20% margin for the year-old battery case — as your "I have this much internet during an outage" budget from now on.

Active adoption-or-renewal suppression rule (working recap): a commercial Expansion Assist prompt is suppressed when there is currently active Customer Success adoption OR renewal work on the account — a state rule, not a per-meeting call and not a signup-age rule. The check is current state near send time, fail-closed on stale or conflicting records.

Case A — Adoption plan marked closed 2024-06-17; no open adoption task.
Classification: NOT SUPPRESSED.

Current-state check at send time:
- Re-query the adoption plan record: status is still "closed" (no silent reopen, no new plan created on this account since 6/17).
- Re-query for any open adoption task on this account; confirm none.
- Re-query for a separate active renewal plan; confirm none.
- If the plan record is stale or conflicts with another source, fail-closed and exclude rather than let the row through on assumption.

What this is NOT: this is not a "recently active = still suppressed" rule. A closed plan with no open task is not active work, regardless of how recently it was closed. Indefinite suppression of recently closed adoption work is exactly the failure mode the rule is built to avoid; closing the plan closes the suppression.

Case B — Renewal plan active; next customer task due 2024-06-24.
Classification: SUPPRESSED.

Current-state check at send time:
- Re-query the renewal plan record: status is still "active" (not silently completed, paused, or canceled since last view).
- Re-query for a separate active adoption plan; confirm none (the rule covers adoption OR renewal, not just renewal).
- Stale or conflicting plan records → fail-closed; do not pass the row through on assumption.

What this is NOT: suppression does not depend on whether a customer task is currently overdue. The plan state is the trigger, not the task due date. An active renewal plan with its next task due 6/24 is still active commercial work today; sending an Expansion Assist prompt would collide with the CS renewal motion regardless of whether anything is due this week. A plan that has been formally completed or canceled would reopen eligibility — quietness inside an open plan does not.

Case C — No adoption or renewal plan; one open support ticket requesting help with an ordinary user-permission setting.
Classification: NOT SUPPRESSED under the active adoption-or-renewal rule.

Current-state check at send time:
- Re-query: confirm no adoption plan (open or otherwise) exists on this account.
- Re-query: confirm no renewal plan exists.
- Note the open support ticket as support-neutral — it does not constitute adoption or renewal work and does not, by itself, trigger this rule.

What this is NOT: an open support ticket is not an active adoption or renewal motion. The 6/12 settled framing is "support-neutral ≠ activation-positive"; support volume is retained as a separate first-signal observation, not folded into the suppression decision. If a different exclusion actually applies here — e.g., missing recent active-admin behavior, or a separate renewal-risk motion I haven't been told about — that is a distinct rule, not this one, and should be cited under its own name rather than smuggled in via "open case."

Net for the 6/18 review: A and C pass the suppression gate (subject to live state re-query at any later send); B is held. None of the three should be re-classified by inferring adoption/renewal activity that isn't currently recorded on the account.

Expansion Assist operational report — redesign

What the mock gets wrong

  The mock puts five qualitatively different events in one funnel:
    1. eligibility (a state determined before exposure)
    2. prompt exposure (a product action)
    3. help request (an inbound customer signal)
    4. Customer Success handoff (a routing decision, often human-initiated)
    5. expansion (an outcome that may or may not flow from any of the above)

  Three things that breaks:
    - Eligible accounts that were never exposed (suppressed at send time, eligibility lost before exposure, not yet scheduled) vanish from the funnel because the next column only counts rows where prompt_sent_at is not null.
    - prompt exposure (system action) and CS handoff (human routing decision) share an handoff_at column with no origin flag, so a self-resolved help request and a CS-initiated adoption handoff read as the same event.
    - A single conversion_rate implies exposure → handoff → expansion is causal. Every row in a not-yet-run design is observational. The funnel shape shouldn't say otherwise.

  The proposed account row has no field for usage-ceiling crossing, no field for help request, no field for non-exposure, and no field for suppression at the planned exposure time — so it cannot answer "why was this account not prompted?" or "where did the handoff come from?" Only "when did things happen, if they happened."

Redesign — two views, no funnel

View 1: account-level detail row (one row per account)

  Each row carries nullable timestamps and explicit state fields for every stage. State + timestamp together let you reconstruct the sequence per account without collapsing stages.

  Identity and cohort
    account_id
    account_name
    cohort_id
    assigned_exposure_week        (design-time scheduled week; nullable if never scheduled)
    row_status                    design_only | shadow | live | reserve | eligibility_lost_pre_exposure
                                  (every row carries this; live panels filter on shadow/live, the rest stay visible)

  Eligibility (determined before exposure evaluation)
    eligibility_state             eligible | suppressed_active_work | suppressed_other | never_eligible | pending_review
    eligibility_determined_at
    eligibility_loss_at           (nullable; only if state changed between waves)
    eligibility_loss_reason       (nullable)

  Exposure
    exposure_state                exposed | scheduled | suppressed_at_send_time | eligibility_lost_before_exposure | not_yet_scheduled | not_eligible
    exposure_evaluated_at         (when send-time suppression was last checked)
    prompt_sent_at                (nullable)
    prompt_suppressed_reason      (nullable; only if suppressed_at_send_time or eligibility_lost_before_exposure)

  Usage-ceiling crossing (observed in product telemetry, separate from prompt)
    usage_ceiling_state           crossed | not_crossed | not_measurable
    usage_ceiling_crossed_at      (nullable)

  Help request (inbound customer signal — distinct from CS handoff)
    help_request_state            none | requested | resolved_without_cs | escalated_to_cs
    help_request_first_at         (nullable)
    help_request_topic            (nullable; uses CS taxonomy)
    help_request_resolved_at      (nullable)
    help_request_resolution       self_served | cs_handoff | product_fix | open

  Customer Success handoff (routing decision — distinct from help request)
    cs_handoff_state              none | initiated | active | closed
    cs_handoff_initiated_at       (nullable)
    cs_handoff_origin             help_request_escalation | adoption_work_open | system_routed | manual_review | design_shadow
    cs_handoff_closed_at          (nullable)
    cs_handoff_outcome            expansion_progressed | closed_without_expansion | open

  Expansion outcome
    expansion_state               none | identified | contracted | first_billed
    expansion_identified_at       (nullable)
    expansion_contracted_at       (nullable)
    expansion_first_billed_at     (nullable)
    expansion_origin              cs_handoff | usage_ceiling | self_serve | help_request | unknown

  Snapshot metadata
    asof_date                     (every row is a snapshot; readers compare snapshots to detect changes)

View 2: five lateral panels (cohort-level)

  No single funnel. Each panel has its own denominator, window, and "what this is not" line. Panels stack vertically in the report — they are not joined by arrows.

  Panel A — Eligibility
    Total accounts evaluated
    Eligible (and, separately, eligible-but-suppressed-at-this-evaluation)
    Suppressed — by reason (active_adoption_or_renewal, manual_billing, unsupported_integration, other)
    Never eligible (with reason)
    Eligibility lost between waves (count, reason breakdown)
    "What this is not": not exposure, not activation, not a rate. A pre-exposure gate state.

  Panel B — Exposure
    Eligible at exposure-evaluation time (re-queried at send time, independent of A's eligible total)
    Prompt sent
    Prompt suppressed at send time (active_adoption_or_renewal, support_open, ceiling_recheck_pending, other)
    Scheduled, not yet sent (with exposure week)
    Eligibility lost before scheduled exposure (with reason)
    "What this is not": not a conversion rate, not a handoff rate, not causal evidence that exposure produces expansion. Shadow-run, observational.

  Panel C — Help requests (in observation window)
    Accounts with ≥1 help request
    By topic
    Resolved without CS handoff
    Escalated to CS handoff (cs_handoff_initiated_at ≥ help_request_first_at)
    "What this is not": not a CS handoff count. A help request that resolves in product or self-serve is a distinct endpoint from a CS handoff. Inbound signal, not routing decision.

  Panel D — Customer Success handoffs
    Accounts with a CS handoff (any origin)
    By origin (help_request_escalation, adoption_work_open, system_routed, manual_review, design_shadow)
    Handoff active at asof
    Handoff closed without expansion
    Handoff closed with expansion (linked to Panel E by account_id)
    "What this is not": not an expansion rate. Closed-without-expansion is a valid endpoint, not a failure. Counts routing decisions, not commercial outcomes.

  Panel E — Expansion outcomes
    Accounts contracted (count)
    Accounts first billed (count)
    By origin (cs_handoff, usage_ceiling, self_serve, help_request, unknown)
    Expansion MRR per account — separate cut, with sample size and caveats
    Day-60 eligibility overlap flag — separate cut, with caveats (does not bundle into this panel)
    "What this is not": not day-30 first-paid, not retention, not a Helio Start read, not a pipeline input, not a paid-acquisition input. Expansion has its own denominator.

Sequence inspection

  The wide account row is the canonical per-account view. Sort the timestamps (eligibility_determined_at, prompt_sent_at, usage_ceiling_crossed_at, help_request_first_at, cs_handoff_initiated_at, expansion_identified_at, expansion_contracted_at, expansion_first_billed_at) and the order is the sequence. Origin flags tell you why each transition happened.

  An optional event log table is a derivation, not a replacement: (account_id, event_type, event_at, event_origin, event_state, row_status, source_event_id). Reconciles to the wide row by account_id + event_at. Default is "derived on read" until someone asks for a persisted copy.

What this design does not do

  - No single conversion_rate column. Rates are per-panel, labeled with the panel's own denominator.
  - No funnel arrows between panels. Panels are lateral.
  - No collapsing of help requests into CS handoffs. The link is an origin flag, not a column merge.
  - No silent drop of non-exposure accounts. Every account has an exposure_state; suppressed_at_send_time and eligibility_lost_before_exposure are visible counts in Panel B.
  - No implicit causality from a not-yet-run design. row_status marks every row; live panels filter on shadow/live only; Panel B's "what this is not" line states observational scope.
  - No retroactive revision. Later states live in their own fields; earlier timestamps are not overwritten.

Questions for Owen before he rebuilds

  1. Is the help request taxonomy the same one Customer Success already uses, or does this report need its own? Same question for cs_handoff_origin.
  2. Event log as a published table, or derived on read? My default is derived on read.
  3. Does Panel E need the day-60 eligibility overlap flag bundled, or kept as a separate cut with its own caveat? My default is separate cut, separate caveat.
  4. Should row_status = design_only rows be excluded by default in the published view, or shown with a clear visual marker? My default is shown, marked — exclusion hides the quarantine work.

Short version: clean it once gently, let him air-dry, keep him from licking it, shorten and soften the next few walks, and only call the vet if a specific change shows up. The two-minute favor at the end of the walk followed by normal weight-bearing fits the same pattern as his earlier burr and thorn incidents, which all settled with home care.

TODAY — CLEAN AND PROTECT

  - Rinse the pad once with lukewarm water or plain saline. Pour it over the pad rather than scrubbing or soaking. Pat dry with a clean towel or paper towel; do not rub.
  - Do not use hydrogen peroxide, rubbing alcohol, iodine, or essential oils on a pad scrape. They sting, slow granulation, and can damage the pad surface.
  - A very dilute chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine solution (the color of weak tea) is acceptable if you want an antiseptic step, but for a clean superficial scrape with no debris it is not required.
  - Leave it uncovered indoors. Air exposure is better for pad healing than a bandage, and a paw wrap holds moisture and dirt.
  - The main thing to control is licking. A short lick or two is normal; sustained licking delays healing and can turn a superficial scrape into a hot spot.
  - If he returns to the spot repeatedly, use an e-collar or a soft cone for a day or two. A light sock secured above the dewclaw with a small strip of cohesive bandage (not wrapped tightly around the paw) works for short outings if he is tolerating it, but take it off indoors.

WALKS — SHORTEN AND SOFTEN

  - Cut the next two to three walks to about two-thirds of the usual length and stay on soft, cool surfaces — grass, shaded sidewalk, dirt path. Skip hot pavement for now.
  - No jogging or running for two to three days. The brief favor at the end of the walk suggests mild discomfort on repeated impact, not injury, so a quick step-back is enough.
  - If he walks cleanly on the shortened route with no favoring, you can return to normal length on the next outing. If he favors again or licks during the walk, stay short another day.

CALL THE VET IF YOU SEE

  - Active bleeding that does not stop with five to ten minutes of gentle, steady pressure.
  - Any swelling, especially between the pads or around a toe.
  - Discharge — cloudy, yellow, green, or foul-smelling.
  - Noticeable warmth in the pad or toe compared to the others.
  - A puncture you did not see initially, a foreign body you cannot easily remove, or anything that looks deeper than a surface scrape.
  - Torn, cracked, or lifted nail, or the scrape is at the nail bed.
  - Favoring the paw that recurs after the walk or persists beyond the next morning; refusal to bear weight at all.
  - Escalating licking that creates a red, moist, raw spot despite your efforts to redirect.
  - Systemic signs — lethargy, loss of appetite, fever-ish behavior, or panting at rest.
  - No improvement after 48 to 72 hours, or anything that looks worse at any point.

WHAT THIS IS NOT

  - Not an emergency. The paw is weight-bearing, no bleeding, no swelling, no embedded object, no torn nail. Treat at home and watch.
  - Not a reason to confine him. Short, soft-surface walks with no running are fine.
  - Not a reason for repeated inspections. Check twice today and once tomorrow morning; over-checking turns a small scrape into a stressed dog.

TALKING POINTS — Priya follow-up for next staff discussion

============================================================

Talking point 1 — When I stop the build over unresolved timestamp semantics

Example: Helio Start day-30 settled-first-cash read for the 52-workspace audit cohort.

The decision the evidence could inform was simple to state and hard to operationalize: how many of those 52 workspaces actually had cash in by day 30. The build was at risk of starting before we pinned three things — whether "first cash" means authorization timestamp or settlement timestamp, which day boundary we were measuring against, and what happens to a workspace that authorized on day 29 but settled on day 31.

I stop before any query is written if any of those three is open. The reason is that each one silently changes the metric. If we count authorization, we count cash that never arrived. If we count UTC midnight against workspace-local timezone, we mis-classify borderline cases. If we exclude day-29 auths from the denominator, we change who the cohort is. None of these are recoverable after the query runs — every one of them changes what the query counts.

What the stop looks like in practice: the unresolved item is recorded under "unresolved assumptions — build-blocking" with the owner (Finance, in this case, because ACH ledger is their system of record), the timestamp field name, the boundary definition, and the boundary-miss treatment. The build doesn't resume until all four are written down.

In the Helio Start case, Finance later surfaced three day-29-authorized / day-31-settled workspaces. Because the rule was pinned before build, the answer was already in place: those three stayed in the denominator, did not enter the numerator, and got a separate window-edge ACH settlement-lag diagnostic row. We did not move the boundary to day 31. We did not call them near-misses. We did not retrofit the rule.

Rule I'll state to the team: stop the build when the timestamp source-of-truth field is ambiguous, when the day boundary is not pinned to a specific timezone, when boundary-miss treatment is not agreed in writing, or when Finance owns a related field and has not confirmed.

============================================================

Talking point 2 — When independent validation is non-negotiable

Example 1: Expansion Assist suppression query, Owen's June 17 dry run.

Owen designed the suppression rule, wrote the query that implemented it, and ran the dry-run that validated it. The dry run surfaced three freshness failures: a usage-ceiling snapshot that was 9 days old against a rule that required ≤48 hours, an integration-depth snapshot past the 7-day limit, and a Customer Success suppression check reading from the nightly cache when the rule required a live system-of-record query within 15 minutes of eligibility evaluation.

If the same person designs and validates, the design errors are invisible to the validator by construction. The validator checks "does this query return what I expected" — but "what I expected" is the design. The freshness rules weren't enforced because the rule lived in the spec, not in the query.

Example 2: Helio Start day-30 read, this time as a validator-not-a-person case. The team's initial number circulated before Finance independently reviewed the ACH ledger against the workspace cohort. Finance's review found the three day-29-auth / day-31-settled workspaces. Without that independent ledger reconciliation, those three would have been invisible and the metric would have over-counted. The validator here wasn't a person — it was Finance's system of record against the team's query, two different views of the same fact, reconciled before the number became official.

Example 3: the mock funnel report Owen brought on June 18. Owen built it; the structure (eligibility → exposure → handoff → expansion as successive stages of one conversion funnel) implied causality from a design that hadn't run. The redesign — five lateral panels with separate denominators, eligible-but-never-exposed kept visible, suppression logged as its own field, help requests not equated with handoffs — only happened because the review function was structurally separate from the build function.

Rule I'll state to the team: validation is non-negotiable when the work generates a number that will be used for a downstream decision, when the same person both designed and queried the rule, when the system of record that would catch a framing error sits outside the build team, or when the freshness of the inputs is itself part of the rule. The validator must be a different person, a different function, or a different system of record. The rare exception — same person doing both — requires Priya's explicit sign-off and is logged. This is already in the kickoff checklist.

============================================================

Talking point 3 — How I surface a late Finance dependency instead of working around it

Example: Helio Start day-30 read. Finance's ACH ledger review arrived after the team's initial day-30 number had already circulated.

The temptation in that situation is to work around it — count day-29 auths as near-misses, slide the boundary to day 31, fold the late input into the read and pretend it had been there from the start. None of those are acceptable. Each one silently redefines the metric and breaks comparison against any prior cohort. Working around a missing Finance input is exactly the failure mode the kickoff checklist exists to prevent.

The pattern I use, with three timing cases:

Case 1 — Finance slips before build. The dependency is named in the kickoff checklist with owner, due date, and the decision it gates. If Finance can't meet the date, that is a re-scope decision made with Priya before any query is written. We do not start the build on a proxy input. If we can't get the input in time for the original deadline, we either move the deadline, narrow the question, or escalate. We don't redefine the question.

Case 2 — Finance slips during build. Stop the affected workstream. Same day, write a one-paragraph impact note: "Without Finance settlement confirmation by [date], we cannot finalize the day-30 numerator. Current read is provisional. Decisions that should not be made on the provisional read: [list]." The note goes to Priya and the affected decision owners in writing. No silent substitution, no proxy field. Build resumes only when the dependency resolves or Priya explicitly accepts the gap.

Case 3 — Finance slips after build. Do not retrofit. Re-narrate the existing read as "based on [inputs available at time of build], pending [Finance input]." Add a separate panel showing the gap and the boundary-miss treatment. Surface the limitation in the same channel where the original read was distributed, in writing. The historical snapshot stays as it was at the time; later Finance input updates a labeled panel, not the original number.

Rule I'll state to the team: when a Finance dependency arrives late, the default response is stop-and-surface, never improvise. If we don't have the input, we say so in writing, with the affected decisions named. We do not paper over it with a proxy, a boundary slide, or a quiet re-definition.

============================================================

These three points reinforce each other. TP1 is the pre-build gate. TP2 is the structural separation that catches what TP1 might miss. TP3 is what happens when the gate fires — the routing, not the workaround.

The deciding question is not "is the unit perfect" but "are the two measured faults the cause, and is the rest of the unit likely to give several more years of service?" The measurements point strongly to yes.

On the $468 repair (warranty):

2. Warranty on the labor — full or prorated; for how long.

On the $468 repair (failure risk):

6. What other components the technician inspected on this visit (indoor blower motor and amp draw, condenser fan motor and amp draw, evaporator coil condition, condensate drain, thermostat behavior under load) and whether anything else is showing wear.

On the $9,240 replacement (scope):
11. Exactly what is included: condenser only, full split system (condenser + coil + line set), new thermostat, permit, haul-off and EPA-compliant refrigerant recovery, any required electrical or ductwork modifications, commissioning and start-up verification.
12. SEER rating of the quoted unit and the rated sound level.
13. Full warranty terms in writing: parts, compressor, labor — and which years are full versus prorated. Whether the labor warranty is through the installer or a third party.
14. Whether the unit was sized using a Manual J load calculation or matched like-for-like to the existing unit. Like-for-like on a unit that has run 11 years is usually fine, but worth confirming.
15. Installer credentials: license number, insurance certificate, who pulls the permit, and whether the install is performed by employees or subcontractors.
16. Rebates, federal energy-efficiency tax credit, or utility incentives that would lower the net cost, and whether the quote already nets them in.

18. The disposal path for the old condenser and the recovered refrigerant.

What this is not

- The repair-vs-replace decision is not the same as a refrigerant, compressor, or coil decision. Those are ruled out by the measurements and are not on the table here.

That keeps the unit running through the heat, costs little, and preserves every option.

Short answer: yes, schedule an evaluation before returning to running — but not as an urgent or same-day visit.

Why now:
- The pattern has crossed two of the prior thresholds. Single-leg hop reproduction qualifies as "symptoms at any sub-step." Stair-descent pain during ordinary use (rather than only delayed post-session) is a new, lower-load reproduction. Three recurrences in roughly six weeks (May 11, June 1, June 15) also reads as "recurring symptoms at similar load."
- Walking being pain-free and the absence of swelling, bruising, limp, instability, focal tenderness, and resting pain keeps this in the "schedule it, don't rush to urgent care" range.

Meanwhile, reasonable activity and symptom limits:

Allowed unless they reproduce pain
- Walking (current baseline is pain-free — keep it that way)
- Cycling, swimming, easy upper-body strength work, pool running if available
- Daily stairs, descending slowly with a handrail if the 2/10 is bothersome

Pause until evaluated
- Running, walk-jog, jogging intervals
- Hopping, jumping, plyometrics, agility, lateral cuts
- Any new load you haven't recently cleared (hill repeats, longer walks, faster pace)

Symptom limits / escalation triggers
- Stop or step back any activity that produces ≥2/10 lateral ankle pain during or within 24 hours
- Stop the day's run and rest the next day if delayed-onset ache returns, even at low intensity
- Move the evaluation up sooner if you develop any of: visible swelling or bruising, focal bony tenderness over the lateral malleolus or talus, instability or "giving way," inability to bear weight normally, escalating pain, pain at rest or at night, a mechanical event (pop/twist/fall), or any numbness, tingling, color, or temperature change in the foot

What to bring to the visit (helps the clinician, doesn't require you to interpret it yourself):
- The location — lateral, often just below or behind the lateral malleolus
- The pattern — pain-free during running, delayed ~2-hour onset on stairs/hop
- The load threshold — ~10+ minutes of easy jogging seems to be the boundary
- Walking and stairs as the current reproducer, single-leg hop as a positive provocative test
- The dates of the three recurrences and the clean sessions between them (May 13, May 20, June 8)
- A sports-medicine physician or a sports-physical-therapist who runs an running assessment is the right fit; they can do a focused exam and decide whether imaging or a graded return-to-run plan is needed.

One thing not to do: don't try to "test through" the single-leg hop or stair descent to see if it still hurts before the appointment. That doesn't add useful information — the answer is already yes — and it can keep the tissue irritated going into the exam.

Assessment of the 73-minute result

The 73-minute runtime is meaningfully below both your 90-minute target and the published ~100-minute claim at 30 W. Against the 90-minute target that's a 17-minute shortfall, roughly 19%. Against the published claim, that's 73% of advertised — on the low end of the 80–95% real-world range I cited when you selected the unit. The 12-hour initial charge was adequate (8–24 h is the typical manufacturer window), so the gap is most likely a partly-formed or partially-aged SLA cell, not a charge-time artifact.

What one conditioning cycle realistically buys

A single full discharge/recharge on a freshly-shipped SLA battery typically gains 5–8 minutes when the cause is incomplete formation or partial state-of-charge on receipt. It does not add battery capacity; it lets existing capacity deliver closer to its rated value. Realistic post-conditioning runtime: ~78–83 minutes — still 7–12 minutes short of your 90-minute target. The probability that one cycle pushes you to 90+ minutes is low, on the order of 10–15%.

Recommendation: return before Monday

I'd skip the conditioning cycle and return. Four reasons:

1. The gap to your named target is meaningful, and one cycle is unlikely to close it.
2. The schedule is tight. Conditioning is discharge (~75 min) + recharge (8 h recommended) + retest (~75 min) + repack. Doing that Saturday leaves Sunday for retest and a return decision; any delay compresses the window dangerously.
3. The asymmetry is wrong. The cost of missing the return deadline (restocking fee, lost refund) is much larger than the cost of skipping a likely-modest improvement attempt.
4. You've consistently declined "close enough" substitutions when a standard was named — the 90-minute target deserves the same treatment.

If you want one more data point before shipping, the cheaper move is a single overnight recharge (no full discharge) plus a Sunday-morning retest. The expected runtime is in the same 78–83 minute range, and you still have Sunday afternoon and Monday morning to ship if it doesn't improve. That isolates "fresh charge" from "true capacity" without spending the return-window time on a deep cycle.

What this is not

This is not a final judgment on UPS runtime claims in general, and not a recommendation to abandon UPS protection. 73 minutes is genuine, useful runtime. It just isn't what this unit's spec promises and what you required of it. A different unit of the same model could land closer to spec (unit-to-unit SLA variation is real); a larger-battery UPS would be the only sure way to clear 90 minutes comfortably.

One practical follow-up if you return: ask the retailer explicitly about restocking-fee policy on a tested unit and whether a swap is available, since the most likely outcome is a same-model replacement that performs a few minutes better rather than a fundamentally different result.

PRINCIPLE: today is isolation and triage, not treatment. Three goals in order — (1) protect people from mold exposure, (2) stop further damage to the ~34 dry prints, (3) decide which of the 8 affected prints need a photograph conservator.

A leak years ago means the box has had time to dry out. If the fuzzy spots are mold, it is most likely dormant or stabilized, not actively growing. That does not make it safe to brush or pull — it means urgency is for proper isolation and assessment, not panic.

────────────────────────────────────────
SETUP — before any more handling
────────────────────────────────────────

Work somewhere with airflow you control: near an open window with a fan pulling air out, or outdoors on a porch or patio. Keep the box away from the kitchen, bathrooms, bedrooms, and anywhere a person with asthma, allergies, pregnancy, or immunocompromise spends time.

PPE, in priority order:
  - A respirator rated N95 or better (KN95 acceptable). A surgical or cloth mask is a stopgap, not protection.
  - Nitrile gloves. Clean dish gloves work if nitrile isn't around. Wash hands after removing gloves even with gloves on.
  - Long sleeves. Hair tied back.

Surface: wipe a clean table or cookie sheet with isopropyl alcohol (70%) or plain dish soap and water, then dry. Avoid carpet, upholstered furniture, and fabric tablecloths — they trap spores.

Have ready, on the clean surface:
  - 8–10 sheets of clean white copy paper
  - A pencil (not pen — pencil won't bleed if the print is damp)
  - Small paper bags or letter-size envelopes
  - A roll of plain white paper towels
  - Optional: a magnifying glass or phone camera on macro mode
  - Optional: a small flashlight or desk lamp for raking light

Do NOT have ready: plastic bags, plastic bins, tape, brushes, cotton swabs, vacuum cleaner, hairdryer, dehumidifier pointed at the prints, isopropyl alcohol anywhere near the prints, vinegar, hydrogen peroxide, "magic eraser," or any cleaning product.

────────────────────────────────────────
ISOLATION — the first physical action
────────────────────────────────────────

Split the box into three groups without touching the affected prints directly. Work over the clean surface so anything that falls can be folded into the appropriate enclosure.

Group A — the ~34 dry, loose prints:
  - Pick up one at a time by the edges with gloved hands.
  - Slide each into its own clean sheet of copy paper, like a sleeve. Don't stack loose prints directly on each other.
  - Write the order number and a one-word description on the paper sleeve in pencil (e.g., "07 porch — three kids"). Do not write on the photo.
  - Set Group A aside in a clean pile, away from the box.

Group B — the 2 prints with fuzzy edge spots:
  - Do not pick up yet. Slide a sheet of clean paper under each one as a spatula and lift paper-and-print together.
  - Place each into its own paper bag or fold a sheet of paper around it as a closed sleeve.
  - Label the outside in pencil: "FUZZY EDGE — DO NOT OPEN — assessment pending." Add date and the order it came out of the box.
  - These stay sealed until you have decided whether they go to a conservator.

Group C — the 6 stuck glossy prints:
  - Do not pick up, do not flex, do not slide paper underneath the stuck corner.
  - Slip the entire cluster onto a single sheet of clean paper as a tray, supporting the whole stack.
  - Fold the paper around the cluster as a loosely closed sleeve — not tight, not airtight.
  - Label: "STUCK — DO NOT SEPARATE — photograph conservator." Date it.
  - These are the only group with a clear, immediate conservator decision. Nothing else you do today changes this.

After Group A is set aside and Groups B and C are sealed:
  - Wipe the work surface again with isopropyl alcohol.
  - Bag the original cardboard box in a paper bag and label it "stored near leak — held for conservator review." It may be useful for the conservator to see storage context.
  - Remove gloves, wash hands, change the surface cover if you used cloth.

────────────────────────────────────────
ASSESSMENT — what you can learn without making things worse
────────────────────────────────────────

For Group B (fuzzy edges), with the print still in its paper sleeve, you can:
  - Look through the paper at the back, not the front. If the paper shows no discoloration, no tide line, no softening, the underlying print is probably structurally intact.
  - Sniff the closed sleeve from a few inches away. A musty or earthy smell suggests active or recent mold. No smell is neutral evidence — dormant mold often has no smell.
  - Photograph each spot in macro through the paper if you want to share with a conservator later.
  - Look at the spot edges: fuzzy and slightly raised = almost certainly mold (filamentous hyphae). Flat discoloration or a tide line = moisture staining, not active mold, still wants a conservator's read.

Things to NOT do during assessment:
  - Don't open the sleeve to "look closer."
  - Don't brush, blow on, or wipe the spot.
  - Don't hold it up to your face or anyone else's.
  - Don't set it on the scanner glass yet — spores transfer to the glass and contaminate everything you scan after.

For Group A (dry loose prints):
  - Hold each one at a low angle under a single bright lamp. Raking light shows surface texture, fingerprints, embossing, and any subtle spotting you'd miss under flat light.
  - Look at all four edges and both faces. Any other fuzzy patches, tide lines, brittleness, stickiness, or curling? Sort into Group B if yes.
  - If Group A is genuinely clean, you can scan them using the workflow you already use for Mom's photos — separate sleeves, front+back pairing, named files. Keep them physically separated from Groups B and C.

────────────────────────────────────────
DECISION — conservator vs home
────────────────────────────────────────

Send to a photograph conservator (no DIY):
  - All 6 stuck prints. Required, not optional.
  - Any print in Group B where the spot is fuzzy or raised (mold), even if it looks small.
  - Any print where the emulsion looks cloudy, sticky, separating from the paper base, or has tide lines.
  - The whole box if you'd rather have one set of expert eyes than triage yourself. Conservators routinely evaluate boxes of mixed condition; an in-person or mailed consultation is normal.

Home treatment is reasonable only when:
  - Group B inspection shows flat discoloration or staining with no raised texture and no musty smell, AND
  - A photograph conservator has either confirmed in writing that it is inert (dust, residual grime, non-living staining) or you have declined formal review and accept the residual risk, AND
  - You keep the print isolated from Group A indefinitely.

For Group A (the ~34 dry, loose prints): home treatment covers rehousing, scanning, and proper storage. That is the entire scope of what home treatment can responsibly do for any of these prints.

Find a photograph conservator through the American Institute for Conservation (AIC) "Find a Conservator" directory, filter by photographs. Most will do a remote consult from good photos if an in-person drop-off isn't convenient. Expect to send clear photos of each affected print, the storage context, and a one-paragraph timeline ("stored near a leak approximately X years ago, brought out June 22, 2024").

────────────────────────────────────────
WHAT HOME TREATMENT ACTUALLY CAN DO
────────────────────────────────────────

  - Rehouse the clean prints in acid-free paper or polyester (Mylar/Melinex) sleeves, vertical or flat, in a clean archival box.
  - Scan the clean prints, preserving front-back pairing and a clear filename convention.
  - Maintain a stable storage environment: roughly 65–70°F and 30–50% relative humidity, dark, no attic/garage/basement.
  - Keep the affected prints physically separate, in clean paper, in the same stable environment, until conservator review.

WHAT HOME TREATMENT CANNOT DO:
  - Separate stuck prints without damaging at least one emulsion layer.
  - Remove mold from a gelatin emulsion without scarring it.
  - Reverse silver mirroring, oxidation, or moisture tide lines.
  - Make a fuzzy spot "go away" with any household product. Don't try.

────────────────────────────────────────
WHAT THIS PLAN IS NOT
────────────────────────────────────────

Not a treatment protocol — Groups B and C are not being "fixed" today.
Not a substitute for a conservator's eyes on Groups B and C.
Not a guarantee that Group A is unaffected — it should be scanned and rehoused, but if any print later develops a fuzzy spot or tide line, treat it as Group B.
Not irreversible — everything in Groups A, B, and C remains in original condition after isolation, so any conservator decision can still be made on the actual artifacts.

────────────────────────────────────────
PRACTICAL ORDER FOR THIS AFTERNOON
────────────────────────────────────────

  1. Move the box to a ventilated spot. Put on respirator and gloves.
  2. Lay out clean surface, copy paper, pencil, paper bags.
  3. Sort into Groups A, B, C using the isolation steps above.
  4. Wipe surface, bag the original box, remove PPE, wash hands.
  5. While the lunch is still going, walk Mom through what was found and what each group means. She does not need to be the decision-maker on the conservator question, but she should know that 6 prints will not be coming back the way they went in.
  6. This evening or tomorrow: photograph Groups B and C through their sleeves, draft a short note for a conservator, and request a consult. Group A can be scanned any time using your existing front-back workflow.

SCALED INGREDIENTS — 24 → 30 servings (×1.25)

  Cucumbers      12         15            15 whole English cucumbers
  Yogurt         3 cups     3.75 cups     1 × 32 oz tub; use ~3.75 cups,
                                            hold ~1/4 cup back
  Chopped herbs  1.5 cups   1.875 cups    ~2 cups lightly packed;
                                            hold ~2 TBSP back
  Lemon juice    3/4 cup    0.9375 cup    ~1 cup (8 fl oz bottle works);
                                            hold ~2 TBSP back
  Olive oil      1/2 cup    0.625 cup     ~3/4 cup; hold ~2 TBSP back
  Kosher salt    2 TBSP     2.5 TBSP      2 TBSP in initial mix;
                                            hold ~1.5 tsp back

The 15 cucumbers lands exact; the yogurt lands on a single 32 oz tub; the lemon juice is one small 8 oz bottle. The rest just rounds up to the next easy measure, which is fine — over-dressing is the larger risk than over-measuring on a 25% bump.


MIXING SEQUENCE

  1. CUCUMBERS (start of prep)
     Slice 15 cucumbers to spec'd thickness.
     Toss with 1 tsp of the kosher salt in a colander set over a bowl.
     Rest 10-15 min, then drain off the liquid. This keeps the yogurt
     from getting thinned out at service, which is the main failure mode
     when you scale a cucumber-yogurt salad up.

  2. DRESSING — INITIAL MIX (large bowl, ~12 qt)
     Whisk together:
       ~3.5 cups yogurt
       ~1 3/4 cups herbs
       ~3/4 cup lemon juice
       ~1/2 cup olive oil
       2 TBSP kosher salt

     Reserve in a small cup or ramekin for final adjustment:
       ~1/4 cup yogurt
       ~2 TBSP herbs
       ~2 TBSP lemon juice
       ~2 TBSP olive oil
       ~1.5 tsp kosher salt

  3. COMBINE
     Add drained cucumbers to the dressing bowl.
     Toss gently but thoroughly so every slice is lightly coated.
     Don't over-toss — yogurt thins and the herbs bruise with handling.

  4. HOLD + ADJUST (10-15 min before service)
     Cover and refrigerate.
     Just before plating, taste and adjust using the reserves:
       - Looks tight/dry after resting  → loosen with reserved yogurt,
                                           drizzle by drizzle.
       - Tastes flat                     → dissolve reserved salt in 1 tsp
                                           of the reserved lemon juice
                                           and stir in.
       - Too sharp                       → a touch more olive oil.
       - Herbs have wilted into dressing → pinch of reserved herbs on top
                                           for fresh aroma.

That keeps about 6% of each wet ingredient and the final half-teaspoon-plus of salt held back, which is the right size adjustment for a 30-serving bowl — enough to fix the batch, not enough to dilute or re-dress it.

That combination — diagnosis matches symptom, the rest of the system checks clean today, and a ~19.7× cost differential ($9,240 vs $468) — is what makes the repair the better first call. Even if the repair has only a low-double-digit probability of resolving the shutdown for the season, expected value is strongly on its side. The 30-day credit makes the worst case bounded: if the same symptom recurs and Mom buys this replacement, the $468 is credited.

What the credit does and doesn't cover

The credit is real but narrowly worded. It applies only if (a) the *same* intermittent shutdown recurs within 30 days, and (b) Mom buys *this* $9,240 replacement from this contractor. It does not cover a different symptom (blower motor seizing in month 4), a different quote, a partial replacement, or a repair-then-replace done in stages outside this contractor. Get the credit terms — amount, qualifying symptom, qualifying replacement, the 30-day clock — on the same written document as the repair quote, not just inside the email body.

Material risk that remains

  1. System age. The unit is 11 years old. Compressor and refrigerant-circuit wear continue on their own curve regardless of the contactor and capacitor. Residential compressor MTTF roughly lands in the 12–18 year band, so this repair is most likely a 1–4 season extension, not a 10-year solution.

  2. Same root cause, different downstream part. The pitted contactor was almost certainly caused by repeated under-voltage hard starts from the weak capacitor. Replacing both should break that loop. But if the pitting was instead driven by a sticky low-voltage control signal or a supply-voltage issue this visit didn't probe, the new contactor can pit again.

  3. The compressor. Compressor amperage checked normal *today*. That's a snapshot. Compressors can develop mechanical weakness (bearing wear, valve wear) that only surfaces under sustained high-load conditions — exactly the kind of stress an Austin afternoon puts on one. If shutdown returns in 30 days and the contactor and capacitor are clean, the compressor becomes the leading suspect, and the credit still applies because the symptom would be the same intermittent shutdown.

  4. Refrigerant circuit, future-facing. No leak detected today doesn't mean no slow leak tomorrow. Eleven-year-old line-set flares, service-valve cores, and evaporator coil solder joints are all candidate leak points. A slow leak wouldn't usually cause intermittent shutdown (it would cause gradual capacity loss), but it's a separate failure mode the repair doesn't address.

  5. Adjacent components not in scope. Blower motor, condenser fan motor, control board, thermostat wiring, and duct static were not part of either quote. Any of those failing next month is a separate event and is not covered by the credit.

  6. Labor warranty is short. 90-day labor / 1-year parts means a defective replacement contactor that fails in month 4 leaves Mom paying labor again. Small dollar exposure, but worth noting.

What changes the call

  - If shutdown happens *during* the visit or *immediately* after, that's a same-visit failure and Mom should not pay for the repair at all.
  - If shutdown recurs within 30 days, the credit triggers: she pays $468 now and applies it against the $9,240 replacement, net $8,772. Replacement then becomes the right call.
  - If a *new* symptom appears (no cooling at all, water leak, burning smell, breaker tripping), the credit language does not apply. Mom should call back rather than assume coverage.

Practical follow-ups to get in writing before authorizing

  - The 30-day credit terms on the same document as the repair quote: amount ($468), qualifying symptom ("the same intermittent afternoon shutdown"), qualifying replacement (this $9,240 quote, this contractor), and clock start (date of repair completion, not quote date).
  - The contractor's name, license number, and the visit date on the quote.
  - Confirmation that the 1-year parts and 90-day labor warranties are documented in writing, not only in the email body.
  - A short note that today's diagnostic readings (capacitor spec, contactor visual, amperage, 18°F split, leak check) were measured today and the compressor is not flagged as degraded at this time.

What this is not

This is not a forecast that the repair will work, a guarantee, or a recommendation to skip the replacement conversation. It is a judgment that the $468 repair is the right first move because the diagnosis matches the symptom, the rest of the system checks clean today, the cost differential is large, and the credit makes the worst case bounded. The decision to replace later — if and when a different failure mode shows up or the same shutdown recurs — is a separate decision and is not foreclosed by trying the repair now.

Reversible comparison method: a window-mat overlay.

Take a piece of card stock, mat board, or even heavy drawing paper cut a little larger than 8x10 (say 8.5 x 10.5 so the border is visible). Cut a centered 8x10 window in it. Lay the painting flat in your normal viewing light. Place the window mat on top, aligned so the opening shows exactly what an 8x10 crop would show. Lift it off to see the full sheet. Photograph both states at arm's length (~50-60 cm) so you can compare without laying it out again. A simpler variant: two L-shaped pieces of matte board arranged to frame an 8x10 rectangle on top of the painting. Equally reversible, and you can slide the window a hair to test "what if the crop origin were slightly different."

Viewing protocol:
  - Same lighting as your painting corner, at the distance a framed viewer would actually stand
  - One look now, set it aside for a day, look again with fresh eyes
  - If you want a stronger test, lean the overlay against a bookshelf or hang the painting briefly with the mat in place so the question lives with you a few days, not just one focused minute

Which tradeoff to favor before cutting: the full sheet.

The 1.25 inches of pale wash on the right is not wasted paper. It's what gives the diagonal shadows somewhere to travel without bumping into the image edge. The plant sitting near the left third is doing the same kind of work as the rule-of-thirds asymmetry you've used in larger studies — it pulls the eye off-center and lets the quiet area do its job. An 8x10 crop compresses both: the plant moves toward center, the breathing room shrinks, and the shadows now terminate at the crop line instead of fading into the sheet. You'd still have a competent, more conventional composition — just a quieter and less interesting one.

The convenience of a standard 8x10 frame is real, but it's a framing problem, not a painting problem. The painting can be matted inside a larger frame, or a custom frame cut later. Once you cut the sheet, you can't add the quiet area back.

So: run the mat-overlay test. If after a few days the cropped view clearly reads better, you've lost only the test setup, not the painting. If the full sheet still reads as the working composition — which I expect — the test has earned you the confidence to keep the sheet as-is and let the framing follow the painting rather than the other way around.
