WHAT HAPPENS IF NOTHING IS DONE

  Six stuck glossy prints (bonded only at corners, no visible image-layer loss beyond the adhered areas)
    - The bond is currently stable but not neutral. Heat, humidity swings, and time all tend to push adhesive joins deeper into the emulsion layer, not the other way. The state today is the *best* state these prints are likely to be in.
    - Left alone, the prints stay inaccessible individually. They cannot be safely viewed, digitized, or returned to albums in their current stuck configuration. They are effectively one 6-print block.
    - If conditions shift (warmer or more humid storage, another summer, a move), the bond can spread or strengthen, which raises both the cost and the loss-risk of any future separation.

  Two fuzzy-edge prints (localized surface mold, not yet in central images)
    - Mold is biologically active. "Localized today" is a snapshot, not a fixed condition. The fuzzy edges are exactly the kind of environment mold continues to colonize, and spores can move to other prints in the same enclosure if isolation slips.
    - These are the more time-sensitive of the two problems. The longer they sit, the higher the probability that the next assessment sees a larger affected area, deeper substrate involvement, or spread to a third print.

WHAT IS RISKED BY AUTHORIZING TREATMENT

  - Humidification and separation of the six stuck prints: the conservator's own note says image-layer loss is currently confined to the adhered corners. Any separation method has some chance of disturbing those corner zones further. The central images are described as intact, and the professional method (controlled humidity, then mechanical separation under conservation lighting) is the lowest-loss route available — but it is not zero-loss. There is a non-zero chance that one or more corners lose a small amount of emulsion that is currently preserved.
  - Surface treatment and stabilization of the two moldy prints: this is the more clearly indicated intervention. The risk here is mostly that surface treatment slightly alters the appearance of the fuzzy edge (which is already compromised), not the central image. Net direction is a stabilization gain, not a loss.

  - Cost: $420 is the fixed total with the $95 assessment fee credited against it. Net new spend is $325. The estimate is described as fixed, so conditions worse than the assessment would need to be flagged and re-quoted rather than silently billed.
  - Inherent trade: any professional handling introduces some manipulation to material that is currently stable in its stuck state. That is the only "preservation by doing nothing" that is given up by acting.

THE ASYMMETRY THAT MATTERS

  - For the two moldy prints, the case for timely treatment is strong. Doing nothing is not a neutral holding pattern; it is a slow progression of an active biological process. Delay has a real cost.
  - For the six stuck prints, the case is more balanced. The current state is preserved by isolation and stable storage, but it is also inaccessible. Treatment buys access and the ability to digitize/return to albums, at the price of some corner-zone risk that does not currently exist.

THE CONCRETE DECISION THE THREE OF YOU NEED TO MAKE

This is a one-shop, one-batch, one-estimate structure. The realistic options:

Recommendation: indoor ride this week, not the Friday commute.

Why:

  - Volume. The commute is ~25 min each way, ~50 min total. The therapist's range is 20-30 min per session, up to 3x/week. Split into two bouts with hours between, the round-trip is two sessions in one day without a clean read on whether either stayed inside the envelope.

  - Commute = obligation to complete. If something twinges on a rise, you're committed to finishing the climb or walking the bike. The indoor bike lets you stop at any moment with no consequence. That asymmetry matters, because the "stop if pain >2/10" rule only works if stopping is actually an option. A commute you can't quit is structurally a running substitute you have to finish.

  - Single-variable rule. The loading program (calf raises, resisted eversion, balance work) is the untested variable this week. Adding an uncontrolled outdoor ride on top stacks two unknowns. The indoor ride is the correct first same-day test of loading + cycling, because resistance is fully controllable and the duration has a clean prior - your June 26 25-min ride was pain-free during and the next morning.

What to do this week:

  - Friday: don't bike commute. Drive or use other transport.
  - One indoor ride, 20-25 min, easy conversational effort, seated, no surges. Same day as loading is fine - that combination is the test.
  - Walks and stairs stay normal.

During-session rule (applies to any easy cycling, indoor or outdoor):

  - Effort: nasal-breathing, can hold a conversation. If you can't talk in full sentences, resistance is too high.
  - Pain gate: stop the session at any pain above 2/10, any sharp or unfamiliar sensation, or any "not right" feeling that isn't normal muscular effort. This is the same threshold the loading program uses.
  - Position: seated, no out-of-saddle surges, no standing climbs.
  - Stopping early is data, not failure. Note the duration and why you stopped.

Next-day rule (this is the gate that actually decides whether to continue):

  The morning after the ride, in this order:
    1. Walk normally - no new limp, no guarding.
    2. Descend stairs - your most sensitive readout. No outer-ankle ache, no new calf tightness, no knee or hip protest.
    3. Single-leg hops, if the therapist has cleared them for self-check - pain-free and symmetric.

  Pass (continue at this level):
    - Pain-free during the ride.
    - Pain-free the next morning on stairs and walking.
    - No new swelling, stiffness, or tightness that wasn't there before.
    - No limp, no guarding.

  Fail (stop and step back to the prior clean level):
    - Any ache above 2/10 during the ride or the next day.
    - Pain on stairs that wasn't there before.
    - Morning stiffness that takes more than a few minutes to walk off.
    - A sensation during the ride that doesn't fully resolve by next morning.
    - Any recurrence of the outer-ankle pattern you've been tracking.

If indoor + loading on the same day is clean this week:

  - Next week you can trial a one-way commute (bike home only, ~25 min, one outdoor session). Treat it as a new first-time test - during-session and next-day rules apply exactly the same.
  - Only consider the full round-trip after a clean one-way, and treat the round-trip as two sessions in one day rather than one.

What this is not:

  - Not a permanent ban on the commute.
  - Not a judgment that the outdoor bike is unsafe.
  - Not a step backward. It's a single-variable test before introducing the variable (outdoor commute) that has higher total volume, less resistance control, and an obligation to complete.

It will hold the sheet if the mat is cut precisely on center, but there is essentially no margin for cutting error or paper shift over time. The visible mat border (1.5" on the sides, 2" top and bottom in a 12x16 frame) is unaffected — the concern is mechanical holding only.

Cutting to 8x10 would eliminate most of that wash and turn a fading diagonal into a hard crop line. The framing problem is solvable with a 12x16 archival mount; the composition is not recoverable once the sheet is cut. The $46 cost difference is the wrong axis for this decision.

  1. How will the sheet be held — corner mounts or a top hinge? Either compensates for the tight overlap mechanically.

The right-side pale wash shrinks from roughly 1.125" visible to about 1" visible — still enough for the diagonals to fade. Worth asking, not worth insisting on.

If the framer says no to both, Option 1 as quoted is still the right call. The 1/8" overlap is a small operational concern, not a disqualifier for what is otherwise the correct framing choice for this sheet.

Yes — under the therapist's pain-free cycling rule as you have it, a controlled 20-minute easy indoor ride today is a reasonable next step. A few specifics to keep the test clean and reversible.

Why it fits the rule:
  - The cycling gate ("pain-free during the ride and the following day") is independent of the running/hop-clearance threshold. Not running and not hopping does not block cycling.
  - The reduced eversion session (2x8) was clean during, immediately after, and the next morning. That is a recent clean signal on the loading side.
  - 20 minutes is the low end of the 20–30 minute band. Stay at 20 today. Do not progress to 25 or 30 in this session even if it feels easy.
  - Indoor with controllable resistance (steady easy gear, low-to-moderate cadence, no surges or standing climbs) is the controlled version.

Side-rules to keep the test isolated:
  - Do not reintroduce the third eversion set (return to 3x10) on the same day as the ride or on the day after. Hold the loading at 2x8 for at least one more session; step the loading back up as its own separate progression.
  - One variable at a time. No new walk distance, no stair stress test, no calf-raise progression today.
  - This counts as one of the up-to-three weekly rides. It does not obligate two more this week.

Stop or defer — what to watch for, by window:

During the ride (immediate):
  - Any lateral right-ankle sensation at all. The rule is pain-free during the ride, so even a faint awareness on the outside of the ankle means stop the ride, not just ease off.
  - A new mechanical event: click, catch, snap, give-way, or sharp localized pain.
  - Pain that increases as the ride continues (stop at the first sign of progression, not when it gets bad).
  - Pain at rest on the bike, or a need to alter pedaling to avoid the ankle.
  - Throbbing, hot sensation, or swelling developing during or in the first 30 minutes after.

Rest of the day:
  - A lateral ankle ache that does not resolve within roughly an hour. Your July 5 reference point was that the 2/10 final-set ache resolved within an hour; anything that lingers past that — or that returns during ordinary walking or stairs later in the day — is a defer signal.
  - A new limp, gait change, focal tenderness, swelling, or bruising appearing after the ride.
  - Restricted stairs that evening. If descending stairs reproduces anything on the lateral ankle, cycling is deferred regardless of how the ride itself felt.

Next morning (the explicit gate):
  - Any lateral right-ankle awareness, ache, or discomfort on walking, on stairs, or at rest = "not pain-free the following day." Cycling rule fails closed: defer cycling, hold the loading dose, repeat the prior dose next session rather than progress.
  - A faint 1/10 on first stair descent that resolves within ~30–60 minutes (the July 5 pattern) is a borderline signal: defer cycling, repeat the same reduced loading dose, do not add a third eversion set, and do not run or hop to "check."
  - Persistent or recurring outer-ankle awareness through the day, gait change, or pain that returns with ordinary walking = stop cycling for the week and bring it to the July 16 reassessment.

Hard stops at any time (these go beyond cycling deferral and warrant PT/sports-medicine contact, not just a pause):
  - Swelling, bruising, focal bony tenderness, limp, instability, inability to bear weight normally, pain at rest, increasing pain under the same load, a new mechanical event, or any neurovascular change (numbness, color change, coldness).

If the ride and the next morning are both clean, you have one clean data point at the low end of the prescribed band. That is a basis to repeat at the same 20-minute dose — not a basis to extend to 25–30 minutes, reintroduce the third eversion set, run, or hop. Each of those is a separate progression and gets its own clean data point before moving on.

What you saw fits mild heat-related panting/exertion rather than heat stroke — he walked normally, stayed responsive, had pink moist gums, settled once back in the AC, and showed none of the worrying signs. The plan below keeps him there.

Rest of the evening

- Keep him in the air-conditioned interior. Close blinds in any room that gets direct sun through the late afternoon/evening.
- Water available, not forced. He can sip as he wants; do not let him gulp a large volume at once, which can trigger vomiting.
- Normal dinner is fine if he wants it; if he skips or only eats half, that is consistent with mild exertion and not by itself a concern. Re-offer in an hour rather than coaxing.
- Skip the evening walk unless he signals he needs to go (pacing to the door, whining). If he does, use the hot-weather protocol in the next section, not the usual walk.
- Quiet house. No rough play, no training, no guests. The goal tonight is a calm, cool, low-stimulation evening.
- Settle him where you are. If he normally sleeps near you, leave that option open; checking on him once during the night is reasonable.
- Optional: if you have a rectal thermometer and he cooperates, a one-time reading is useful to confirm he is not trending up. Normal dog temp is 101–102.5°F. You do not need to keep checking.

Adjusting necessary outdoor breaks while it is hot

- Timing. Aim for the coolest part of your window — typically the first 60–90 minutes after sunrise or the last 60 minutes before sunset. "After dusk" in humid weather is not the same as cool: air temperature and pavement temperature both lag the sun. Use the back-of-the-hand test: press the back of your hand to the sidewalk/asphalt for 5–7 seconds. If you cannot hold it comfortably, the surface is too hot for his pads.
- Purpose. Potty only, not exercise. Three to five minutes is the ceiling; cut the trip the moment he has done what he needs to do.
- Route. Shade and grass/dirt over pavement where possible. Avoid the sun-exposed side of the block. Carry water and offer a small amount on the way back if he is panting.
- Skip if he is already restless or panting indoors. That is a sign he is not handling the ambient heat well today; an extra potty lap will not help and may make things worse.
- Cool-down protocol on return. AC, water, calm. No ice baths, no ice water, no cold hose spray on a hot dog — rapid surface cooling constricts vessels and traps heat inside. A damp towel on the belly/inner thighs, room-temperature water to drink, and AC is the right ladder.
- Tomorrow. If today's pattern repeats (humid, warm, dusk walk), assume the same protocol. Do not step back up to a normal-length walk until you have two consecutive days where he comes back cool and unbothered.

Signs that require urgent veterinary care, not continued home monitoring

Go to an urgent/ER vet tonight if any of the following appear:

- Gums change from pink and moist. Watch for: bright red, brick red, purple, bluish, pale, white, or tacky/dry. Capillary refill time (press a gum until it blanches, count how fast color returns) over 2 seconds is a red flag.
- Breathing does not settle within 10–15 minutes of being in the AC, or he pants hard at rest once calm. Any noisy breathing, rasp, gagging, or repeated swallowing is also a flag.
- Body temperature at or above 104°F rectally, or below 99°F.
- Vomiting or diarrhea, especially if repeated, or with blood.
- Collapse, weakness, or inability to stand/walk normally.
- Disorientation, staring into space, confusion, not recognizing you, head pressing.
- Seizure, tremor, or sudden severe muscle stiffness.
- Excessive thick drool, foaming at the mouth, or sudden extreme restlessness that does not improve in AC.
- Unresponsiveness, or a level of lethargy where he cannot be roused to interact normally.

Two judgment calls worth naming:

- Panting that improves meaningfully inside 5–10 minutes and stays improved is reassuring. Panting that keeps recurring in AC, or gets worse rather than better, is not.
- A dog who vomits once or twice after gulping water on a hot day is different from a dog who keeps vomiting, looks bloated, or whose belly feels tight. If you see the second pattern, that is the ER, not the morning vet.

One boundary worth stating: tonight is home monitoring, not a vet visit. If the next 12–24 hours are uneventful — he eats, drinks normally, gums stay pink, breathing is quiet at rest, he moves normally, no vomiting — you are fine to call your regular vet at normal hours tomorrow if anything subtle is still nagging, and otherwise resume routine with the hot-weather break protocol above.

- "Incremental labor" is redefined as: minutes spent on a predefined trial subtask that would not have been performed, or not performed the same way, without the trial. Counted across every contributor (Sam, prep cook, anyone else) and summed.
- This is the same metric the June 28 baseline used; it was just contributed by Sam alone. The 57-minute baseline is the sum, not "Sam's shift." If a second contributor had been on the trial on June 28, the 57 would already have included their minutes. Nothing about the June 28 record changes.

3. Per-shift log: one chronological sheet, not per-person siloed ledgers
- Columns: Start | Stop | Person | Trial subtask | Minutes (= Stop minus Start) | Notes.
- Rules:
  - Each row is one contiguous interval. When a person switches subtasks, stop the row and start a new one.
  - One row per minute-block. If two people are on trial tasks concurrently, each interval is attributed to the person working that minute. No minute appears in two rows.
  - If a single person multitasks two trial subtasks at once, log only the primary one for those minutes; pick the subtask they are actively executing. Passive watching doesn't count.
  - Gaps between rows are not counted. Idle, normal-service tickets, breaks, and waits don't count.

OVERNIGHT PRECAUTIONS (do now, before you stop for the night)

1. Confirm the dishwasher's local shutoff (under-sink, on the supply line feeding the dishwasher) is fully closed — gentle clockwise until it stops. You already did this. Verify by trying to gently turn further; it should not move.

2. Place a dry, light-colored paper towel flat on the cabinet floor in two positions: one directly under the supply connection, one under where the dishwasher drain hose enters the cabinet. These are sentinels. If either gets wet overnight, the position tells you which side the moisture came from. Take a phone photo of the dry cabinet floor now — that is your "before."

3. Lay a dry towel or shallow pan under the supply connection as a backup catcher, in case the shutoff seat itself is not sealing perfectly.

4. Open the cabinet doors for ventilation. A small fan blowing into the cabinet speeds drying.

5. Remove anything stored in the cabinet that you do not want wet (cleaning supplies, bags, the bin if it has a soft bottom) and set it on a dry counter overnight.

6. Avoid running the kitchen sink overnight. Any tap use pressure-cycles the cold supply line and can re-leak if the connection is loose. If you must run water briefly, expect the drip to potentially return.

7. If you have a leak sensor or smart water monitor (Flo, Flume, Moen, leak detector puck), make sure it is armed. If you have none, lay a couple of dry paper towels as broad sentinels under the full under-sink area.

8. Optional: flip the dishwasher's circuit breaker off overnight. There is no outlet near the water per your check, but isolating the appliance entirely removes any electrical exposure on the appliance side.

9. You do not need to shut off house main water overnight. The local shutoff is doing the isolation work. If the local shutoff itself is weeping from the stem when closed (valve seat problem), then shut off the house main for the night and call this an urgent-call trigger in the section below.

10. Keep your phone audible if anyone will be asleep, in case a leak sensor alerts.

DISTINGUISHING SUPPLY FITTING FROM DRAIN LEAK (no dismantling)

Important honesty note before the tests: the fact that closing the local shutoff stopped the drip is consistent with both a supply-side leak and a drain-side leak that simply finished draining. A drain hose holds water after a cycle, so the drip would naturally stop a few minutes after the cycle ends whether or not you closed the shutoff. The four tests below are how you separate them.

Run them in this order. Each is reversible.

Test A — Is the local shutoff actually holding? (Tonight, 1 hour, dishwasher off)
  - Local shutoff stays CLOSED.
  - Place a fresh dry paper towel under the supply connection.
  - Do not run any water in the house for 1 hour.
  - If the towel is wet: the leak is upstream of the shutoff (wall-side supply piping or the shutoff valve seat itself). Plumber-fix, not dishwasher-fix. This is an urgent-call trigger.
  - If the towel is dry: the shutoff is holding. Move to Test B.

Test B — Supply side under static pressure, dishwasher off (Daytime, 5 minutes)
  - Open the local shutoff gently (counter-clockwise, just enough to restore pressure).
  - Do NOT start the dishwasher.
  - Run the kitchen sink cold tap for 30–60 seconds, then close it.
  - Watch the supply connection for 3 minutes. Count drops.
  - Then watch for 3 more minutes without the sink running. Count drops.
  - Interpretation:
    - Drip during or right after sink use, dry otherwise: supply-side leak at the dishwasher connection (loose compression nut, worn ferrule, or hose failure). Likely a one-visit plumber fix.
    - Dry the entire 6 minutes: supply side at the dishwasher connection is sound under household pressure.

Test C — Drain side without cycling the dishwasher (Daytime, 5 minutes)
  - Local shutoff stays open from Test B.
  - Do NOT start the dishwasher.
  - Fill the sink partway with the stopper in, then pull the stopper (do not use the disposal). Or run the sink with stopper in for 2–3 minutes, then drain.
  - Watch both the supply connection and the drain hose area during draining.
  - Interpretation:
    - Drip during sink drain only, and the water is grey, soapy, or has food bits: drain-side leak. Could be the drain hose connection, the air gap (if you have one — small chrome cylinder on the sink), the disposal knock-out, or the drain tailpiece.
    - Dry during sink drain: drain side is likely sound under this load. Note that a dishwasher cycle pushes more water through the drain than a sink basin, so this is necessary but not sufficient.

Test D — Definitive 24-hour static-pressure test (only if B and C are dry)
  - Local shutoff open, dishwasher OFF, door closed.
  - Place fresh dry paper towels under both the supply connection and the drain hose area.
  - Wait 24 hours without running the dishwasher.
  - If supply towel is wet, drain towel dry: supply-side leak at the connection under static pressure — plumber, likely ferrule or supply nut.
  - If drain towel is wet, supply towel dry: drain-side leak at the hose connection or air gap — plumber for the drain side.
  - If both dry: the connection holds under static pressure; the leak only appears during a cycle. Then run one supervised cycle (you present, watching under the sink) as the final discriminator.

If a supervised cycle is needed (Tests B, C, D all clean, dishwasher is the only trigger):
  - Run a normal cycle with the cabinet door open and you watching.
  - Note where water appears first and how clean/dirty it is.
  - Stop the cycle if water reaches any electrical area or the cabinet starts pooling more than a tablespoon.

Do not use any drain chemical, PTFE tape, or plumber's putty until you know which side is leaking. Tape and putty on a supply connection under pressure can mask and worsen a leak. On a drain connection they are usually unnecessary and can hide the failure mode.

URGENT PLUMBER CONDITIONS (call tonight or first thing tomorrow — do not wait for a regular appointment)

Call for same-day or 24-hour service if any of these appear:

1. The drip does NOT stop when the dishwasher's local shutoff is closed. This means you cannot isolate the leak. Worsening is more likely than not without isolation.

2. Water reaches or pools near any electrical outlet, junction box, appliance plug, the dishwasher's electrical connection, or any wall switch. You said no outlet is under the sink — confirm none is at floor level where water could reach.

3. Cabinet floor shows new swelling, soft spots, flaking laminate, dark discoloration, or a musty smell. Active absorption means the leak is feeding the cabinet base faster than it can dry.

4. Water appears outside the cabinet: on the kitchen floor, on the wall below the cabinet, on the baseboard, or seeping into an adjacent room. The leak is no longer contained.

5. The drip rate visibly increases over an hour (faster drip, more pooling) rather than stabilizing. Worsening leaks do not self-correct.

6. The local shutoff valve itself is weeping from the stem (handle area) when closed, or the handle will not fully close. The shutoff has failed; you cannot isolate. Shut off the house main and call tonight.

7. The water is grey, brown, soapy, or has food particles. That is drain-side, and drain-side leaks can worsen quickly with normal sink and dishwasher use, and may involve the disposal knock-out or the drain stack.

8. The house water meter (if readable) shows movement with all fixtures off. That means the leak is upstream of the shutoff, or there is a second silent leak. Either way, escalate.

9. You see or smell sewage. That points to the drain stack or a failed drain seal, not a supply fitting.

10. The dishwasher itself shows water (front, base, door, or inside the tub) rather than the leak being only at the under-sink connection. That is a different failure (door seal, tub seal, fill valve, pump) and likely needs appliance service, not a plumber — though a plumber can sometimes diagnose inlet-side dishwasher failures too.

Non-urgent path: if the local shutoff holds the leak completely overnight, the cabinet stays dry, and no worsening signs appear, you can schedule a normal plumber visit in 1–3 days. Bring your observations to the call: clean water, located under the supply connection at the dishwasher, two tablespoons per cycle, local shutoff stops it, cabinet dried with no swelling, no outlet nearby, no ceiling below you (Cherrywood is a single-story layout). That description lets the plumber bring the right parts — typically a 3/8" compression ferrule and nut, or a replacement braided supply line — and resolve in one visit. If you have the May 6 plumbing work order from the cold-water shutoff repair, have it handy for context; that work was a different connection but the same plumber may know the under-sink layout already.

3. Test on scrap first: same cotton cold-press, same paints, same dilution. Match humidity and timing to what you had on the study.

4. Try a clean, dry, soft brush lightly dragged along just the bloom's outer edge into the muzzle — no water. This sometimes knocks down a cauliflower edge without adding any moisture. If that's enough, stop.

5. If dry-brushing isn't enough, move to a barely-damp clean brush: load, then blot on tissue until the brush leaves almost no track on a dry paper towel. Touch only the transition edge, working from the pale-muzzle side just into the bloom's outer edge to pull a small amount of pigment outward. Lift with dry tissue immediately after each stroke. One or two passes, not a sequence.

6. Stop after that one pass. Let the sheet dry fully (15–30 min, longer if humid). Re-evaluate at viewing distance.

Stopping point: leave some texture. Aim for "soft shadow variation," not "invisible." If the boundary now reads as a gradual cheek-to-muzzle transition at normal distance, you're done — even if close-up you can still see some irregularity. The close-up view is not the relevant view for a backlit fur study.

What to avoid:
    Re-wetting the bloom's interior (carries pigment into the pale muzzle)
    Glazing over the bloom (darkens it; does not soften edges)
    Scrubbing, repeated passes, or "one more" lift cycles (roughens the paper and produces a more visible patch than the original bloom)
    Any moisture within a clear margin of the eye and nose

If after one barely-damp pass the boundary still reads as a hard cauliflower line at viewing distance, the next move is to consider a different crop or accepting the bloom as texture — not a second wet pass in the same zone.

Immediate triage for the Monday onboarding-email gap. The picture is a transport-layer acceptance miss (provider accepted 160 of 201 trigger records), not an audience, copy, or eligibility problem. The 79.6% is well outside the 97-99% band, so the cause is real and worth isolating before any replay. The 3-recipient gap between eligible (204) and triggered (201) is a separate small question and should not be conflated with the 41-trigger gap.

1. Immediate containment (next 60-120 minutes)

  a. Freeze the workflow. Pause any scheduled follow-up sends that share the trigger key, exclusion list, or sender identity. This is a stop-the-bleed step, not a diagnosis. No live sends until the replay evidence is in hand.

  b. Snapshot the four lists, with timestamps, and lock them as read-only views:
     - 204 eligible (as of the original audience build)
     - 201 trigger records (with their internal trigger IDs)
     - 160 with provider message IDs (provider-accepted)
     - 41 trigger records with no provider message ID
     The 3-eligible-but-not-triggered records should appear only in the first list and be flagged for separate review.

  c. Capture current unsubscribe state and current eligibility state for all 204, as of right now. Do not use the eligibility state at trigger time. The right boundary for any replay is the fresher state.

  d. Pull worker logs for the submission window covering all 201 records. For each trigger, capture: submission attempt count, last HTTP status from the provider, last error code/message, latency, retry behavior, and queue depth at the time.

  e. Pull provider-side activity for the submission window. For each of the 201 trigger records, ask the provider for any message-id, delivery event, open, bounce, deferred, or drop event keyed on recipient address and the time window. Also pull the provider's status page / incident log for the window.

  f. Do not send anything until (d) and (e) are complete and reconciled. Replays start from the reconciled list, not from the 41.

2. Layer-by-layer diagnosis

  Layer A: Trigger generation (204 eligible -> 201 trigger records).
  - Are the 3 missing records new-eligible-since-build, suppressed by a race, or never triggered? If never triggered, they are a separate bug and out of scope for the 41-replay decision. If suppressed by a race, do not touch them now; flag for a follow-up.

  Layer B: Worker submission (201 -> 160). This is where the 41 live. For each of the 41, classify:
  - no attempt at all (worker never picked it up)
  - attempt failed before provider ack (timeout, 5xx, network)
  - attempt returned provider ack but message ID was not captured (race between response parsing and persistence, webhook-vs-poll mismatch)
  - attempt returned provider rejection (4xx with reason: suppress, bounce-precheck, policy, list-unsubscribe, etc.)
  These four cases have different correct responses. Cases 1 and 2 are the most replay-safe. Case 3 is the dangerous one because it can mean the provider actually accepted the message but the message ID never made it back into our record. Case 4 is generally not safe to replay unless the rejection reason has cleared.

  Layer C: Provider acceptance (160 -> ?). For the 160 with message IDs, check provider delivery state. Some will be delivered, some will be in deferred/pending, some will have soft-bounced. This is informational for now and feeds the post-mortem, not the replay decision.

  Layer D: Delivery. Same as C, but tracked against the original send window so we can compare to the 97-99% historical baseline.

3. Why no blanket resend, and how duplicates get avoided

  A blanket resend to the 41 is wrong for three independent reasons:
  - Some of the 41 may actually be silent successes at the provider (Case 3 above). Replaying them duplicates the send.
  - Current unsubscribe and eligibility state is fresher than trigger-time state. Anyone who unsubscribed or became ineligible between trigger and now must be excluded from any replay.
  - The cause of the gap is unknown. Replaying before you know the cause means you are also replaying whatever corrupted the first round, and you cannot tell replay outcomes apart from primary outcomes in the data.

  Duplicate-prevention logic for any replay:
  - The trigger record ID is the internal idempotency key. The provider message ID is the provider-side idempotency key. Both must be checked before any send.
  - For each candidate replay recipient, query the provider for any message sent to that address in the last 24 hours with the same template/sender fingerprint. If yes, exclude.
  - Mark each replay as `replay_of=<trigger_record_id>` in both our records and any provider tag/metadata the provider supports, so post-hoc reconciliation can separate primary from replay.
  - Replay must be a distinct, named campaign/run with its own delivery metrics, not folded back into the primary send.

4. Evidence required before any controlled replay

  All of these must be on hand and reviewed before replay begins:
  - Reconciled 41-list with the four-case classification from Layer B, with worker log evidence per record.
  - Provider-side query result for each of the 41, covering the original submission window and the current state.
  - Current unsubscribe list and current eligibility state for the 204, timestamped.
  - Confirmation that the worker uses trigger record ID as idempotency key, and that this is enforced at the provider (not only in our DB).
  - Provider incident / status-page check for the submission window.
  - A named small batch size and a per-batch approval gate (for example, first batch of 10, then 10, then remainder, each with a 10-15 minute observation window).
  - A stop rule for the replay: any new provider error, any duplicate detection, any unsubscribe spike, any new eligibility change.

5. Replay protocol (only if/when 4 is satisfied)

  - Replay only the subset of the 41 that is in Cases 1, 2, or 3-cleared (Cases 3 where provider confirms no message was sent) AND is still eligible AND is not on the current unsubscribe list.
  - Exclude Case 4 rejections unless the specific reason has documented clearance.
  - Exclude anyone who received any provider-confirmed message in the original window.
  - Send in small named batches with the per-batch approval gate above.
  - Tag each replay with `replay_of=<trigger_record_id>` and the original trigger timestamp, both internally and in provider metadata where supported.
  - Track replay outcomes as a separate panel: attempted, accepted, delivered, bounced, opened, clicked, replied, unsubscribed. Do not fold into the primary send's metrics.
  - Defer any statement about overall Monday send rate until primary and replay panels are reconciled separately.

6. What this is not

  - It is not a deliverability or sender-reputation conclusion yet. Provider delivery data for the 160 is not yet pulled.
  - It is not a copy or audience-segment problem. The gap is at the provider-acceptance boundary, not the audience or template.
  - It is not an activation or churn signal. Activation and churn for this cohort remain read on their normal definitions and windows; this gap does not change those readings.
  - It is not a basis for changing any other workflow's exclusion filter, send time, or audience. The gap is scoped to this one workflow and submission window until evidence shows otherwise.
  - It is not a forecast, pipeline, retention, or causal claim. Replay metrics, if any, are operational recovery data, not performance data.

Immediate next move I'd recommend: do (1a) through (1e) now, then stop and reconcile before any send decision. The replay is a separate, later decision gated on the evidence in section 4.

Diagnostic sequence to distinguish Safari tracking failure from a real signup decline.
Working frame only — no causal claim until Step 5 closes.

0.  Frame the question and the boundaries before looking
    Observation to test: Wednesday Safari front-end signup_start is sharply lower
    while backend application-session creation is near the seven-day average.
    Hypotheses to discriminate:
      (A) Safari-side tracking failure (client emission, transport, ingest,
          identity, or dashboard).
      (B) Real signup decline concentrated in Safari visitors.
    Explicitly NOT on the hypothesis list:
      - pricing_page_v3 registry cleanup. It carried no traffic and no rollout
        rules; do not treat it as cause without evidence. If the diagnostic
        in Steps 1–2 forces it onto the list, note the evidence; otherwise
        leave it off.
    Define "sharp" and "near" before pulling numbers, e.g. < -2 sigma vs the
    trailing 7-day same-hour baseline (timezone-aligned, hour-of-day matched,
    not raw day-over-day) and +/- 5 percent of baseline for the backend claim.

1.  Confirm the discrepancy shape — browser x event matrix
    Build the cut for the 24h window vs the trailing 7-day baseline:
      rows:    Safari (iOS, macOS, by version), Chrome, Firefox, Edge, other
      columns: pricing-page session (server access log by UA),
               pricing-page view (client pageview),
               CTA / plan select,
               signup_start (client),
               signup form POST (server),
               application session create (server, canonical),
               workspace/account create (server).
    Read the cut before going deeper:
      - Gap is Safari x signup_start only  -> tracking is the prime suspect.
      - Gap is Safari x all client events -> SDK init / snippet / CSP.
      - Gap is Safari x everything, including server sessions -> real decline.

2.  Browser / client layer (Safari tracking hypothesis)
    2a. SDK load and init
        - Did the analytics snippet actually load on Safari in the window?
          Check the SDK's first-byte / init event and 4xx-5xx rates on the
          analytics endpoint by UA.
        - Any deploy, snippet change, CSP nonce change, third-party-cookie
          posture change, or CDN config change Wednesday morning?
        - For pricing_page_v3: confirm registry returned 0 percent rollout
          and no traffic was served from it. Recording this to rule it in or
          out is fine; naming it as cause is not.
    2b. Safari-specific failure modes
        - ITP and storage: did anonymous_id persist across the visit? ITP
          7-day caps and storage eviction can orphan the id and the
          identity merge silently drops the event.
        - iOS Safari page lifecycle: background-tab freeze, visibilitychange,
          beforeunload beacons. If signup_start is fired on a transition
          Safari drops, the event never lands.
        - sendBeacon availability and quota; fetch keepalive fallback path.
        - Cross-site tracking prevention (Safari 17+): if the analytics
          endpoint is on a different site than the pricing page, beacons can
          be blocked silently.
        - Service Worker conflicts on Safari that intercept the pricing
          page's network requests and prevent the SDK from firing.
    2c. Version spread
        - Is the gap concentrated in one Safari version (e.g. only 17.x,
          only iOS, only macOS)? Version-specific gap -> Safari bug or SDK
          regression. Uniform across all Safari -> ITP / transport.
    2d. Live reproduction
        - Controlled Safari session against staging with the production
          snippet version: does signup_start fire server-side? Then against
          production with the same UA: does it land?
        - Network tab in Safari: is the analytics POST attempted,
          completed, or absent? That single observation discriminates
          client-not-sending from downstream-dropping.

3.  Analytics pipeline layer
    3a. Client -> ingest
        For the window: how many signup_start events did the client attempt
        to send on Safari (analytics endpoint access log, by UA) vs how
        many the collector received?
          - Big gap -> client not sending or transport blocked (Step 2).
          - Equality -> downstream drop (3b onward).
    3b. Ingest -> warehouse
        Bot filter, sampling rule, rate limiter, or reclassification step
        selectively dropping Safari events? Was the event taxonomy changed
        (event name string changed) so the dashboard shows zero even though
        events are landing?
    3c. Identity resolution
        Did anonymous -> identified merge succeed for Safari visitors? If
        Safari cannot link the anonymous session to the identified user
        post-signup, the "Safari signups" cohort collapses in the dashboard
        while the backend session still exists.
    3d. Sampling / data cleaning
        Was a sampling rule activated or a quota threshold hit? Safari
        mobile events are commonly sampled first if the rule is bandwidth-
        or token-based.
    3e. Dashboard vs warehouse
        Pull the raw signup_start count for Safari from the warehouse, not
        from the dashboard. If the dashboard shows the dip but the
        warehouse shows parity, the issue is a dashboard filter, time
        bucket, or property-mapping artifact. That outcome is itself a
        useful finding; it is not a real decline.

4.  Backend / source-of-truth layer
    4a. Application session creation
        Re-check the seven-day average claim with a same-hour-of-day
        comparison, not raw day-over-day (Wednesday has its own hour
        pattern). If same-hour comparison is also flat -> strong evidence
        the gap is frontend-only.
        Cut by UA on the server: are Safari visitors still creating
        application sessions at the baseline rate? If yes -> they are
        signing up; the client is not reporting it.
    4b. Funnel integrity, server-side
        pricing-page request -> signup form render -> signup form POST ->
        email-confirm click -> application session create -> workspace
        create. Compare the funnel on Safari vs other browsers. If the
        divergence is only at the client event signup_start and every
        server-side step is at baseline, the gap is instrumentation.
    4c. Account / workspace creation by UA
        New workspaces in the 24h window whose earliest signup request
        carried a Safari UA, vs baseline. This is the canonical "real
        signup" signal. Cross-check with first-action events and login
        events for the same cohort.

5.  Disconfirming the real-decline hypothesis
    Working conclusion is "Safari tracking failure" only if all hold:
      (a) Safari pricing-page sessions are flat or up vs baseline,
      (b) Safari backend application-session creation is flat in the
          same-hour comparison,
      (c) non-Safari signup_start is normal in the same window.
    If any of (a)–(c) fails, the working conclusion flips to a real
    decline (or a mixed picture), and the diagnostic continues rather
    than closes.

6.  Containment before the root cause is closed
    - Do not publish a "real signup decline" narrative from the dashboard
      number alone.
    - If the gap is purely instrumentation, a short operational note is
      appropriate ("Safari signup_start under-reported on [date]; backend
      signups unchanged"). No decline announcement, no action beyond
      fixing the pipeline.
    - If Step 5 indicates real decline, open a separate thread; do not
      let the Safari-tracking investigation absorb it.

What this sequence is not
    - Not a verdict. The output is a discrimination rule, applied once
      Steps 1–5 close.
    - Not a fix. The diagnostic identifies the layer; the fix follows
      only after the layer is confirmed.
    - Not a treatment of pricing_page_v3 as cause. It had no traffic and
      no rollout rules. It stays off the hypothesis list unless evidence
      from Step 1 or Step 2 forces it in.

What to put in front of Owen and Ines now
    - The claim under test and its boundary conditions (Step 0).
    - The working frame is "Safari tracking vs real decline," not "real
      decline," until Step 5.
    - The dashboard-only number is not the source of truth; backend
      same-hour parity and warehouse parity are the deciding evidence.

Given a single small attached tick, Kibo acting normally, fine-tipped tweezers already on hand, and no substances applied, here is the conservative sequence.

Removal
1. Steady Kibo's head. Behind-the-ear ticks often provoke shaking or scratching, so a brief settle (helper at chin/cheek, calm voice, treat) helps. No muzzle needed unless he has a history of object-near-ear reactions.
2. Part the fur so you can see where the mouthparts meet the skin. The engorged part is the body; the narrow attachment buried in the skin is the head.
3. With the fine-tipped tweezers, grasp the tick as close to the skin as possible, at the mouthparts, not the body.
4. Pull straight up with steady, even pressure. Do not twist, jerk, or squeeze the body. A slow, firm pull for 2-3 seconds is normal; it will release rather than snap.
5. If mouthparts break off and stay in the skin: do not dig. Clean the area and leave them; they usually work themselves out over several days. A small dark speck remaining is not an emergency.

Aftercare (bite site only)
- Wipe the area with dilute chlorhexidine or povidone-iodine. Plain mild soap and water is also fine. Pat dry.
- A thin layer of antibiotic ointment is optional; if applied, watch that he doesn't lick it off.
- Watch him for the next few hours for any sudden facial/muzzle swelling, hives, vomiting, or breathing change. That is the one truly urgent scenario in the immediate post-removal window (acute allergic reaction; rare but real).

What to do with the tick
Either is fine; pick one.
- Save it: seal in a small zip bag or jar with a damp cotton ball, or submerge in rubbing alcohol. Label with the date and site (left ear, behind). If Kibo develops symptoms in the next 2-4 weeks, the vet can identify the species, which materially changes what to test for.
- Or photograph it (top view, ideally next to a coin for scale) and dispose: seal in a bag, submerge in alcohol, or flush. Do not crush with bare fingers.

Central Texas note: Lone Star ticks are the most common biter here, and they transmit ehrlichiosis. A photo showing the female's single white dot on the back, if present, helps later identification, but is not required today.

Local signs to watch (bite site, 1-7 days, sometimes longer)
- Spreading redness, swelling, or warmth beyond the immediate bite
- Discharge, crusting, or a sore that doesn't scab cleanly
- Persistent scratching or head-shaking focused on that ear
- A small firm nodule that doesn't resolve in 2-3 weeks (granuloma; cosmetic, not urgent)

Whole-body signs to watch
Acute window (minutes to 24 hours):
- Facial swelling, hives, sudden restlessness, vomiting, or breathing change → urgent vet or emergency clinic immediately

Days 3-30 (main window for tick-borne illness in Texas):
- Fever cues: warm dry nose, shivering, lethargy
- Reluctance to move, stiff gait, or shifting lameness (joint pain)
- Swollen lymph nodes (under the jaw, behind the knees, in the shoulders)
- Loss of appetite lasting more than a meal
- Vomiting or diarrhea that is new or persistent
- Unusual bruising or pale gums (rare; indicates platelet involvement)
- Eye or nose discharge, jaundice (yellow tint to whites of eyes or gums; rare but serious)
- Any neurological change: head tilt, facial droop, wobbly gait, seizure

When to call the vet
- Same-day urgent: any item in the acute allergic-reaction window above
- Within 24-48 hours: any combination of fever, lethargy, appetite loss, lameness, or vomiting in the 3-30 day window
- Next-day routine: bite-site infection signs (pus, expanding redness, persistent discharge)
- Mention the tick bite and the date even if calling for an unrelated reason in the next 30 days

What this is not
- Not a reason for a same-day vet visit given the normal presentation you described.
- Not a reason for prophylactic antibiotics. Those are not given absent symptoms or known high-risk attachment duration (deer tick >24-36 hours in a Lyme-endemic area, which is not the Texas pattern).
- Not a reason to restrict Kibo's normal activity. Monitor the site and behavior only.

Frame: paper fully dry, warm area is one transparent glaze, horizon opening intact. That puts you in the safest correction zone for cotton cold-press — a thin cool glaze over a transparent warm layer is the lightest-touch way to neutralize and unify the bank without disturbing paper or horizon light. Lifting is available as a single-pass option, not a campaign. Test every move on a scrap of the same paper first; the painting is not the place to find out how a glaze or a lift will behave.

Test setup (before you touch the painting)
  Cut a small piece of the same 300 gsm cotton cold-press. Lay down a warm stroke of the same pigment and dilution you used on the bank, let it dry fully, then practice on it:
    - one barely-damp lift pass
    - one dilute cool glaze over the dried warm stroke
  Judge on the scrap. If the glaze reads too dark, too cool, or muddy on the scrap, thin it or shift the mix before going to the painting.

Step 1 — single restrained lift, only if you want to lighten before glazing
  Brush: soft round, size 6 or 8 (kolinsky or quality synthetic). Dampen it, then blot firmly on a clean towel until it feels almost dry.
  One directional stroke across a small section of the warm bank — top to bottom, or following the cloud form. Do not scrub. Do not retrace.
  Immediately press a dry tissue to the stroke with no rubbing. Lift the tissue straight up.
  Let dry fully. Judge at normal viewing distance.
  If the warmth drops noticeably, repeat on the next section with the same single-pass protocol.
  If pigment does not release cleanly on the first stroke, stop. A transparent warm glaze binds into the cotton fiber; forcing it roughens the surface more than it helps. Move to Step 2 only and accept the warmth as is.

Step 2 — cool glaze to neutralize and unify the bank
  Mix, roughly in this order:
    - mostly water — the glaze should read as tea-colored, not milk-colored; thinner than the existing warm layer, not the same weight
    - ultramarine as the primary cool — it granulates on cold-press and is the complement of the warm pigment, so it grays and cools without going muddy
    - a whisper of quinacridone rose — same family as the violet sky, so the cooled bank stays in the same color world instead of reading as a flat cool patch sitting on top of a warm one
    - a tiny touch of raw sienna or burnt sienna — this is what revives granulation. Ultramarine alone granulates mildly; ultramarine plus a small amount of an earth pigment granulates strongly on cold-press and gives the bank the texture it currently lacks
  Aim for a cool violet-gray, slightly lighter than the darkest part of the warm bank and slightly darker than the violet sky.
  Application:
    - Work on the warm bank only.
    - Keep a wet edge at least a quarter inch below the pale horizon opening — that dry buffer protects the light.
    - One directional pass per area. Do not retouch while wet.
    - Let dry fully before judging.

Step 3 — only if the upper edge of the bank now reads as a hard line against the violet sky
  After Step 2 dries fully, take a clean brush, damp it, blot it almost dry. One soft stroke along the upper edge of the bank, traveling into the bank (away from the pale opening). This pushes the boundary down a hair and softens the transition.
  Dry fully. Judge.
  Do not stroke toward the horizon opening.

Step 4 — only if the bank still feels too uniform after Step 2
  A second, even more dilute pass of the same mix, but with the raw or burnt sienna bumped up a fraction. Single pass. Dry fully. Judge. This adds break-up of texture without deepening value.

Stop rules
  One lift attempt (or none). One cool glaze. Judge.
  If the bank now reads as cooler, with visible texture, and the horizon light is preserved — stop. The study is done.
  If the bank still reads as too warm or too solid at normal viewing distance, stop anyway. This is a study, and one encouraging correction is the goal, not a finished piece. Forcing more correction will roughen paper more than the original problem and is not worth it. Record what you learned and let the next study carry the next question.

What not to do
  Do not scrub, even gently.
  Do not rewet the same area to "try again" — that lifts paper fiber, not pigment.
  Do not glaze wet-on-wet over the existing warm layer; you will get backruns and muddy mixing.
  Do not flood the bank; the glaze should be thinner than the existing warm layer.
  Do not work on or near the pale horizon opening. The dry buffer above the glaze is what protects it.

After the session
  Air dry fully for a few hours. If you must use a hair dryer, low setting, keep it moving, and hold it back.
  Judge at normal viewing distance in north-facing light if possible.
  Wait a day if you can — glazes shift as they cure, and the cooled bank may read better tomorrow than it does today.

Short answer: same scanner, same flatbed workflow, same two people, same Saturday file format and ID-preserving filename pattern. Only the geometry changes for P007, only the exposure changes for P014. No cleaning, no in-software re-mapping, no re-ID, and the eight prints in treatment stay where they are.

Pre-session
- Only the 32 dry loose prints P001–P032 on the work surface. The eight in professional treatment remain at the conservator's facility; they are not brought in, opened, scanned, named, or referenced.
- Same scanner, same clean flat surface, same two reviewers (Mom + Marcus), same dry clean hands or cotton gloves as Saturday.
- Keep the existing inventory doc and the runbook open beside the scanner so every change is logged in the same place.
- Inherit Saturday's resolution, color depth, file format, and paired front/back filename pattern. The two adjustments below are the only deltas.

P007 front — glare on part of the image
- Cause: specular reflection off the print's glossy surface at the scanner's lamp angle.
- Fix the geometry, not the print. Place a clean, acid-free paper or light-card spacer with a window cut slightly larger than the print between the print and the lid so the lid glass is no longer in optical contact with the print. That removes Newton's rings and most of the offending reflection without touching the print. If a spacer is not workable, reposition P007 on the platen so the reflection falls off the obscured area.
- Do not: wipe, brush, blow on, or otherwise clean the print; apply liquid, anti-static spray, or pressure; bend or shim-tilt the print; re-shoot with a camera.
- Capture one scan with the new geometry. Review at 100% with both reviewers. Accept only if the previously obscured area now reads cleanly and no new artifact (banding, focus shift, color cast) appears. If not, repeat with a different platen position — do not adjust contrast or apply sharpening in software.

P014 back — handwriting too faint
- Cause: the Saturday exposure was set for the print's typical reflectance and under-exposed the lighter verso where the writing sits.
- Fix the scanner exposure, not the print. Rescan the back side only with positive exposure compensation (about +1 to +1.5 EV equivalent, or the scanner's brightness/darkness slider set to expose the writing), holding resolution, color depth, focus, and sharpening settings identical to Saturday. If the first attempt is still unreadable, do one further pass at about +0.5 EV more; do not stack multiple boosted rescans.
- Do not: apply sharpening, contrast boost, levels/curves, noise reduction, despeckle, color re-mapping, or any "enhancement." The deliverable is the raw, exposure-corrected scan. The writing is allowed to stay faint in the file as long as it is readable.
- Pair the new P014 back with the existing P014 front (which passed Saturday's review). Do not rescan the front.

Two-person verification
- Both reviewers open the two new files at 100% on a calibrated display.
- P007 front: confirm the glare-obscured area now shows usable detail; confirm tone and color match the surrounding image and the other 31 fronts; confirm no new artifacts.
- P014 back: confirm the handwriting is now legible; confirm nothing else on the back is blown out or altered by the exposure bump; confirm the front/back pairing still belongs together.
- Both reviewers initial and date the inventory entry. Do not accept on one reviewer's word; do not skip.

File and inventory handling
- Filename: keep Saturday's paired front/back filename. Append a version suffix to the rescanned side only, e.g. P007_front_r1.tif and P014_back_r1.tif. The Saturday file of the same side is renamed, not deleted, to make its superseded status explicit (e.g. P007_front_r0_superseded.tif). The print is the source of truth; the files are the digitization of it.
- Inventory doc: add a short rescan note per side — date, reason (glare on P007 front, faint handwriting on P014 back), the single parameter change (spacer / exposure bump), reviewer initials. Do not reassign or rename the print IDs. Do not open a new range; the eight treated prints remain unassigned until they return with final condition notes.
- After verification, re-sleeve P007 and P014 in their original positions in the storage order. Do not flip, rotate, or otherwise disturb the other 30 prints during this session.

What this procedure is not
- Not cleaning, retouching, or any chemical or mechanical treatment.
- Not a software fix — no sharpening, contrast boost, noise reduction, despeckle, cloning, or re-mapping of any kind.
- Not a re-shoot with a camera or different scanner.
- Not a re-ID. P007 stays P007, P014 stays P014; nothing is written on the prints.
- Not an opening, handling, or assignment of the eight treated prints. They stay at the conservator's, unassigned, until they return.

Boundaries held: 32 dry loose prints P001–P032 only; two-person check throughout; original print is the source of truth and Saturday's scan of each rescanned side is preserved (renamed), not deleted; rescan logged with date, reason, single parameter change, and two initials.

Kibo's site at day 5 — short answer: yes, that fits a minor local reaction (or a small retained-mouthpart granuloma, which behaves the same way at this stage). Nothing in what you've described points to infection, systemic illness, or allergic reaction today.

What you're describing is the typical post-tick-bite trajectory: a small, mildly raised, pink papule with a dry/crusted center, stable or slowly shrinking over days, with no heat, drainage, expanding redness, or pain. Foreign material from the bite (tiny mouthpart fragments, saliva proteins) can keep a small bump simmering for 1–3 weeks. The dry center is consistent with normal healing, not pus.

Day-to-day care (gentle, do-nothing-by-default)

  - Don't scrub, pick, squeeze, or soak it. Don't apply ointments, essential oils, alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, or topical antibiotic creams unless a vet has specifically directed it. Many topicals are worse than the bite if Kibo licks them.
  - Don't try to dig out anything dark in the center. If retained mouthparts are present, the skin will usually wall them off and either extrude them or quietly encapsulate them. Forcing them out causes more trauma than it solves.
  - Keep Kibo from scratching or rubbing the spot. Most dogs ignore a 4 mm papule; if he works at it, a brief T-shirt or e-collar only as long as needed is reasonable. Persistent focused licking/scratching is itself a sign to call.
  - Look at it once a day, same light, same angle. A daily photo (with a ruler or coin next to it for scale) is the single best evidence tool if anything changes. You want comparable images, not memory.
  - No change to walks, food, or routine is warranted based on what's there now.

Routine vet call (within a day or two, not urgent)

  - The bump grows — clearly larger than 4 mm, or the same size at 2–3 weeks without shrinking.
  - Redness expands beyond a small ring around the bump, especially a slowly spreading flat red patch that looks like a target or has central clearing. (Erythema migrans — early Lyme rash — can appear anywhere from a few days to ~30 days post-bite; day 5 is on the early edge but not impossible.)
  - A small dark speck in the center persists and the site becomes intermittently inflamed or Kibo keeps bothering it.
  - Any new rash, hives, or itchiness elsewhere on the body.
  - Mild lethargy, reduced appetite, or subtle lameness that lasts more than 24 hours.

Urgent / same-day vet call

  - Spreading redness with warmth, swelling, increasing pain, or any drainage from the site (cellulitis / abscess pattern).
  - Facial swelling, hives, sudden itch all over, vomiting, or breathing changes (allergic reaction — uncommon this late but not impossible).
  - Fever-ish signs: panting at rest, warm ears, marked lethargy, refusal to move.
  - Joint swelling, shifting lameness, reluctance to move, or noticeable weakness.
  - Ataxia, wobbly gait, or ascending weakness (tick paralysis is rare and usually tied to an attached tick, but flag any neurological change).
  - Any collapse, repeated vomiting, or blood in stool/urine.

Two regional notes worth keeping on your radar for the next several weeks

  - The Lone Star tick is the most common biter in the Austin area. Beyond the usual tick-borne diseases, it can transmit alpha-gal syndrome — a delayed allergic reaction to mammalian meat (beef, pork, lamb) that can develop weeks after a bite. Not relevant to today's site, but worth knowing in case Kibo has any future vomiting, facial swelling, or hives after eating.
  - For tick-borne illness incubation windows generally: RMSF 2–14 days, ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis 1–2 weeks, Lyme typically weeks. So the relevant observation window for systemic signs isn't just today — it extends through roughly the end of August. Keep notes, not just impressions.

The hallway wall is the safest of the three for this piece. Direct west sun on the living-room wall is the dominant risk, and cooking humidity in the kitchen is a meaningful secondary one that the acrylic does not address at all.

Why the hallway wins on the actual exposure profile

- West light from roughly 3:00 to 5:00 pm is direct, low-angle, and intense. Two hours of direct sun a day compounds. UV-filtering acrylic blocks most ultraviolet (commonly in the high-90s percent range for quality conservation glazing), but visible light, especially the warmer, more energetic wavelengths that dominate late afternoon, still fades watercolor pigments gradually. The acrylic meaningfully slows fading; it does not stop it. The damage from direct sun is dose-dependent, so the worst pattern is repeated daily exposure on the surface the eye naturally rests on.
- Kitchen humidity is a different category of threat. Watercolor paper is hygroscopic, so it expands and contracts with humidity swings; over time this can lift edges, distort the float-mount register, or telegraph through the mat opening. Steam and cooking aerosols also deposit on glazing and frame surfaces and can migrate to the paper edge. UV acrylic does nothing for any of this — it is a glazing material, not a vapor or humidity barrier.
- The hallway's indirect light and steadier humidity give a much lower cumulative dose on both axes. The trade-off is real (you'll view it from farther away), but viewing distance does not change the painting's preservation; light and humidity do.

Practical placement precautions for the hallway

- Hang on a wall that does not receive a direct sightline to any window. Indirect ambient light is fine; raking direct light across the surface is what you want to avoid at all hours, not just 3:00–5:00.
- Keep the frame off exterior walls by an inch or two if you can, and out of any spot where temperature drops at night (behind a door, opposite an uninsulated exterior wall). Stable conditions beat marginally "better lit."
- Keep clear of heating and cooling supply registers, return grilles, and any spot directly above a radiator. Forced air dries paper unevenly and can lift edges of a float-mounted sheet over months.
- Maintain household humidity in the rough 40–55% range. A basic hygrometer near the painting is worth it; sustained readings outside that band are the most common silent cause of paper distortion and foxing in framed work.
- Mount with secure hardware so the frame hangs flat and does not vibrate when doors close. Vibration over years can shift a float-mounted sheet inside its window.
- Hang so the lower edge sits roughly at eye level for the typical viewer in that hallway; this preserves the lower-right pencil signature's visibility and avoids the painting being shaded by a passerby's shadow at close quarters.

Ongoing care, not as a chore but as a light check

- Once a season, look at the painting in raking light (stand to one side so light skims across the glazing) for any haze on the acrylic, edge-lift on the sheet, or change in the mat or backing. A microfiber cloth on the acrylic is fine; do not use ammonia or spray cleaners near the frame.
- If you ever notice afternoon sun reaching the hallway wall during a season change (low sun in winter can sneak into places summer light misses), reposition the frame a few feet rather than waiting for visible fading. Fading in watercolors is not reversible.
- Keep the painting away from the kitchen as a hard rule. Even with the acrylic, grease and steam are the kinds of contaminants that are very hard to undo later.

What the UV acrylic is actually doing for you here, so the framing of risk stays honest

- It is meaningfully reducing the UV portion of the daily dose, which is the most aggressively damaging part of sunlight for organic pigments and paper.
- It is not eliminating visible-light fading, it is not a humidity or vapor barrier, it is not a thermal shield, and it does not substitute for placement. Its job is to slow one component of one risk on the better-lit of your two viable walls.

If you want a single rule of thumb for the next few years: hallway, indirect light, stable humidity, eyes-on check twice a year. That posture is what will keep the sheet, the signature, and the pale wash on the right looking the way it does now.

Noted — no plan changes will be made automatically. Here are the standard options for absorbing a temporary spike during a planned migration window, with the tradeoff each one carries:

1. Do nothing. Let the spike land, accept any rate limits, throttling, or per-event overage charges.
   Best when you have lots of headroom and overage is cheap.
   Risk: hard caps can fail the migration outright.

2. Pre-stage / flatten the spike at the application layer before cutover.
   Batch non-critical work, raise cache TTLs, defer heavy jobs, move backfill out of the window.
   Zero vendor changes, fully reversible.
   Only works if the spike source is something you control, not the migration itself.

3. Buy a one-off burst pack or event credits, leaving the base plan untouched.
   Targeted, doesn't alter recurring billing, easy to walk back.
   Usually worse unit economics than a tier upgrade, and not every platform offers it.

4. Temporary tier uplift with a hard scheduled reversion.
   Upgrade for the migration window, downgrade the day after.
   Cleanest headroom, but requires manual scheduling and a real calendar reminder — the missed-revert is the classic failure mode here, so I'd want the revert date written down before the upgrade is requested, not after.

5. Request a short, time-boxed quota bump from the vendor.
   Some platforms will grant a temporary lift for a known event if you ask in advance.
   Free, supported, but needs lead time and a written confirmation of the exact numbers and end date.

6. Move the migration window itself to a lower-traffic slot.
   Doesn't reduce absolute usage, but reduces user-visible impact.
   Useful if the failure mode is customer-facing latency, not a hard cap.

Here is the comparison. Both options have identical coverage — $40K personal property and $300K liability — so the only real difference is the deductible and the premium.

  OPTION A — $1,000 deductible, $312/year
  OPTION B — $2,500 deductible, $276/year

Annual savings from raising the deductible: $36.
Extra out-of-pocket per property claim: $1,500.

The math, stated as break-even

Option B is only a net win if the savings ($36 × years held) outweigh the extra $1,500 you absorb on a claim.

$36/yr × N = $1,500  →  N ≈ 41.7 years.

That is: you would have to go ~42 years between property claims just to break even on the lower premium. Anything shorter than that and Option B has cost you more.

Stated as a probability question

Equivalently: for any given year, a renter needs to face a property-claim probability of at least 2.4% (36 / 1500) for Option A to be the cheaper choice in expectation. Industry-wide renters claim frequency for property loss (theft, fire, water, etc.) is well above that threshold for most households. Add the recent Cherrywood upstairs-leak episode — water-backup is one of the more common covered losses and is exactly the kind of event the $5K water-backup endorsement is sized for — and the expected-value case for Option A gets stronger, not weaker.

What the deductible actually applies to

Important nuance worth flagging before you call: a renters-insurance deductible applies to property loss, not liability. So a $2,500 deductible makes you worse off only if you have a covered property loss (theft, fire, water damage to your belongings, etc.). It does not change your exposure on a liability claim, which is unchanged at the $300K limit. So the question really is "how likely are we to file a property claim in the next policy term" — and given water-backup endorsement, two adults working, a dog in the household, and an upstairs neighbor who has already leaked once, "very low" is not a safe assumption.

Pattern check

You and Sam previously chose the higher-premium option on the Cherrywood policy to get replacement-cost treatment and a lower deductible ($84/yr extra for replacement cost, deductible at $500). The logic there was the same: small annual premium to cap out-of-pocket exposure on a real event. By that standard, the inverse move here — saving $36/yr by raising your deductible by $1,500 — is a worse tradeoff than the Cherrywood decision was.

Recommendation

Keep the $1,000 deductible at $312/year (Option A).

The $36 annual saving is not large enough to justify $1,500 of additional per-claim exposure, the break-even horizon (~42 years between claims) is implausibly long, and the household's recent water-loss history makes the relevant claim probability meaningfully above the 2.4% threshold.

Two things worth confirming with the insurer before you lock it in by Friday afternoon:

  1. Does the $2,500 deductible apply per occurrence or per claim year? Some carriers structure it as a flat per-incident; others treat it as an annual aggregate. Get that in writing.
  2. Is the higher deductible still paired with the same $5K water-backup endorsement, or does that endorsement carry its own (often separate, sometimes smaller) deductible? Water-backup often does — which would change the calculus materially if it stays at $1,000 while property goes to $2,500.

The current picture fits normal resolution of a tick-bite reaction: the acute inflammation (pink, raised bump) has settled and only a small dry scab remains, with no heat, drainage, swelling, tenderness, or enlargement, and normal behavior. That's the expected trajectory at day 14.

1. Leave the dry scab alone.
  - Picking, peeling, or scrubbing it risks reopening the wound, introducing bacteria, and restarting the local inflammation that just resolved.
  - Don't apply ointments, creams, alcohol, hydrogen peroxide, or essential oils to the site.
  - If he scratches at it with the hind paw and reopens it, that's itself a routine-call trigger (see below), but until then, no intervention is needed.

2. Cleaning is minimal and only when there's a real reason.
  - Routine cleaning is not needed at this stage. The scab is doing its job.
  - If the area gets visibly dirty (after a yard session, a bath, sweaty weather, or pollen), a single gentle wipe with a soft cloth or gauze moistened with plain warm water or sterile saline, then pat dry, is enough.
  - Don't soak the scab. Don't use antiseptic wipes, chlorhexidine, or peroxide on intact healing skin — they damage new epithelium and slow closure.
  - Keep the area dry after walks and baths. The skin fold behind the ear traps moisture, which is the main local risk factor at this stage.

3. Routine (non-urgent) veterinary call would be warranted despite the overall improvement if any of these appear:
  - Local:
    - The scab persists for several more weeks without falling off naturally, or a small firm lump develops under or around it (possible retained mouthparts / tick-bite granuloma — common, benign, but worth a look).
    - New or returning redness, heat, swelling, or itch that makes him scratch.
    - Mild drainage, crusting that spreads, or a slowly enlarging bald patch.
    - Any new skin change that doesn't normalize within roughly 4–6 weeks total from the removal date.
  - Whole body (these overlap with the tick-borne disease monitoring window — separate category):
    - Low-grade lethargy, reduced appetite, or a low-grade fever feel.
    - New limping, joint stiffness, or seeming sore somewhere not obviously injured.
    - Repeated vomiting, diarrhea, or a notable change in drinking or urination.

The urgent-care red flags from the August 1 guidance still apply and are unchanged: spreading redness with pain, marked swelling, pus, behavioral collapse, breathing change, jaundice, sustained fever, sudden lameness, or neurological signs. None of those are present here.

One separate note on the timeline: tick-borne disease incubation in dogs is typically 2–4 weeks (Lyme, ehrlichia, anaplasma, RMSF vary by region and pathogen). Day 14 is still inside that window, so the next 2–4 weeks remain a passive monitoring period for whole-body signs — no testing or preventive antibiotics are indicated purely because of the bite, but any of the routine triggers above is a reasonable reason to call rather than wait for an urgent one.

Anchor the figure with a cool cast shadow on the floor only, in two dry-down glazes. Never on Kibo.

  Setup before any pigment:
    - Re-trace where the light rim sits on Kibo's back and keep a deliberate clean gap around that edge. The rim is the priority. If anything below forces a choice, the rim wins.
    - Keep Kibo out of the immediate area while the glaze is wet. He will step in it.
    - Have two cool mixes ready in the palette, the second slightly stronger than the first, both transparent.

  Mix recommendations (paper is cotton cold-press and fully dry):
    - Penumbra mix: very dilute ultramarine plus a hair of burnt sienna, mostly water. The burnt sienna is small enough that the read stays cool, but it stops the blue from going synthetic against warm fur.
    - Umbra mix: the same two pigments, just less water. Ultramarine still leads; burnt sienna is the bridge to the fur.
    - Avoid Payne's gray and any black-based gray. Neutral is exactly the pasted-on problem you are trying to leave.

  Sequence:

    1.  Penumbra glaze first, broader and softer.
        - Damp (not wet) brush, well-loaded and not dripping.
        - Lay it only on the floor, fading away from Kibo. Stop short of the fur with a clean, deliberate margin. Aim to read as cast shadow, not as edge shading on the figure.
        - No glaze on Kibo himself. Cool pigment pulled into rust fur will dirty both.

    2.  Dry fully. Not surface-dry, bone dry, including any dampness in the gap next to Kibo. Cold-press holds moisture longer than it looks; give it several minutes past the point the surface seems dry.

    3.  Umbra glaze second, narrow and dense.
        - Smaller brush, same cool hue, slightly stronger.
        - Sit it only at the contact line where Kibo meets the floor and the small wedge under his chest and tucked haunches.
        - Keep this glaze short. It is the anchor, not the body of the shadow. The penumbra does most of the work of grounding him.

    4.  Dry fully again.

    5.  Stop and look at normal viewing distance before any third pass. A day or two of looking is even better.

  If after the second dry-down the shadow still reads pasted-on:
    - Most likely cause is that the umbra is too short. Tighten it under the chest and tucked limbs rather than darkening across the whole shadow.
    - Second most likely cause is that the penumbra is too uniform. Soften the far edge with a barely damp clean brush and a dry tissue lift while the glaze is still damp, and only on a test scrap of the same paper first since this paper's tooth catches lifts differently than the dry glaze will.
    - If either step puts the rim at risk, stop. A study with a preserved rim and a slightly weak shadow reads better than a study with a strong shadow and a lost rim.

  Things to actively avoid on this pass:
    - No glazing on Kibo's fur. The cast shadow lives on the floor; the rim stays clean.
    - No wet-into-wet into the warm fur.
    - No reworking the existing fur wash. If more cool is needed, build it on the floor side of the rim, not on the fur.
    - No Payne's gray, ivory black, or tube neutral.
    - No facial details yet. The face will want a different light cue than the rim, and is easier to commit to once the ground is settled. Save it for a separate pass when the cast shadow is fully dry.
