Temporary plan for the 40 stabilized photographs through the A/C outage. Conservative, reversible, no interventions on the materials themselves.

WHAT THIS IS NOT
- Not opening the boxes to inspect individual prints. Sleeves are clear, condition was just stabilized by the conservator on Aug 9, and any handling now adds more risk than six hours at 67% RH.
- Not wiping, brushing, fanning, drying, or treating any surface. Sleeves are the only interface.
- Not adding desiccant packs, silica gel, rice, fans pointed at the boxes, or anything that would drop the box interior humidity faster than the room humidity.
- Not refrigerating or freezing. Condensation risk on rewarming is worse than the current exposure.
- Not removing prints from sleeves for any reason.

WHY SIX HOURS AT 67% RH IS NOT A CRISIS BY ITSELF
- Mold growth on stable photographic paper generally needs sustained RH well above 65% for 48-72 hours or longer. Six hours is short of that window by a wide margin.
- The boxes and sleeves act as a buffer, so the interior of a closed box lags the room by a noticeable amount.
- The visible signs you would expect from a real problem are absent: no condensation, no odor, no tackiness, no visible change. That is consistent with the prints being fine.

RELOCATION
- Pick an interior room away from exterior walls, direct sun, and HVAC supply vents. Interior hallway closet, interior bedroom closet, or an interior wall of the living room or dining room are good options.
- Avoid basement, attic, garage, kitchen, bathroom, laundry, near windows, and anywhere with a known moisture source.
- Keep the boxes closed and flat during the move. Support from the bottom, do not tilt them on edge, do not stack anything on top.
- Once placed, leave them undisturbed for the rest of the day. Do not move them again unless conditions clearly worsen.

ROOM CONDITIONS TO MAINTAIN
- Aim for the room to settle back into the 40-55% RH range over hours, not minutes. If you run a whole-home dehumidifier or the HVAC has a dehumidify mode, that is fine. A point-source dehumidifier in the same room on a low setting is also fine if it pulls RH down gradually, which a normal residential unit does.
- Do not aim a dehumidifier or fan directly at the boxes.
- Keep the room temperature stable. Avoid cranking the A/C down hard once it is fixed; a gradual return to normal is the goal.
- If the repair runs late and you have no cooling, prioritize getting interior room RH below 60% over lowering temperature.

MONITORING WITHOUT OPENING
- Place a small battery hygrometer-thermometer on the shelf near the boxes, not inside them. Note the reading once after placement.
- Glance at the hygrometer two or three times during the day. That is enough.
- From outside the boxes only, look at the box exteriors: any surface dampness, darkening, warping, or visible mold.
- Do not lift lids. Do not open sleeves. Do not unwrap anything.
- Do not move the boxes to "check on them." Movement is the main avoidable risk during this window.

SIGNS THAT WARRANT CONSERVATOR ADVICE
- Visible condensation on the outside of the boxes, on sleeves, or anywhere in the room near the prints.
- Any new musty, sour, or "old basement" smell from the boxes when you are near them at normal distance.
- Any visible mold: white, green, gray, or black fuzzy or powdery growth, including a single small spot.
- Tacky or sticky surface on a sleeve or box exterior.
- Cockling, warping, rippling, or any visible distortion of paper or sleeves.
- Sustained indoor RH above 70% for more than a few hours, or any reading above 75%.
- Indoor temperature swings larger than about 10°F day-to-night, or conditions staying above about 80°F for many hours.
- A/C repair is delayed past today and humidity is climbing or holding high.

IF NONE OF THOSE APPEAR
- Treat the exposure as a stress event the prints came through. Once A/C is restored and room RH is back in the normal range, leave the boxes where they are for another 24 hours to let interior and exterior humidity equalize gradually before any future handling.
- Do not re-sleeve, re-box, or re-inventory on the day A/C returns. Defer that until the prints have re-equilibrated to normal room conditions.

RECORD-KEEPING
- One short note is enough: date, approximate duration of elevated RH, peak reading if you caught it, where the boxes were moved, and any of the conservator-trigger signs observed or not observed. This protects the provenance of P001-P032 and the treated eight if anything is questioned later.
- Do not open boxes to confirm condition as part of this note.

Net effect: keep them still, keep them closed, let the room come back to them, and treat any of the trigger signs as the line for escalating, not the duration of the event itself.

Short answer: replace the tire before riding to work again. A boot is a get-home-or-get-to-the-shop tool, not a fix for ordinary commuting.

Why visible casing is the deciding fact:

The sidewall is structural. The casing plies you're seeing through the cut carry the tire's load in flex and tension every revolution. A cut that exposes casing means those plies are severed at that spot, so the remaining plies now take disproportionate load right there. A boot sits between the tube and the inside of the tire. It can keep the tube from extruding through the hole, but it does not restore the missing plies and it does not stop the cut from propagating under repeated flexing.

"Holds pressure" and "no bulge" describe the tube and the tire at rest. Under commute loading — your weight, curb impacts, sustained flexing over miles — the cut can zipper, a bulge can develop mid-ride, and a sidewall blowout is possible. A sidewall blowout on a loaded commute is a crash-and-injury event, not a flat-and-walk-home event. The current state is not predictive of the loaded state.

This is the same scenario your mechanic resolved in February 2024: ~8 mm sidewall cut with visible casing, tube and rim fine, tire replaced for $58. That call was correct, and the same logic applies here. The fact that nothing has visibly changed since you found it doesn't change the structural finding.

What a boot is actually for:

A boot is a roadside emergency measure to keep the tube from poking through a hole long enough to walk or slow-ride the bike home or to a shop at very low speed and light load. It is not a substitute for replacement when you intend to keep loading the tire on a normal commute.

Practical options for the next commute:

  - Replace the tire (yourself or via shop) before the commute.
  - If a replacement isn't possible in time, do not commute on this tire. Use transit, a rideshare, or get a lift for that one ride, and get the bike to the shop for replacement separately.
  - Keep the boot in the saddle bag for genuine "I have to get this bike home" emergencies, not for daily use.

Verification: $18,960 ÷ 52 = $364.6154…, which rounds to $364.62. The arithmetic is right; the labeling is the problem. Here is the distinction.

What Marcus's calculation actually computes
It divides the mature Helio Start cohort's refund-adjusted cash by the count of admitted workspaces in that matched cohort. The result — $364.62 per workspace — is the observed average organic cash per admitted workspace in this specific group: pricing-page-referred, organic-through-Q3, 52 workspaces, cash already net of same-day full refunds, zero-cash credit invoices, and the three later refunds mapped on Aug 13. It is a descriptive mean of cash collected from this cohort, not a cost figure.

What a paid CAC requires
A customer acquisition cost is a ratio of acquisition spend to acquired customers, and it is meaningful only when (a) there is a real acquisition cost on the numerator, (b) there is a defined acquisition channel or mix on the denominator, and (c) the comparison isolates the incremental effect of that spend versus a baseline. Concretely, a paid CAC read needs:

1. Paid-media spend attributable to the cohort (campaign cost, creative/tooling cost, agency or platform fees, allocated overhead).
2. An acquisition channel definition (which channels, which campaigns, which time window, which geos, which audiences).
3. An incremental comparison: response in the paid-exposed group versus a matched holdout or organic baseline, so the read measures lift caused by the spend rather than demand that would have arrived anyway.
4. A response definition tied to the channel (e.g., a pricing-page signup, a first paid, a paid-active at day 90) and consistent rules about refunds, chargebacks, and assisted conversions.
5. A cohort the spend actually bought, not a cohort that arrived through organic surfaces.

Why this cohort produces none of those
- There is no paid-media spend on the numerator. The organic-through-Q3 boundary means no acquisition dollars were committed against this group. The numerator is cash collected, not cost incurred.
- There is no acquisition channel defined for these workspaces. They came in through pricing-page referral under the pre-Q3 organic boundary; no paid campaign, no mix, no channel-level response data exists for them.
- There is no incremental comparison. There is no holdout, no geo split, no time-window test, and no paid-vs-organic contrast. The cohort is uniformly organic, so "without paid spend" is not a controlled counterfactual here — it is the only state we have.
- The response side (cash) is not a paid-channel response. It is observed cash from organic-arriving workspaces. Dividing cash by workspace count tells you what those workspaces paid, not what it cost to bring them in.
- Calling $364.62 a CAC inverts the ratio. A CAC is cost ÷ acquired customers; this is cash ÷ organic customers. The two ratios answer different questions even when the numbers happen to match.

What "incremental cost of acquiring a workspace" would actually require
To produce that number, we would need a separate, designed test: a paid-channel pilot with preregistered CAC target, payback window, and stop-loss; a randomized or geographically separated exposure; a matched organic holdout; account-level joining of spend to acquired workspaces; the same refund-adjusted cash treatment applied to the paid cohort; and the same account-level support evidence. None of that infrastructure exists for the matched organic cohort, and creating it retroactively from this group is not possible — the organic cohort cannot tell you what would have happened with paid spend behind it.

What this number is good evidence for
The matched organic cohort supports descriptive, account-level analysis: refund-adjusted cash per workspace, post-admission effort, zero-contact share, separate pre-admission and billing contact lines, and the joint read of mature retention, refund-adjusted cash, and account-level support that any later paid-acquisition proposal must pair together. Those are real and useful, and Owen's Aug 14 join already paired each workspace's refund-adjusted cash with account-level support at the account level. None of those descriptive uses turn into a CAC by dividing by 52.

What should happen with Marcus's draft
The $364.62 figure should be relabeled as "observed average refund-adjusted cash per admitted workspace in the matched organic Helio Start cohort through Aug 9" — with the Aug 13 refund mappings called out — and kept inside the descriptive account-level evidence pack. It should not be quoted as an allowable CAC, a paid-acquisition benchmark, a payback input, or a basis for authorizing a paid test. The mature retention, refund-adjusted cash, and account-level support evidence remain bundled for any future paid-acquisition proposal; that bundle is necessary but not sufficient, because the paid-cost side still has to be produced by an actual paid test, not inferred from an organic cohort.

Bottom line
$364.62 is a true arithmetic result and a meaningful descriptive statistic for this organic cohort. It is not a CAC, it does not measure incremental acquisition cost, it does not support a paid test on its own, and treating it as allowable paid-acquisition CAC would put a paid-acquisition claim in front of stakeholders using evidence that contains no paid-acquisition cost. The right next step is to keep the descriptive bundle intact and require a designed paid-channel pilot, with its own preregistered CAC target and stop-loss, before any paid-acquisition number is circulated.

The $14 difference is simple subtraction (58 − 44 = $14), so I'll proceed without a calculator tool.

Recommendation: the puncture-protected 700×32 at $58 installed.

Tradeoff, framed honestly:

- The lighter 700×32 saves $14 once. A single commute-ending failure (pinch flat, sidewall cut, wet-road slip that demands an unexpected stop) costs far more than $14 in lost time, recovery, or damage to a freshly replaced tube/casing. With your stated priorities — rough pavement, occasional wet conditions, predictability over rotational weight — the cheaper tire is paying for savings you don't value and accepting failure modes you do.
- The puncture-protected casing is the part that matters for your conditions: extra rubber/puncture belt reduces flats from road debris, and the slightly heavier, more robust casing is more resistant to the kind of sidewall failure that just sidelined your current tire. "Lighter" in commuter tires usually means thinner casing — which is the opposite of what you want on rough pavement and is worse, not better, in wet grip because it runs closer to the wear threshold.
- Wet-condition grip on rough city pavement comes mostly from tire volume, tread pattern, and casing integrity, not from saving a couple hundred grams of rotational mass. At 700×32 (a comfortable commuter width), the rotational-weight difference between two same-size tires is small enough that you won't feel it; you will feel a flat or a cut.
- $14 over the life of a tire (typically 2,000–3,000 miles for a commuter) is roughly half a cent per mile. It's not a meaningful economic decision.

What the cheaper tire is actually trading away is exactly the failure mode you just experienced (a sidewall cut that took the bike off the road for a shop trip) plus the puncture risk that hits hardest when you're commuting on a schedule in mixed weather.

Go with the $58 puncture-protected tire. The $14 isn't the deciding axis — the deciding axis is which tire is less likely to put you back in the shop or on a sidewalk walk-home.

Method: primary owns the minutes, secondary stays a flag.

Pick one tag per contact as the primary. Every other tag on that contact is a secondary flag — present/absent only, no minutes claimed. One rule, applied to all 66 contacts:

- Single-tag contacts (43): the one tag is primary. No ambiguity.
- Mixed contacts (23): the tag CS flagged as primary in the notes, if any; otherwise the first issue type mentioned in the note. Document the rule once and apply mechanically.

This gives 66 primaries whose minutes sum to exactly 684, because each contact's minutes are owned by exactly one primary tag. No double-count, no per-tag minute split, no invented precision.

Three operating reads from that one assignment:

1. Primary-tag minutes table. Tag, contact count, minutes, share of 684. Sums reconcile: 66 contacts, 684 minutes, 21 distinct workspaces. This is the headline issue-mix view.

2. Secondary-tag incidence. For each tag, the count of contacts where it appears anywhere — primary or secondary. This is the "issue surface" view: it shows which topics co-occur without claiming minutes for the co-occurrence. Useful for spotting compound issues.

3. Co-occurrence pairs. Among the 23 mixed contacts, which (primary, secondary) pairs appear, and how often. Frequency only, no minutes. This is where you see "permissions often travels with automation-design" or similar patterns.

Compound-issue indicator: 23 of 66 contacts carry more than one tag. That fraction (34.8%) is the share of contacts where complexity compounds, independent of minutes.

What this is not:

- Not a minute-weighted issue mix within a contact. You don't have per-tag minutes for the 23 mixed contacts, and you are not inventing any.
- Not a capacity, staffing, demand, or forecast read.

LOAD-DEPENDENT REAR-WHEEL RUB — likely causes, parking-lot checks, whether to accept the bike

"Rhythmic" plus "only with my weight on the bike" means something is moving into the tire's path when rider load flexes the frame, fork, or wheel a small amount. The tire, tube, and casing look fine, so the issue is mechanical. In rough order of likelihood:

1. Brake pad or rotor contact under load
   - Rim brakes: pads were set just clear on the stand, but rider weight flexes the seatstays enough to close the gap. Or the pads were simply placed too close during the install. A new tire can also change the effective rim position slightly, which puts one pad too close.
   - Disc brakes: a slightly warped rotor (common after transport or a wheel re-dish), a caliper that is not perfectly centered, or loose caliper bolts. Rotors flex more under load than on a stand, so a slight warp becomes a rub point you can hear each revolution. Loose caliper bolts let the whole caliper shift under load.
2. Frame, fender, or chainstay clearance
   A 700x32 is wider than the typical 700x25 or 700x28 commuter tire. Even with no visible bulge, the carcass spreads slightly under rider weight. If the frame was already close to the old tire's edge, the new one may now kiss the chainstay, seatstay, or a fender stay under load but not on the stand. This is a real wear risk — riding it would abrade the new tire's casing, exactly the kind of damage that ended the last tire.
3. Wheel not fully seated in the dropouts
   A quick-release skewer that was not clamped firmly enough, or a thru-axle not torqued to spec, lets the wheel shift fore-aft or laterally under load. The shift brings the rim closer to one pad or pulls the rotor into the caliper. This is the one that worries me most for a commute — sustained pedaling load is harsher than a parking-lot roll, and a rear wheel that shifts mid-ride is a serious safety event.
4. Wheel out of true from the install
   New tire and tube change spoke load balance. The shop should have re-checked trueing after the tire was mounted and seated, not before. A small hop or side-to-side wobble in the rim reads as a rhythmic rub that was not present on the old tire.

QUICK PARKING-LOT CHECKS YOU CAN DO RIGHT NOW

- With your weight off the bike, look down the line of the rim or rotor as a helper spins the wheel slowly. Any visible hop, side wobble, or a single-spot rub mark on the rotor = the wheel or rotor is out of true.
- Disc brakes: with the wheel off the ground, squeeze the brake lever firmly once and release. On a mechanical disc caliper this recenters the pads via the slide mechanism. Re-spin and see if the rub is gone. If so, it was a centering issue and is a 60-second fix with a 5 mm Allen and a torque wrench.
- Rim brakes: sit on the bike, both feet on pedals, and have a helper look at the pad-to-rim gap on both sides under load. If one side visibly closes to near zero, the pads need re-centering or the wheel needs re-seating.
- Tire clearance: sit on the bike loaded, helper watches the gap between tire and chainstay, seatstay, and any fender on both sides. If the gap closes or the tire touches the frame under load, it is a clearance issue and the bike is not safe to ride as-is.
- Wheel security: grab the top of the wheel and try to rock it fore-aft in the dropouts. Any movement means the QR or thru-axle is not holding. Do not ride.
- QR lever: when fully closed, the lever should leave a clear imprint in your palm. If it swings closed with no resistance in the last 90 degrees, the cam is not engaging and the wheel is loose.

WHAT TO TELL THE SHOP

Tell them the rub appears only with your weight on the bike, not on the stand. That tells them it is a load-geometry problem, not a static-alignment problem. Ask them, in order, to:

  a. Verify wheel true and dish after the new tire is mounted and seated.
  b. Confirm QR skewer or thru-axle torque to spec, and that the wheel does not shift under hand pressure in the dropouts.
  c. Check brake pad-to-rim or pad-to-rotor clearance under load — either with you sitting on the bike or with a known-weight stand-in.
  d. Check tire-to-frame and tire-to-fender clearance at full load, both sides.
  e. True the rotor or rim if the rhythmic rub persists after the above.

A re-check on the stand after a fix is not sufficient. They need to reproduce your weight on the bike before they hand it back.

SHOULD YOU DECLINE TO RIDE

Yes. Decline acceptance and leave the bike with the shop. Reasons:

1. Load-dependent geometry changes are exactly what an acceptance test is supposed to catch. The shop did not catch it; you did. Until they verify it under load, you have no evidence the bike is safe for sustained riding rather than a parking-lot loop.
2. If the cause is brake rub under load, riding it to work would generate heat and wear on the pad and rotor or pad and rim surface that was just installed. That is damage you would be paying for.
3. If the cause is a wheel not fully seated, sustained pedaling load is more demanding than a parking-lot roll. The condition can worsen between the shop and your office, and a rear wheel that shifts under load is a safety event, not a nuisance.
4. If the cause is frame clearance, the new tire would be grinding against the frame or fender with every revolution under load. That abrades the casing of a tire you just paid $58 to install, the same kind of damage that ended the previous tire.
5. From a practical standpoint, leaving the bike is the only way to keep the diagnosis on the shop's side of the counter. Riding it and bringing it back gives them a defensible "you rode it" line if a later issue is related.

If you must get the bike home because you walked or biked-share there, do not ride it on the road. Push or walk it. A one-mile walk with a brake or frame rub under load is harmless to the bike. Riding it would be the mistake, and your ankle is in a clean three-day gate window right now — losing it to a sketchy bike handling decision would not be a good trade.

In short: the tire itself looks fine. The install or the geometry around the new tire does not, and it has not been verified under the conditions you will actually use it in. That is the shop's problem to resolve before you accept the bike, not yours to discover on the commute.

Today's picture (shallow scrape on the pad edge, oozing stopped with pressure, full weight-bearing, no flap, no embedded material, no gapping on toe flexion) fits a minor superficial abrasion. Home care is reasonable. The thresholds below are the real decision points, not the wound itself.

Cleaning today
  Use lukewarm tap water or sterile saline. Low-pressure rinse from a cup or slow faucet, 30–60 seconds. Pat dry with clean gauze or paper towel — do not rub.
  Acceptable: dilute chlorhexidine (0.05%) or a very dilute povidone-iodine solution (pale tea color) if you have it; saline or water alone is fine for this depth.
  Avoid: hydrogen peroxide, rubbing alcohol, essential oils, tea tree, vinegar, undiluted ointments, and any topical antibiotic without vet direction. Peroxide/alcohol damage granulating tissue; dogs lick; some topicals are toxic if ingested.

Short-term protection
  Goal: keep it clean, dry, and shielded from licking for ~5–7 days until a firm scab forms.
  Covering during outings and overnight: a non-adherent pad (Telfa-style) over the wound, then a soft wrap or a breathable dog bootie/sock. No sticky adhesive directly on the wound or on fur.
  Change the cover once daily. When you swap it, leave the paw uncovered for 30–60 minutes while supervised so it can air-dry.
  If he reaches the cover or keeps licking, use an e-collar or inflatable collar during the uncovered window and overnight.
  No puddles, mud, lawn chemicals, orlicking in between changes. If the cover gets wet or soiled, replace it.

Activity
  Shorten walks to ~5–10 minutes for the next few days, leash only, on flat smooth surfaces.
  Hard-surface sidewalks are fine; avoid gravel, broken pavement, hot asphalt (back-of-hand test, 7 seconds), sand, and ice-melt-treated paths.
  No running, jumping, fetch, stairs-for-exercise, or dog-park play until the pad is closed, dry, and non-tender on palpation.
  Recheck the pad visually before each outing — if it reopens, oozes again, or looks deeper, hold walks to just potty breaks and call the vet.

Same-day vet call (routine appointment or phone triage, not the ER)
  Bleeding that restarts and doesn't stop within 5–10 minutes of clean gentle pressure.
  Increasing redness, swelling, warmth, or visible pain over the next 24–48 hours.
  Discharge that turns thick, creamy, yellow, green, or develops odor.
  New or worsening lameness, favoring, or refusal to bear weight at any recheck.
  Wound gapes, edges separate, or a flap you didn't see before becomes visible.
  Licking that reopens the wound or keeps it constantly wet despite covering.
  Anything you can't rinse out of the wound bed.
  Systemic signs: off food, lethargy, feverish feel, restlessness out of proportion.

Urgent care / ER (go today, not wait for a routine slot)
  Pulsing or spurting bleeding (arterial).
  Pad torn with a visible flap, deep gash, or exposed deeper tissue.
  Large or deeply embedded object you can't easily lift out, or suspicion a fragment broke off inside.
  Rapidly swelling, hot, very painful paw with refusal to bear any weight after a few hours.
  Pale gums, collapse, vomiting, or any sign of shock.

Quick 24–48 hour checklist
  Reinspect once in the evening and again tomorrow morning — same checks: dry? flat? non-tender? no discharge?
  Trimming hair away from the wound edge helps keep discharge from matting in.
  If tomorrow's recheck shows a clean, dry, non-tender scab with full weight and no licking, you're on track. If anything on the same-day list appears, make the call; anything on the urgent list, go in.

Bottom line: this is a home-care scenario today, with explicit go-still thresholds rather than vague reassurance. The two real risks over the next 48 hours are infection (red/warm/swollen/discharge/pain) and self-trauma (licking reopening it), and both have clean triggers above.

This morning's event is a soft re-injury of a healing surface, not a fresh wound. The single pinpoint bleed that stopped within a minute of gentle pressure, combined with weight-bearing normally, no gape on toe flexion, and no swelling, heat, discharge, odor, debris, or flap, is consistent with the licking breaking through the new epithelial layer rather than reopening the original scrape in any structural way. The disturbance does change one thing: because the scabbed surface has been broken again, treat any new finding over the next 24–48 hours as if the wound were freshly opened, not mid-healing.

Cleaning (right now, before re-covering)

  - Rinse the paw briefly with cool water or sterile saline to remove saliva and any outdoor grit. A gentle stream from a cup is enough; you don't need to soak.
  - No hydrogen peroxide. No alcohol. Both damage the new epithelial cells you are trying to preserve. You already know this from the March 4 decision; same rule applies.
  - Pat dry with clean gauze or a lint-free paper towel. Don't rub.
  - If you have dilute chlorhexidine 0.05% (the standard pet wound rinse), one quick wipe over the spot and the surrounding pad is reasonable. If not, plain saline or water is fine. Skip povidone-iodine; it stings and stains the pad.
  - Re-check the spot after drying: no flap, no gape, no embedded material, no fresh bleeding when you gently blot. If any of those change, that is the first decision point below.

Re-covering (the part that failed last night)

  - The loose sock was the failure mode, not the bandaging. The cover needs to stay on through normal movement, friction on the floor, and the dog's attempts to remove it.
  - Layer order: non-adherent pad (Telfa or similar) directly over the spot, sized to cover just the affected pad edge. Then a thin layer of rolled gauze if the pad moves around. Then a self-adherent cohesive wrap (Vetwrap-style) around the paw and just above the carpus — snug enough that two fingers slip underneath but not so loose it slides. Stretch the wrap as you go; don't pull it tight at the top edge.
  - Then the sock. Two changes that meaningfully reduce slip-off:
      1. Size down, or use a baby/child sock that ends below the carpus rather than above it. Less leverage for the dog to work it down.
      2. A single strip of 1-inch medical tape at the top of the sock, wrapped once around the limb above the carpus, sticky side to the sock only (not to fur). Acts as a cuff. Easy to remove later by cutting the tape, not pulling the wrap.
  - Alternative if the sock keeps failing: a proper dog bootie with a Velcro or zip closure. These hold better than a pulled-on sock but must be removed at night so the paw can air out and you can re-check the spot.
  - Walks: keep the cover on for outdoor walks today; take it off for the in-house rest periods so the pad can dry. Each time you remove the cover, re-check the spot against the criteria below before putting a fresh one on.

Cone decision

  - Yes, use an e-collar for the unsupervised and resting windows. The fact that the sock came off and licking produced a bleed means the cover alone is not enough to break the lick cycle. The cone doesn't have to be on all day; it has to be on when you cannot actively interrupt him.
  - Specific windows where the cone should be on:
      - Overnight and any nap longer than ~20 minutes
      - Any time you leave the room, even briefly
      - First 30–60 minutes after you re-cover the paw (licking temptation is highest right after handling)
  - During supervised calm time (you're on the couch, watching him), the cone can come off IF he leaves the paw alone. The moment he looks at it or starts to turn, the cone goes back on.
  - Type: a rigid plastic cone is the most reliable. Inflatable collars and soft cones are better tolerated but many dogs can still reach a front paw with them. If you have only a soft collar, test it under supervision before relying on it overnight.
  - The cone is a contingency, not a fixture. Once the surface has re-epithelialized (typically 2–4 days for a superficial pad scrape if he leaves it alone), you can drop the cone during supervised time first, then overnight, then drop the sock during indoor rest. Don't drop all three at once.

Same-day veterinary call thresholds (call your regular vet today or tomorrow)

Call during normal hours, same day, if any of these appear:
  - Bleeding recurs and doesn't stop within 2–3 minutes of gentle direct pressure
  - The spot looks wider or deeper than this morning, or you can see a flap, a defined edge, or a gape when the toes flex (this morning it didn't gape; if that changes, call)
  - New swelling, increased warmth, or the pad becomes tender when you press gently around the spot
  - Any discharge: cloudy, yellow, green, or foul-smelling. Clear pink-tinged ooze in the first few hours after re-injury is normal; anything colored or smelly is not
  - He starts favoring the paw or shows a limp at any point, even briefly
  - You find embedded material you can't rinse out with cool water
  - He repeatedly removes a properly-secured cover within the first 24 hours despite the cone. That means the licking drive is high enough that home containment isn't going to hold
  - Behavioral change: inappetence, lethargy, hiding, or guarding the paw when you approach

Urgent-care / emergency-vet thresholds (go now, regardless of hour)

Go directly to urgent or emergency care if any of these appear:
  - Active bleeding that does not stop with 5 minutes of firm direct pressure
  - Sudden, visible swelling of the whole paw or digits, especially with heat
  - The wound gapes open, or you can see deeper tissue (subdermal, fat, tendon)
  - A torn nail or bleeding from the nail bed, separate from the pad scrape
  - Pale, white, or tacky gums, or any sign of shock concurrent with the paw issue
  - Repeated vomiting, collapse, or unresponsiveness
  - A suspected deeper foreign body (a thorn fragment, glass) that you can feel but can't extract with gentle saline rinse
  - He bites or snaps when you try to inspect, beyond normal paw sensitivity — that can indicate significant pain and warrants hands-on assessment

Monitoring for the next 24–48 hours

  - Re-check the spot twice today (midday and before bed) and once tomorrow morning, each time the cover is off.
  - The re-injury extends the clock. Treat the next 48 hours as the new healing window. If the spot is dry, flat, and pink at the 48-hour mark with no licking attempts, the cone can be retired first, the sock second.
  - Walks today: keep them short, on clean dry pavement, cover on. Avoid grass, dirt, and any surface that could reintroduce debris into the broken surface. If the pavement is hot, skip the walk — Kibo's pad tolerance is lower while the surface is open, and heat on a broken pad is a separate irritation.
  - Don't apply any ointment unless your vet has previously approved one for Kibo. Some dogs lick off topical antibiotics and the ingestion can matter; some human ointments (especially anything with zinc or cortisone) are not safe for dogs.
  - One observation that is reassuring but should not change the plan: a single pinpoint bleed that stops in under a minute and produces no other change is exactly the kind of soft re-injury that heals with protected time. The risk is not the bleed itself; the risk is the licking habit continuing to break the surface before it sets.

Bottom line: you likely need to buy nothing, provided two short clarifications from the instructor go your way. The only realistic purchase is a tube of Hansa yellow, and only if the instructor requires it for a specific exercise.

What you already have, no questions:
  Palette, masking tape, rigid board, two water jars
  Ultramarine blue, burnt sienna, quinacridone rose, phthalo blue

Reasonable substitutions (covered without buying):

Paper — 9x12 cold-press block for "one full sheet or two quarter sheets"
  The clinic's wording reads as a choice, not full-sheet-only. Your block gives multiple 9x12 sheets; each is roughly 108 sq in versus a true quarter sheet's ~165 sq in. The trade-off is area per sheet, not material quality, since 140 lb cold-press matches the spec. You can pull two sheets and have roughly comparable total area to two quarter sheets. Where it might feel tight: a single very large wet-on-wet wash that wants full-sheet room.

#8 round for #10 round
  Workable. Holds less water/pigment, so the largest single-stroke washes come out a bit smaller. Fine for most wash-and-edges work. The difference will only show on demos that need the largest single stroke.

3/4" flat for 1" flat
  Workable. Strokes run ~25% narrower. Fine for edges and broad washes; you'd just take an extra pass for the widest strokes.

What you would need to buy, and only if confirmed:
  Hansa yellow — only if the instructor rejects azo as a substitute for a specific exercise.
  Where the difference actually shows:
    - Mixing greens with ultramarine or phthalo: Hansa Yellow Light stays cleaner and more sap-like; azo yellow leans warmer, so the mixes read more olive/muted. Not wrong, just different.
    - Warm/cool yellow comparisons: Hansa is cool, azo is warm. If a demo depends on the cool yellow, substitution loses that contrast.
    - Plain yellow washes (sunlight, light areas): azo is fine, just warmer.
  A 5 ml tube is plenty for a one-day clinic.

Ambiguity to confirm with the instructor:

1.  Is "one full sheet or two quarter sheets" a real choice, or does at least one planned exercise require full-sheet area specifically? If quarter sheets (or close-to-quarter sheets from your block) work, you're covered. If full sheet is mandatory for a specific demo, ask whether the instructor will have spare paper on hand or whether you need to buy one full sheet.

2.  Is azo yellow acceptable for the exercises, particularly any green-mixing or warm/cool yellow demo? If yes, no purchase. If no, a single small tube of Hansa yellow is the only buy.

If both questions resolve in your favor — block-of-9x12 accepted, azo accepted — you walk in with what you own and buy nothing.

If the first question fails, the purchase is one full sheet of 140 lb cold-press (or rely on the instructor's spare stock if offered).

If the second question fails, the purchase is one small tube of Hansa yellow.

If both fail, you buy both. Low cost either way; no reason to decide before the email reply.

P037_back.tif SIZE MISMATCH — NON-DESTRUCTIVE COMPARISON & QUARANTINE
2024-09-02

Premises held throughout
  - Neither file is opened, copied, moved, renamed, or overwritten yet.
  - Newer mtime does NOT decide which is the master.
  - The verified master is whichever file matches the scanning-session log's
    recorded capture parameters and shows no post-capture modification.
  - Resolution is by independent evidence, not by recency or by "the
    external drive is the backup, so it must be right."
  - The original photograph stays in its archival sleeve until Phase 5
    and is handled only under the existing two-person convention.

Phase 0 — Freeze the current state (reads only, no writes)
  0.1 Write down both full paths, the exact 12 KB size delta, and each
      file's current atime / mtime / ctime / birthtime into a notes file
      kept OUTSIDE the photo directories. Capture these BEFORE running
      anything that reads the files, since most reads update atime.
  0.2 Do not open either file in Preview, Photoshop, Finder QuickLook,
      Lightroom, or any app that can write sidecar files, QuickLook
      caches, ._ AppleDouble files, or extended attributes. A GUI
      preview alone is enough to leave fingerprints in some workflows.
  0.3 Stay on the command line until Phase 4. If a tool needs a writable
      scratch path, use a clearly named _scratch directory that is not
      inside the photo set.

Phase 1 — Read-only evidence capture (single pass per file, in place)
  Run each of these on BOTH files independently and record results
  side by side. Nothing here modifies the file's content; the only side
  effect is an atime bump, which is acceptable since you recorded the
  pre-read atime in 0.1.

  A. Cryptographic hash of the whole file:
       shasum -a 256 <full-path>      # macOS
       sha256sum <full-path>         # Linux
  B. File system metadata:
       stat <file>
  C. TIFF structure + every tag (the highest-yield single read):
       exiftool -G -s -a <file>
     If exiftool is not installed, fall back to:
       tiffinfo <file>               # libtiff
       identify -verbose <file>      # ImageMagick, less complete
  D. First 16 bytes of the file (sanity check it is actually a TIFF and
     not, e.g., a renamed JPEG, a partial download, or an HTML error):
       xxd <file> | head -n 1
     Expect: 49 49 2A 00 (little-endian) or 4D 4D 00 2A (big-endian).

Phase 2 — Match against the scanning-session log
  For each field below, decide which file is consistent with what the log
  recorded for the P037 back capture. The log may not have a checksum,
  but it should have most of these:

    Scanner make/model            -> TIFF Make, TIFF Model
    Scanner firmware              -> TIFF Software (should read as
                                     scanner firmware, not "Adobe",
                                     "Apple Preview", "ImageMagick",
                                     "GIMP", etc.)
    Capture datetime              -> TIFF DateTime, EXIF DateTimeOriginal,
                                     EXIF DateTimeDigitized (should fall
                                     inside the recorded session window)
    Resolution (DPI)              -> TIFF XResolution / YResolution /
                                     ResolutionUnit
    Color mode                    -> TIFF PhotometricInterpretation,
                                     SamplesPerPixel, BitsPerSample
    Color profile                 -> ICC Profile descriptor / size
                                     (should match the scanner profile
                                     documented for that session)
    Compression                   -> TIFF Compression (LZW or None for
                                     archival masters; JPEG-in-TIFF is
                                     a strong re-save signal)
    Operator / session notes      -> EXIF Artist, EXIF Copyright, IPTC,
                                     XMP (only if your log records them)

  Strong signals a file was RE-SAVED after the session:
    - Software tag is no longer the scanner firmware.
    - DateTime / DateTimeOriginal is later than the recorded session end.
    - ICC profile was stripped or replaced.
    - Compression changed (e.g., LZW -> JPEG, LZW -> Deflate).
    - EXIF thumbnail was added or removed.
    - Image dimensions differ from what the log says.
    - Pixel content is identical but byte size differs (a re-encode).

  Strong signals of pristine scanner output:
    - Software tag = scanner firmware string.
    - DateTime within the recorded session window.
    - Resolution, color, bit depth, compression all match the log.
    - ICC profile is the scanner profile documented for that session.

  A 12 KB delta on a TIFF is a very common footprint for an ICC profile
  add/strip, an EXIF/XMP block add, or a compression re-encode at the
  same pixel dimensions. Treat that as a hypothesis to confirm against
  the log, not as a conclusion on its own.

Phase 3 — Choose the verified master (no file moves yet)
  The file whose Phase 2 evidence is consistent with the scanning-session
  log across the most INDEPENDENT parameters is the verified archival
  master. The other file is the post-session-modified file and is the
  suspect.

  If both files show editor fingerprints, or both have suspicious
  DateTime values, or neither matches the log cleanly, do not guess.
  Skip to Phase 5 — that is exactly the case Phase 5 is for.

Phase 4 — Quarantine the suspect (non-destructive, fully reversible)
  4.1 Create the quarantine directory alongside the photo set, never
      inside it, e.g.:
        _quarantine/2024-09-02_P037_back_size-mismatch/
  4.2 Move the suspect file there with mode and timestamps preserved:
        mv -p <suspect-path> \
           _quarantine/2024-09-02_P037_back_size-mismatch/
      If the move crosses filesystems and `mv -p` cannot preserve:
        rsync -aE <suspect-path> \
              _quarantine/2024-09-02_P037_back_size-mismatch/
        # re-hash the destination; only after the hash matches, rm the
        # source
  4.3 Rename the quarantined file to encode its status, never to lose
      the original identity:
        P037_back.tif.SUSPECT_2024-09-02_does-not-match-session-log
  4.4 Write a sibling manifest in the quarantine directory, in plain
      text, containing:
        - date and time of quarantine
        - full original path
        - SHA-256 of the file as quarantined
        - size and mtime at the moment of quarantine
        - which Phase 2 signals failed and why
        - SHA-256 and size of the file left in place (the candidate
          master)
        - pointer to the scanning-session log entry used for matching
  4.5 Do NOT delete the quarantined file. Do NOT modify it. It is
      evidence, not trash, until the master is independently re-confirmed.

Phase 5 — Independent confirmation (only if Phase 2 was inconclusive)
  This is the only phase that touches the original photograph. It is
  invasive enough that it warrants deliberate handling, not reflex.
  5.1 Two-person handling per the standing convention. The photograph
      stays in its archival sleeve until the scanner bed is ready.
      Minimize exposure to room light.
  5.2 Re-scan P037's back at the SAME settings recorded in the log:
      DPI, bit depth, color mode, ICC profile, compression. Name the
      new capture so its role is explicit, never overwriting either
      candidate:
        P037_back.tif.RESCAN_2024-09-02_two-person-verification
  5.3 Hash the rescan and compare its TIFF tags and pixel content to
      BOTH candidate files. Whichever candidate the rescan matches is
      the verified master. The non-matching candidate joins the
      quarantine directory from Phase 4.
      If the rescan matches NEITHER candidate, that is more serious
      than a single-file mismatch and warrants a separate review
      before any further file moves. Stop and document.
  5.4 Immediately re-sleeve P037. Two-person file check before and
      after re-sleeving, per the standing rule for the original
      photographs.

Phase 6 — Documentation before closing the incident
  6.1 In the inventory / index note for P037, record:
        - the size delta observed today,
        - the Phase 2 evidence used to identify the master,
        - the SHA-256 of the master now in place,
        - the quarantine path and filename,
        - the rescan outcome (only if Phase 5 was needed),
        - the timestamp and operator(s) for any move or rescan.
  6.2 Do not silently rename the in-place file. Its existing name is
      the name the rest of the index references for the front-to-back
      pairing; renaming it now would break that record.
  6.3 As a separate, smaller follow-up pass — not as a generalization
      from today's incident — hash the other ten treated-photo TIFF
      pairs against their counterparts on the external drive. A size
      delta is not assumed for any of them; this is just a quick
      equality check now that the comparison tooling is in hand.

What this is NOT
  - Not an assumption that the external drive is the master because it
    is the backup. Either side may have been modified after the last
    sync; the log is the reference, not the storage role.
  - Not a recommendation to delete the smaller or larger file. Size
    alone is not a discriminator.
  - Not an instruction to overwrite the in-place file with the
    "matching" candidate before independent confirmation. The in-place
    file remains the operational master until evidence replaces it.
  - Not a reason to handle the original photograph more than necessary.
    Re-sleeve it as soon as the comparison work is done.
  - Not a forecast that other files in the set have the same issue.
    P037 is the only confirmed mismatch today; do not generalize.
  - Not a license to open the files in a viewer "just to look." Any

    writes that complicate the next comparison.

## Operating principles for this restore

- Master path (`P037_back.tif`) → written from the verified external copy, verified again, checksummed.
- Evidence path → the altered laptop file is renamed to a non-master name; never `P037_back.*`. It is moved out of the masters tree entirely so it cannot be picked up by any future "find all masters" operation.
- No in-place edits. No `cp` directly to the master path before the evidence copy is renamed. No checksum of a file at a master path that has just been written.
- Two independent verifications: one before the evidence copy is moved (proves which file is which), one after the master is in place (proves the master is the verified one).
- Session log appended, not rewritten.

---

## Step 0 — Set up a working directory and snapshot current state

Do this from the directory that contains both files. Adjust the path if `P037_back.tif` lives in a subdirectory of the treated-photo folder.

```
WORK=/tmp/p037_restore_$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ)
mkdir -p "$WORK"
cd /path/to/treated_photo_folder    # contains P037_back.tif
ls -la P037_back.tif                 # note current size, mtime, ctime
```

Capture the exact byte size and both timestamps into `$WORK/pre_state.txt`. You said the laptop file is 12 KB larger than the external; size alone is enough to tell them apart at every step.

## Step 1 — Compute SHA-256 of both files BEFORE any move or copy

This is your pre-action evidence record. Do it now, on the files at their current paths.

```

```

Then for the external file. Mount the external drive read-only if possible; if not, just use it normally but do not write to it.

```
EXTERNAL=/Volumes/ExternalDrive/path/to/P037_back.tif      # macOS path
# or: EXTERNAL=/mnt/external/path/to/P037_back.tif        # Linux path
sha256sum "$EXTERNAL" > "$WORK/pre_sha256_P037_back_external.txt"
cat "$WORK/pre_sha256_"*.txt
```

Save these two lines. They are the only place where the unaltered laptop file and the unaltered external file are individually fingerprinted before any copy or rename.

## Step 2 — Capture file-level metadata of both files

Use `exiftool` if available; `identify -verbose` from ImageMagick is a fallback but reads TIFF less cleanly. You already did this non-destructively — re-record it into the work directory so the session log is self-contained.

```
exiftool -j -a -G1 -FileName -Directory -FileSize -ImageWidth -ImageHeight \
  -BitsPerSample -Software -DateTimeOriginal -CreateDate -ModifyDate \
  -FileModifyDate -FileAccessDate -FileInodeChangeDate \

exiftool -j -a -G1 -FileName -Directory -FileSize -ImageWidth -ImageHeight \
  -BitsPerSample -Software -DateTimeOriginal -CreateDate -ModifyDate \
  -FileModifyDate -FileAccessDate -FileInodeChangeDate \
  "$EXTERNAL" > "$WORK/pre_meta_P037_back_external.json"
```

The fields that establish provenance for the external as the verified scan:
- `ImageWidth`, `ImageHeight`, `BitsPerSample` → must match the scanner's original spec
- `DateTimeOriginal` (EXIF TIFF tag 36867, embedded by the scanner) → must match the scanner session
- `Software` → should be empty or the scanner's vendor string, NOT the access-editing application
- `FileModifyDate` and the software-save timestamp on the laptop file → the laptop file's distinguishing feature

Important naming choice baked in:
- `P037_back` retained as a fragment so the link to the original scan session is preserved in the filename itself.
- `__ALTERED_accessapp_save` is the literal role tag.
- `2024-09-07` is the discovery date, not the alleged save date — you do not know the exact laptop save timestamp without re-checking `FileModifyDate`; date-stamping from discovery keeps the filename honest.

Under your load rule (any week, duration OR frequency), each next-run decision is set by Monday morning's baseline and the gap since 9/8:

  - Green path: Monday baseline is clean (walking and stairs both pain-free, no swelling, no focal tenderness) AND there are at least 3 clean days between 9/8 and the next run. Next run stays at 34 minutes, same easy effort, same route. Do not extend. Do not add a second run that week unless 9/8's pattern is fully gone and the run is unambiguously clean.
  - Yellow path: Monday baseline is mostly clean but a faint awareness lingers on stairs, or a mild ache returns later in the day, or the gap is only 2 clean days. Shorten the next run to about 30 minutes and keep it easy. Reassess after that run; do not stack a second run that week.
  - Hold path: Monday baseline is not clean — pain on stairs, ache with ordinary walking, any swelling, any focal tenderness, any limp, any instability, pain at rest, or any symptom that's worse than 9/8. Rest day or two. Substitute pain-free walking or easy cycling only. No jogging until you have a fully clean baseline and PT has signed off on the next step. Two consecutive soft late-onsets at the same ceiling also puts you on this path until PT re-checks.

What would warrant clinical follow-up

These are the same STOP gates you've been using, restated so the boundary is unambiguous:

  - Swelling, bruising, or visible change at the lateral ankle
  - Focal bony tenderness when pressing the specific spot
  - Limp or inability to bear weight normally
  - Instability, giving way, or a feeling of "something shifting"
  - Pain at rest or pain that's getting worse rather than fading
  - Pain or ache that returns at the same or a lower load on the next run
  - Any new mechanical event (roll, twist, sharp pop)
  - Numbness, tingling, color change, or temperature change in the foot

Also warrant a check: the same soft late-onset pattern showing up on the next run at 34 minutes (two in a row), or any symptom that doesn't fully resolve to baseline within roughly 24–48 hours of 9/8. Either of those is the trigger to loop PT back in before the next extension attempt — the pattern is more useful information to a clinician than the single-session intensity.

What this is not

This is not a regression to where you were in June. There is no resting pain, no stair pain, no focal tenderness, no instability, and 9/8 was a controlled easy effort at a level you earned over two clean 32-minute weeks. It is also not a clean pass at 34 — the pattern recurred, which is why 34 becomes the ceiling for at least one more session, not a stepping stone to 36. Treat it as a useful boundary read: you now know where the current soft limit is, and the next run is the test of whether 34 holds cleanly or whether it needs another week at the same dose.

Practical sequence for cutting one 22x30 sheet into four 11x15 quarters while keeping the painting surface untouched, the two deckled edges preserved on the cut pieces, and front/back never confused after cutting.

Step 1 — Identify the painting side (front)

Cold-press paper has a textured side ("tooth") and a smoother back. Confirm the front with three cross-checks:
- Touch: drag a fingertip lightly across each side. The textured side feels slightly grippy; the back is smoother.
- Oblique light: tilt the sheet near a lamp. The textured side shows tiny cast shadows in the tooth.
- Watermark: most artist-grade sheets carry a maker's watermark. Read flat, it reads correctly from the front and appears mirrored from the back.

Commit now: textured side = front, smooth side = back. Don't second-guess later.

Step 2 — Identify the two deckled edges

The deckled edges are the original irregular, slightly wavy/untrimmed sides — usually a touch thicker and fuzzier than the maker-cut edges. The other two edges will be straight and clean.

Note which two parallel sides are deckled. The cuts below run perpendicular to those edges (from deckled edge to deckled edge), which splits each deckled edge in half between two adjacent quarters rather than trimming it away.

Step 3 — Place face-down and pencil-mark the back

Put the sheet face-down on the board. The front is now against the board and fully protected; the back is up, where all your marks and cuts will happen.

In one corner of the back, pencil a small "B" or a short diagonal slash. This is a temporary reference; you'll replace it with marks on each quarter in Step 6.

Step 4 — Pencil the cut lines on the back

Using the ruler and pencil (still on the back only):
- Measure 11" along the 22" dimension and tick at each edge.
- Measure 15" along the 30" dimension and tick at each edge.
- Connect the ticks into two perpendicular lines that divide the sheet into four equal 11x15 rectangles.
- Verify with the ruler that opposite ticks line up and the rectangles are square.
- Keep lines light so they don't ghost through to the front.

Step 5 — Cut

- Use a fresh, sharp blade. A dull one crushes the tooth.
- Press the ruler firmly along the first pencil line; it must not shift.
- First pass: light scoring, just breaking the surface. Keep the blade vertical and pull it along the ruler in one smooth stroke.
- Repeat passes (3–5 total for ~300 gsm paper), deepening the score each time. Don't try to sever in a single pass.
- The paper will separate along the score. If it doesn't release, finish by folding gently along the score and creasing it open, or continue passes until it does.
- Repeat for the second perpendicular line. You now have four quarters.
- Keep your free hand clear of the knife path the entire time.

Step 6 — Mark each quarter's back

The full-sheet corner mark from Step 3 is now split and ambiguous. On the back of each quarter, write the same small mark in the same corner — e.g., a tiny "B" or slash in the upper-right of the back, with the deckled edge oriented the same way for every piece. Never write on the front.

Step 7 — Store flat

- Stack the four quarters with their fronts and backs aligned, deckled edges on the same side.
- Interleave clean paper (or glassine) between pieces if they'll sit together, so the texture stays clean.
- Place a flat board on top with light, even weight — heavy weight crushes the tooth. A second clean board plus a few books is enough.
- Keep them dry, away from splashes, dust, and direct sun. Avoid sealed plastic in a humid room (trapped moisture cockles the paper).

Result: four 11x15 quarter sheets, painting surface untouched, each with one original deckled edge preserved as a feature, and each individually marked on the back so you can never flip-mistake a piece.

Short answer: yes, skip Wednesday's commute. Take transit. Here is why and what to bring the mechanic.

WHY SKIP
- Long lever travel is not the same as no brake — the pads still bite — but the bite point is much later in the pull. In traffic that means more hand travel before any deceleration, and your hand is closer to the bar when it finally engages. That is the wrong condition for an intersection stop or a panic grab.
- A commute introduces variable conditions (cars, pedestrians, wet pavement, possibly downhill) where consistent lever feel matters. A brake that engages unpredictably late is exactly the one you don't want to learn the hard way about.
- The change showed up right after a tire install. That timing is a strong clue something shifted during the wheel-out / wheel-in work: cable tension, pad seating, caliper piston retraction, possibly even a slight rotor nudge. It deserves diagnosis, not operation.
- Transit is available and Thursday is already booked. One commute day is a small cost; a marginal brake on a morning ride is not a small cost.
- Your past calls on bike issues have been right (the Jan 14 rotor pulse turned out to be a slightly bent rotor with glazed pads; the Aug 19 sidewall was real damage). Don't ride on "should be fine."

WHAT TO TELL THE MECHANIC
- Symptom in your words: the rear brake lever now pulls most of the way to the bar before the pads engage. Engagement point is much farther than before the tire change.
- Recent work: rear wheel removed, new tube/tire installed, wheel re-seated.
- What you already checked and what you found: wheel spins freely with no rub; no rim wobble when rotating; no visible fluid at the caliper or lever; new tire is seated and inflated.
- What you did not feel: no pulsing, no scraping, no grinding, no intermittent engagement. The change is lever travel length, not lever feel.
- Ask for, in this order:
  1. Confirm brake type first — mechanical cable disc, hydraulic disc, or rim. Your "no fluid leak" check is only meaningful for hydraulic. If it's cable-actuated, the issue is almost certainly cable/housing, not fluid.
  2. Pad and rotor condition — thickness, wear indicator, contamination (oil, chain lube, degreaser), glazing, parallelism to rotor.
  3. Reset the caliper pistons if hydraulic — they often don't fully retract after a wheel removal, which directly produces long travel.
  4. Bleed or top off the system if hydraulic and travel is still long after the pad reset.
  5. Check cable tension, housing compression, ferrule seating, and any kinks if mechanical.
  6. Adjust the lever reach / bite-point adjuster if the lever has one.
  7. Confirm rotor is true and clears both pads uniformly through a full wheel revolution with the brake released (no rub at any single point).
- Ask them to test the bike after the work in the shop lot: a hard stop from speed, a controlled slow stop, and several repeated pulls to confirm consistent lever feel and a bite point well before the bar.

ONE THING NOT TO DO
- Don't ride it "a few miles to see if the travel goes back to normal." Lever travel does not self-correct, and a longer-than-expected lever pull during a sudden stop on a hill or behind a car is the exact condition to avoid.

WHAT THIS IS NOT
- Not a structural failure. Not a sign the new tire is bad. Not an emergency — the brake still works, just later than it should.

The repair was localized (reseated ferrule, readjusted rear brake) and your parking-lot test was clean at low speed with loading. That's a sufficient green light for a first ride, not for an aggressive or uncertain one.

Pre-ride (in the lot, before you leave):
  - Lever feel matches the shop: firm, quick engagement, no extra travel, clean return when released.
  - Ferrule still fully seated at the cable-housing stop; no kink, no frayed strand at the lever or rear caliper.
  - One or two loaded low-speed stops, same as the parking-lot test.
  - Rear tire firm; fender clears the tire under load (same work block).
  - Helmet, lights if needed; route that avoids long descents and heavy-brake traffic.

Early-ride (first few miles):
  - First real stop at ~5–10 mph, then one at ~15 mph within the first mile or two — confirm the same firm lever, no rub, no click.
  - Default to front brake for the first few stops; use the rear brake lightly. The front is your primary stopper (~60–70%), and you're not stress-testing the rear cable yet.
  - Listen for ticking/clicking from the housing, scraping from the caliper, or rhythmic fender rub.

Stop and walk the bike if any of these appear:
  - Lever goes soft, pulls closer to the bar, or doesn't return cleanly.
  - Any pulsing through the lever under braking.
  - New rub, click, grind, or scrape from the rear-brake area.
  - Ferrule visibly displaced.
  - Rear tire soft, or any handling change (pulling, wandering).

A clean round-trip Friday is enough data to call the rear brake settled. Anything anomalous in that first ride is a "walk back / shop" signal, not a "push through" signal.

The cauliflower is a moisture-mismatch artifact. Mechanism in one line: when the brush is drier than the bead but the surrounding paper is past its wet-into-wet window, the brush pulls bead water OUT into setting paper — that water carries dissolved pigment with it, and the water finds irregular paths through partially-dried fibers. The lobed cauliflower shape is the fingerprint of that path-of-least-resistance flow.

Why each part mattered:

1. Pigment collected near the taped lower edge because the tape is a hydrophobic barrier. Wash water carried pigment to the lowest point and pooled there as a bead. The bead stays wet longer than the rest because it's a deeper accumulation.

2. "Sheen had begun to disappear" means the surface water film was already gone across the sheet. The paper there had started to set — pigment is bonding into the drying fibers. Sheen gone = wet-into-wet window is closed.

3. A drier brush into that scene: the brush drank bead water (correct instinct) but then released that water, with its dissolved pigment, into adjacent paper that couldn't accept it uniformly. Drier-brush-into-wet-bead-into-setting-paper is the textbook cauliflower recipe.

The mismatch, plainly: the brush was calibrated to the bead (wet) instead of to the sheet (setting). The bead wanted lifting earlier — while sheen was still active — or not at all.

---

Practice sequence before Saturday

Goal: keep bead, paper sheen, and brush moisture in one regime at all times. The rule is that the brush matches the sheet, not the bead.

Setup (repeat for each round):
  - Tape an 11x15 quarter sheet on all four sides; burnish edges
  - Tilt the board ~5–8° so gravity pulls the wash toward the taped edge slowly and evenly — enough to flow, not enough to pool
  - Two water jars (rinse + clean pickup), one cloth or paper towel for blotting
  - One scrap of the same paper off to the side for brush-moisture testing

Brush calibration (the test):
  - Touch the loaded brush to the scrap. If it leaves its own bead, it's too wet. If it just dampens, it's right. Target is damp, not loaded.
  - "Drier brush" in this context meant past damp — dry enough to drink from the bead but not wet enough to give back into setting paper.

Three timing windows — these are the operating boundaries:
  - WET (sheen present, both surfaces glossy): soft edges, gradients, lift a forming bead NOW
  - CRITICAL (sheen just gone, paper still cool to touch): last chance to soften a forming edge with a damp brush; do not rewet a bead
  - DRY (paper room-temp, no surface moisture): leave it; corrections happen later with a barely-damp brush or a single dilute glaze, never by scrubbing

The bead protocol:
  - Bead forms while sheen is active → use a damp brush to PULL the bead UP into the still-wet surrounding wash. Wet-into-wet redistribution. Pigment moves; paper stays wet. No backrun possible.
  - Bead forms after sheen disappears → leave it. It dries as a darker edge that usually reads as a horizon, shadow boundary, or compositional accent. Trying to fix it is what makes cauliflowers.
  - The only acceptable touch-up on a dry bead edge is a barely-damp brush (dampened, blotted nearly dry) with one soft pass. Stop after one pass.

Three rounds before Saturday:
  1. Plain graded wash, no bead intervention. Just observe sheen timing on your specific setup. Note the second the sheen disappears — that's your critical window closing.
  2. Same wash, deliberately let a small bead form at the taped edge. While sheen is still active, lift it with a damp brush. Watch the pigment redistribute without a backrun.
  3. Same wash, let a bead form and ignore it until dry. Judge it as a feature. This is training yourself to accept the bead-as-edge instead of rescuing it.

On the existing practice sheet: leave the cauliflower. The rest is usable, and the sheet already taught you the lesson. Don't re-wet, don't scrub. When fully dry you can soften one edge with a barely-damp brush if it reads as a hard line, or glaze once with very dilute mix if it really bothers you — but for clinic prep, that's optional, not necessary.

For Saturday itself, the single thing to watch is the moment sheen disappears. That's your cue: any bead at the tape line is now a feature, not a problem.

Two follow-up studies below. Each uses one quarter sheet from your prepared stack, runs one variable across a small grid, and ends with the sheet fully dry and judged at normal viewing distance. Neither involves scrubbing, lifting, glazing over a wet edge, or returning to a finished scene.

Common rules for both
  Use a single mixed wash for the whole study (one pigment pool, kept consistent) so color is not a variable.
  Tape the quarter sheet flat. Mask only the outer border if you want a clean frame for judging; do not mask between cells.
  Lay every stroke once. No second pass to "fix" anything mid-session. If a cell floods or beading is severe, blot once with a dry brush and leave that cell alone.
  Judge only after the sheet is fully dry. Photograph each cell flat, in the same light, from normal viewing distance.
  Each study is one short session (20-40 minutes) and is complete at the listed final cell. Do not extend to a 7th cell "to check one more thing" — that is a different question for another session.

Study 1 - Bead and brush-moisture control
  Purpose: Isolate which combination produces a bloom/bead when you return to a wash. Variables are sheen state at the moment of return and brush moisture at the moment of return. Pigment, brush size, stroke speed, and stroke length are held constant.

  Setup
    One 11x15 quarter sheet, taped flat.
    Divide into 6 cells, roughly 2 columns x 3 rows, each cell about 2" x 4". Light pencil tick-marks at the corners only.
    One large round brush for the base stroke (e.g., #12 or #14).
    One smaller round brush for the return stroke (e.g., #8).
    One mid-tone wash mixed once and kept in a single pool. A granulating mix (e.g., ultramarine + a touch of burnt sienna) makes bead/tide lines easy to see. Avoid anything heavily staining.
    Two water jars and a paper towel for controlled brush moisture.

  Variables
    Sheen state at return: 3 levels
      S - still wet and shiny (sheen present)
      D - just dulled (sheen gone, paper still cool and damp)
      X - touch-dry to a clean finger but still cool
    Brush moisture at return: 2 levels
      damp - brush loaded, then dragged once firmly across a paper towel
      wet  - brush fully loaded, no towel drag
    Cells: 3 x 2 = 6 (S/damp, S/wet, D/damp, D/wet, X/damp, X/wet).

  Procedure
    1. Load the large brush. Lay one continuous top-to-bottom stroke in cell 1, continuing straight into cell 2, then 3, without lifting - this keeps stroke speed constant. Do not reload between cells in the same row.
    2. Note the time at the end of the stroke.
    3. At the target sheen time for cell 1, load the smaller brush to the target moisture level and make ONE short return stroke along the bottom inch of the cell, lifting at the cell boundary.
    4. Repeat across the row, adjusting only the time delay and the brush moisture.
    5. Repeat for rows 2 and 3.
    6. Stop. Do not revisit any cell.

  Recording (one line per cell, written on a scrap before you forget)
    Cell | sheen target | brush moisture | actual seconds to return | observation after drying (no bloom / faint tide / clear bloom / flooding)

  Stopping points
    After the 6th cell, the study is done.
    If a cell is visibly flooding or beading heavily during the pass, blot once with a dry brush and stop that cell - do not chase it.
    Do not glaze, lift, scrub, or rewet any cell. The blooms you produce are the data.

  What this is NOT
    Not a painting. The sheet goes into the reference pile, not the wall.
    Not a glaze or lift study. Adding layers later would obscure the very thing you are measuring.
    Not a color study. One wash, one pool, end of discussion.
    The output is a 3 x 2 map: which sheen x moisture combinations stay clean, which bead, which bloom. That map is what you carry into the next large wash.

Study 2 - Timing for soft versus hard edges
  Purpose: Isolate the time gap between two adjacent wet shapes that share a boundary, and read off when the shared edge stays soft versus when it goes hard. Pigment, brush, shape, size, and stroke direction are held constant.

  Setup
    One 11x15 quarter sheet, taped flat.
    Divide into 6 cells, single column or 2 x 3 grid, each cell about 2" x 3". Pencil corner ticks only.
    One medium round brush (e.g., #8 or #10).
    Same mid-tone wash pool as Study 1 (single pool, single session if you want; otherwise mix fresh to the same ratio).

  Variables
    Only one variable: seconds between shape A and shape B in the same cell.
    Time points: 0, 10, 20, 30, 45, 60 seconds.
    Six cells, one time point each. Draw the cell assignment on a scrap first so you do not lose track mid-session.

  Shape protocol (same for every cell)
    Shape A: a small soft oval, painted with one stroke of the side-loaded brush, letting the wash feather on its own. Stop short of the cell boundary by about 1/4" on the side that will meet B.
    Wait the target time.
    Shape B: an identical oval placed so it touches A along a short shared boundary of about 1/2". One stroke, side-loaded, no second pass.

  Procedure
    1. Mix wash. Note start time.
    2. For cell 1: paint A. Start a timer. At 0 seconds (immediately), paint B.
    3. For cell 2: paint A. Wait 10 seconds. Paint B.
    4. Continue through cell 6 (60-second gap).
    5. Stop. Do not paint a 7th cell.

  Recording (one line per cell, written on a scrap before the sheet dries and the timing detail fades)
    Cell | target gap | actual gap | observation at normal viewing distance after drying (invisible shared edge / soft transition / visible but soft / hard tide line)

  Reading the results
    The cell where the shared edge becomes invisible or barely visible is your soft-edge window.
    The cell where a crisp tide line first appears is where you crossed out of the soft zone.
    The 20-second cell from the clinic should land inside or just past that boundary - that is confirmation, not a failure.

  Stopping points
    After the 6th cell, the study is done.
    Do not rewet any hard edge "to soften it." That is the exact move you are trying to stop making on finished paper.
    Do not glaze over the cells later in the same session. If you want a glaze test on these shapes, that is a separate future study on a fresh sheet.

  What this is NOT
    Not a finished painting. The sheet is a timing reference, not artwork.
    Not a glaze, lift, or scrub test. The whole point is to read the edge as it dried.
    Not a study of brush size, pigment choice, or surface texture. One brush, one wash, one shape.
    The output is a single number range: "soft-edge window is approximately X to Y seconds at this brush, this wash, this paper, this room." That range is what you carry into the next cylinder exercise.

How the two studies connect
  Study 1 tells you when you are allowed to return to a wash at all (which sheen x moisture combinations stay clean).
  Study 2 tells you how fast you have to move when shapes share a boundary (the soft-edge time window).
  Together they replace two instincts with two short references. Future wash work consults both before the first stroke, not after the bloom.

Suggested placement
  Each study fits inside one short sitting (20-40 minutes) and uses one quarter sheet. If you want to do both in one session, do Study 2 first (it is quieter, single brush, single variable) and Study 1 second (more setup, two brushes, two variables). Let the second sheet dry fully before judging either - judging wet cells is a known way to overcorrect.

Short answer: do not promise the 26 yet. Hold the count at "intent" and ask the supplier for a guaranteed minimum trimmed yield in writing before confirming the chef-owner's number.

Why the current estimate is not enough to commit against:

1. The supplier gave a range (27–30), not a guaranteed minimum. The advance-count protocol only works when the yield floor is known, not estimated. Estimates are design input; commitments need a number you can be held to.

2. There is a recent, directly relevant precedent. For the September 13 dinner (30 chicken guests), the supplier's pre-trim estimate was 36 portions; after final trim on September 12 the case produced 33, which was 8% below estimate. The dinner still worked only because the 4-portion kitchen contingency absorbed the shortfall, leaving exactly the 30 plated meals. That contingency absorbed a real, observed variance — it did not have spare capacity.

3. Apply that same variance to the new numbers. 26 portions needed against a 27–30 estimate is a 1–4 portion cushion at the estimate level. After a similar trim haircut (≈8%), a 27-floor estimate becomes roughly 25 actual, which is below the 26 target. Two portions of kitchen contingency is not enough buffer against an estimate, because the contingency is the buffer — it cannot also be the committed production.

4. Historical sale-run yields (44–45 portions from the 30-pound case on June 28, July 26, August 16) are not a substitute here. Those used the larger sale-run case with a different trim expectation; the private-dinner case scale and trim path are what produced the 33/36 outcome on September 13, and they are what the 27–30 estimate is built on.

What to do now, in order:

a. Reply to the inquiry as a soft hold: 28 adults on October 19 is workable, chicken count and contingency will be confirmed after supplier confirmation, no seconds advertised.

b. Ask the supplier for two things in one message: the case size being quoted (so we know we're comparing like-for-like to the September 13 case), and a guaranteed minimum trimmed yield for that case. Without a guaranteed minimum ≥ 26, the count does not get locked; with a guaranteed minimum ≥ 28, you can promise 24 plated + 2 kitchen contingency and have a real floor under it.

c. Do not pre-stage against an estimate. Pre-staging the tested sequence is fine, but production sizing waits for the guaranteed number.

What this is not: this is not a rejection of the October 19 dinner or of producing 26 portions. It is the same advance-count rule that worked on September 13 — the rule that kept 30 guests fed when the actual came in three portions below estimate. The chef-owner's 2-portion contingency is structurally right; the missing piece is the supplier's guaranteed minimum, not the protocol.

If the supplier cannot or will not guarantee a minimum trimmed yield, the honest answer to the host is that the chicken count cannot be locked at 24 plated until that guarantee exists, even if the estimate range looks comfortable.

15-minute practice — three skills, three blocks, no composition.

0:00–2:00  WARM-UP / FEEL
- Load a mop or large round; tap off the excess so the brush is full but not dripping.
- Three test strokes on scrap: barely-wet, full bead, flooded.
- Goal: register the visual difference between an alive bead and a dying one before the timed work starts.

2:00–7:00  BEAD CONTROL ON EVEN WASHES (5 min)
- 4–6 vertical strips, each ~2.5 cm wide, full paper length.
- One continuous pass each, top to bottom, never lifting.
- Vary speed and bead size across strips: the slowest-with-least-bead strip should look the same as the fastest-with-most-bead strip — that's the muscle you're training.
- No backtracking. If the bead runs dry mid-strip, finish the strip; start a new one for the next attempt.

7:00–10:00  RE-WET WARNING (3 min) — confirms yesterday's finding
- Lay two horizontal strips and let them go fully matte (sheen completely gone).
- Strip A: with a clean wet brush, make one stroke across the dried wash. Watch the bloom form on that single return stroke — this is what not to do.
- Strip B: same starting wash, but where you'd want to extend it, lift and start fresh on dry paper beside it instead.
- Pair them side by side so the contrast stays visible on the page.

10:00–15:00  20-SECOND EDGE WINDOW (5 min)
- Paint a saturated rectangle (~8 × 10 cm).
- Drop clean water along four edges at 10s, 20s, 20s (repeat), 30s after the rectangle is laid.
- Expect: 10s = diffusion runs far past the line; first 20s = controlled soft transition (the target); second 20s = same target, locks the timing in your hands; 30s = hard edge, paint already set.
- Label each edge with its time so the page reads as a reference sheet later.

Stop at 15:00 even if the last edge is still wet. The point is the timing feel, not the painting — the page should read as a reference sheet, not a picture.

3. Midpoint meetup. Drive to a midpoint or the endpoint of the route and join Sam for the last easy stretch back toward the cars. Bring water/snacks; you skip the hardest middle portion.

4. Spectator-and-cooldown. Drive to the trailhead, walk a short warm-up loop on flat ground nearby, hang at start/finish while Sam does the full route, walk an easy cooldown together at the end.

- A genuine near-fall or twist — do not walk it off
