Short answer: the IRA/SEP/SIMPLE box is blank, so the answer to the software is "from a pension or annuity" — NOT from an IRA, SEP, or SIMPLE.

What the form is telling you:

  - Blank IRA/SEP/SIMPLE box → this is from a qualified employer plan (most likely a 401(k), 403(b), or a traditional pension). It is not from a personal IRA.
  - Distribution code 7 → "Normal distribution." On a qualified plan this means Mom has reached the plan's normal retirement age (or 59½ with separation from service). Code 7 specifically signals no 10% early-withdrawal penalty under the code itself. For an IRA the same code just means age 59½ or older.
  - Gross distribution = taxable amount → the entire distribution is taxable. There is no after-tax basis in this plan to recover (typical when all contributions were pre-tax, as in a 401(k)).

What this means for the software flow:

  - Route to the pension/annuity section, not the IRA section.
  - Enter the full gross amount as taxable.
  - No early-withdrawal penalty line (code 7 already accounts for that).
  - Any federal income tax withheld on the form is still reported separately on the federal return — that part is unaffected by the code or the IRA box.

What this is NOT:

  - Not a QCD (Qualified Charitable Distribution) — code 7 would not be used for a QCD; QCDs use code G or Q on Form 1099-R and are typically issued by an IRA, which is also ruled out here.
  - Not an RMD-year signal by itself — code 7 covers normal-age distributions generally; if Mom was the required beginning date age this year and the plan flagged an RMD, you'd see a different code (often 7 with the year-of-age minimum amount, or a plan-specific flag). The form you've described doesn't carry an RMD indicator, so treat this as a normal age-based distribution unless Mom's plan documents say otherwise.
  - Not an IRA rollover source — you can't roll a 401(k)/pension distribution into another IRA through the software's IRA-rollover flow without checking form-specific boxes; the blank IRA box already removes that branch.

What to double-check before clicking through:

  - Box 1 (gross distribution), Box 2a (taxable amount), and any Box 4 (federal income tax withheld) numbers against the year-end retirement statement. From the Jan 9 session these already matched, so no new reconciliation needed unless the printed form differs from the values she keyed.
  - Box 7 distribution code letter/number: confirm it is exactly "7" (single digit). If the form shows "7" followed by another letter that's a separate signal.
  - The plan name and EIN in Box 11/12 — the software may ask, and they should match the year-end statement.

If the software offers a follow-up like "Was this a total or partial distribution?" or "Did you roll this over?" — answer those based on what actually happened (Riley would know from Mom), but the IRA/pension split above is settled by the blank box.

The AGI gate and the IRA-vs-pension gate are independent. Entering the AGI unblocks e-file identity verification, but it does not unblock the substantive interview. Mom still has to answer the IRA-vs-pension question, and that answer depends on what the 1099-R itself shows.

HOW THE VISIBLE 1099-R FIELDS DRIVE THE IRA-VERSUS-PENSION PROMPT

Form 1099-R is used for distributions from many account types: traditional IRAs, Roth IRAs, SEP-IRAs, SIMPLE IRAs, 401(k)s, 403(b)s, governmental 457(b)s, qualified pensions, profit-sharing plans, and nonqualified annuities. The software's "IRA or pension" question is asking what TYPE of account paid the distribution because:

  - The line on Form 1040 differs (qualified-plan distributions land on 5a/5b; IRA distributions land on 4a/4b).
  - The 10% additional tax rules (Form 5329) differ by account type.
  - RMD treatment, QCD eligibility, and basis recovery are account-type-specific.
  - Form 8606 (nondeductible IRA basis) only matters for IRAs.

The form itself carries most of what the software needs to infer the type:

  Box 1   Gross distribution paid in 2024.
  Box 2a  Taxable amount (before any 2024 return adjustments).
  Box 2b  Federal income tax withheld (some forms use Box 4 instead).
  Box 3   Distribution code(s). The strongest clue.
  Box 4   Federal income tax withheld (alternate location).
  Box 5   Employee contributions / Designated Roth contributions. For IRAs this is usually nondeductible basis territory.
  Box 6   Net unrealized appreciation. Only for employer-securities distributions.
  Box 7   Distribution amount. Sometimes used for annuity contracts.
  Box 8   Other. Sometimes indicates "PS 58 costs" or similar employer-plan items.
  Box 9a  Total employee contributions. Cumulative basis in a pension or annuity plan.
  Box 9b  Total designated Roth contributions. For designated Roth accounts.
  Box 10  Amount allocable to IRR (income on retirement contracts).
  Box 11-15  State information.

Why Box 3 is the dominant signal: letter codes are overwhelmingly IRA / Roth / SIMPLE. Numeric codes are overwhelmingly pension / qualified plan / nonqualified annuity. The IRA-specific letters are:

  G  Direct rollover
  H  Direct rollover to a Roth
  J  Early distribution from a Roth IRA, no known exception
  Q  Qualified Roth distribution
  R  Recharacterized IRA contribution
  S  SIMPLE IRA early distribution under 2 years
  T  Roth IRA distribution, not qualified
  U  Qualified charitable distribution from an IRA (age 70½+)

Codes D, E, and F are nonqualified-plan codes. Letter codes appearing on a pension/qualified-plan 1099-R are unusual and worth a stop.

Secondary signals:

  - Trustee/payer name in the upper-left corner. Banks, brokerages, mutual fund companies, and "IRA custodian" wording point to an IRA. Employers, pension plan administrators, and benefit-plan wording point to a pension or qualified plan.
  - Box 5 / 9a / 9b presence. IRA basis tends to live in Box 5; pension basis tends to live in Box 9a.
  - The January 9 reconciled year-end statement already describes the account as one or the other — that's the cleanest source.

FACTS MOM MUST VERIFY BEFORE ANSWERING

  a. The legal account type. Is it her IRA at a custodian, or a pension/qualified plan from a former employer? The account name on the year-end statement usually settles it.

  b. The distribution code. A code she does not recognize, or one with a "may include" annotation (for example, "B — may include 2"), is a stop signal, not a guess signal.

  c. Whether she took a QCD in 2024. A QCD shows up as Code G on the 1099-R. This is an IRA-specific election that the software may or may not handle automatically, and the substantiation needs to match.

  d. Whether she took an RMD in 2024 and whether the full RMD was satisfied. Shortfall has penalty-relief implications.

  e. Whether she did any rollover in 2024. Direct rollovers produce Codes G or H, and the software needs to know whether the distribution is a nontaxable rollover (and whether any part is taxable because of after-tax basis).

  f. Whether she has basis. If Box 5 or Box 9a is non-zero, the situation is more involved than the plain IRA-vs-pension prompt suggests; an incorrect answer can quietly mis-state the taxable portion.

  g. Whether this 1099-R is the only 2024 1099-R she received. Multiple 1099-Rs from different accounts must each be entered with its own type.

  h. Re-verify boxes 1, 2a, and 2b/4 against the January 9 reconciliation. They already matched; it's worth a second pass now that the AGI is no longer blocking, so the substantive interview starts from a confirmed baseline.

WHEN TO STOP AND ASK THE PLAN ADMINISTRATOR

  - She does not recognize the trustee or payer name on the 1099-R.
  - The distribution code is unfamiliar, has a "may include" suffix, or is missing.
  - Box 5 or Box 9a shows a basis amount she cannot reconcile with her own records.
  - The gross distribution, taxable amount, or withholding do not match her year-end statement (they did match on January 9; a new discrepancy is a stop).
  - She took an RMD and the 1099-R does not clearly indicate the RMD portion — the administrator can confirm whether the full RMD was distributed and whether any part was a QCD.
  - She had a rollover across account types (IRA to 401(k), 401(k) to IRA, or Roth conversions) and the form's wording is ambiguous.
  - Boxes 11–15 (state information) do not match her state-return plan.
  - The plan administrator already declined to issue a corrected 1099-R for the prior mailing address (confirmed January 9) — but if any OTHER field becomes relevant to the IRA-vs-pension choice and the form is silent, ask in writing before answering.

WHEN TO STOP AND ASK A TAX PROFESSIONAL (CPA / EA)

  - The distribution code is one she does not understand and the plan administrator cannot explain in plain English.
  - There is a basis amount (Box 5 or Box 9a) and Form 8606 (or the pension-basis equivalent) was never filed in prior years.
  - The 1099-R shows a return-of-contribution, a recharacterization, or an excess-contribution removal.
  - A QCD appears on the 1099-R (Code G) but the charity, amount, or substantiation is unclear, OR she made a QCD but the form does not show Code G.
  - An RMD was required and either was missed, partially taken, or taken late — Form 5329 penalty relief is a judgment call.
  - The distribution code indicates disability, death, divorce, or IRS levy.
  - The software's IRA-vs-pension answer changes the Form 1040 line and the resulting tax differs from her expectation based on prior years.
  - She cannot tell whether the account is traditional, Roth, SEP, SIMPLE, or an employer plan, and cannot determine it from the form, the statement, or the administrator.

WHAT THIS IS NOT

This is a checklist of what the visible 1099-R fields mean for the IRA-vs-pension prompt, what to verify before clicking through, and where the stop-and-ask lines are. It is not tax advice and not a recommendation about software-versus-EA. The pattern that has held for Mom's other tax items — reconcile against the year-end statement, ask the administrator when a field is unclear, reserve the EA for judgment calls — fits this prompt the same way.

One practical note: now that the AGI is visible, Mom does not need to rush through the rest of the interview in one pass. The software should let her save progress. The AGI gate opens at the e-file verification step; the IRA-vs-pension gate sits earlier in the substantive interview and is the one where careful answers, not fast ones, are what matter.

Reject IND-031-04 means only that the AGI Mom entered does not match what IRS has on file for her primary SSN. It is one of the two most common e-file rejects and almost always resolves on the next attempt once the number is correctly verified. Nothing in the reject itself implies identity theft or a problem with her 2024 return — just a mismatch on the prior-year AGI check.

The likely causes, in rough order:

1. Transcription error on her end. The most common cause by far. The prior-year AGI is one number on a specific line of the 2023 Form 1040 (line 11). It is easy to misread line 11 (AGI) as line 9 (total income) or line 12 (taxable income), or to misread a digit. It is also easy to transpose two digits when copying.

2. The number she transcribed is from a different document. State return, a worksheet, a summary screen, or a draft — none of these are the AGI the IRS verifies against. Only the AGI on the federal 1040 (line 11) that was actually filed and processed for 2023 counts.

3. IRS has a different figure. Uncommon but possible: IRS made an adjustment to her 2023 return during processing, or she amended 2023 after the original filing and IRS's record is now the amended AGI. If she did amend 2023, the amended AGI is what IRS is comparing to, not the original.

4. Filing-status mismatch. If 2023 was filed jointly and 2024 is single, or vice versa, the primary-taxpayer AGI check still uses the AGI from the 2023 return as filed. The number is the same in either direction — but it is worth confirming she is looking at the 2023 return she actually filed, not a draft for a different status.

What to re-verify on the printed 2023 return, in order:

- Confirm it is the federal Form 1040 (or 1040-SR) and the return that was actually filed and accepted, not a draft.
- Read line 11 directly: "Adjusted gross income." Do not use line 9 (total income) or line 12 (taxable income) or line 15 (tax).
- Copy every digit, including leading zeros if any, and confirm there are no commas or dollar signs included. IRS expects the numeric value.
- Note whether 2023 was filed jointly or single. If jointly, the AGI is still one number for the joint return — enter the joint AGI exactly as it appears.

If rechecking the printed 2023 return does not produce a successful e-file, the cleanest independent source is IRS Get Transcript (online at irs.gov, or Form 4506-T by mail). The "Tax Return Transcript" shows the AGI IRS has on record for the year. Online retrieval is fastest — usually immediate. This resolves the ambiguity if the printed return and IRS records do not match for any reason.

Do-not-guess rule: do not have her try variations of the AGI hoping one works. IRS locks the e-file identity check after a small number of failed attempts, and a temporary lock would make the rest of the season harder. Two careful, verified attempts is the right budget.

If the second attempt also rejects, the practical fallbacks are:

- IRS Get Transcript to confirm the AGI IRS has, then enter that exact number.
- Use the prior-year PIN option instead, if she has one (the reject code covers either AGI or PIN mismatch, so the software should offer both).
- File on paper. The e-file identity check does not apply to paper filing. Paper is a clean fallback for a simple return like hers; the trade-off is a longer refund timeline.

Effect on the earlier software-vs-$325 EA decision: this AGI issue does not change it. Software remains appropriate if the remaining review is comfortable; the EA's value is judgment, review, and notice support, not different forms. A guided-software user with a simple return hitting a standard prior-year-AGI reject is squarely within what the software is designed to handle.

Practical next step: re-read line 11 of the 2023 filed 1040 with Mom, copy it exactly into the software, and resubmit. If it rejects again, pull the IRS Tax Return Transcript online before a third attempt.

IND-031-04 means the prior-year AGI Mom entered for electronic identity verification does not match the IRS Master File. The e-file was rejected; nothing was accepted, and the 2024 return is still due. The right fix depends on which condition caused the mismatch, so walk through the steps in order rather than retrying with different guesses.

STEP 1 — CONFIRM THE NUMBER MOM ACTUALLY ENTERED
Re-open the return in the software and look at the exact value entered for the 2023 AGI. It must be from her 2023 Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 11 (Adjusted Gross Income). It is not:
  - line 9 (total income)
  - line 15 (taxable income)
  - the 2024 AGI (easy swap when the software shows both years)
  - the 2023 refund, withholding, or bank-1099 interest
  - a number re-typed from a tax summary email that rounded or summarized
If the entered value is not line 11 of the 2023 return, correct it and retransmit. Do not change it to a guess.

If the entered value does match line 11 exactly, go to Step 2.

STEP 2 — DETERMINE WHETHER THE 2023 RETURN HAS BEEN PROCESSED
This is the step most skips. IND-031-04 with the correct line-11 value almost always means IRS does not yet have a 2023 AGI on its Master File, even though Mom filed. Check status:
  - If Mom expected a 2023 refund: use IRS "Where's My Refund?" at irs.gov/refunds with SSN, filing status, and exact refund amount.
  - If no refund or that tool isn't helpful: sign in to her IRS online account at irs.gov/account and pull the 2023 tax account transcript.
  - If she can't go online: request a transcript by mail via "Get Transcript." Allow 5–10 calendar days.

Three outcomes:
  (a) The transcript shows a 2023 AGI and it differs from what Mom entered — use the transcript value. That is what IRS has. Retransmit.
  (b) The transcript shows no 2023 record, $0, or "return not yet processed" — IRS hasn't posted 2023. Go to Step 3.
  (c) The transcript shows the same AGI Mom entered but the rejection persists — that is an administrative issue, not a data issue. Call the IRS e-file help line listed on the rejection notice.

STEP 3 — IF THE 2023 RETURN WAS FILED BUT NOT YET PROCESSED
The 2023 AGI on Mom's filed return is real; it just hasn't reached the IRS Master File yet. Three honest paths:

  (i) Wait for 2023 to finish processing, then retransmit 2024. This is the cleanest path when there's no deadline pressure. Paper-filed 2023 returns commonly take 6–10 weeks from receipt to post (sometimes much longer); e-filed 2023 returns usually post within 21 days but can lag in peak season. The IRS "Where’s My Refund?" status turning to "Refund Sent" or the transcript populating is the signal that 2023 is now on file.

  (ii) Enter $0 as the prior-year AGI only if the software explicitly allows it AND the truthful answer to "Did you file a 2023 return?" in that software's flow is one of: "no," or "yes, but it has not yet been processed." Most guided software won't accept $0 if the prior-year question is answered "yes" with no processing confirmation; it will demand the actual AGI. Don't misrepresent the filing status to force the $0 path — that's an inaccurate return, not just a workaround.

  (iii) Paper-file the 2024 return. See Step 4.

If Step 3(i) is workable, it's usually preferable — e-file is faster and produces an electronic acknowledgment.

STEP 4 — PAPER-FILE THE 2024 RETURN
Paper filing bypasses the AGI/identity-match verification entirely, so it sidesteps IND-031-04 completely. Practical points:
  - Print the federal return from the software, sign and date page 2, mail to the IRS service center address the software prints for her state of residence. Use certified mail or USPS with tracking so there is proof of mailing.
  - The state return is a separate envelope and mailing.
  - Processing is 6–8+ weeks, longer if there's any error. There is no electronic confirmation of receipt.
  - Choose this when waiting isn't workable (deadline, refund timing) and the $0 path isn't available.

WHAT NOT TO DO
  - Don't retransmit with the same rejected AGI; the rejection will repeat.
  - Don't substitute a different "AGI-looking" number hoping one matches. There is only one correct prior-year AGI on file with IRS for any given year.
  - Don't enter an Identity Protection PIN or prior-year PIN unless Mom was actually issued one — IND-031-04 is AGI, not a PIN code (PIN mismatches are IND-032 / IND-033).

WHAT THIS IS NOT
  - A rejection is not a filed return. The 2024 return has not been accepted by IRS; it remains due.
  - A mismatch is not, by itself, an audit flag or fraud signal. It just blocks e-file until the AGI matches the Master File.
  - This is not a reason to switch from software to a paid preparer mid-return. The decision she made earlier (software vs. enrolled agent) doesn't change because of IND-031-04; the issue is mechanical, not judgment-based.

The narrow path: confirm the entered value is line 11 of the 2023 Form 1040; check IRS processing status via transcript or online account; then choose (a) retransmit with the correct/transcript value, (b) wait for 2023 to post and retransmit, or (c) paper-file 2024. Don't mix (b) and (c) — pick one and let it run.

SHADOW-REPLAY ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
post-corrected-nine-fixture / pre-production-release

Purpose: define what the shadow replay must demonstrate before any production-release decision on the shared-state contract. The replay is one gate between the corrected nine-record fixture test (Feb 11) and the separate production-validation gate that follows. Shadow-replay success is not release approval.

  What shadow replay is
    - Nonproduction replay of a frozen production-source snapshot through the versioned shared-state transformation, observed by the three production consumer surfaces (Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, lifecycle preflight) using each consumer's actual query path.
    - Uses historical "current-as-of" snapshots, not live production state.
    - Produces no production writes, no customer-visible effects, no override of any consumer's routine output.
    - Required to demonstrate: (a) cross-consumer agreement and (b) correct fail-closed behavior at production scale.

  What shadow replay is not
    - Not production validation.
    - Not a release decision.
    - Not a substitute for the production-validation gate that follows it.
    - Not evidence that the transformation is operationally stable, audit-clean at scale, or safe to leave running unattended.
    - Not authorization to flip the contract live.

  Input freeze (must hold for the entire replay)
    1. Source snapshot: a single point-in-time export of every governed source field across all accounts/workspaces/destinations in the test window, with SHA-256 hash, row count, and timestamp recorded.
    2. Consumer query paths: frozen at the commits used in the corrected nine-fixture run; no parallel rewrites during replay.
    3. Transformation code: pinned to the commit on which Daniela's corrected version sits — the one without prior-value inheritance for qualifying-human-admin. Any re-pin is a new replay.
    4. Freshness threshold and conflict-resolution rules: frozen at the values documented in the shared-state contract comment.
    5. Prior-value state must be preserved in the snapshot, so the "must NOT inherit" assertion is tested, not assumed.

  Coverage — minimum record mix in the replay population
    - Default: full production population for the test window. A sampled replay is acceptable only if the sample design reproduces the four-state distribution below at >=95% confidence; in that case the unsampled remainder must still be re-run before release.
    - The nine January mismatch fixtures included verbatim, with their prior-value state preserved.
    - Each of the four field-state categories must be present with explicit counts:
        (a) current value present and supported
        (b) current value present but stale (older than freshness threshold)
        (c) current value missing / null
        (d) current value conflicting across sources
    - The specific class the corrected fixture was designed to catch — prior qualifying-human-admin = true, current = null — must be present in the replay, not only represented in fixtures.

  Cross-consumer agreement — pass conditions
    For every record in the replay population:
    1. HS reporting, EA selection, and lifecycle preflight derive the same current governed value for each governed field from the shared-state read.
    2. Where any of the three consumers currently computes from its own source rather than the shared-state read, the replay must record both the consumer's current answer and the shared-state answer, and the pass condition is that the shared-state answer matches what the consumer's own source would have produced (i.e., the shared state is at least as fresh and as correct as the consumer's local view).
    3. Any cross-surface divergence in a record's governed value must be attributable to documented intentional difference (e.g., workspace-vs-account unit, different as-of window), not to a transformation defect.
    4. Per-record output: governed field, prior value, current source value(s), freshness timestamp, conflict flag, consumer-by-consumer output, pass/fail.

  Fail-closed behavior — pass conditions
    For every record where the governed field is missing/null, stale, or conflicting:
    1. All three consumers output HOLD. No selection, no exposure, no preflight pass.
    2. The transformation must not carry forward a prior "true," must not default to "true," and must not default to "false" when the current value is unsupported. HOLD is the literal output.
    3. Lifecycle preflight marks the record as send-suppressed, not as eligible-with-a-note.
    4. HS reporting classifies the record as held, not as admitted or assisted.
    5. EA selection treats the record as not-eligible: no neutral exposure, no expansion attribution, no contact.
    6. Held rows appear in the exception manifest; held rows do not appear in any numerator (selected, eligible, exposed, contactable, send-ready).
    7. Held rows generate no customer-visible artifact — no prompt, no email, no in-app message, no CS task, no neutral exposure.
    8. Specifically for the prior-value-true / current-null case: the replay must demonstrate that the corrected transformation does not inherit the prior "true," and that no consumer (HS, EA, preflight) treats the record as qualifying because of the prior value.

  Provenance and reproducibility — pass conditions
    1. Deterministic: same frozen inputs + same transformation commit -> same outputs.
    2. Per-record decision log: record id, governed field, prior value, current value(s), freshness timestamp, conflict-resolution outcome, output.
    3. SHA-256 of source snapshot, transformation commit, and each consumer query commit recorded and linked from the replay artifact.
    4. The replay can be re-run from frozen inputs without contacting live production systems.

  Operational containment — pass conditions
    1. No writes to production tables from the replay run.
    2. No override of any consumer's routine production output.
    3. No customer-visible side effect of any kind.
    4. Replay artifact filed in the approved managed folder; row counts and hashes verified before sign-off.

  Scale and stop conditions
    1. Replay passes only if every pass condition above is met for the full replay population.
    2. A single held-but-not-hold-output instance is a fail. A single prior-value-inherited instance is a fail. A single cross-consumer disagreement that cannot be attributed to documented intentional difference is a fail.
    3. A failing replay blocks the production-validation gate; it does not block a re-run after a documented fix and a fresh fixture pass on the affected cases.

  Post-replay, pre-production-validation
    - Replay artifact and a one-page summary (population size, four-state distribution, pass/fail counts, any divergences with attribution, any anomalies) filed alongside the shared-state contract document.
    - Corrected narrative: shadow replay passed; production validation has not occurred; the contract is not live.
    - The next gate is a separate production-validation pass (the Daniela pattern — first pass, then second pass with assertions). Its assertions, expected outputs, stop conditions, and audit window must be specified before it begins, and it remains a state-changing-event-class review regardless of replay outcome.

  What this gate does not authorize
    - Flicking the contract live, even on a small slice of the population.
    - Removing the per-row prior-state preservation from any later test.
    - Treating fixture success + replay success as joint evidence of release-readiness.
    - Reclassifying the work as a routine measurement change rather than a state-changing release.

Staging freshness alarm — acceptance criteria for automatic-clear, audit-history, fail-closed preservation, and held-row non-release.

Scope. These criteria define how the lifecycle-export freshness alarm transitions out of "active," how its incident history is preserved, and what it explicitly cannot do to held rows. They do not modify row release authority, suppression rules, freshness SLA, connector-state checks, or the named-human recheck process. The alarm remains a monitoring signal only.

----

1. Automatic-clear criteria.

The alarm auto-clears when ALL of the following are satisfied at the moment of the verification run:

  a. A fresh source-to-consumer refresh has completed and been corroborated. This mirrors the January 30 pattern: Daniela (or the on-call transport owner) repairs the refresh job, then Owen and Ines perform a fresh current-state check rather than reviving prior eligibility.

  b. Source as-of and consumer as-of converge within the freshness SLA. Specifically: consumer as-of is no older than source as-of, or consumer as-of is within the SLA window defined by Owen. Until that window is formally set, the default is "consumer as-of ≥ source as-of at the time of the verification run."

  c. The convergence is verified by the same monitoring path that detected the divergence, not by an independent signal that could itself be misaligned or stale.

  d. The verification runs against current state. It does not compare against a pre-incident stored snapshot, a cached as-of, or a value written during the alarm-active window.

The alarm does NOT auto-clear based on:
  - Time elapsed since the alarm was raised.
  - Manual acknowledgment by an operator.
  - A separate operator action that has not been corroborated by a current as-of comparison.
  - Absence of new divergence events (no news is not the same as verified-good).
  - Re-running of earlier "eligible" flags or stored freshness markers.

If convergence cannot be verified — for example, source connector down, consumer refresh halted, as-of timestamps not writeable, or verification job failing — the alarm remains active. A stale or failed verification path fails closed.

----

2. Audit-history acceptance criteria.

Every state transition of the alarm is logged with all of the following fields:

  - Timestamp (UTC) of the transition.
  - Actor: "system" for auto-detected transitions, or a named human (e.g., "Owen rerun," "Ines recheck," "Daniela transport repair confirmed"), or an automated verification-run identifier.
  - Trigger: which acceptance criterion in section 1 was satisfied (1a, 1b, 1c, 1d), or which operator action triggered the transition.
  - As-of values at the moment of transition: source as-of, consumer as-of, and divergence magnitude in minutes.
  - Lag duration: elapsed time from alarm-raise to alarm-clear.

The audit log is append-only. No row of the audit log is overwritten, deleted, or rewritten by the auto-clear path. The earlier standing rule against erasing audit history by removing non-running flag records still applies: alarm flags do not transition to "non-running" in a way that erases the active incident. The cleared state is a new appended row that references the prior active row.

Held rows retain their original hold timestamps, hold reasons, and held-by attribution. The auto-clear does NOT modify hold metadata on any row. If a row was held at 14:00 with reason "export lag — source as-of 4:00 AM vs consumer as-of 3:00 PM," that record remains unchanged after the alarm clears at 16:00.

If a verification run fails, that failure is logged with the same fields. Three consecutive verification failures escalate to a named human — Owen for within-surface, Riley for cross-surface or expansion-assist.

The audit log also records the alarm's "active" duration as a single derived field, computed at the moment of clear, not interpolated later.

----

3. Fail-closed preservation (cross-cutting).

Alarm-clear does NOT change the disposition of any held row. Specifically:

  a. The alarm has no write path to row state. It cannot transition a row from "held" to "eligible" or from "held" to "released." A code review or query against the row-state table must show zero state transitions during the alarm-active window except those explicitly authorized by a separate governed action with a named actor.

  b. Row release requires the existing recheck process: a named human (Owen for within-surface Helio Start, Ines for lifecycle messaging, or the appropriate lane owner) performs a fresh current-state check on each row, confirms current eligibility against current state, and only then releases under existing authority. This is the same procedure used on January 30, where recheck preceded release and the two were distinct events.

  c. Held rows remain held through alarm-clear. If the auto-clear occurs at 16:00 and the recheck has not yet been performed at 16:30, the row is still held at 16:30. The recheck schedule is set by the lane owner and does not depend on alarm-clear timing.

  d. If a held row's underlying state has shifted during the lag — for example, a workspace deactivated, a suppression added, an external authority revoked, a connector-state value changed — the row remains held under the new state even after alarm-clear. The recheck discovers the new state; it does not assume pre-lag state is restored. The recheck result, not the alarm-clear, determines the new disposition.

  e. Fail-closed posture is re-established or maintained after alarm-clear. The next send attempt requires the full existing preflight: freshness check, suppression check, connector-state check, and any other gates that applied before the incident. Alarm-clear is informational. It does not bypass, shortcut, or satisfy any preflight gate.

----

4. Held-row non-release by the alert (cross-cutting acceptance test).

The alarm passes acceptance only if the following sequence is observed end-to-end:

  a. Baseline: known-good state, no lag, no rows held by the freshness gate.

  b. Synthetic lag injected: source as-of frozen, consumer as-of continues. Observed: alarm raises within SLA; audit log records the "active" transition with all required fields; all rows that would otherwise be eligible remain held fail-closed.

  c. During alarm-active window: query the row-state table. Confirm zero rows transitioned state. Confirm no suppression was bypassed. Confirm no held row was sent. Confirm no connector-state override occurred.

  d. Lag repaired. Observed: alarm auto-clears only after criteria 1a–1d are satisfied. Observed: rows remain held. Observed: hold metadata on rows is unchanged.

  e. Existing recheck process run by named humans (Owen and/or Ines). Observed: only then do rows transition to released, and only those rows that pass the fresh recheck.

  f. Audit log shows the full sequence — raise → active → cleared → release — with named actors at each human-driven transition and trigger fields at each system transition.

The acceptance test fails if any of the following occurs:

  - Alarm clears without convergence verified under criterion 1b.
  - Any row transitioned to eligible or released during the alarm-active window.
  - Any row transitioned to released without a named recheck actor.
  - Audit log entries missing for any state transition.
  - Hold metadata on a row was modified by the auto-clear path.
  - A suppression or connector-state check was bypassed because the alarm was clear.

----

5. What this specification is not.

  - Not a release authority. The alarm cannot release rows.
  - Not a modification of the suppression check, freshness SLA, or connector-state check.
  - Not a replacement for the named-human recheck process with an automated one.
  - Not evidence that the alarm is production-safe. This defines acceptance criteria for a future validation pass; passing that pass is a separate event.
  - Not applicable to cross-surface or expansion-assist state changes. Those remain Owen's lane for within-surface and Riley's lane for cross-surface.
  - Not a settlement of alarm-monitoring ownership or on-call rotation.
  - Not retroactive. It applies forward from the date the criteria are adopted; it does not re-classify prior incident handling.

----

Open items to resolve before this can be adopted:

  - Owen to define the convergence window for criterion 1b (default above is a placeholder).
  - Owner of the verification job in criterion 1c — same monitoring path as divergence detection, or a paired run?
  - Escalation routing for three consecutive verification failures (Owen within-surface, but who for the alarm-monitoring run itself?).
  - Where the audit log lives, who reads it, and how it is preserved across the contractor's February 23 closeout.

If you want, I can put this into a doc or update the lifecycle ownership working document so the criteria are persisted alongside the existing recheck procedure and suppression-check labels.

Assessment of whether to drive, plus the precautions you asked for.

Drive-or-not call

The leak is slow, not catastrophic. About 8 psi lost overnight with no audible hissing now and no sidewall damage is consistent with a screw acting as a partial plug in the center tread, which is the classic repairable zone. At 27 psi against a 35 psi spec, the tire is underinflated but serviceable for a very short, low-speed drive on city streets.

That said, "should I drive it" depends on distance and route:

  - Shop within roughly 3 miles, surface streets only, no highway: reasonable to drive directly, slowly, straight there.
  - Shop requires highway driving or is more than a few miles away: don't. The risk profile gets worse fast with sustained speed and heat on an underinflated tire. Better alternatives in order of preference: a mobile tire service that comes to you, a tow, or have someone bring a 12V inflator and follow you while you drive the short distance at low speed.

Screw handling

  - Leave the screw in place until a technician pulls the tire and inspects from the inside.
  - It is very likely slowing the leak. Pulling it can convert a slow seep into a fast one on the spot.
  - It also tells the tech the entry angle and depth, which determines whether the puncture is repairable and where the internal patch needs to go.
  - Do not add any external sealant (Fix-a-Flat type product) before the shop visit. It makes the internal inspection messier and some shops refuse to work on tires that have had sealant in them.

Adding air for a short trip

Reasonable, with the right framing:

  - You are not "fixing" the tire. You are buying a safe pressure margin for a short drive only.
  - If you reinflate, do it right before leaving. A 12V portable inflator or a gas-station air compressor both work. Inflate to roughly 30 to 32 psi, not the full 35. Full pressure gives a false sense of security and the tire will drop again; the goal is just enough margin to keep the sidewall from folding under load at low speed.
  - Drive immediately. Do not inflate, wait an hour, then drive — you will likely arrive underinflated.
  - After you reinflate, watch the tire for 2 to 3 minutes. If pressure drops noticeably in that window, do not drive.

Drive precautions for the trip

  - Speed: stay well under posted limits. Treat 30 mph as a soft ceiling.
  - Route: avoid highways, freeways, and any sustained high-speed stretch. Take the most direct surface-street path.
  - Acceleration and braking: gentle. Hard inputs load the tire harder and generate more heat in an underinflated carcass.
  - Cornering: avoid anything sharper than a normal gentle turn. The rear can get loose on an underinflated rear tire, especially in a RWD car. FWD is more forgiving but still take it easy.
  - Cargo and passengers: minimize. Less load = less sidewall flex = less heat.
  - Bring the inflator in the car if you have one. If pressure visibly drops during the drive, stop and reinflate rather than pressing on.

Stop-driving conditions during the trip

Stop immediately and pull over safely if any of these happen:

  - Pressure drops visibly, or you hear hissing or any sudden air sound.
  - TPMS warning light comes on (you are already below the threshold at 27, so a light may already be present; a change in behavior is what matters).
  - Vibration, thumping, or pulling to one side that wasn't there before.
  - Visible bulge, blister, or any change in the tire's shape, especially the sidewall.
  - Pressure falls below roughly 20 psi. That is the rough line where sidewall damage risk rises sharply.
  - Any handling change that makes the car feel unstable.

If you have to stop on the road, change to the spare rather than reinflating again and continuing. If no spare, call for roadside service rather than limping further.

What the shop should assess when you arrive

This is what you're paying them for, so ask for it explicitly:

  - Dismount the tire from the wheel and inspect the puncture from the inside. Tread-area punctures of small diameter (screw, nail) are normally repairable with a plug-and-patch from the inside; a plug alone is not considered a permanent repair by industry standards.
  - Check the puncture's location, angle, and whether it went all the way through. Center tread is best; shoulder and sidewall are not repairable and would mean replacement.
  - Inspect the sidewall for any heat or underinflation damage from running low. Given the modest underinflation and short duration, damage is unlikely but worth confirming.
  - Check remaining tread depth. If the tire is already near the wear bars, replacement rather than repair may be the better call.
  - Confirm the wheel and rim are undamaged and the valve stem is intact while the tire is off.
  - Road-force balance after reinstallation, especially since rear-tire balance affects stability.

After the repair, normal safety practice is to recheck pressure and visual condition after 24 to 48 hours and again within the first week.

What this is not

This is not a recall-grade or catastrophic failure situation. It is a slow leak from a likely-repairable center-tread puncture, and the right move is a careful short drive to a competent tire shop rather than either ignoring it or replacing the tire on the roadside. The decision you actually need to make is just: how do you get the car to the shop safely, and what conditions make you stop and call for service instead.

The sketch is conflating two different things: **triage pressure** (how long, how wide) and **exception nature** (what kind of hold). Those are categorically separate signals, and the five terms you flagged each imply different handling:

- **Entitlement** — the account doesn't qualify to receive the action at all. Resolution is entitlement work (plan, role, eligibility confirmation), not "send sooner." Hours-open is irrelevant to whether the prompt should fire.
- **Qualifying-human-admin** — there's no human admin to act, hold, or confirm. The right work is finding/confirming the human, not escalating to override the gap.
- **Authority** — the system lacks documented authority to act on this row (lifecycle messaging authority, suppression authority, cross-team sign-off). The right work is authority confirmation; "older + wider" doesn't manufacture authority.
- **Suppression** — deliberately fail-closed. This is the most dangerous conflation: an old, wide-reaching suppression should *never* look high-priority for action. The score should be hard-bounded by suppression state, not nudged toward override by age/breadth. If anything, long-open suppression is a documentation/audit signal, not an action signal.
- **Cosmetic reporting** — display/labeling issues that gate no action. They're not in the same priority class as the four above. Squeezing them into one number with entitlement/authority failures is the wrong shape.

Two structural problems on top of the category conflation:

1. **Surface-count is not an independent signal.** Three affected surfaces can be one propagation issue, not three problems. Breadth without a root-cause reading inflates priority without adding work.
2. **"Surface" isn't a defined unit.** Workspace? account? destination? exception class? Mixing units is the same mistake the cross-surface card fell into (14 + 7 + 11 = 32 proved nothing).

### What I'd recommend for the next pass

Separate the **exception type** (a categorical primary term — one of the five above, mutually exclusive) from the **operational pressure modifiers** (age, breadth, customer-blocked time, etc.), and apply **hard gates** that override the score:

- Suppression → held, regardless of score. Score only drives *audit/documentation* follow-up, not action.
- Entitlement / authority / qualifying-human-admin → score routes to the right workstream (entitlement team, governance, admin-confirmation), not to "send faster."
- Cosmetic → separate track; lowest default priority; no urgency modifier.

If Owen wants a single priority number for the dashboard, it should be the **operational-pressure score only**, with the exception type printed alongside it as a label, not folded into the number. That preserves the triage value (age + breadth) without letting it manufacture urgency where urgency is the wrong response.

The sketch isn't wrong that age and breadth matter — they're real operational signals. It's wrong that they substitute for, or can be summed with, what kind of exception this is.

CRITIQUE OF OWEN'S 1pt/hr + 10pts/surface RULE

Five problems with the sketch:

1. No field criticality. Cosmetic display labels and entitlement conflicts earn the same 10pts/surface. They aren't the same class. One doesn't gate action; the other does.

2. Categories conflated. Owen's single "exception" bucket treats pending external authority, missing or conflicting evidence, active CS-work, and active opt-outs as interchangeable. They have different unblock paths and different time behaviors.

3. Age dominates severity. A 50-hour cosmetic error outranks a 1-hour entitlement gap under 1pt/hr. The "age should not erase field severity" principle is broken at the scoring layer, not just the interpretation layer.

4. Active holds aren't represented. Held-fail-closed rows accumulate priority points while held. Age-while-held is normal for external-authority waits, not urgency. The score rewards waiting.

5. The composite reads as customer impact. A single priority number will be read as severity, and severity will be read as customer consequence. Field completeness is operational state, not customer consequence. The score cannot be defended as a customer-impact metric and shouldn't be used like one.

RECOMMENDED TRIAGE ORDER

Sort, do not score. The order is tiered, not numeric.

PRIMARY SORT — Field criticality tier:

  Tier 1 — Hard release gates
    1a. Missing or conflicting evidence
        Entitlement view conflict, missing suppression manifest, stale authority timestamp, conflicting CS-work status.
        Cleared by fresh artifact, fresh release-time check, or decision-time reconciliation. Internal-clearable.
    1b. External-authority dependency
        Entitlement, qualifying-admin, suppression check, authority timestamp pending from external owner.
        Cannot be cleared by internal action. May be slow or stalled. Allowed to age without penalty.
    1c. Active CS-work or adoption work in progress
        Correctly routed; clears when work closes or is reclassified. Not a state failure.
    1d. Active customer opt-out
        Correct honoring; permanent until customer reverses. Not a state failure.

  Tier 2 — Soft action gates
    A specific next action is blocked (need fresh evidence before send, need owner decision before routing). Not a release blocker.

  Tier 3 — Discovery-only
    Field-incomplete but usable for Owen's within-surface review. Not eligible for any release path.

  Tier 4 — Cosmetic / non-gating
    Display, copy, formatting. Does not gate action or release. Ages without operational consequence.

SECONDARY SORT — Within Tier 1 only, by unblock-path urgency:
  1a (internal-clearable evidence gaps) → 1b (external-authority waits) → 1c (in-progress work, passive) → 1d (permanent state, minimal attention).
  Each has different SLA behavior. External waits are not urgency by virtue of waiting.

TERTIARY SORT — Surface scope, within same tier + same sub-tier:
  Single-surface items first; cross-surface items flagged for wider blast radius.
  Cross-surface does NOT promote a Tier 3 or Tier 4 item above a higher tier.

QUATERNARY SORT — Age, tiebreaker only, within same tier + sub-tier + scope:
  Older item = more likely to have lost context, more likely the holder moved on, more likely a reminder is owed.
  Age is NEVER used to promote a lower-criticality item above a higher-criticality item.
  Active holds age normally while held; that aging is not urgency.

WHAT THIS IS NOT
  Not a customer-impact ranking.
  Not a beta-pool readiness score.
  Not a single composite number.
  Not a tool for promoting cosmetic items by age.
  Not a substitute for field-owner evidence or a fresh release-time check.
  Not a basis for releasing held rows without their specific gate clearing.

WHAT THIS IS
  A triage order for operational attention.
  A fail-closed default: items only clear when their tier-specific gate is met.
  A map from field ownership to unblock path:
    Owen — warehouse and system fields (definitions, units, as-of, freshness, suppression check orchestration).
    Ines — lifecycle and support fields (suppression, hold, fail-closed controls, message-branch state).
    Daniela — transport, refresh, and source dependencies.
    AE/CS — narrative fields.

ONE-LINE RULE FOR OWEN

  Sort by field criticality tier (1a/1b/1c/1d → 2 → 3 → 4), then surface scope within tier, then age as final tiebreaker. Field severity never gets demoted by age. Active holds age normally; that is not urgency. Cosmetic items stay at the bottom regardless of how long they sit. No single composite number, and no claim that priority equals customer impact.

The $360 difference and the digit pattern are worth a closer look before any second submission.

  The numbers: $31,482 (transcript) and $31,842 (filed-return copy). Read digit by digit:
    31,482  =  3  1  4  8  2
    31,842  =  3  1  8  4  2
  The middle two digits are swapped. That is the cleanest single-character error a person can make on a copied figure, so the copy is the leading suspect.

What the 20-minute meter check actually tells us:

  Rules out:
    Any continuous leak large enough to push ≥ ~2 gal through the
    meter during the window — i.e., a sustained leak at roughly
    6 gal/hour or more during the window you watched.

  Does not rule out:
    A slow continuous leak below meter resolution (many residential
    meters' leak indicators don't reliably spin below ~1 gal/hour,
    and a 20-min window may not register even that).
    An intermittent leak — one that only flows when an appliance
    triggers it (washer, dishwasher, ice maker, recirc pump cycle).
    A leak downstream of the meter you watched (irrigation branch,
    water-heater recirc loop, hose bib, external fixture).
    A leak in shared plumbing that gets billed to your statement
    (only relevant if the meter isn't a true unit submeter).
    A billing/read artifact — one read actual and one estimated,
    misaligned cycle lengths, a read catch-up.

Plausible causes, roughly ordered by how often they match this
pattern in residential settings:

  1. Silent toilet flapper leak. Flapper doesn't fully seat; tank
     seeps into bowl at roughly 0.5-2 gal/hour. No sound, no visible
     water. This is the single most common cause of "no visible leak,
     bill doubles." A dye test catches it definitively.

  2. Water-heater recirculation pump running more than it should, or
     a small leak on the recirc loop. A pump set to "continuous" or
     on a tight schedule can move 50-150 gal/day on its own with no
     other fixture open.

  3. Irrigation/sprinkler zone that ran in January — unusual but not
     impossible (manual run, system left on schedule through a warm
     spell, maintenance testing).

  4. Intermittent appliance supply-line leak (washer, dishwasher,
     ice maker) that only flows when the appliance calls for water.
     These often go silent in a 20-min no-use window.

  5. Increased legitimate use you didn't track — guests staying over,
     more laundry, longer showers, a bath routine, a new appliance
     with high draw (e.g., a humidifier on continuously through dry
     weather).

  6. Building-side or shared-plumbing usage billed to your statement,
     depending on how submetering is set up at Cherrywood.

  7. Read artifact — December read estimated high (carrying a prior
     lower-use period forward), January read actual catches up; or
     billing-cycle lengths not matching calendar months.

What I'd suggest next — all reversible, all evidence-building, no PM
contact yet:

  - Pull hourly or daily usage from the utility portal if it offers
    it. This is the same data source that identified the May 2024
    guest-toilet leak (continuous draw 1-5 AM). A continuous baseline
    shift across January points to a continuous leak; an intermittent
    pattern points elsewhere.

  - Dye-test every toilet in the unit. Food coloring in the tank,
    do not flush, check the bowl in 15-20 minutes. Cheap and
    definitive for flapper leaks.

  - Run a longer meter observation. Overnight or a 4-hour window,
    watching the leak indicator (small triangle or diamond on the
    meter face) the whole time. A slow continuous leak shows as
    steady rotation; an intermittent leak shows as nothing during
    quiet hours.

  - Check the water-heater recirc pump — is it set to continuous,
    on-demand, or scheduled? If continuous or tight-scheduled, change
    it to on-demand or a wider schedule and compare next statement.

  - Verify what the meter actually measures: unit submeter, building
    master with allocation, or directly billed. If it's a building
    master, allocation rules matter and other units' usage can land
    on your number.

  - Confirm whether both statements were actual reads or if one was
    an estimate, and whether the cycle lengths are the same.

  - If all of the above are clean, then ask Cherrywood PM one narrow

    adjustment request — just fact-gathering.

What this is NOT, yet:

  - Not a confirmed leak.
  - Not a confirmed billing error.
  - Not grounds for a leak-adjustment request to Cherrywood PM.

  - Not a reason to withhold payment, escalate, or bring in a third

  - Not resolved.

Worth tracking while you investigate, in one place:

  - Utility portal hourly data for January, if available
  - Result of toilet dye tests on every toilet in the unit
  - Result of longer meter observation (overnight or 4-hour)
  - Water-heater recirc pump current setting, and what it was before

  - Any plumbing, irrigation, or shutoff events at the building in

  - Your own usage log if you start one (showers, laundry loads,

8-HOUR NO-USE WATER METER TEST — PLAN

Purpose
Hold all water activity constant except for a small set of recorded necessary uses, and observe whether the meter moves beyond those known events. The test is diagnostic, not a fix. A pass (no unexplained movement) does not prove zero leaks; a fail (movement without a logged cause) is a strong signal but not a final repair order.

Window selection (no overnight)
- Pick an 8-hour block where Riley is home, awake, and not about to need a bathroom mid-block. Best shape: morning start, e.g. 8:30 AM–4:30 PM, after a bathroom stop and before significant drinking.
- Confirm Sam's schedule: Sam home and committed to the protocol, OR Sam not home at all (in which case Riley manages Kibo solo).
- Avoid: days with scheduled laundry, cleaning, building maintenance, irrigation, expected visitors, or apartment inspections.
- Check building notices for sprinkler tests, boiler work, scheduled shutoffs that could affect pressure or flow readings.
- Avoid a heavy-storm day: pressure swings can trigger fire-system or irrigation back-up behavior.
- Avoid a hot afternoon with expected outdoor watering if the building has a hose bib that grounds crew might use.

Preparation (T-24h and earlier)
Equipment to gather:
- Phone or camera with timestamps turned on.
- Notepad or notes app for the event log.
- Measuring pitcher or kitchen scale (1 g water ≈ 1 mL).
- Optional flashlight for the meter pit or closet.
- Optional stopwatch.

Pre-fill all expected water needs before T-0:
- Riley's drinking water: bottles, with measured amounts written on them.
- Pitcher for the fridge: pre-filled and refrigerated before T-0.
- Coffee and tea: pre-made, or skipped for the test day.
- Kettle: skip; use microwave or cold brew if needed.
- Ice: pre-made and stored in a cooler; turn off the ice maker.
- Cooking water: skip cooking that needs water, or pre-stage measured water for one planned use.
- Cleaning: no cleaning during the test.

Kibo plan for daytime (key constraint):
- An adult dog typically drinks roughly 30–50 mL/kg/day; over 8 hours this is about a quarter to a third of daily intake. Pre-stage 1–1.5 L in a sealed, marked bottle.
- Kibo's bowl: fill to a measured amount (volume or weight), photograph the level, place bowl at T-0.
- Kibo's potty needs are handled by walks outside, not indoor water use. Schedule 2–3 walks during the block (one mid-block, one late). Walks do not consume indoor water.
- If Kibo drains the bowl, refill from the pre-staged bottle only; log the refill amount and time. If a second refill is needed (storm day, hot day, post-walk), a second sealed bottle is the refill source. Do not refill from any tap.
- Kibo is never denied water. The protocol manages how it is offered, not whether.

Appliances and fixtures to neutralize before T-0:
- Refrigerator ice maker: turn OFF; empty the ice bin; if there's a water dispenser, lock or disable it.
- Dishwasher: confirm not running; do not start during the test.
- Washing machine: do not run during the test; if a cycle was imminent, run it before T-0 so supply settles.
- Toilet(s): confirm fill valves are seated and not hissing; angle-stop valves under the tank fully open.
- All faucets: closed, not dripping.
- Outdoor hose bib(s): closed; do not use.
- Humidifier on HVAC (if present): turn off for the test if feasible — it draws water continuously and will show up as use.
- Water softener (if present): note its regeneration schedule; if a regen is due inside the test window, shift the window to avoid it.
- Water heater: don't touch. Its thermal expansion and refill behavior is normal and should not be counted as leak, but if the pressure-relief valve discharges, log it.

Household briefing for Sam (if home during the test):
- No showers, baths, dishwasher, laundry, or outdoor water use.
- Toilet flushing allowed only as a logged event with before-and-after meter photos. One planned mid-block flush is usually enough; if more are needed, each is recorded.
- Ice maker, water dispenser, humidifier all off.
- Refrigerator door: minimize opens; do not use dispenser.
- A printed note on the fridge and bathroom mirror helps.

Before photo evidence (T-0, in this order)
1. Wide shot of the meter location, showing the meter in context (unit, pit, closet, and what unit number it serves).
2. Close-up of the meter face, square-on, with the register reading fully visible. Include a piece of paper next to the meter with date, time (with timezone), and "TEST START" written legibly, OR ensure phone camera timestamp is visible in the photo.
3. Second close-up of the low-flow indicator (small triangle or rotor) — capture it at rest, ideally a short 10-second video of it still, to confirm baseline.
4. Photo of the utility portal or app showing current usage rate, if available — a corroborating digital witness.
5. Photo of Kibo's filled water bowl with measured level visible.
6. Photo of all staged water (Riley bottles, refill bottle, kettle-skip state, ice-maker-off confirmation, empty ice bin).

T-0 start
- Record start time (with timezone, -06:00 Central) in the log.
- Confirm: all faucets closed, no audible toilet refill, ice maker off, dispenser locked, humidifier off, no scheduled irrigation.
- First meter observation: write the exact odometer reading in the log (digits, including any small dials). Note position of the low-flow indicator (still or direction).
- Begin the hourly observation cadence.

During the test (every 30–60 minutes)
- Glance at the meter: odometer digits, sweep hand, low-flow indicator.
- Walk the unit: listen for running water, look under sinks, around toilets, behind the washing machine, near the water heater for any moisture.
- Log every entry with timestamp and what was observed.
- Photo of the meter at hours 2, 4, 6, and at end (same angle as T-0).
- Any Kibo water refill: record exact volume added and time.
- Any toilet flush: BEFORE photo of meter, flush, AFTER photo of meter; record the exact digits before and after to capture the delta for that flush.
- Any unexpected sound (hiss, drip, refill): mark the moment, then check the meter within 60 seconds.

Stop / invalidation conditions
Stop the test and re-run from T-0 if any of the following occurs without a logged explanation:
- Odometer advances by a digit (or fractional digit) beyond what the log accounts for.
- Low-flow indicator spins during a check-in when no logged use occurred in the prior 15 minutes.
- Audible running water or visible moisture anywhere in the unit.
- Toilet running intermittently (tank refilling on its own). This is itself a finding; the 8-hour no-use test as designed cannot complete. Pivot to a flapper diagnostic instead.
- An appliance cycle that was supposed to be off turns out to be on (ice maker, humidifier, dishwasher, washer).
- A scheduled irrigation or sprinkler event fires during the window.
- A plumbing event outside the unit: building shutoff, fire-system test, neighbor event that affects pressure or flow at this meter.
- Power outage affecting meter electronics or smart-meter gateway.
- Severe weather causing main breaks or pressure swings.
- Anyone in the household forgets the protocol and runs water without logging.

A test that ends with no unexplained movement is a pass for the configured 8-hour window only. It does not rule out a leak with a period longer than 8 hours (a 24-hour irrigation timer, a weekly softener regen, a flapper that only leaks after a long fill cycle). Re-running on a different day, or extending to 24 hours, is a separate decision.

After photo evidence (T+8h, in this order)
1. Same wide shot of the meter location as the T-0 wide shot.
2. Same close-up of the meter face, same angle, with date/time/timezone paper note saying "TEST END".
3. Same low-flow indicator close-up, ideally another short video.
4. Photo of utility portal or app showing total usage for the day.
5. Photo of Kibo's bowl showing remaining water and its measurement.
6. Photo of the log sheet (paper or app screenshot).

Details to record in the log
- Date, start time, end time (with timezone; -06:00 Central).
- Meter identification: unit number, meter serial if visible, meter type (gallons vs cubic feet), register digits.
- Start odometer reading (exact).
- End odometer reading (exact).
- Delta = end minus start.
- Event log, every entry with timestamp and volume impact:
  - Toilet flushes: gallons (1.6–3.5 typical; or measured delta).
  - Faucet use: duration times estimated flow (or measured delta).
  - Kibo water added: measured volume.
  - Any appliance cycle that did run despite the protocol.
- Meter check-ins: every 30–60 minutes, what was observed (digits, low-flow indicator status, sweep hand).
- Hourly photos: file names matched to timestamps.
- Environmental notes: weather, indoor temperature, HVAC behavior, any sounds of running water.
- Confound notes: any appliance or fixture that remained on and might explain small movements (humidifier, water heater behavior, ice maker if not actually off, water softener regen).
- Anomaly notes: anything unusual, with the response taken.
- A short plain-language conclusion, in one of two forms:
  - "Odometer advanced X.X gallons over 8h; logged uses account for Y.Y gallons; unexplained = Z.Z gallons."
  - "Odometer did not advance; low-flow indicator did not move at any check-in; no unexplained use detected in this window."

What this result is, and is not
- It IS a controlled observation of one meter's behavior over one 8-hour window.
- It IS evidence that can support or refute a hypothesis of continuous use, but only for the conditions of the test.
- It is NOT a leak audit of the plumbing system.
- It is NOT a repair order, billing correction, or claim against any party.
- It is NOT a substitute for a licensed plumber's assessment if the result is ambiguous or positive.

A strict follow-up variant
If the controlled-use test is ambiguous, a second pass with the unit's main shutoff valve closed for the same 8-hour window removes the confound of "did I forget to log something" entirely. That variant requires Kibo to be out of the unit (a walk, a daycare day, or a same-day vet/grooming drop-off) and a portable toilet solution for Riley and Sam. Plan it as a separate, opt-in step rather than the default.

ASSESSMENT: Non-atomic rollback is itself a release blocker.

Reasoning, narrow:

1. The shared-state contract's central premise is coordinated consistency across the five consumer views (Helio Start, Expansion Assist, activation reporting, lifecycle messaging, CS-nudge dependencies). A non-atomic rollback is, by definition, partial reversion — which is the structural form of the silent-source-change / downstream-override / stale-eligibility-reuse failure mode the prior incident pattern has already demonstrated. A rollback that does not restore all consumers to a single prior state in a single transition is a contract violation, not a rollback.

2. The fail-closed guarantee is undefined under non-atomic rollback. There is no clean "all held" or "all released" intermediate state — some consumers revert, others do not, and during the window consumers can disagree on held-vs-released, eligible-vs-ineligible, or pre-change-vs-post-change. The intentionally-stale-case rule (held rows remain held, no prior-eligibility re-inheritance) cannot be enforced across consumers that have partially reverted.

3. The audit-trail premise breaks. The Feb 18 work — preserving governed UTC source timestamps — exists precisely so cross-consumer ordering is provable. A non-atomic rollback generates multiple rollback events at different consumer clocks, which then require reconciliation by external time authority, which contradicts the governed-UTC work just completed. A non-atomic rollback is not a single auditable event.

4. Held-row preservation cannot be guaranteed during partial reversion. A faster-rolling-back consumer can re-expose a workspace that a slower consumer still holds fail-closed (or vice versa). Either direction produces silent eligibility re-use or silent suppression bypass — both previously observed failure modes.

5. The Feb 18 shadow replay established cross-consumer agreement on values, ordering, as-of, and freshness. That agreement is necessary but not sufficient. Cross-consumer agreement on a single rollback transition is the harder guarantee, and it is the one a non-atomic rollback cannot provide.

Conclusion: a non-atomic rollback capability is incompatible with the shared-state contract as designed. The contract either is atomic-rollback-coordinated or it does not exist. The blocker is structural, not procedural. This is an assessment, not a release decision; the existing "no production release approved" boundary is preserved.


COORDINATED ROLLBACK BEHAVIOR the next rehearsal must prove:

The rehearsal must demonstrate a single rollback event that:

1. Carries one rollback ID and one governed UTC timestamp, recorded identically in every consumer's audit log before any consumer begins reversion.

2. Captures a frozen pre-rollback state manifest per consumer view (row counts, SHA-256 hashes, suppressed/held/released classifications, source timestamp), verified and persisted before reversion begins.

3. Reverts all five consumer views to that manifest state under a single transaction, with no consumer entering a transitional state observable to any other consumer or to operators.

4. Stays fail-closed throughout the rollback window. If any consumer fails to revert, all consumers remain at the post-change state (or a defined rollback-fail-closed state) until the failing consumer is reconciled. No partial reversion is exposed.

5. Preserves held rows. For every row held pre-change (external authority, conflicting connector state, active CS work, intentionally stale), the held classification is preserved through and after rollback. Rollback does not re-inherit prior eligibility.

6. Preserves the audit trail of the change being rolled back, not overwriting it. The rollback event is a new event with its own provenance; the change event remains visible and is not silently undone.

7. Has operator visibility at every step. At all times during rollback, an operator can see which consumers have reverted, which have not, what the rollback ID is, and what state the system is in.

8. Requires operator initiation and operator confirmation of completion. Rollback is not automatic on a consumer error; it is an explicit, governed action with a named initiator.


REHEARSAL EVIDENCE the next rehearsal must produce:

1. Pre-rollback manifest, per consumer view: row count, SHA-256 hash of state, list of held rows with hold reason (external authority / conflicting connector / active CS / intentionally stale), list of released rows with release evidence.

2. Rollback trigger record: initiator name, governed UTC timestamp, rollback ID, scope (which change is being rolled back, identified by its original change ID).

3. Per-consumer rollback confirmation log. Each of the five consumer views produces a confirmation entry containing: the rollback ID, the pre-rollback manifest hash it reverted to, the timestamp at which reversion completed (in governed UTC), and a confirmation that no consumer-local state delta exists outside the rollback scope.

4. Post-rollback fixture replay. Re-run the Feb 18 agreed shadow fixture (or its successor) against all five consumers and confirm identical agreed values, ordering, as-of, and freshness outcomes to the pre-change fixture run. This proves rollback restored prior agreement, not just internal consistency within each consumer.

5. Held-row audit. For every row classified as held pre-change, confirm post-rollback classification matches. Specifically, the count of held rows per category must equal the pre-change count.

6. Rollback-window timing record. The elapsed time from rollback trigger to all-consumer-confirmed-reverted, recorded in governed UTC. The rehearsal must specify a maximum window; a rollback exceeding the window fails closed.

7. Failure-mode rehearsal. At least one consumer is configured to fail rollback (simulated timeout, simulated conflicting state, simulated missing manifest). Evidence must show: (a) the failing consumer is detected, (b) the system stays fail-closed throughout, (c) no held row is re-exposed by other consumers, (d) recovery procedure is documented and executed before any re-attempt.

8. Audit-log integrity check. The rollback event appears exactly once in each consumer's audit log with consistent rollback ID; the change event being rolled back remains visible and is not overwritten. No consumer emits more than one rollback record for the same ID.

9. No-customer-regression check. No live prompt was triggered by the change or rollback, no customer-visible activation/expansion decision was reversed, no audience row was sent during the rollback window, no inbox/state change reached a customer.

10. Recovery-from-rollback evidence. If the change is to be re-applied after a successful rollback, it travels the same change-control path (fresh manifest, fresh checks, fresh release) — not silent re-application. The rehearsal demonstrates this path or documents why it is not yet needed.

11. Operator-visibility log. Screenshots or recorded console output showing operator-visible state at each rollback milestone (trigger, in-progress, per-consumer-confirmed, complete / failed), with timestamps in governed UTC.

12. Load-condition evidence. The rehearsal runs against realistic queue depth (not empty system), so rollback timing and held-row behavior under load is measured, not extrapolated.


WHAT THIS IS AND IS NOT:

This is an assessment of the rollback design and a specification of what the next rehearsal must demonstrate. It is not approval of a production replay, not scheduling of the rehearsal, not a release decision, and not evidence that the Feb 18 clean shadow replay was sufficient on its own. The existing "no production release approved" boundary remains in force. The next rehearsal is admissible as evidence for a future production-release decision only if it produces the items above; nothing in this response weakens that standard.
