The single most important fact is that your freezer is currently reading 24°F, which is below both the 32°F freezing point and well below the 40°F food-safety threshold. Combined with the physical state of the food, that is a clean keep/refreeze verdict on everything you described.

Per-item judgment (February 22, 2025, ~17:30 CT):

Safe to keep, safe to refreeze:
  Sealed chicken portions (hard, ice crystals). The strongest evidence in this report: visible ice crystals mean the chicken never crossed 32°F, so it never fully thawed at any point during the event. Keep as-is. Refreezing is safe; expect minor texture or moisture loss on later cooking. That is a quality call, not a safety call.
  Frozen vegetables (hard, ice crystals). Same logic. Safe. Refreezing generally preserves vegetable quality well.
  Bread (still frozen). Safe. Quality preserved through refreezing.

Quality loss only, no safety issue:
  Ice cream (soft at the edges, still cold, partly frozen). At 24°F, ice cream at the edges will be soft no matter how long it sits there. The fact that it is still cold and partly frozen means it did not pass into the fully-melted/warm zone. Safe to eat. After re-hardening, expect ice-crystal texture. Discard is optional and is a quality call, not a safety call.

For any other freezer contents you did not describe, the working test is:
  Still hard with visible ice crystals at 24°F -> safe to keep and refreeze.
  Fully thawed to a soft or liquid state during the event with unknown time at warm temperatures -> not present in what you described; apply case-by-case judgment if found elsewhere.
  Cross-contamination from leaking raw onto ready-to-eat food -> not present per your report.

What I cannot infer from what you reported:
  The maximum temperature the freezer reached during the three-hour window. 24°F is the current reading; we do not know if it peaked higher and is now recovering, peaked lower, or is still rising.
  The exact duration the door was actually ajar. "About three hours" is your estimate.
  Whether 24°F is your freezer's normal running temperature, an elevated recovery temperature, or a sign of a residual problem. (A normal full freezer runs at or below 0°F.)

Practical follow-up before treating this as closed:
1. Confirm the door is now fully closed and latched and the seal looks intact. Something allowed it to drift ajar while groceries were being put away; identify the cause (package leaning against it, damaged gasket, warped door, misaligned latch) so it does not recur.
2. Verify the freezer returns to its normal operating temperature (0°F or below) over the next few hours. If it stalls above roughly 10°F, the compressor, door, or seal needs attention.
3. Recheck the thermometer in a few hours to confirm the reading is falling, not still climbing.

What this is not:
  Not an assessment of any freezer contents you did not describe.
  Not a finding that the freezer is functioning normally. 24°F is well above 0°F, and the reason the door came ajar matters.
  Not a guarantee about the maximum temperature reached during the event.
  Not a standing rule for future events of this kind. Each event is its own assessment, and the next one may land differently.

Working from the fixed fact that the door was ajar for three hours, and without sensory evaluation of the food, here is the conservative assessment. I am separating what we can determine from what we cannot, because we do not have a continuous internal temperature log.

1. What we know and what we do not know

Known:
  - The freezer door was not sealing for approximately three hours.
  - Warm-room air infiltrated continuously during that interval.

Not known and not safely inferable from a single current air reading:
  - The peak air temperature inside the cabinet during the three hours.
  - How long the air stayed above 40 degrees F.
  - Whether each individual package crossed 40 degrees F, for how long, and whether it fully thawed.
  - The starting temperature of any specific item.

You previously stated that the duration above 41 degrees F cannot be inferred from the air reading alone, and the same constraint applies here. The three-hour interval plus an unknown peak temperature is the most honest framing, and it drives the conservative path below.

2. Decision framework without smell or taste

Allowed evidence:
  - Hardness of the item (solid, slushy, liquid).
  - Visible ice crystals inside the package.
  - Visible purge or free liquid in meat or fish packages.
  - Package frost and recrystallization patterns.
  - Independent thermometer readings placed inside the cabinet before any decision is made.
  - A separate, instrumented cooler if items need to be held at a verified temperature while you decide.

Disallowed evidence:
  - Smell.
  - Taste.
  - "It looks fine."
  - Time alone as proof of safety.

3. Per-category keep or discard

3.1 Raw meat, raw poultry, raw fish, raw shellfish
  - Discard. Pathogens of concern (Salmonella, Listeria, Staphylococcus aureus toxin, Clostridium perfringens, etc.) can multiply at refrigerator and warmer temperatures and some toxins are heat-stable. A three-hour unknown-temperature event does not let us rule out extended time above 40 degrees F. Refreezing does not make unsafe food safe.

3.2 Cooked meat, cooked poultry, cooked fish, gravies, broths, soups with meat
  - Discard for the same reason. Cooked protein is a higher-risk substrate than raw.

3.3 Casseroles, frozen meals, pot pies, pasta with meat or dairy sauce, frozen pizza with meat or cheese
  - Discard unless you have continuous evidence the package never crossed 40 degrees F. You do not, so discard.

3.4 Ice cream, frozen yogurt, gelato, sorbet (dairy or egg-containing)
  - Discard on quality and on safety. Texture alone is a tell that it thawed and refroze, and dairy or egg bases are perishable.

3.5 Frozen vegetables (plain, no sauce)
  - If still rock-hard with visible ice crystals: refreeze promptly and use soon. Texture loss expected.
  - If soft or partially thawed but still cold by thermometer: cook immediately, then either eat or freeze the cooked product.
  - If fully thawed and you cannot verify temperature: cook thoroughly before consuming. Do not refreeze raw thawed vegetables without cooking.

3.6 Frozen fruit
  - If still hard with ice crystals: refreeze.
  - If thawed but still cold: cook, bake, or smoothie-process before consuming. Do not refreeze for fresh eating.

3.7 Bread, rolls, muffins, baked goods (no custard, no cream)
  - Refreeze even if thawed. Risk profile is low. Discard only if you see visible mold after thawing.

3.8 Pies, pastries, cheesecakes, cream-filled items, meringue, custard
  - Discard. Dairy and egg fillings support pathogen growth and reheating is not a reliable control for some toxins.

3.9 Hard cheese blocks (cheddar, parmesan, swiss)
  - Refreeze if still very cold. Lower water activity than soft dairy. Quality loss likely but safety risk is lower.

3.10 Butter
  - Refreeze if still cold. Salted butter is relatively forgiving.

3.11 Frozen juice concentrates
  - If still frozen or slushy, refreeze. If fully thawed, refrigerate and use within a few days. Acidic, lower risk.

3.12 Commercially vacuum-sealed raw fish of especially high value
  - Same rule applies: discard unless you have continuous evidence the package stayed at or below 40 degrees F. Cost is not a safety input.

3.13 Ice cube trays, ice from auto dispenser, ice packs
  - Discard ice that fully thawed during the event. Refreeze only if it never thawed. Ice that fully melted and refroze can harbor environmental contamination.

4. Restore protocol for the freezer

  1. Close the door fully now. If a fast-freeze or quick-freeze switch exists, engage it.
  2. Do not open the door to inspect food yet. Each opening slows recovery.
  3. Place two independent thermometers in the cabinet: one near the top-front (the warmest point when recovering) and one in the center-back. Use a third if you can.
  4. Log time, top-front temperature, and center-back temperature at 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, and 24 hours.
  5. Empty cabinet typically recovers to 0 degrees F in roughly 4 to 6 hours; full cabinet in roughly 8 to 12 hours; large chest freezer up to 24 hours.
  6. Do not load newly purchased frozen food into the cabinet until both thermometers are stable at or below 0 degrees F.
  7. When the cabinet is back at 0 degrees F, do one short, organized open: sort contents into four piles by physical state.
     a. Still rock-hard with ice crystals: refreeze immediately, label with today's date, use first.
     b. Soft or slushy but cold by thermometer: cook today before any other use, then refreeze the cooked product if appropriate.
     c. Fully thawed and you cannot verify sub-40 temperature: hold in an instrumented cooler at or below 40 degrees F while you decide per the per-category rules above.
     d. High-risk items already categorized as discard: bag, seal, and remove from food areas so they are not accidentally consumed.
  8. Clean any spilled juices, ice, or thawed food residue with hot soapy water, then a sanitizer suitable for food-contact surfaces. Dry before restocking. This is hygiene, not sensory evaluation.
  9. Confirm the door seal by closing on a sheet of paper and trying to slide it; repeat around the gasket. If the door was ajar because of a failed seal, ice buildup, a faulty latch, or a recent shift of the appliance, document and address before restocking.

5. Monitoring after the event, without smell or taste

  - Primary instrument: the two thermometers placed during recovery. Read and log them at fixed times for 24 hours.
  - Secondary checks after recovery: hardness, visible ice crystals, visible purge in meat and fish packages, frost pattern on package exterior. These are physical-state observations, not sensory evaluations.
  - Keep a written log with: discovery time, estimated door-ajar duration, closing time, time to reach 0 degrees F, items kept with reasoning, items discarded with category, cleaning steps, gasket check result, and the thermometer readings at each interval.
  - Set a reminder to recheck the freezer at 24 and 48 hours after recovery. A freezer that fails to hold 0 degrees F after this event is itself a problem and should be treated as one before restocking.

6. What this assessment is not

  - Not a guarantee about any specific package without that package being individually inspected and, where required, held below 40 degrees F during the decision.
  - Not a substitution for the per-category rules above.
  - Not a substitute for a continuous temperature log if you ever need to defend keeping a specific item.
  - Not advice on whether the appliance itself needs service; that decision follows the gasket, latch, and temperature-hold checks in step 9 and the 24- and 48-hour rechecks.

The single decision-driving sentence: with a three-hour door-ajar interval and no continuous internal temperature log, treat the high-risk categories (raw and cooked animal protein, dairy- and egg-based prepared foods, ice cream) as not safely refreezable, and let only physical-state plus thermometer evidence clear the lower-risk categories.

Sublimits, waiting periods, service-type exclusions, or "consultation vs. treatment" definitions are commonly buried below summary level.
  - The insurer's reconciliation of why the medication was allowed under the behavioral benefit while the consultation on the same visit was excluded as behavioral services.

The internal contradiction: the insurer treated the $50 trazodone as a covered behavioral benefit subject to the $250 deductible. That necessarily means they accept the underlying encounter as a behavioral claim subject to the deductible — not as something categorically outside coverage. On that same encounter, they excluded the $78 consultation under "behavioral services excluded." Both cannot be true at once. Either:
  (a) the visit is behavioral, in which case the consultation is "behavioral treatment" and should run through the deductible rather than being categorically excluded, or
  (b) the visit is not behavioral, in which case the medication should not have been allowed under the behavioral benefit in the first place.

The insurer has not yet produced the contract text, the diagnosis code, or the line-by-line adjudication that would let either reading stand. That is what you ask for next.

  2. Keep the $50 medication line in the same hold while the underlying diagnosis question is open — paying the medication cleanly while the consultation is contested can be read as accepting the insurer's categorization of the visit, which weakens the dispute. If you'd rather pay the medication and dispute only the consultation, that's also defensible, but flag it explicitly so the framing is yours, not the insurer's.
  3. Send a written request to the insurer (member services or claims, on paper or in the portal message thread — not by phone alone) asking for:
     a. The complete policy provision cited for the "behavioral services excluded" exclusion — full text, including any subparagraphs, definitions, endorsements, and any waiting-period clauses that could apply to behavioral coverage.

     d. The annual deductible status as of the claim date and the running balance after this claim.
     e. A written explanation reconciling the medication allowance (as covered behavioral benefit) with the consultation exclusion (as behavioral services excluded) on the same visit.

I don't have the specifics of this $78 exclusion on file (no EOB, claim number, CPT code, policy section, or disposition language stored), so the framework below is the diagnostic structure — once you have the answers, the actual reconciliation logic narrows to one or two of these paths. Default posture per your standing rule: decline, request documentation, hold payment, pay only after reconcile.

POSSIBLE RECONCILIATIONS (claim disposition vs. policy wording)

A. Disposition misapplies a valid exclusion — the cited exclusion is for service "X" but the billed service is "Y." Example: exclusion is for cosmetic surgery; billed service is reconstructive after injury. Appealable.

B. Disposition applies the right exclusion to the wrong facts — exclusion targets "experimental/investigational" but the treatment is FDA-approved, in standard use, with peer-reviewed support. Appealable with clinical documentation.

C. Bundling/edit disposition that documentation overcomes — service was truly separate and distinct but a modifier (-59, -X{EPSU}, -25) was missing, rejected, or the NCCI edit was misapplied. Appealable.

D. Disposition matches policy correctly — the service is genuinely excluded, the language is unambiguous, and the application is factually correct. Accept.

E. Disposition is technically correct but the provider could have billed differently — covered under a different CPT/HCPCS, or required PA that wasn't obtained, or split-able into covered components. Provider-side fix; not a true policy appeal.

F. Disposition cites "non-covered" but it's actually applied to deductible or wrong cost-share tier — processing/coordination error. Confirm before paying; provider may need to write off or rebill.

G. Disposition is correct but the amount ($78) is computed wrong — allowed amount, copay, or coinsurance percentage was applied incorrectly. Worth verifying math even if exclusion stands.

The "explanation" question is which of A–G fits the actual text of the disposition and the actual policy wording. You can't tell from the disposition alone; you need both side by side.

POLICY QUESTIONS (ask the insurer — get the section number, page, and verbatim text)

1. What is the exact policy provision (section, page, effective date) cited for this exclusion? Provide the verbatim language.
2. Does that provision name the CPT/HCPCS code billed, or the category of service, or both?
3. What is the policy's definition section say about the terms used in the exclusion (e.g., "cosmetic," "experimental," "medically necessary," "maintenance")?
4. Is there a "medical necessity override," "exception," or "clinical review" clause that could apply?
5. Are there any riders, amendments, or endorsements that modify this exclusion for the date of service?
6. What are the covered-services provisions that arguably cover this — and why does the plan read them as not applying?
7. What is the appeals/grievance procedure, the deadline (often 180 days from EOB), and the escalation path (internal review → external review)?
8. Does the exclusion apply in all settings, or only certain places of service / provider types?

CODING QUESTIONS (ask the provider's billing office, and verify against the EOB)

9. What CPT/HCPCS code was billed? What ICD-10 diagnosis codes? What place-of-service code?
10. What were the CARC and RARC codes on the EOB (the denial reason codes)? Get them verbatim.
11. Was any bundling edit applied (NCCI, modifier indicator, N20-type)? Which specific edit?
12. Were appropriate modifiers appended (-59, -25, -X{EPSU}, etc.)? If not, why?
13. Is there an alternate covered code that describes the same service? Could the service have been split?
14. Does the diagnosis code support medical necessity per the policy's clinical criteria?
15. Was prior authorization required, and was it obtained? If obtained, what was the auth number and approved scope?

CLAIM QUESTIONS (ask both the insurer and the provider; reconcile across both)

16. Claim number, date(s) of service, provider NPI, facility, in-network or out-of-network status?
17. Full money trail: billed amount, allowed/negotiated amount, plan paid, other insurance paid, contractual adjustment, patient responsibility ($78 = full PR or portion?).
18. Was the claim processed under the correct plan year, deductible met status, and family vs. individual accumulator?
19. Was coordination of benefits correctly applied (Medicare, other group, COB)?
20. Was the claim filed timely per the policy's filing deadline?
21. Is the $78 part of a global period, bundled payment, or capitation arrangement?
22. Has the provider submitted any correction, appeal, or rebill? If yes, where does that sit now?
23. What is the exact disposition language from the EOB — quoted verbatim, including any remark codes (N-code, MA-code, etc.)?

NEXT STEP

Hold payment. Send a written request to both the insurer and the provider asking for the items in questions 1, 9, 10, 16, 17, and 23 verbatim, plus the policy section text and the EOB. Once you have the disposition language and the policy language side by side, the reconciliation path becomes one of A–G above, and the decision (accept vs. appeal) follows from which scenario fits. If the answer is D, pay. If A/B/C/F, appeal with the documentation those categories require. If E, push the provider to rebill before any payment.

If you can paste the EOB disposition language and the policy section text, I can map it to one of A–G directly.

REVIEW: Bounded field-level lifecycle-preflight visibility fix (Ines + Daniela, 2025-02-25)

What the proposal as stated covers
- Per governed field: source owner, source as-of, consumer as-of, freshness result, hold reason.
- Customer field values stay under existing access controls.
- Feed-level timestamp remains as transport diagnostic only, not a freshness substitute.
- Missing/stale/conflicting continues to hold.

What is missing or under-specified before implementation and production replay approval

1. Field scope is not enumerated.
The proposal says "each governed field" but does not list which fields are governed, how the governed-field set is versioned, who owns the source-of-truth list, or how an operator verifies the displayed set matches the canonical set. A field added, removed, or renamed must not silently fall outside the view. Required: the named governed-field list with a frozen hash per release, surfaced in the view.

2. Timezone and canonical form of the two as-of timestamps is not stated.
The Feb 14 shadow replay failed exactly because lifecycle preflight parsed six timestamps as local time while HS and EA preserved UTC. The proposal must specify that source as-of and consumer as-of are rendered in the governed canonical form (UTC) with display-only Central conversion, identical to the Feb 18 correction. A display-only Central rendering without the canonical UTC primary is a reintroduction of the same defect.

3. Field-level freshness SLA is not defined per field.
"Freshness result" requires a limit to evaluate against. Owen's freshness SLA is referenced in the alarm acceptance criteria but is not committed here. Required: per-field freshness limit, default value, who owns the limit, and what "stale" renders as on the field (warning vs critical), consistent with the existing feed-level alarm thresholds. Stale means held, not advisory.

4. Hold reason taxonomy and rendering are not specified.
"Hold reason" must be a closed, enumerated set (missing field, stale source, stale consumer, conflicting source vs consumer, conflicting across consumers, suppressed, external-authority absent, CS-work active, opt-out, etc.), not free text. Each reason must map to a defined remediation lane and must not release eligibility on its own.

5. Cross-field / cross-consumer aggregation is not addressed.
The view shows per-field state but does not say how an operator reads the combined row decision when fields disagree. Required: a clear per-row rollup rule — held if any governed field fails, with the failing field(s) enumerated; never silently green; never override a held field with another field's freshness.

6. Failure to render is not handled.
The proposal assumes the view always renders. Required: behavior when the view cannot render a field (rendering error, missing schema field, stale view itself) — must fail closed (hold), surface an operator-visible banner, and audit the render failure. The view is not allowed to silently drop a governed field.

7. Audit history is not specified.
The staging alarm acceptance criteria required append-only audit with UTC, actor, trigger, source/consumer as-of, divergence, lag duration, references to prior active records. The field-level view needs the same: every visible-state transition (render, refresh, hold, alarm interaction) logged; view-render events auditable; held-row timestamps, reasons, and attribution preserved; alarm clear does not write row state.

8. Concurrency / refresh behavior is not specified.
How does the view refresh — on operator load only, on a defined cadence, on every feed event? Required: explicit refresh contract, staleness indicator on the view itself (the view's own as-of), and behavior when the underlying payload is older than the view's render time. The view itself must not become a freshness alarm substitute.

9. Alarm interaction is not specified.
The Feb 20 feed-level freshness alarm remains the transport diagnostic. Required: explicit statement that the field-level view does not replace the alarm, does not clear it, does not suppress it, and does not authorize release when the alarm is active. The field-level view is a deeper drill-down, not a parallel authority.

10. Rollback interaction is not specified.
The Feb 19 release-blocker finding requires coordinated rollback. Required: behavior of the field-level view during a coordinated rollback — view must roll back with the rest of the consumer state, must not show post-rollback field state as if it were pre-rollback, and must record the rollback ID and governed UTC timestamp in its audit. The view cannot be a partial-revert island.

11. Access controls and redaction are stated but not detailed.
"Customer field values would remain restricted under existing access controls" — required: explicit redaction boundary (which identifiers, which values, which role can see what), and a verification step that no governed-field display path leaks customer values to an unauthorized role. The field-level visibility is for governed metadata, not for payload content.

12. Idempotency and replay agreement are not addressed.
The Feb 18 correction required preserving idempotency and event distinction across consumers. Required: the field-level view must produce identical governed-field state across HS, EA, and lifecycle preflight for the same input; a divergence must itself be a held condition and an auditable event.

13. Acceptance test is not specified.
The proposal lists no test sequence. Required: a bounded acceptance test analogous to the alarm acceptance test — synthetic missing, synthetic stale source, synthetic stale consumer, synthetic conflict across consumers, recovery, render failure, and access-control verification — each with the expected field-level render, expected row decision, expected audit entry, and expected held outcome. No customer sends, no production state changes.

14. Approval boundaries and "what this is not" are not in the proposal.
Required: explicit statement that the field-level view is not release authority, not suppression override, not connector-state override, not evidence that the shared-state contract is live, not retroactive, not a substitute for the named-human recheck, not authorization for downstream overrides or silent source changes. Implementation must carry these in the design doc and the operator surface.

15. Decision-time interaction with other gates is not stated.
The Feb 16–18 minimum production gate also requires a fresh decision-time manifest, cap fit, and 24-hour post-release audit. Required: statement of how the field-level view feeds the manifest (per-row held-row list with reasons), how it participates in cap fit, and what the 24-hour audit observes about the view itself.

16. Operator visibility of the view's own integrity is missing.
Required: visible schema version, visible governed-field-set hash, visible last-refresh timestamp, visible active-alarm status, and visible rollback state — all on the view itself, not on a separate page.

17. Notification / handoff to Ines and Owen is not specified.
The Feb 19 rehearsal evidence required named initiation and completion. Required: named human accountable for the field-level view's daily operation, escalation path when the view cannot render, and the handoff document so the role does not depend on Daniela being present.

18. The proposal does not name who classifies field-level holds under the categorical exception-priority model.
A "missing field" hold is a hard gate. A "stale source" hold is a hard gate. A "stale consumer" hold may be a soft gate. Required: each hold reason classified in the model so triage order and unblock path are defined, not invented at decision time.

19. Cost of false comfort is not addressed.
A more detailed view can read as "more verified" when it is only more visible. Required: explicit statement that visibility is not verification, and that the named-human recheck remains required for release regardless of how green the field-level view appears.

20. Boundary against the operator's temptation to act on partial state is not stated.
Required: the view must not expose any "release anyway" affordance; it is a hold-explaining surface, not a release-enabling surface. No button, link, or shortcut from the view to a release action.

Recommendation
Do not implement yet. Return the proposal with these twenty items as required additions. Re-circulate when (a) the governed-field list with hash is attached, (b) the per-field freshness limits are committed, (c) the hold-reason taxonomy is enumerated, (d) the audit and rollback interactions are specified, (e) the acceptance test sequence is written, and (f) the "what this is not" boundaries are stated in the proposal itself.

RECOMMENDATION (trip to office, now): walk the bike the six blocks to the parallel neighborhood street and ride the rest of the way in on that street.

REASONING:
- The posted detour combines three independent risk multipliers — 45 mph posted speed, no shoulder, and low dawn light. You are not under a deadline that would force accepting that exposure, so the default is fail-closed: refuse the segment.
- Walking 6 blocks is roughly 6-10 minutes. It is comparable to or less than the bus option once you include the bike-retrieval trip the bus option forces.

- It keeps the bike with you and ends on a low-traffic neighborhood street, which is also your cleanest return-trip option. No stranded lock, no second retrieval trip.

WHY NOT LOCK + BUS:
- Strands the bike at the closure.
- Adds ~15 minutes you don't need to add.
- Does not actually solve the route problem — you still face the same closure / detour on the way home, just deferred.

A few concerns before this goes anywhere. None of them are stylistic — they're content.

1. "Failed" is too strong for a pending-state message. It reads as a verdict on a process that may still be in flight or that the customer could resolve. The current body uses "inactive" — neutral observation. Swapping in "failed" is a factual and tonal escalation. If the trigger is a "No" returned from the connector-auth field, "we couldn't authenticate the connection" or "the connection couldn't be verified" is closer to what we actually know. If it's a genuine failure after retries, "failed" is fair but the message then needs to acknowledge that explicitly, and it doesn't.

2. The body treats reconnect as the finish line. "Once the connection succeeds, your workspace will be ready" — that's not true. Helio Start readiness needs admin proof, supported billing, simple deployment, external authority, current entitlement, AND a first integration that can be connected in the first week. Connector success moves one gate; it doesn't complete setup. Same conflation pattern as the "your connector is verified, so your account is fully authorized and entitled" draft we already flagged.

3. No assisted path. Per the connector-access-gap brief, No and Not sure are routed to assistance before workspace admission. "Reconnect it now" assumes the right next step is do-it-yourself. For permissions gaps, agency ownership, manual billing, imports/migrations, reconnect isn't the answer — assistance is. The message doesn't acknowledge that, and doesn't say where those customers go.

4. Subject + first sentence land as alarming + conclusive. For a customer still mid-setup, "Your connection failed" + "Reconnect it now" reads as the system rejecting them rather than asking them to try again. The current "inactive" framing is gentler and more accurate.

Two things worth asking Ines before touching the copy:

- What state actually fires this? (auth check still pending, auth returned No, retry exhausted, post-assisted handoff back to customer?) The right wording depends on the trigger.
- Is there a companion branch or message that routes the cases where reconnect isn't the right action, or does this stand alone?

I'd rather not rewrite until we know the trigger. The connector-auth field is stored separately from admin proof, and Ines already suppresses connection prompts while the answer is pending — so this message sitting in the "pending-state" lane is itself worth pinning down before we change wording.

    Your Helio workspace administrator proof and connector
    authentication are both verified, and your entitlement is
    current. The remaining readiness input is confirmation of
    external-system owner authority, which Customer Success

    released. Setup prompts will stay held until that confirmation

    readiness check. The connector does not need to be
    reconnected, and your existing verifications are unchanged.

What this rewrite fixes vs. the prior draft:

- Names the actual blocker: external-system owner authority, framed as a separate readiness input reviewed by Customer Success — not a setup failure.
- Preserves the three verified fields (admin proof, connector authentication, entitlement) as still-valid, so the applicant is not silently reclassified.
- Holds setup prompts explicitly, in line with the standing rule that setup_prompts stay held while external authority is pending.
- Replaces the reconnect ask with a "connector does not need to be reconnected" line, so the message neither implies a connector failure nor requests a connector action.
- Points to a Customer Success follow-up email after the readiness check, matching the existing confirmation text ("We'll review connector access and email you after the readiness check") without conflating the connector step with the external-authority step.

The message makes no claim about why the external-authority review is pending, no timing promise beyond the existing CS email-after-readiness-check behavior, and no instruction that would relabel the applicant as having failed connector authentication or as finally ineligible.

The member's reading isn't wrong — it just lands a little past where the passage actually stops.

What the passage supports: she reversed. She set the bag on the step (committed it to leaving), waited through the daylight and the dusk, and then chose the threshold's other side. She is staying tonight. The reversal is real, and the member is right to call it a choice.

What the passage doesn't quite support: the word "finally." The bag comes back inside, but it comes back zipped. It's not unpacked, not slid under the bed, not put away in a closet. She carries it upstairs and leaves it beside where she sleeps — within reach, still ready. The narrator hasn't settled the question; she has deferred it. The text gives us a "not tonight," not a "no."

That distinction matters because it preserves the same tension the "Not tonight, she said, and turned the key" passage preserves, and that the unopened-letter-under-the-tax-papers passage preserves. In each case, the narrator refuses the moment without foreclosing the future. The bag beside the bed is structurally similar to the letter under the papers she revisits every April: a thing kept in a state of being-ready, in a place she'll have to encounter again. The choice isn't closed; it's stored.

So one defensible reading is the member's: the reversal is the answer, and bringing the bag in is the narrator coming home to the life she's in. Another defensible reading is that this is a postponement with its own return built in — she is staying tonight, but the bag is zipped, and tomorrow the front step is still there. Whether the first reading or the second becomes true is something the book has to keep earning. The passage, on its own, holds both.

For the discussion: the strongest move is probably to notice that the bag's *condition* is doing more work than its *location*. Zipped is not the same as unpacked. The narrator hasn't put the leaving behind her; she's put it beside her pillow.

The two readings share the same gesture — the bag being inside rather than at the door — and diverge only in what that gesture means over time.

A packed bag inside keeps the threshold uncrossed for tonight. That is the postponement reading: departure stays materially possible, but not now. It is also the stay reading: not setting the bag by the door is choosing to remain, even provisionally. The packed state preserves the option without exercising it; the inside location defers the crossing without foreclosing it.

From inside this moment the two are not yet distinguishable. Postponement is what a stay looks like before enough evenings have passed to name it; staying is what a postponement looks like before the bag is moved again.

Question that keeps both readings open: what would have to happen next — the bag unpacked, or simply more evenings with it by the closet — for this to settle into one reading rather than the other?

Here's how to retain and reconcile the $12.01 1099-INT, what to verify before deciding whether any filing follow-up is necessary, and why the $0.17 difference is not, by itself, a basis for amending.

WHAT THE TWO FIGURES REPRESENT

  - The 1099-INT is the bank's official IRS form. Box 1 ($12.01) is
    the authoritative taxable interest for the 2024 tax year.
  - The year-end dashboard figure ($11.84) was a preliminary total
    captured before the bank issued the 1099-INT. It is informational
    for reconciliation, not for filing.
  - The 1099-INT arrived after Mom's federal e-file was accepted.
    The accepted return therefore reflects the dashboard figure, while
    the IRS now holds the bank's 1099-INT separately. This is timing,
    not a discrepancy in the sense of an error.

WHY THE $0.17 LIKELY EXISTS (RECONCILE, DON'T CORRECT)

Common, benign causes for a small positive variance between a dashboard
total and a year-end 1099-INT:

  - Interest that posted in the final day(s) of December, after the
    dashboard's as-of date.
  - Year-end accrual adjustments on interest-bearing balances (banks
    sometimes include interest accrued through 12/31 even if not yet
    credited).
  - A dashboard that displays a snapshot of "posted" interest rather
    than "accrued through year-end" interest.
  - Rounding behavior on the dashboard (rare for 17 cents, but possible
    if interest was split across sub-accounts).

A 17-cent delta is well within the normal noise band for these
timing/rounding effects and does not imply the bank misreported or
that the dashboard was wrong.

WHAT TO VERIFY BEFORE DECIDING ON ANY FILING FOLLOW-UP

Do these in order, and stop if anything fails:

  1. The 1099-INT itself.
     - Payer name, payee name, and TIN match Mom exactly.
     - Box 1 is $12.01 (whole dollars and cents).
     - Box 3 is blank or zero (no backup withholding took place).
     - This is the original 1099-INT, not a "Corrected" 1099-INT.
     If any of these are off, hold and reconcile with the bank.

  2. The bank's own records agree with $12.01.
     - Pull the December statement and the bank's year-end interest
       summary (often available in online banking as a tax-document
       or 1099-INT detail page).
     - Confirm the bank's posted-interest total for 2024 equals $12.01.
     - Confirm the bank has not issued, and is not preparing, a
       corrected 1099-INT with a different amount.

  3. There is no other 1099-INT for 2024.
     - Review every account Mom held in 2024: checking, savings,
       money market, brokerage cash sweep, certificates, closed
       accounts that paid interest before closure, joint accounts,
       and any trusts or POD accounts.
     - If additional 1099-INTs surface, the picture changes. Total
       across all 1099-INTs is what matters, not any single one.

  4. What the original return actually used.
     - Confirm the accepted federal return reported $11.84 (or $12.01
       if she updated before filing) on Form 1040 line 2b.
     - The IRS matching system will reconcile any tiny gap from the
       bank's copy; this is not a filing error.

  5. State filing, if applicable.
     - $0.17 is immaterial at any state level. No state return
       changes are warranted on this alone. (Texas has no state
       income tax; if Mom is elsewhere, the same $0.17 reasoning
       applies, with a possible check of the state's amendment
       threshold.)

Only proceed once 1-5 check out. If any step fails, the question of
amendment changes; otherwise it does not.

WHAT THE DECISION CRITERIA ACTUALLY ARE

The right question is not "is the filed number different from the
1099-INT," but "does the difference produce a meaningful change in tax
liability, and is amendment the appropriate tool."

  - Tax effect of $0.17 of additional taxable interest.
    At any reasonable marginal rate, the federal tax difference is
    roughly $0.02-$0.04, and is frequently $0.00 once standard
    deduction and bracket interactions are accounted for. There is
    no meaningful federal tax change.

  - Schedule B threshold.
    Schedule B is required only when total taxable interest exceeds
    $1,500. $12.01 is far below that. Schedule B is not triggered
    by this 1099-INT.

  - Form 1040-X purpose.
    An amended return is for corrections that change the tax owed or
    refund by a meaningful amount, or for changes to filing status,
    dependents, credits, or deductions. $0.17 of interest is below
    any practical threshold for amendment.

  - IRS automated matching.
    The IRS holds its own copy of the 1099-INT and reconciles against
    filed returns automatically within defined tolerances. A $0.17
    gap will not generate a CP2000 notice or any other inquiry.

  - Cost/risk of amending for this alone.
    Form 1040-X adds processing time, can delay a refund or trigger
    correspondence, and provides no tax benefit. Filing it solely to
    correct $11.84 to $12.01 is not warranted.

Conclusion: no 1040-X, no IRS contact, no state amendment. Retain

The existing five fields (integration-depth, active-admin-behavior, usage-ceiling, entitlement-derived state, CS-first suppression) are either entitlement-derived or rule-derived. A manually-maintained bucket field sits in a different category and would create:

    - A freshness problem. CSM-maintained fields degrade immediately: a "High" from January is not a "High" from March unless someone re-asserts it. There is no SLA in the proposal.

    - A circular-dependency risk with the CS-first suppression rule. Accounts with open CS renewal work are already suppressed by state. A "renewal likelihood = High" bucket would tend to track those same accounts. If both signals feed the same prompts, the question becomes: which one is authoritative, and what happens when they disagree?

    - A scope-bleed risk. "CSM-maintained" means CS is, in effect, curating state that Growth, Expansion Assist, and Helio Start will read. That is a different change-control posture from the existing five fields, and it pulls CS into the freshness-alarm and fail-closed responsibility set.

On governance, the three missing pieces are not minor and cannot be answered inline. Each requires its own acceptance test, alarm, fail-closed behavior, and audit:

    - Source owner: who in CS is accountable for keeping the field current, on what cadence?
    - As-of rule: when a CSM changes a value, what timestamp governs (change time, next account review, scheduled refresh)?
    - Freshness limit: how long can the field be stale before consumers treat it as missing?

Recommended response to the CS lead:

  - Acknowledge the underlying concern. Renewal-risk visibility is real, and it is already partially served by the CS-first suppression rule plus CSM judgment.

  - Decline the pre-replay scope expansion. The replay verifies the contract that exists. Adding fields during replay confounds verification.

  - Identify what would need to be true for a sixth field to be added at all. Named source owner. Defined as-of rule. Freshness SLA plus alarm plus fail-closed behavior. Explicit distinction from the existing CS-first suppression rule. Acceptance test designed. Audit trail specified.

  - Propose the right order. After the replay passes and the release decision is made, treat the sixth field as a new change under separate change control with its own gates, not as a precondition to the existing replay.

  - Reframe the "block the replay" framing. The replay is not a launch. Even a clean replay is gated by a separate verified release decision. Holding the contract at five governed fields is not "launching without renewal likelihood"; it is verifying what is already designed before adding scope.

Two things I would not do:

  - Treat this as a preference negotiation. The right comparison is governance, not enthusiasm.

  - Conflate it with the broader CS work in flight. The CS-first suppression rule, the four rows held during the March 4 warning, and the fresh checks Owen and Ines performed on March 5 are separate items. A sixth field does not help any of them, and adopting it now would not accelerate the March 5 release decisions.

Recommendation: keep `renewal likelihood` outside the controlled replay.

The five settled inputs (external authority, connector authentication, entitlement, qualifying-human-admin status, active Customer Success adoption or renewal work) each have one source owner, an explicit as-of time, and a freshness limit. `renewal likelihood` has none of those.

- Source owner: the value would draw on Customer Success judgment, account history, usage signals, and possibly a model. None is authoritative alone, so no single owner exists to defend it.
- As-of time: a projection is not a snapshot, so there is no clean moment to bind it to.
- Freshness limit: a projection ages non-linearly and the policy for staleness is not defined.

Adding it now would weaken the field standard rather than extend it. The replay is testing those five governed inputs plus the freshness alarm and held-row behavior. Admitting a field that fails all three requirements makes that test harder to defend and risks reading the contract as softer than the five fields actually are.

Active Customer Success adoption or renewal work is already represented as a distinct current-state field. `renewal likelihood` would either duplicate that field or sit on top of it, conflating observation (this account has open renewal work) with inference (this account is likely to renew). The offer has real upside and a real structural problem, and they're in different clauses. Worth separating them before any conversation with the chef-owner.

What I'd treat as the actual stakes:
- Seasonal-menu authority and private-dining authority are meaningful creative ownership, not a title change.
- Quarterly profit participation aligns incentives in a way wages don't.
- Sam already carries substantial private-dining load in practice (the standardized chicken work, the Jan 25 dinner, the February test dish). Some of this is formalization of what's already happening, plus genuine scope expansion.

The structural problem is not the two of those — it's the workload proposal sitting next to them: two additional closes per month plus open-ended availability when private events shift. Read together, that's an open-ended call on Sam's nominal nights off, with the profit participation functioning as the implicit compensation for time that should have been off the table in the first place. That's the leak you're worried about, and it's written into the offer rather than left ambiguous.

Clause-by-clause, as written:
1. Seasonal-menu development authority — needs a defined approval gate (Sam proposes, chef-owner approves, with what criteria?), and a refusal right if exec/ownership overrides his call. Without those, "authority" is consultative, not authority.
2. Private-dining program authority — needs scope: max events per month/quarter, event-type definition, budget ceiling, chef-owner veto conditions. Sam has been operating this informally and well; formalizing it is fine if it's bounded.
3. Quarterly profit participation — needs a formula. What's the denominator? What counts as profit (private-event revenue in or out?)? Is there a baseline below which nothing pays? What's the measurement window? Vesting on departure? Without these it's a number on a page.
4. Two additional closes per month — designated nights or floating? Predictable schedule or substituted on short notice? This clause is fine if it's designated; it's a different conversation if it's floating.
5. Open-ended availability when private events shift — this is the one to push back on hardest. As written, it converts every schedule reshuffle into a Sam night, with no notice floor, no refusal right, and no compensation structure beyond the profit participation that's already been promised.

What a bounded version of the offer would look like, worth proposing before acceptance:
- Seasonal menu: Sam proposes, chef-owner approves against defined criteria, refusal right preserved.
- Private dining: scope cap (events/month, event-type, budget), chef-owner veto defined in advance, refusal right preserved.
- Two additional closes: designated nights, predictable, with at least X days' notice for substitutions.
- Availability for private-event shifts: defined trigger (e.g., ≥14 days' notice → Sam is lead; <14 days → Sam available if schedule permits, refusal permitted without justification), with a stated refusal rate the restaurant accepts as normal, not exceptional.
- Capacity floor preserved in writing: minimum nights off per week, minimum full weekends per month, whatever matches your actual baseline.
- Profit participation: explicit formula, baseline, threshold, measurement window, vesting.
- Review point at 6 or 12 months, with either side able to walk without penalty.

The shape of the conversation I'd want to have before signing: this isn't "we don't want the offer," it's "we want the offer with the capacity leak closed." The chef-owner extending it likely didn't intend for it to function as an unlimited availability clause; making that explicit protects the relationship, not threatens it.

Acceptance hasn't happened, and that's the right state for it to be in. The negotiation posture is the actual decision right now, not the yes/no.

One thing I'd want to know before forming a stronger view: are the two additional closes net-new (on top of current load) or substituting for existing closes? And is the profit participation replacing any current compensation, or additive? Those change the math meaningfully.

What we know: pigment was blotted with water while still wet, the seal is intact and non-tacky, and a pale blue shadow remains. What we don't know from the message: the seal type (polyurethane, varnish, shellac, wax, oil, conversion), the pigment (some "staining" blues — phthalo, ultramarine, indigo — bite harder than others), how many seconds passed between splash and blot, and the wood species or finish age. The plan below is built so none of those unknowns can hurt you: every step is tested before it touches the visible spot, and each step has an explicit stop.

Before you start
  - Let the blotted area dry fully. Water blot + further wet work too soon can drive pigment in instead of lifting it.
  - Photograph the shadow in even daylight now, so you have a true before image. Your eye will adjust.
  - Gather: two soft microfiber cloths, one soft cotton cloth, distilled water, a drop of pH-neutral dish soap, and clean paper towels. Nothing else belongs on the tray.

Rule that runs through the whole sequence
  - One variable at a time. Technique, then dwell time, then pressure — never all three at once.
  - Press-and-lift, never scrub. Scrubbing on a sealed surface is how you burnish the seal or push pigment into micro-defects.
  - Each step gets a hidden-area test first. The painting-corner side or back edge of the same piece is fine. Wait five to ten minutes after the test and check for sheen change, tackiness, or color lift before going to the visible spot.
  - If a step doesn't visibly help on the first two attempts, stop at that step. More repetitions at the same aggressiveness rarely help and only raise the risk of finish damage.

Step 1 — dry pickup
  - Dry microfiber, single light pass, then a fresh section for a second pass.
  - Purpose: catch any loose pigment sitting on top of the seal that the original blot missed.
  - Stop if: cloth comes away noticeably blue and the spot doesn't lighten, or if the finish sheen changes at all.

Step 2 — barely-damp microfiber with distilled water
  - Wring the cloth until it feels almost dry. Press onto the shadow for five seconds, lift straight up. Blot dry immediately with a clean cotton cloth.
  - Repeat twice if the cloth shows faint color transfer, then stop and reassess.
  - Purpose: lift water-soluble pigment the original blot didn't reach.
  - Stop if: no improvement after the second lift, if color transfers but the spot doesn't lighten correspondingly (pigment is bonded), or if the finish dulls, hazes, or feels grabby.

Step 3 — pH-neutral soap solution
  - One drop of dish soap in a small bowl of distilled water. Fresh microfiber, wrung nearly dry, same press-and-lift, blot dry. Follow with a plain distilled-water rinse cloth, then blot dry.
  - Purpose: lower surface tension so a thin film of pigment releases.
  - Stop if: any of the Step 2 stop conditions appear. Soap residue left on the surface will itself dull the sheen, so the rinse matters — if the cloth leaves a faint film, that's the residue, not the pigment.

When to stop entirely
  - Any change in sheen, gloss, or smoothness of the finish — even subtle. That is the seal telling you it has had enough, and continuing will trade a faint blue shadow for a permanent dull spot.
  - Any tackiness or softening where the surface was dry and firm before.
  - Pigment doesn't visibly lift after two or three gentle attempts at the same aggressiveness. Further passes at the same level risk burnishing the seal without helping.
  - Pigment smears or spreads instead of lifting. That means it has bonded or the seal has a micro-defect; mechanical action will only enlarge the affected area.
  - You're unsure whether what you're seeing is improvement or damage. Stop, dry the area, walk away, look again in an hour.

Things not to use
  - Rubbing alcohol, acetone, mineral spirits, nail polish remover, vinegar, lemon juice. Any of these can dull or cloud finishes we can't identify, and shellac and wax will dissolve under them.
  - Baking soda, soft scrub, toothpaste, melamine sponges, scrubbing pads. All are abrasives. Even "gentle" abrasives scratch seals.
  - Heat of any kind. No hair dryer, no warm cloth. Heat can set pigment and cloud some finishes.
  - Prolonged wet contact. Don't lay a wet cloth on the spot and walk away. Brief dwell, blot dry.

If the shadow doesn't lift by the end of Step 3
  - You've done the safe sequence. The right move is to leave it.
  - A pale blue shadow on an intact seal is stable and far less visible than wet pigment. Several watercolor pigments fade further with normal indoor light over weeks. Worth a check in a month before deciding anything else.
  - Future options, only if it still bothers you and only after the surface has rested: a polish matched to the specific finish (which requires identifying the finish), or a conservator/refinisher for that small area. Neither is urgent, and neither is promised to remove the shadow.

Quick summary
  Dry pickup -> barely-damp distilled water (press-lift, blot) -> soap solution (press-lift, rinse, blot). One variable at a time, hidden-area test before each step on the visible spot, hard stop on any sheen change or after two or three ineffective attempts at the same level.

SIDECAR-RECONSTRUCTION AND AUDIT-LOG PROCEDURE
Draft v1 — 2025-03-22, for Riley review
Trigger: P014/P015/P016 metadata sidecars missing after a catalog export while the image scans themselves are intact and hash-identical to the prior export. The procedure is general; it applies wherever an original record existed as (primary artifact) + (structured metadata sidecar or field set), and the sidecar/field set is now missing or incomplete while the primary artifact survives.

0. WHAT THIS IS AND IS NOT

Is:
  - An append-only reconstruction method that records what was preserved, what was copied from a contemporaneous non-sidecar source, and what remains unknown.
  - A provenance-preserving replacement for a missing sidecar or field set.
  - A way to keep the loss event visible in audit history.
  - A way to make affected records discoverable without upgrading them to verified status.

Is not:
  - A permission to invent values for fields whose source is missing or uncertain.
  - An upgrade of paper-log, recall, or external-recollection entries into file-verified metadata.
  - A merge of reconstructed entries into the original archival index without a separate addendum.
  - A removal of the export-defect event from history.
  - A license to act on recollection as identification, subject, or person-name.
  - A way to bypass hold / fail-closed behavior on rows whose fields remain unsupported.

1. PROVENANCE TIERS (strict order; do not silently mix)

  Tier 1 — File-verified (current):
    Primary artifact bytes are present in a known location, and one or more of:
      (a) cryptographic hash matches a prior recorded hash,
      (b) file size / dimensions / extractable properties match a prior record,
      (c) produced or re-scanned under named-operator, governed-UTC conditions.
    Only Tier 1 justifies a write into the primary index without an addendum.

  Tier 2 — Contemporaneous structured evidence (different medium):
    A contemporaneous record from another medium (paper log, manifest, signed release artifact, timestamped audit log) attests to a specific field value at a specific time. Real and admissible, but not file-verified for the current artifact. Medium and source must be cited explicitly per field.

  Tier 3 — Reconstructed from contemporaneous evidence:
    Used only where Tier 1 and Tier 2 both attest to a value AND the reconstruction is mechanical (e.g., a derived field whose inputs are both Tier 1/Tier 2). Reconstruction does not elevate its sources; it is labeled.

  Tier 4 — Lead / recollection:
    A person's recollection or attribution (Mom's identification note, a curator's later comment) not corroborated by Tier 1 or Tier 2. Recorded, not used to modify archival metadata. Stored alongside, not inside.

  Tier 5 — Unknown / missing:
    No source supports the value. Gap recorded, not filled.

2. FIELD-LEVEL CLASSIFICATION (every field gets one)

  V — verified (Tier 1 only)
  P — paper-log / contemporaneous non-sidecar source (Tier 2)
  R — reconstructed from Tier 1 + Tier 2 evidence (Tier 3)
  L — lead / recollection (Tier 4); stored as comment, not as a field value
  U — unknown / missing (Tier 5); gap retained, value empty

  A field is never written without an explicit label. The label travels with the field in the sidecar (as a per-field annotation), in the audit log, and in any downstream index that ingests the sidecar.

3. AUDIT-LOG SCHEMA (append-only)

  One entry per event. Existing entries are not edited or removed. A new entry may correct a prior entry by referencing its event_id; the original entry remains.

  Fields (minimum):

    event_id            locally unique, monotonic
    timestamp_utc       governed UTC, never local
    operator            named person who performed the action
    action              controlled verb-noun vocabulary:
                          sidecar_missing_confirmed
                          image_hash_recomputed
                          hash_match_recorded
                          paper_log_field_copied
                          sidecar_field_written
                          label_applied
                          archival_index_updated
                          addendum_appended
                          lead_recorded
                          gap_retained
                          export_defect_logged
                          independent_check_signed
                          closure_manifest_recorded
                          procedure_revised
                          ...
    target              record ID, file path, or field name affected
    prior_state         what was true before this event (or "absent")
    new_state           what is true after this event (or "no change")
    source              concrete pointer to evidence:
                          paper_log_page=<n>, line=<m>
                          prior_export_manifest_sha256=<hash>
                          fresh_rescan_sha256=<hash>
                          contemporaneous_audit_id=<id>
                          ...
    confidence_label    V / P / R / L / U
    cross_references    list of related event_ids and external artifact IDs
    rationale           one-sentence plain-language reason

  Storage: append-only JSONL or audit.txt per affected record, filename versioned, location whose own hash is recorded in a manifest. Hash the log itself at session end and record the hash plus event count as the closure manifest.

  Example entry (illustrative, not real data):

    {"event_id":"P014-007","timestamp_utc":"2025-03-22T16:14:03Z",
     "operator":"<named>","action":"paper_log_field_copied",
     "target":"P014.source_box","prior_state":"absent",
     "new_state":"Box 4","source":"paper_log_page=12,line=3",
     "confidence_label":"P","cross_references":["P014-001"],
     "rationale":"Paper log attests to source box for P014 at scan time."}

4. FILE-SYSTEM HANDLING

  4.1  Do not modify the primary artifact bytes.
  4.2  Do not overwrite any existing sidecar, even a partial one.
  4.3  Where the original sidecar is missing:
         - Write a NEW sidecar with a suffix that signals reconstruction
           (e.g., P014.xmp.reconstructed) so it cannot be confused with an original.
         - Populate only fields whose source is Tier 1, 2, or 3.
         - For every populated field, embed the per-field confidence label
           (V / P / R) and a per-field source pointer.
         - For every field whose value is unknown, write label U with an empty
           value and an audit-log pointer to the gap-recorded event. Do NOT
           guess, interpolate, or copy a value from a similar record.
  4.4  For each Tier 4 lead (Mom's identification note, a curator's later
       comment), do NOT put it in the sidecar. Record it in a sibling file
       (P014.leads.txt or equivalent) or in an addendum to the inspection
       document. The lead stays separate from archival metadata.
  4.5  Retain the export-defect event itself as a record (one line in the
       audit log under action=export_defect_logged) so the loss is visible in
       history. Do not bury it inside another action.
  4.6  The original archival index entry, if any, is not overwritten. It may
       be annotated with a pointer to the addendum; nothing else changes.

5. RECONSTRUCTION SEQUENCE (ordered)

  Step 1 — Confirm the loss.
    Locate the primary artifact and any partial sidecar. Confirm the sidecar
    (or specific field set) is missing. Confirm it is also missing from the
    backup or prior known-good export. Record action=sidecar_missing_confirmed
    naming both locations and timestamps. If the loss is systemic across an
    export, also record action=export_defect_logged with scope.

  Step 2 — Verify the primary artifact.
    Compute the current hash of the primary artifact bytes. Compare to:
      (a) any prior recorded hash from a prior export, manifest, or earlier
          audit;
      (b) a fresh rescan or re-fetch under named-operator conditions.
    Record action=image_hash_recomputed and action=hash_match_recorded. A
    match elevates the artifact's identity to Tier 1 for THIS reconstruction.
    A mismatch halts and escalates (decision point D3).

  Step 3 — Inventory Tier 2 evidence.
    For each field the sidecar should contain, identify whether Tier 2
    evidence (paper log, manifest, audit) supports a value. Record the
    inventory in the audit log; do not yet write the sidecar.

  Step 4 — Write the reconstructed sidecar.
    For each field with Tier 1, Tier 2, or Tier 3 support: write the value
    with its confidence label (V / P / R) and a per-field source pointer.
    For each field with no support: write label U and an empty value, with
    a pointer to the gap-recorded event.

  Step 5 — Record leads separately.
    For each Tier 4 lead: write to the sibling leads file or the inspection
    addendum. Do NOT write into the sidecar. Record action=lead_recorded
    with the source pointer.

  Step 6 — Append to archival history.
    Write an addendum to the inspection / catalog document that names:
      - the affected record(s);
      - the export-defect event;
      - the hash-match evidence;
      - the fields written at each confidence label;
      - the leads stored separately;
      - the gaps retained as U.
    The addendum does not merge into the original archival index; it travels
    alongside it. The original index entry, if any, may be annotated with a
    pointer to the addendum and is not overwritten.

  Step 7 — Independent check.
    A second operator (not the writer) re-reads the sidecar and audit log,
    verifies hash and source pointers, and signs off under
    action=independent_check_signed.

  Step 8 — Closure manifest.
    Hash the audit log itself and record the hash plus total event count
    under action=closure_manifest_recorded. This is the closure record.

6. LABEL AND NAMING CONVENTIONS

  Reconstructed sidecar filename:
    <original-name>.<ext>.reconstructed
    e.g., P014.xmp.reconstructed, P014.xmp.reconstructed.json

  Per-field tags inside the sidecar:
    conf="V" | conf="P" | conf="R" | conf="U"
    src="<source pointer>"
    Fields with conf="L" are not written into the sidecar at all.

  Leads file (sibling, never merged into sidecar):
    <record-id>.leads.txt

  Addendum to inspection / catalog document:
    Title format:  "<Record IDs>: sidecar reconstruction, <YYYY-MM-DD>"
    Header statement: this is an addendum, not a replacement of the
    original entry.

  Audit log filename:
    <record-id>.audit.jsonl   (one event per line, append-only)

7. DECISION POINTS (escalate to Riley; do not write past these)

  D1  A field cannot be supported by Tier 1/2/3 but downstream consumption
      depends on it (gates a send, a hold, a count, a Customer Success
      action). The field stays U and the row stays held. No inference.
  D2  Paper log and another contemporaneous source disagree on a field value.
      Record both at Tier 2 with respective sources, do not pick one.
      Escalate.
  D3  Fresh rescan hash does not match the prior recorded hash. Halt. The
      primary artifact's identity is no longer Tier 1 for this record.
  D4  A Tier 4 lead (e.g., Mom's identification note) is being asked for as
      an identifier (catalog title, person-name). Leads are not promoted to
      identifiers by this procedure. Escalate.
  D5  The export defect appears systemic across more records than originally
      scoped. A separate decision is needed about widening or halting.
  D6  Writing any field would change cross-surface semantics, suppression
      behavior, eligibility, reporting, or messaging. This is not routine
      sidecar work under the shared-state boundary rule. Escalate.
  D7  Language is being written (release note, catalog entry, public
      statement) about the reconstruction. Wording can overclaim
      ("recovered", "restored", "verified") when the actual state is
      partial. Escalate.

8. VALIDATION CRITERIA (before reconstruction is closed)

  V1   Hash of primary artifact matches a prior recorded hash OR a fresh
       rescan under named-operator conditions. Hash, algorithm, and source
       are in the audit log.
  V2   Every populated sidecar field carries conf and src tags; no field is
       unlabeled.
  V3   Every field with conf="U" has an empty value and a gap-recorded
       pointer in the audit log.
  V4   Every Tier 4 lead is in a sibling leads file or inspection addendum,
       NOT in the sidecar.
  V5   The export-defect event is present in the audit log under
       action=export_defect_logged with date, scope, and named operator.
  V6   An addendum to the inspection / catalog document names the affected
       records, the loss event, the hash-match evidence, the labels, and
       the gaps. The addendum does not replace the original entry.
  V7   A second operator has signed off under
       action=independent_check_signed.
  V8   The audit log itself is hashed at session end; hash and event count
       are recorded as the closure manifest.
  V9   The original archival index, if any, is unchanged except for an
       annotation pointing to the addendum. Original entry is not
       overwritten.
  V10  No cross-surface state changed as a result of the reconstruction.
       If a send, hold, count, or message moved because of this work, the
       work is not a reconstruction; it is a state change, and that is a
       different procedure.

9. IMMEDIATE APPLICATION — P014 / P015 / P016 (2025-03-22)

  Known evidence:
    - Image scans intact, hash-identical to prior export. Tier 1 once
      re-verified.
    - Sidecar files missing from BOTH current export AND backup. This is
      the export defect; it is recorded, not silently bridged.
    - Paper log retains: photo ID, source box, scan date (Tier 2) and
      Mom's identification note (Tier 4).

  Recommended next actions under this procedure:

            sidecar_missing_confirmed for each, plus one

    Step 2 — Recompute hash of each image; compare to the prior-export

    Step 3 — Inventory paper-log fields per photo:

              - person/subject Tier 4 (Mom's note — not a field value)
    Step 4 — Write P014.xmp.reconstructed, P015.xmp.reconstructed,
            P016.xmp.reconstructed with:
              photo ID       conf="P" src=paper_log_page=<n>,line=<m>
              source box     conf="P" src=paper_log_page=<n>,line=<m>
              scan date      conf="P" src=paper_log_page=<n>,line=<m>
              image hash     conf="V" src=fresh_rescan_sha256=<hash>

    Step 5 — Put Mom's identification note in P014.leads.txt,

    Step 6 — Addendum to the P014/P015/P016 inspection / catalog

    Step 7 — Independent check by a second operator (not the writer).

    - Move Mom's note from a Tier 4 lead into a sidecar field.
    - Write the reconstructed sidecar under the original filename (the

    - Delete or overwrite any partial sidecar if one exists.

Single soft stool after grass, with everything else normal, is most often a grass-irritation event in dogs rather than Salmonella. Salmonella incubation in dogs typically runs 6 to 72 hours, sometimes out to 7 days, and the early picture usually starts with fever or appetite drop rather than one isolated soft stool. That said, the recall context legitimately raises the floor: treat this as grass-caused unless anything changes in the next 24 to 48 hours, but watch more carefully than you would for a routine grass event.

HOME MONITORING PLAN

Hydration
  - Keep fresh water available at all times; do not restrict.
  - Quick dehydration check tonight and again tomorrow morning: lift the lip — gums should be pink and slick, not tacky or sticky; gently tent the scruff — skin should snap back within a second.

Feeding
  - Hold the next regular meal by 1 to 2 hours; then offer the normal diet in a smaller portion (about half).
  - If a second soft stool or any vomiting appears, switch to a bland diet for 24 to 48 hours: boiled skinless chicken (no salt, no oil) plus plain white rice, in small frequent meals — a few tablespoons at a time, 3 to 4 times daily.
  - Continue offering food. If Kibo refuses more than one full meal, or interest drops across the day, that is a signal.

Hygiene (Salmonella is zoonotic; this matters more than usual right now)
  - Wash hands with soap and water after handling food, bowls, stool, or Kibo.
  - Do not let Kibo lick faces, especially children, anyone pregnant, anyone immunocompromised, or elderly household members.
  - Pick up stool promptly; bag and dispose in household trash, not compost, not the yard.
  - Wash bowls in the dishwasher on a hot cycle, or hand-wash with very hot soapy water. Same for the scoop and any surface the recalled kibble touched.
  - Disinfect food-prep surfaces that contacted the recalled bag with a dilute bleach solution (about 1 tablespoon bleach per quart of water) or a disinfectant labeled effective against Salmonella.
  - Retain the recalled lot number L25-0317A and the packaging — useful if the regular vet wants to cross-reference.

Monitoring over the next 48 hours
  - Stool: count, consistency, color, presence of blood or mucus.
  - Appetite: continued interest in food, willingness to eat.
  - Energy: normal walk behavior, alertness, interest in you.
  - Vomiting: any retching or bringing food up.
  - Temperature: only if you have a rectal thermometer and Kibo tolerates it. Normal is 101 to 102.5°F. Anything above 103°F is worth a call.
  - Abdomen: soft and non-tender on gentle palpation. A tense, swollen, or painful belly is a signal.

CONTACT THE REGULAR VET (call, not urgent visit)
  - A second soft stool or any diarrhea within 24 to 48 hours.
  - Any vomiting, even a single episode.
  - Appetite drop or refusal of one full meal.
  - Subtle energy drop — skipping the walk, less interested in you.
  - Blood, mucus, or black/tarry stool.
  - Slight fever above 103°F.
  - Symptoms persisting or worsening past 48 hours.
  - When you call, mention the recalled lot L25-0317A and the March 22 meal so the clinic has the context.

GO TO URGENT CARE / ER NOW
  - Repeated vomiting (two or more episodes in a short window, or any persistent retching).
  - Repeated diarrhea within 24 hours, especially with blood.
  - Profound lethargy, collapse, weakness, or unresponsiveness.
  - Fever above 104°F, or temperature below 99°F.
  - Pale, white, blue, yellow, or tacky gums; skin tent that does not snap back.
  - Abdominal distension, severe pain, or a "prayer posture" (front down, rear up) that does not resolve.
  - Difficulty breathing.
  - Any sign of sepsis: rapid heart rate you can feel, shivering, cool extremities, confusion.

For now this is a one-stool event most consistent with grass. The recall context does not change the plan dramatically; it raises the threshold a little and adds the hygiene layer. If tomorrow's stool is normal and everything else holds, this resolves cleanly. If anything in either column above appears, call or go.

VALUE-SEPARATION STUDY — warm counter vs. cool window

Goal: find the minimum warm-wash value that holds perceptual ground against a fixed cool wash, with brush load, paper, and per-layer wash timing held constant.

Setup
  - One quarter sheet, light pencil grid: 3 horizontal strips, vertical line down the middle of each strip
  - Same brush, same water, same pigment:water ratio for both pigments, same per-layer timing (apply wet-on-dry, full dry before the next layer)
  - Held: brush load, paper, wash timing
  - Variable: only the number of layers on the warm side

Constant: cool window wash
  - Ultramarine, 2 layers wet-on-dry on the left half of every strip
  - Apply layer 1 to all 3 strips in sequence, wait until just dry, apply layer 2 to all 3 strips
  - Same dilution per dip, same brush reload each pass

Variable: warm counter edge (burnt sienna, right half of each strip)
  - Strip 1: 1 layer
  - Strip 2: 2 layers, full dry between
  - Strip 3: 3 layers, full dry between each
  - Same dilution per dip as the cool wash

Procedure
  1. Lay out pencil grid
  2. Cool pass 1 across all 3 strips, then cool pass 2 across all 3 strips
  3. Warm pass 1 across all 3 strips
  4. Warm pass 2 on strip 2 only; warm pass 3 on strip 3 only
  5. Full dry, then observe

What to record after full dry
  - Which strip keeps the warm edge reading as a distinct, warmer plane against the cool (i.e., where value separation survives the dry-down)
  - Whether the boundary stays clean or muddies (pigment lift at the seam)
  - Whether the warm chroma comes through or is flattened by the adjacent cool

Estimated time: roughly 15–18 minutes including drying intervals.

What this isolates
  - Only the warm-wash value (layer count) changes; everything that drove the prior wet-to-dry convergence — load, paper, timing — is held constant

What this does not test
  - Wet-into-wet timing, soft edges, different pigments, hue-temperature effects, composition, or any change to the cool-wash value

The tension is well-formed and the three scenes alone don't resolve it — which is probably the structural point.

What each reading is actually claiming:

Reading A (genuine adaptation): The community has produced a working response to a problem the institution can't solve at the source. "Resilience" is accurate description of what's there. The repeated repairs aren't a failure of the practice — they're institution doing what institution does (band-aid), while the residents have found what works. The planner is naming something real.

Reading B (renamed avoidance): The underpass keeps flooding because nobody addresses the cause (drainage, capacity, upstream land use). The "resilience" label lets the planner credit the institution for the community's stopgap while never having to fix the structural problem. Residents do the labor; the planner does the framing.

Where the planner's narration is doing work:

The sequence matters. In your three scenes, the rerouting appears before the planner names it — that ordering gives the practice some independence from the label, which leans slightly toward A. But the planner is also the one assembling the three repair cycles into a "repeatedly" pattern before introducing the framing; choosing to show three failures of repair before naming the workaround is itself editorial. So the planner curates what the reader sees the workaround against. That curation is closer to B.

Two things would tip it without fully settling it:

1. Whose voice is the planner's. If the planner is inside the institution (a department memo, a planning document) the label is more plausibly strategic; if outside (an observer, a chronicler) it's more plausibly descriptive. The voice's relation to the institution changes what the naming act does.

2. Whether the planner shows the workaround breaking — a flood that closes the reroute, an injury, a missed emergency, a season where it stops working. A workaround shown as fragile makes "resilience" read more clearly as institutional comfort. A workaround shown as load-bearing and durable makes the label closer to accurate, and the harder question becomes why the institution hasn't learned from the community it sits next to.

Discussion question that holds both readings open, if you want one:

"If the workaround is resilience, who is being asked to be resilient — and is that a different question from who's being asked to fix the underpass?"

Or more pointed: what's the smallest detail in any of the three scenes that would let a reader tell whether the planner is describing a community or managing one?

Two-sided reading:

Side A — adaptation. The character is genuinely finding a new way to live. The avoidance of the institution is incidental, even necessary: going back would require something they can't give, or would flatten what they've built. What looks like refusal is actually lateral movement, and the new shape holds on its own.

Side B — avoidance. The adaptation is real but partial. It works for the visible self; the institutional contact (the appointment, the visit, the form, the door not knocked on) remains undone. The new life is structured around not going back, and the cost shows up in smaller ways — a name not said, a question dodged, a hand not extended.

Both can hold. The book seems to be testing whether the adaptation would survive contact with the institution, or whether it was built precisely so it never has to.

Opening question (conversational, holds both sides):

"When [character] seemed most settled, did that read like something they'd grown into, or something they'd built around the thing they weren't going back to?"

Why this works as an opener: "settled" asks people to describe what they noticed on the page rather than argue a reading; "grown into" vs. "built around" lets the room split on whether the calm is gain or cover without forcing either one, and the institution stays unnamed, so the group can fill in which one they mean. It opens interpretation instead of asking for agreement with a thesis, which is where your group tends to land best.
