DECISION FRAMEWORK — Q4 LIFECYCLE SYSTEMS CONTRACTOR CASES
(framework only; no selection made)

THE THREE CASES

Case 1 — No contractor
Case 2 — Half-time operations contractor, 6 months, $36,000
Case 3 — Full-time-equivalent contractor, 4 months, $48,000

Intended work in scope of all three cases: repeatable audit preparation, campaign inventory, operator enablement.
Out of scope in every case: a fifth shared-state consumer, Helio Start paid acquisition, engineering release work, replacement of Owen's and Ines's owner lanes.

---

AXIS 1 — WORKLOAD RELIEVED

Each case relieves different work; the relief profile has to match what actually burdens the team rather than what looks cheap on paper.

Case 1 — No contractor: zero workload relief. The three intended workstreams (audit prep, campaign inventory, operator enablement) remain on Owen, Ines, and the existing Lifecycle Systems operators. The August 5 mature-cohort support-effort readout and the August 6 source-age alert release confirmation both landed on the same week that would be Q4 planning; if those two are a leading indicator, adding three new workstreams on top of routine single-path operating evidence is the capacity picture Case 1 implies. Case 1's "workload relieved" line is therefore not zero — it is zero in absolute terms, but the implicit effect is that existing operators absorb the new work and something else has to give.

Case 2 — Half-time for six months: partial relief across the full window. Audit prep and campaign inventory are the more easily-partitioned deliverables — they have clean handoff points and bounded acceptance. Operator enablement is the harder one to halve because it tends to require context, follow-up, and continuity. Realistic expectation: roughly two of the three workstreams are meaningfully unblocked; operator enablement is closer to a delayed start than to real relief. Six months gives runway but does not give a full quarter of dedicated focus.

Case 3 — FTE-equivalent for four months: more relief in a shorter window. All three workstreams can move in parallel. Four months is roughly one quarter, which lines up with a defined deliverable set but not with sustained operating rhythm. Risk on this axis is the inverse of Case 2: the work fits the window, but the contractor leaves before the deliverables are absorbed into routine operation, which can create a recurrence of the original workload plus a transition tax.

The framework question under this axis: which mix of relief (full + short vs. partial + long vs. none) matches the actual shape of the burden as it sits today, and which match preserves the routine operating evidence cadence (Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, CS auto-nudge path) the bounded period depends on?

---

AXIS 2 — EVIDENCE REQUIRED

Each case carries a different evidence burden to be defensible in the Q4 planning thread.

Case 1 — No contractor: the evidence burden is the lightest in absolute terms but the heaviest in implicit terms. The implicit claim is "existing capacity is sufficient." That claim needs evidence of its own: current operator load, a credible queue of the three intended workstreams with effort estimates, and an explicit statement of what gets deferred or dropped to make room. Without that, "no contractor" reads as a decision made on cost grounds rather than a decision supported by capacity evidence.

Case 2 — Half-time for six months: medium evidence burden. Need a written scope split (which two of three workstreams, what "half-time" means in hours/week, what handoff and acceptance points look like), a named start and end date, a definition of "operations contractor" that sits inside the existing shared-state scope, a confirmation that the contractor touches none of the four established consumer paths in a way that creates a fifth consumer, and a clear exit condition that does not strand deliverables mid-cycle.

Case 3 — FTE-equivalent for four months: the heaviest evidence burden. In addition to everything Case 2 needs, Case 3 needs a four-month delivery plan with milestone gates, an explicit transition plan that names who absorbs what after the contractor exits, a definition of how the four-month window interacts with the live-evidence period and the May 30 / June 5 / August 6 checkpoint cadence, and evidence that the contractor's faster throughput does not crowd out the operator lanes the work is supposed to relieve.

Across all three cases, the standing rule from prior sessions holds: any claim stronger than the evidence is the wrong claim. "Mature," "companywide," "launch," "GA expansion," "paid-acquisition," and "fifth consumer" language must stay out regardless of which case is selected.

---

AXIS 3 — PROTECTION OF EXISTING OWNER LANES

The standing owner lanes as of August 6, 2025:

  Owen — routine single-path ledger, denominator, exception taxonomy, source/freshness documentation, surface scope, age ordering within tiers, routine holds, stale/conflicting records
  Ines — prompt-hold language, CS checks, operator-facing message-state guide
  Daniela — engineering release controls, transport, source reliability, shared-state repair, rollback
  Riley — cross-surface eligibility/reporting/messaging changes, disputed semantics or ownership, incorrect shared-state contracts, suppression fail-open risk, new exception types or reversals, stop signals, executive/board/customer-facing/high-stakes language

These four lanes must remain intact through the live-evidence period and do not prejudge later outcomes. The framework question is which case protects them best.

Case 1 — protects the lanes trivially because no new actor enters the system. Risk: the lanes are protected in name only if existing operators are stretched to the point of dropping routine checks. Lane protection here is actually capacity protection; the lane content is fine, but the lane stewardship may not be.

Case 2 — protects the lanes provided the contractor's work stays in three specific workstreams (audit prep, campaign inventory, operator enablement) and does not draft governing language, make release calls, or stand up new consumer views. The cleanest test: if the contractor's deliverables could be reassigned to Owen or Ines without rewriting scope, the lanes are intact. If reassignment would require a scope change, the contractor has drifted into lane territory.

Case 3 — same lane test as Case 2, but with higher drift risk because a full-time-equivalent over four months is more likely to be handed end-to-end pieces of work that touch adjacent surfaces. The stronger mitigation is a written lane-boundary addendum (not a separate lane, a boundary document) reviewed before work begins.

The standing rule that applies across all three: discovery, beta, launch, pricing-page approval, or a fifth consumer must not be reopened through this hire. Any case that drifts there has failed on this axis regardless of workload relief.

---

AXIS 4 — WORK THAT MUST REMAIN OUT OF SCOPE

The user's prompt already lists four out-of-scope items; the framework should treat them as floor, not ceiling. Additional out-of-scope categories the established context already requires:

  Any fifth shared-state consumer (the August 4 pre-release review and the August 6 production confirmation both rest on a four-consumer scope)
  Any Helio Start paid-acquisition framing, pricing-page exposure, or paid-channel claim
  Any engineering release work, transport changes, rollback authority changes, or source-reliability redesign (Daniela's lane)
  Any replacement or dilution of Owen's routine single-path ownership or Ines's messaging/lifecycle governance
  Any rewrite of the CS auto-nudge prompt-hold language without source-owner review, semantic mapping, and freshness-limit documentation
  Any claim about contractor output that rises to mature, companywide, GA-expanded, launch, causal, forecast, pipeline, retention, revenue, or legacy-retirement
  Any suppression fail-open behavior, manual release of a held decision, or assumption that an adjacent message inherits eligibility from a held or suppressed decision
  Any cross-surface eligibility/reporting/messaging change without Riley's participation; any disputed semantics, new exception types, reversals, or stop signals without Riley's lane

Cases 2 and 3 in particular must carry these as written exclusions in the contractor's scope, not as unwritten norms. Case 1 needs them as preserved constraints on whatever existing operators pick up.

---

HOW THE FOUR AXES INTERACT

The four axes are not independent. The selection will trade between them:

  Workload relief and lane protection can pull in opposite directions: more relief (Case 3) tends to increase drift risk into lanes; less relief (Case 1) tends to stretch the lanes themselves.
  Evidence required and time horizon interact: shorter windows (Case 3) need more upfront planning evidence; longer windows (Case 2) need less milestone density but more cumulative handoff evidence.
  Out-of-scope enforcement is cheapest in Case 1 (no new actor), more expensive in Case 2 (one new actor, six months), and most expensive in Case 3 (one new actor, four months, higher throughput).
  Across all three, the live-evidence period (CS auto-nudge operating evidence, source-age alert operational evidence, Helio Start bounded-GA reporting) is the protected surface; the contractor's work must sit beside it, not inside it.

---

WHAT THE FRAMEWORK DOES NOT YET DO

This is a comparison and decision framework, not a selection. The selection still requires:

  Confirmation of which three workstreams are highest-priority (audit prep, campaign inventory, operator enablement) and which two are the right pair if Case 2 is selected
  The current operator load and queue, so "no contractor" can be defended on capacity rather than cost
  The transition / absorption plan for Case 3

The editor's answer does three things, in this order:

1. Affirms the cataloging split is intentional. "Care that could become control" is not a hedge — it is a designed dual-register. The novel is meant to be readable as either, and the editor is confirming both were aimed for.

2. Refuses resolution on the ending in both directions. "Neither absolution nor a final verdict" is sharper than the usual ambiguity disclaimer. It forecloses two specific closures: it will not say the narrator is forgiven, and it will not say the narrator is condemned. That's a stronger stance than "I won't decide."

3. Punts the load-bearing question. Attention vs accountability is the actual axis the ending turns on, and the editor explicitly says the novel does not adjudicate it. So that one stays open for readers, not closed by authorial intent.

That third move is the one worth sitting with. The editor is willing to defend the design of the ambiguity and the refusal of resolution, but declines to say what the novel itself decides about whether attention has crossed into accountability. Authorial authority is being invoked to keep a question open, not to close it.

It maps onto the Brixton split, but not symmetrically:

  - "Care and attention" vs "converted neighbors into data / made intimacy managerial" — the editor says both are intended, not competing readings. The dual reading is the point.
  - "Avoided responsibility for the narrator's choices" vs "refused a clean resolution" — the editor's framing is a third position, not a midpoint. Refusing both absolution and verdict is not the same as refusing to take a stand; it is a specific refusal of two particular stands.

One thing to note if you ever want to press the framing: the editor's distinction between attention and accountability is itself a clean binary. The novel's actual texture may not be that clean — there are probably scenes where attention is accountability, or where the line the editor is drawing does not hold. The editor's answer is generative as long as it is treated as one more interpretive voice, not a final word.

Three findings from the clinic, restated narrowly:

  - ~3 min re-entry: too wet. The cool wash bled back and the dark travelled into the warm doorway edge.
  - ~7 min re-entry: workable window. Cool shape held, warm edge kept its separation.
  - Fully dry re-entry: too dry. The rain mark landed as a hard sit-on-top, no settling into the wash.

So the re-entry timing variable now has a known working point (the ~7 min window) and two failure modes on either side. The next study should hold ~7 min re-entry constant and vary one other thing.

The natural next-variable candidates, each varying exactly one thing:

  1. Brush moisture on the rain mark (full damp vs barely damp vs nearly dry), holding 7-min re-entry, same paper, same pigment, same dilution, same rain-mark size and value. Tests whether a drier brush softens the rain's edge into the cool wash without breaking the cool shape.
  2. Rain-mark value (full value vs one step lighter vs two steps lighter), holding 7-min re-entry and a consistent damp brush. Tests whether a less-saturated rain reads as rain without sitting so sharply.
  3. Rain-mark pigment (same three-pigment set, swap which one carries the rain), holding 7-min re-entry and damp brush at one consistent value. Tests whether a different pigment settles more softly at the same load.
  4. Cool-wash dilution (current load vs one step lighter), holding 7-min re-entry. Tests whether a lighter cool wash gives the rain more breathing room to settle in.

Which direction do you want to go? Or is the instructor steering you toward a specific one?

CONTROLLED PERSONAL-PRACTICE SEQUENCE
Intermediate position for the dark rain interruption

Scope: one sheet, personal practice only. No title, no signature, no frame, no third pass. Bounded to the three-pigment practice.

Held constant (do not change from the established courtyard-shadow study):
- Paper: same 140-lb cold-press sheet
- Pigment mix: same three-pigment mix
- Brush: same brush
- Brush load: same load, same one-firm-blot on a clean paper towel before each wash
- Cool wash: same continuous application, same ~20-second bead-wicking interval, same one-touch softened edge, same no-return rule once the sheen dulls, same full dry before continuing (paper cool to the touch, not glossy)
- Warm edge: same pass — thin, a full value step lighter than the cool wash, no added orange, no extra pigment
- Rain interruption: same pigment mix, same dilution, same small controlled strokes

Varied (the single controlled change in this session):
- The position of the dark rain interruption in the sequence. Moved from the late reference (after both washes are fully dry) to an intermediate reference (after the cool wash is fully dry, before the warm edge is applied). Pigment mix, paper, and brush load stay constant.

Pre-run scrap test (instructor standing advice, ~3 minutes):
- On a scrap of the same paper, lay down a short cool wash at the same load and blot.
- Let it fully dry — paper cool, not glossy.
- Apply one short stroke of the rain interruption at the same dilution.
- Let it dry.
- Lay one short warm-edge pass at the same dilution over the dried interruption.
- Confirm three things before running the main sheet:
  (a) the interruption sits cleanly on the dry cool wash without blooming
  (b) the warm edge sits cleanly over the dried interruption without muddying or lifting
  (c) neither wash is disturbed
- If any of those fail, do not run the main sequence. Adjust dilution or wait longer and re-test on scrap.

Sequence on the study sheet:

Step 1 — Cool wash (held constant)
- Apply the cool wash in one continuous pass.
- At ~20 seconds, do the one-touch softened edge.
- Stop touching once the sheen dulls.
- Wait for full dry: paper cool to the touch, not glossy. Do not rush this.

Step 2 — Intermediate rain interruption (the test)
- With the cool wash fully dry, apply the dark rain interruption directly to the dry cool wash.
- Keep it small and contained — a few short, controlled strokes — so it does not take over the street wash.
- Do not rework any area where the interruption has begun to set.
- Let the interruption dry fully (paper cool, not glossy) before continuing.

Step 3 — Warm edge (held constant)
- Apply the warm edge pass as in the established study: thin, a full value step lighter than the cool wash, no added orange, no extra pigment.
- One controlled pass. No return strokes after the sheen dulls.
- The warm edge now sits over the dried rain interruption, not under it.

Step 4 — Stop and dry
- No third pass.
- No refinement of the rain interruption.
- No signature, no frame.
- Let the sheet dry fully (paper cool, not glossy) before any evaluation.

What "preserved" means in this sequence
- Continuous cool wash: the cool wash is applied, softened, and fully dried before any other paint touches the sheet. Nothing interrupts its continuous application or its dry state.
- Warm edge: the warm edge is applied as a complete, thin, value-separated pass on top of the dried rain interruption. Its value separation from the cool wash is preserved because it is the last pass on a fully dry sheet.

Stop conditions (any one is enough)
- Rain interruption blooms into the cool wash on the scrap test or the main sheet.
- Rain interruption lifts or muddies when the warm edge is laid over it.
- Warm edge does not sit at its established thinness and value after the interruption.
- Cool wash is disturbed at any point.
- Paper is glossy or tacky when the next step is about to begin — wait, do not proceed on a wet sheet.
- Mechanical event: paint shift, tear, flood, lifted bead.

Evaluation (only after the sheet is fully dry)
- Does the rain interruption read as a dark interruption rather than a stain or a stamp?
- Has the warm edge retained its value separation from the cool wash after drying?
- Does the cool wash still read as continuous and uninterrupted?
- Is the interruption contained, or did it take over the street wash?

What this is NOT
- Not a finished painting. No title, no inventory entry, no sale or exhibition commitment.
- Not a teaching setup. Personal practice only.
- Not a change to pigment mix, paper, brush, brush load, cool-wash procedure, warm-edge value, warm-edge dilution, or rain-interruption dilution.
- Not a test of more than one variable. Only the rain-interruption position is varied.
- Not a verdict. A clean run tells you the intermediate position works in this sheet; it does not lock it in as the new default. A failed run tells you where the limit is; it does not retire the practice.

Q4 LIFECYCLE SYSTEMS CONTRACTOR PRE-READ — FINAL
Prepared: August 18, 2025
For: August 21, 2025 Q4 contractor workshop
Audience: Priya (decision), Riley (escalation lane), Owen / Ines / Daniela (lane review)
Purpose: Make the decision structure explicit. No recommendation. No preselection.

DECISION STRUCTURE
The August 21 workshop is being asked to evaluate three cases against a single decision frame, not to select a case today. The frame is three questions:

1. What repeatable work is documented in the June–July sample, and how much of it could each paid case absorb by December 31, 2025?
2. What evidence would distinguish owner leverage (contractor absorbs routine work) from added coordination (contractor shifts work from "do" to "review")?
3. What work remains categorically with Owen, Ines, Daniela, or Riley regardless of case selected?

This update adds the side-by-side matrix, the December capacity cut, the leverage-vs-coordination evidence tests, and the categorical carve-outs. It does not select a case.

CASE MATRIX (SIDE-BY-SIDE)

  Dimension              | No contractor        | $36,000 half-time          | $48,000 4-month FTE
  -----------------------|----------------------|----------------------------|-----------------------------
  Start date             | n/a                  | October 1, 2025            | No earlier than November 1, 2025
  End date               | n/a                  | ~March 31, 2026 (6 months) | ~February 28, 2026 (4 months)
  Months elapsed by 12/31| 0                    | 3 (Oct, Nov, Dec)          | 2 (Nov, Dec)
  Total committed cost   | $0                   | $36,000                    | $48,000
  Monthly run rate       | $0                   | $6,000                     | $12,000
  Nominal capacity by 12/31 (est.)| 0 hrs       | ~240 hrs                   | ~320 hrs
  Onboarding constraint  | none                 | none                       | agency onboarding required
  Owner-lane protection  | baseline             | scope + decision carve-outs| scope + decision carve-outs +
                         |                      |                            | agency lag acknowledged
  Coordination overhead  | none                 | bounded if scope-bounded   | bounded if scope-bounded and
  risk                   |                      |                            | decision rights bounded

  Notes:
  - Nominal capacity envelopes assume ~80 hrs/month (half-time) and ~160 hrs/month (FTE). Actual contracted hours must be confirmed before treating these as firm.
  - Both paid cases can cover presentation-detail reconciliation per the Finance / Procurement constraints.

SAMPLED WORKLOAD BY DECEMBER
The documented June–July sample anchor is approximately 6 hours per month of presentation-detail reconciliation that should not require Riley's judgment. This is the only specific figure documented in the supplied sample. The full sample inventory beyond this anchor should be confirmed before the workshop treats the numbers below as final.

  Anchor accumulation by December 31, 2025:
    No contractor case:       0 hrs accumulated on contractor; ~36 hrs remains on owner lane over Oct–Dec
    $36,000 half-time case:    18 hrs of anchor work accumulated; ~240 hrs contractor capacity available
    $48,000 4-month FTE case: 12 hrs of anchor work accumulated; ~320 hrs contractor capacity available

  Anchor share of available capacity envelope:
    $36,000 half-time case:    ~7.5% (18 / 240)
    $48,000 4-month FTE case: ~3.75% (12 / 320)

Decision-relevant read: both paid cases can absorb the documented anchor in full by December. The relevant difference is not whether the anchor is absorbable (both yes) but how the remaining capacity is scoped, what additional repeatable items enter scope, and what coordination overhead the additional scoping introduces. The $48,000 case has more headroom per anchor hour but starts one month later and arrives through agency onboarding. The $36,000 case has less headroom but starts sooner and is simpler to stand up.

Open items for workshop confirmation:
  - Full June–July sample inventory beyond the 6 hrs/month reconciliation anchor
  - Contracted hour commitments for each case (nominal envelopes are estimates)
  - Whether additional capacity in either paid case is intended for scope expansion or held as reserve
  - Whether the $48,000 case's November 1 start and agency onboarding are firm or negotiable

EVIDENCE TESTS — LEVERAGE vs. ADDED COORDINATION
The brief separates leverage from added coordination with observable signals. None are pre-decided; each is a measurement the workshop can adopt as a monthly checkpoint beginning the second month of any paid engagement.

Leverage signals — target: present and stable or improving over time.
  1. Routine items resolved by contractor within agreed scope, per month
     (named-item count; denominator = sampled scope)
  2. Owner hours spent on routine items inside contractor scope, month-over-month
     (target: decreasing or flat-low)
  3. Reconciliation cycles completed per month
     (named-item count; denominator = reconciliation backlog)
  4. Cycle-time for sampled items
     (target: contractor ≤ owner baseline)

Coordination overhead signals — target: bounded ceiling, decreasing over time.
  1. Escalations back to owner per week
     (count; target: low and decreasing for items inside scope)
  2. Owner review / QA hours per contractor deliverable
     (ratio; target: bounded ceiling per item)
  3. Items requiring owner judgment per month
     (count; target: stable-low for items inside contractor scope)
  4. Items reworked or returned for correction per month
     (count; target: low and decreasing)

Net test: if leverage signals are present and coordination overhead signals are bounded, the contractor is producing owner leverage. If coordination overhead signals grow without a proportional rise in leverage signals, the contractor is adding net work, not removing it. A monthly checkpoint against these signals should be adopted by the workshop before any paid engagement begins.

CATEGORICAL CARVE-OUTS — WORK THAT REMAINS WITH EACH OWNER
Regardless of case selected, the following lanes stay with the named owner. The contractor does not absorb these under any of the three cases.

Owen stays with (routine single-path ledger):
  - Routine ledger maintenance and denominator integrity
  - Exception taxonomy and freshness documentation
  - Surface scope and age ordering within tiers
  - Routine holds and standalone exception handling
  - Stale or conflicting records that fail closed

Ines stays with (messaging + lifecycle governance):
  - Prompt-hold language and Customer Success check-ins
  - Lifecycle governance and messaging alignment
  - Operator-facing message state and the corrected operator-facing message-state guide

Daniela stays with (transport + source reliability + engineering release):
  - Transport and shared-state contracts
  - Source reliability and shared-state repair
  - Rollback and engineering release control
  - Cross-surface consequence handling

Riley stays with (high-stakes only):
  - Cross-surface eligibility, reporting, or messaging changes
  - Disputed semantics or ownership questions
  - Suppression fail-open risk review
  - New exception types or reversals
  - Stop signals
  - Executive, board, or customer-facing language
  - Contractor scope disputes and case-selection questions

Out of scope for the contractor under any case:
  - Decision authority on lifecycle policy
  - Customer-facing message approval
  - Release and rollback authority
  - Owner-lane judgment calls
  - Any item currently owned by Owen, Ines, Daniela, or Riley per the carve-outs above

BOUNDARY REMINDER
This brief presents three cases against a single decision frame. It does not recommend a case. The decision remains with Priya and the workshop after reviewing the matrix, the December capacity cut, the evidence tests, and the categorical carve-outs. No case is preselected.

Five minutes is a useful working window, with one known cost.

  Why it earns that label:
    - The cool wash stayed continuous, which is the main thing 3 minutes
      did not give you.
    - The warm doorway edge held clear. At 3 minutes it did not. So 5 is
      past the continuity-and-edge threshold.
    - The bloom is a single-locus artifact at the dark mark's entry point,
      not a wash-wide failure. It tells you the paper at that spot was
      still active enough to backflow when the brush touched it. That is
      a manageable cost, not a disqualifier.

  What 5 min is and is not:
    - It is a window where the cool wash stays continuous and the warm
      edge holds.
    - It is not a clean window. A small bloom is the price of entry at
      the interruption point.
    - It is not yet the upper bound. We do not know how much further the
      window runs before the wash sets enough that the dark mark stops
      integrating.

  One next study — push the upper bound:

    Hold everything from this morning exactly:
      - paper (140 lb cold press)
      - blue + brown pigment mix and dilution
      - brush and brush load for both the cool wash and the dark mark
      - large cool wash coverage
      - warm doorway edge goal

    Single change: place the dark rain interruption at ~7 minutes instead
    of 5. Do not change the mark's pigment, dilution, or brush. Let the
    wash dry on the board the same way you did today.

    What to watch, in order of informativeness:
      1. Bloom at the dark-mark entry — does it shrink or disappear?
      2. How the dark mark sits — is it still integrating into the wash,
         or is it starting to land on top with a harder, less-fused edge?
      3. Warm doorway edge — should hold at least as cleanly as at 5.
      4. Cool wash continuity — should hold.

    How to read the result:
      - Bloom shrinks AND mark still integrates  -> the window extends
        past 7; next probe can move further out.
      - Bloom shrinks AND mark sits on top with a hard edge  -> 7 min is
        at or just past the upper bound of integration. 5 min is then a
        confirmed inside-window timing with a known, locatable cost, and
        you have a real bracket.
      - Bloom persists with little change  -> the bloom is not primarily
        timing-driven at this brush load. The next variable to isolate is
        brush moisture or pigment concentration at the dark mark, not
        timing. Do not chase further timing changes until that is sorted.

    One bound on the study itself: do not extrapolate past 7 in a single
    pass. If 7 turns out too dry, you would learn less than from one clean
    7-minute read. Keep it one probe, then judge after the wash dries.

Conservative plan: ride in this morning, do not ride home this afternoon. The 108°F heat-index window (3-7pm) is the dangerous part; the morning ride is in front of it.

1. Ride in this morning
   - Depart in the coolest part of your window, earlier the better.
   - Pre-hydrate ~16-20 oz water in the hour before leaving; a few sips during the 25-minute ride.
   - Light-colored, breathable kit; sunscreen on exposed skin; sunglasses; helmet as always.
   - Two short rises are fine at morning temps — same load as your normal ride, no new variable.
   - Lock the bike at the office and leave it there.

2. Skip the ride home
   - This is the fail-closed call. A 25-minute ride home peaking inside the advisory window is the exact scenario you've avoided in past August heat (8/1, 8/10, 8/17 style conditions), and the bike stays where it is overnight.
   - Do not "just retrieve it later" — coming back for it in the same advisory window is the same risk as riding home in it.

3. Return-trip options, in order of preference
   - Rideshare with Sam if she's heading that way and the timing fits — lowest walk/exposure.
   - Rideshare on your own if the bus stop walk is more than a block or two in 100+ heat.
   - Bus if the stop is close, shaded, and you can minimize wait time.
   - Whichever you pick, decide it before the afternoon so you're not improvising at 5pm.

4. At the office during the window
   - Keep sipping water through the afternoon; don't wait for thirst.
   - One electrolyte serving mid-afternoon is reasonable if that's already part of your routine — not a reason to start something new today.
   - Stay out of direct sun on any breaks.

5. Hydration specifics (conservative)
   - Morning: water before, small amount during, normal breakfast fluids.
   - Midday at office: steady sips, not chugs.
   - Avoid a new caffeine load or alcohol as a "cool down" — both work against you in heat.

6. Clothing
   - Light-colored, loose-weave or technical moisture-wicking top.
   - Either long-sleeve sun shirt OR short sleeves + sunscreen on arms; pick whichever you've used before without issues.
   - Sunscreen SPF 30+ applied before the ride; reapply to face/neck at the office if you'll be outside at all.
   - Sunglasses with UV protection (you already ride with them).

7. Stop conditions — change the plan if any of these appear
   - Morning air is already unusually humid or warm at departure, or the advisory has been pulled forward to cover the morning window — downgrade to rideshare/bus both ways, retrieve the bike tomorrow.

Three things to compare, three questions. Walking through each one with what the captured history actually shows.

1) DO THE PLAN DATES AND FEES MATCH THE WRITTEN CONFIRMATION?

The Aug 19 written confirmation (from the supplier) said:
  - Active start date: August 13, 2025
  - Term: August 13, 2025 – August 12, 2026 (12 months)
  - No recurring plan fee
  - $150 early-termination charge (ETC)

This bill (Jul 22 – Aug 21, 2025) shows:
  - kWh split landed on Aug 13, 2025 — matches the confirmed start date
  - Bill falls inside the confirmed Aug 13, 2025 – Aug 12, 2026 term
  - No recurring plan fee line — consistent with "no recurring plan fee"
  - No early-termination charge — consistent (we're inside the term, not exiting it)

So dates and fee treatment match the confirmation. Nothing on the bill contradicts what the supplier wrote on Aug 19. One thing the bill period itself does NOT confirm — because it can't, from a single statement — is the 12-month end date of Aug 12, 2026; that remains a forward-looking commitment from the supplier's confirmation letter.

2) WHY IS THE PERIOD SPLIT THIS WAY?

The supplier bills on a fixed calendar cycle (Jul 22 – Aug 21, 31 days), not on plan-term boundaries. Because the fixed plan started mid-cycle on Aug 13, the supplier prorated the kWh by allocating each day to whichever plan was active on that day:

  Jul 22 – Aug 12 = 22 days, 296 kWh → prior variable plan
  Aug 13 – Aug 21  =  9 days, 128 kWh → new fixed plan
  22 + 9 = 31 days ✓
  296 + 128 = 424 kWh total over 31 days

The kWh are divided, not double-counted. Each day of usage belongs to exactly one plan. The split point is the Aug 13 plan-change date, not the billing-cycle start. This is standard proration — the same mechanic you'd see if you switched plans on any day other than the first day of a billing cycle.

A couple of grounded read-outs from the split itself:
  - Overall household run-rate: 424 / 31 ≈ 13.7 kWh/day
  - Fixed-plan segment run-rate: 128 / 9 ≈ 14.2 kWh/day
  - The 9-day fixed-plan sample is too small and too early in the term to be a meaningful test of the plan's headline rate — it's just a sanity check that kWh are landing where they should.

3) WHAT THE SUPPLIER'S ESTIMATED ALL-IN RATE POINTS DO AND DON'T GUARANTEE

The three points the supplier quoted (14.1¢ at 500 kWh, 13.5¢ at 1,000 kWh, 13.3¢ at 2,000 kWh) are reference prices — designed for shopping and comparison, not for bill reconciliation. Here's the honest read:

What they DO:
  - Give you three "all-in" prices at three specific monthly usage levels. "All-in" bundles the energy charge, TDU/delivery pass-through, and any base fee into one number, so you can compare this fixed plan against the 15.2¢ variable offer at a glance.
  - For your household's ~820–1,050 kWh range, the 1,000 kWh point (13.5¢) is the relevant one — your effective rate should land somewhere near it.
  - They let you sanity-check whether the fixed plan still beats the variable plan at your usage band, which is exactly the comparison you ran on Aug 11 and Aug 12.

What they DON'T guarantee:
  - They are NOT a tariff schedule. Three points at 500/1,000/2,000 kWh don't disclose the underlying rate structure — whether it's flat per-kWh, tiered, or flat-with-base-fee. From the three points alone you can't fully reconstruct what you'd pay at, say, 870 kWh. (A prior session showed an inferred model — ~$6 base + tiered per-kWh — that reproduces all three points exactly, but that's a reconstruction, not a disclosed tariff.)
  - They are NOT a price cap. Your actual all-in rate at your real usage could be slightly above or below the nearest reference point, depending on the plan's structure. The headline rate is a reference, not a ceiling or floor.
  - They don't include every charge. "All-in" typically means energy + TDU + base fee. Sales tax and certain regulatory riders may still appear as separate line items.
  - They don't tell you what rate was applied to THIS bill's fixed-plan segment. The 128 kWh / 9 days sample is too short to test the 13.5¢ estimate, and we don't have the rate lines or dollar totals from this statement yet.
  - They don't tell you what rate was applied to the 296 kWh variable-plan segment. That segment was billed under the prior plan's variable pricing for Jul 22 – Aug 12, which could be the 14.8¢ starting rate from your Aug 1 enrollment, the 15.2¢ from the Aug 11 comparison, or some other value the supplier used for those specific days. The headline figures don't reach backward into the variable plan.
  - They aren't predictive. They're forward-looking reference points; seasonal usage swings will move your effective rate even if the plan structure is unchanged.
  - They don't replace the full EFL/ESI documents. The base fee (if any), tier breakpoints, ETF conditions, renewal mechanics, and renewable content all live in the Electricity Facts Label / disclosure document — not in the three headline points.

Bottom line for the comparison you're doing:

The rate points answer the shopping question ("is fixed at 13.5¢ better than variable at 15.2¢ at my usage?"). They do NOT answer the reconciliation question ("did this bill apply the rates the supplier said it would?"). For that, you'd need the rate lines and dollar totals from this specific statement. What this bill alone DOES tell you is that the plan-change boundary was honored on Aug 13, the kWh were allocated correctly between the two plans, no plan fee was added, and no ETC was triggered. The plan is behaving the way the Aug 19 confirmation said it would, at least at the structural level.

    - Do the second run only if both the 35-min test session AND its following-day check are clean. If the next-day check is not clean, skip or shorten the second run; the week does not advance duration in either direction.
    - Treat the 35-min session as one test, not a new standard. A single clean session-plus-following-day pair at 35 min is load-testing, not clearance. Do not retest 35 min the very next week just because this one was clean.

  4. STOP CONDITIONS DURING THE 35-MIN SESSION

    Stop the run for any of:
      - Focal ankle pain (inside or outside, including the recurrent lateral / inside-right-ankle pattern), especially if it is new, increasing, or one-sided.
      - Limp, giving way, instability, sharp or mechanical sensation.
      - Swelling, bruising, focal bony tenderness noticed during the run.
      - Pain at rest after you stop.
      - Neurovascular change — numbness, color change, persistent pins-and-needles beyond normal.

    Stop does not mean "walk home slow and see." Stop means end the running portion. Walking home at an easy pace is fine if gait is normal and there is no focal pain.

  5. ROLLBACK / NEXT-DAY CONDITIONS

    The following-day (and through ~48h) check covers the same list plus:
      - Focal ankle pain at rest, on stairs, or during ordinary walking.
      - Swelling, bruising, focal bony tenderness.
      - Limp or compensated gait you did not have before.
      - Recurring symptoms at the same or lower load — i.e., something that showed up during the test and returns later, or a symptom that emerges during next-day walking that was not there at the 30-min baseline.
      - Pain at rest.
      - New mechanical event or neurovascular change.

    If any of those appear:
      - Skip the second run that week. Do not retry 35.
      - Step back to the last clean 30-min session in the standard shoes. Repeat the 30-min baseline one or two more times before any further duration test.
      - Recurrent focal ankle pain still triggers clinical follow-up, same standing rule.

    If both the 35-min session and the following day are clean:
      - Do the unchanged 30-min second run on the next nonconsecutive day, same effort, and still check the day after it.
      - That second pair is a re-confirmation of the 30-min baseline, not a second 35-min test.

  6. WHAT THIS IS NOT

    - Not a clearance. Not a new standard duration. Not an automatic step toward 40 min.
    - Not a reason to add a third run, change shoes, change route, change effort, or add hills.
    - Not paired with any other new load variable in the same week.
    - Not a basis, on its own, for declaring continuous running "established" — that framing still requires multiple clean pairs, which you do not yet have at 35.

  Net shape of the week: one 35-min easy test early, one recovery day, one clean following-day check, one unchanged 30-min easy run, one more following-day check. If all four observation points are clean, you have one clean 35-min pair to add to your record — and a standing decision that 35 is still a test, not a baseline.

Interpretation

  The 5- and 6-minute results are not a contradiction; they describe two sides of a transition in surface wetness at the moment the dark mark lands.

  At 5 minutes, the wash was still wet enough that the pigment and water from the interruption mark pushed outward into the surrounding damp wash. The mark softened into a small bloom. The wash continuity and warm edge still held because the diffusion was local.

  At 6 minutes, the wash had lost enough surface moisture that the mark sat on top rather than diffusing. It reads slightly crisp — present, but a little separate from the surface it interrupted. The wash and warm edge were again preserved.

  So neither version is "right" or "wrong"; both keep the harder constraint (wash and warm edge) intact, and they differ in whether the rain mark integrates into the damp surface or sits on a drier one. The 5-minute bloom is closer to rain hitting a wet surface; the 6-minute crisp is closer to rain hitting a surface that has just begun to dry. Aesthetic preference, not correctness, picks between them.

Is 5.5 minutes the right next test?

  Yes, and the reason is specific. The 5→6 result puts the bloom-to-crisp transition inside a one-minute window. A 5.5-minute study, with everything else held constant, tests whether the transition is gradual (intermediate softness, slight halo, mark still legible) or sharp (still bloomy or already crisp). That answer decides what kind of working window you actually have:

    - If 5.5 lands as a slightly softened but legible mark, the window is broad enough that timing alone gets you close, and 5.5 is a usable working point for these conditions.

    - If 5.5 looks like a weaker version of one of the two, the window is narrow and timing alone won't resolve it. Then the next move is to vary something inside the mark itself (pigment load, brush dampness at the moment of interruption) rather than chase the clock.

  Either outcome is useful; the value of 5.5 is that it tells you which kind of window you're in.

Controls for the 5.5-minute study

  Same as 8/31 — only one thing changes:

    - Same paper (140-lb cold-press)
    - Same blue-plus-brown pigment mix and dilution
    - Same brush, same load
    - Same large cool wash, same warm-edge goal
    - Single controlled change: interruption timing = 5.5 minutes from wash start
    - 15-minute hard cap; drying is part of the test
    - No refinement, no third pass, no lifting, no glazing after the second pass dries
    - Judge the result after the second pass has dried, not while wet

  No title, no signature, no exhibition or sale framing. This stays in the practice-study lane.

Caveats worth holding

  The window shifts with room humidity, paper dampness, pigment load, and how continuous the wash was. A 5.5-minute result on one Sunday is a working point for those conditions, not a permanent rule. Worth jotting the room and paper state alongside the timing when you record it.

  "Crisp" at 6 and "bloom" at 5 are observations about the mark, not a verdict on either version. The 8/24 study, the 8/31 study, and the proposed 5.5 are three points on the same curve; together they describe the transition, and the next step after 5.5 follows from where it lands — not from a decision made in advance.

  Holding off, for now, on changes to pigment load in the dark mark, paper, board tilt, heat, or any third pass. Any of those added now would make the 5.5 result harder to read, and the point of the next study is to map the transition cleanly.

  So: yes, the 5.5-minute study is the most useful next test, with timing as the only variable and everything else held to the 8/31 conditions.

Assessment of the two options (uniform 60-minute warning window across all five governed fields vs. differentiated warning windows by field, source-reliability tier, or consumer).

  OPERATIONAL USEFULNESS

  Uniform 60-minute gives operators a single mental model: any staleness warning they see carries roughly 60 minutes of runway before the freshness limit expires. No per-field memorization, no per-consumer lookup, no conditional escalation rule to recall under time pressure. That simplicity has real operational value during a period when operators are still learning the system's hold-and-refresh cadence (see the Aug 28 CS question about reusing a 10:00 proceed at 10:30 — that question would be harder to answer cleanly if warning timing varied by surface).

  Differentiated windows could in principle be tuned: a fast-volatility field could carry a longer warning, a slow-volatility field a shorter one. But tuning requires per-field evidence we do not yet have. We have only a handful of Q3 field-specific-hold observations (the five rows Owen surfaced on Sep 2, plus the Aug 6 source-age alert), which is enough to confirm the alert-and-hold path fires and resolves, not enough to design a per-field calibration. Tuning now would be configuring ahead of evidence.

  ALERT NOISE

  Uniform 60-minute bounds noise symmetrically: each governed field's warning fires at a consistent lead time relative to its own freshness limit. If two fields have different freshness limits, their absolute lead times differ, but the operator-facing signal (one warning, ~60 min to act) is uniform. That symmetry is itself a noise-reduction property — operators do not have to weight warnings differently.

  Differentiated warning times without evidence risks asymmetric noise: some fields get over-warned (stable sources that rarely approach the limit), others under-warned (volatile sources where 60 min is genuinely tight). Until we know the per-field volatility distribution, we cannot tell which way the asymmetry cuts. Worse, any asymmetry introduced mid-period would be very hard to interpret in the Q3 evidence — every later observation would be confounded with the configuration change that produced it.

  COMPARABILITY

  This is the strongest argument for uniform 60-minute through the Q3 evidence period. The period exists to gather bounded operating evidence under a stable configuration so that observations are directly comparable across time. Any mid-period differentiation — whether by field, by source-reliability tier, or by consumer — creates a configuration regime change that splits the evidence into "before" and "after" sub-periods. The smaller those sub-periods get, the less useful the evidence becomes for any subsequent review (Sep 19 lock, Sep 24 quarter-close, or later).

  Uniform 60-minute also keeps the warning lead time independent of the freshness limit, which is what makes the evidence interpretable: hold age, refresh latency, breach frequency, and disposition timing can all be reported on their own scales without a hidden coupling to operator warning behavior.

  WARNING TIME vs. CUSTOMER-DECISION LOGIC

  These are two distinct concepts and the assessment depends on keeping them separate:

    - Warning time = operator-facing signal that a governed source is approaching its freshness limit. Its job is to give the named source owner enough runway to refresh before the limit expires. It governs operator readiness, not customer treatment.

    - Customer-decision logic = at the moment a nudge decision is scheduled, given current state of all governed fields, what disposition applies (proceed, valid suppression, or hold). The freshness limit is the boundary condition here; the decision itself is per-decision and per-field.

  The Aug 28 operator question illustrates the separation directly: a 10:00 proceed was being considered for reuse at 10:30, but a required source's freshness limit governs whether the 10:30 decision can use current state at all — that is decision logic, not warning logic. A uniform 60-minute warning window does not change any of that; it only affects how much advance notice operators get before the freshness boundary is reached. Differentiating the warning would risk coupling these two layers in operator mental models (a longer warning on a field starts to feel like that field is "more important" to the decision, when in fact every governed field's freshness limit applies independently to the decision).

  RECOMMENDATION

  Keep the uniform 60-minute warning configuration through the Q3 evidence period.

  Reasoning, in order of weight:

    1. Comparability. The Q3 evidence period is for accumulation under stable configuration. Mid-period differentiation is a confound we cannot afford in a period whose output feeds the Sep 19 lock and the Sep 24 quarter-close decision.

    2. Separation of warning time from customer-decision logic. These are distinct concepts; the uniform lead time reinforces that separation rather than blurring it.

    3. Lack of tuning data. We have early evidence the alert-and-hold path fires and resolves, not enough to calibrate per-field warning windows. Designing differentiation now is configuring ahead of evidence.

    4. Bounded alert noise. Uniform lead time gives a consistent operator signal across fields, which is itself a noise-reduction property during a learning period.

    5. Reversibility. The decision is to defer differentiation, not to reject it. After Q3 evidence is gathered and the Sep 19 lock / Sep 24 review are behind us, a per-field tuning proposal grounded in observed volatility, breach frequency, and refresh latency would be a reasonable follow-on — but it would be a new decision, not a continuation of the current one.

  WHAT THIS RECOMMENDATION IS AND IS NOT

  It is:
    - A routine configuration choice during an evidence-gathering period
    - A choice to preserve comparability of Q3 observations
    - A choice to keep the warning layer from coupling to the decision layer
    - Reversible at the next natural review point

  It is not:
    - A claim that 60 minutes is the optimal universal warning window
    - A permanent rejection of differentiated warning times
    - A change to any freshness limit, governed field, source owner, suppression rule, or customer-decision rule
    - An expansion of surface scope, an authority change, or a re-opening of the legacy config
    - A statement that early Q3 evidence (the Aug 6 alert, the Sep 2 five-row worksheet, the Aug 28 operator question) has already settled the question — those observations support the recommendation but do not prove 60 minutes is forever-right

  OPERATIONAL ESCALATION CONDITIONS

  The recommendation holds unless a specific Q3 observation shows 60 minutes is operationally broken for a specific field — for example, a chronic breach pattern where a named source owner cannot refresh within 60 minutes, or a cluster of warnings that operators consistently ignore as unactionable. Either of those should surface as a routine exception to Owen, not as a configuration change driven from outside the routine lane. If one emerges, it is evidence for a post-Q3 tuning proposal, not a reason to break the Q3 configuration now.

  In short: keep it uniform through Q3, treat the period as the evidence base it is designed to be, and revisit differentiation only after the evidence is in hand.

Chicken fried rice is the natural fit — cold rice is what you want, the eggs scramble in, spinach wilts at the end, scallions and lime finish it, and it reheats well. Yield: about 3 generous portions (2 tonight, 1 reserved for Sam).

PAN: 12-inch skillet, nonstick or well-seasoned cast iron.

INGREDIENTS (with rough quantities for 3 portions):
  - Cooked rice: ~4 cups, cold from the fridge (best texture)
  - Roasted chicken: ~1 to 1.5 cups, shredded or chopped small
  - Eggs: 2
  - Corn: ~3/4 cup (drained if canned)
  - Spinach: 3 to 4 handfuls, roughly chopped
  - Scallions: 3 to 4, whites and greens sliced in separate piles
  - Lime: 1, halved
  - Oil: 2 tbsp neutral
  - Soy sauce: 1.5 to 2 tbsp
  - Optional: 1 small garlic clove (grated), pinch white pepper, 1 tsp sesame oil at the end

TIMED SEQUENCE (clock starts when you begin prep):

  0:00  Mise en place (about 5 min):
        - Shred/chop chicken, slice scallions, chop spinach, halve lime
        - Beat the 2 eggs in a small bowl with a pinch of salt
        - If rice is clumpy, break it up with damp hands or a fork

  0:05  Preheat skillet over medium-high. When hot, add 2 tbsp oil; let it shimmer.

  0:07  Aromatics, about 1 min:
        - Scallion whites in, stir 30 sec
        - Garlic in if using, stir another 30 sec

  0:08  Eggs, about 2 min:
        - Pour beaten eggs in; let them set 15 sec, then scramble into small curds
        - Push eggs to one side of the pan (or scoop into a bowl and return later)

  0:10  Chicken + corn, about 3 min:
        - Add chicken and corn, stir-fry until chicken is heated through

  0:13  Rice + sauce, about 6 min:
        - Add rice, breaking up remaining clumps
        - Drizzle 1.5 to 2 tbsp soy sauce over the rice
        - Toss, then press flat for 30 sec to build a little crust, flip, repeat
        - Keep it moving so nothing burns

  0:19  Spinach, about 1 to 2 min:
        - Add chopped spinach, toss until just wilted (60 to 90 sec)

  0:21  Off heat:
        - Squeeze HALF the lime over the pan; toss
        - Add scallion greens and the optional sesame oil; toss once

  0:22  Portion and reserve:
        - Scoop about 1/3 of the pan into Sam's container
        - Cool on the counter 5 min, then fridge, lid on
        - Plate your portion(s), squeeze remaining lime to taste, eat

REHEAT FOR SAM (after service):

  Microwave (easiest):
    - Sprinkle 1 to 2 tsp water over the rice
    - Cover with a plate or paper towel (slightly ajar), microwave 60 to 90 sec on high
    - Stir, then another 30 to 60 sec
    - Finish with fresh scallion greens and a fresh squeeze of lime — this matters, the lime loses brightness in the fridge and the fresh hit covers most of the reheat softening

  Skillet (better texture):
    - Splash of water or oil in a small pan over medium, 3 to 4 min, stirring occasionally

  Storage: airtight container, fridge up to 3 days. Do not freeze — eggs and spinach do not thaw well.

NOTES:
  - Cold day-old rice is the biggest texture win. If your rice is freshly cooked, spread it thin on a plate or sheet pan for 5 to 10 min while you prep.
  - Realistic reheat quality: about 80 to 85% of fresh. Eggs and spinach are the softest on reheat; the fresh lime and scallion finish at serving closes most of that gap.
  - If the chicken is bone-in, pick it carefully and discard skin and any small bone fragments — easy to miss in fried rice.
  - Low cleanup if you use the skillet for everything, one bowl for the eggs, one cutting board for the chopping.

Diagnosis in one line: this is a mid-cycle drain failure. Standing water tells you the pump didn't finish; the hum on restart tells you the pump is getting power but can't move water — most often a clogged filter/sump, a jammed impeller, or a blocked drain line. The pump drawing current against a stall is the main reason to act conservatively now: every restart attempt can overheat the pump windings, which turns a service call into a pump replacement. This is an appliance fault, not a safety emergency.

Shutdown sequence (in order):
1. Stop/cancel the cycle. (Done.)
2. Cut power to the dishwasher at the breaker before any further inspection or restart attempt. The hum = energized stalled motor. Open the labeled breaker; if it's shared and unlabeled, leave it for the tech rather than guess. Don't treat the door latch or child lock as a power cutoff.
3. Leave the dishwasher supply valve under the sink as-is. Open is correct — closing it doesn't help drainage, and prior Cherrywood supply-side leaks presented under the sink before they appeared on the floor. Glance under the cabinet for moisture around the supply line, the drain hose connection at the disposer or sink tailpiece, and the cabinet floor. You said no floor leak; confirm the cabinet specifically.
4. Keep the door cracked enough for airflow but Kibo-blocked. Standing sump water holds residual detergent and any sharp debris that may be causing the jam — paw risk is glass/bone fragments in the water, not the water itself.
5. Don't bail the water yet. Leaving it in place preserves the level, smell, and floating debris for whoever services it.

Safe user checks (no disassembly, breaker still off):
  A. Filter: most built-in dishwashers have a bottom filter assembly that twists out by hand (usually quarter-turn). Lift it out, rinse it, look at the underside and mesh for debris — glass, bone, pits, fruit-stone fragments, label bits, olive pits. The Dec 2023 incident was a filter that hadn't fully seated, so confirm the re-seat is correct on reassembly (quarter-turn until it stops, not loose).
  B. Sump well: with the filter out, shine a flashlight into the cavity. You're looking for anything that could jam the impeller. Don't reach in with bare fingers — use tongs or a stiff plastic utensil to lift out debris. A wet-dry vac (shop mode, no electrical contact with the unit) is also reasonable.
  C. Air gap: if there's a small chrome cylinder on the sink near the faucet with a cap, pop the cap and look inside. A clogged air gap will silently stop a dishwasher from draining. Not all installs have one — if you don't see it, skip.
  D. Disposal: if the disposal was ever replaced, a plastic knockout plug inside the disposer port must be punched out or the dishwasher will never drain. With the dishwasher breaker still off, running the disposal for ~10 seconds with cold water flowing can clear a loose blockage at the inlet. Don't reach into the disposal.

If you found and removed debris and want to test:
  - Bail or wet-vac most of the standing water first (reduces overflow risk if the drain is still slow).
  - Restore breaker power.
  - Run the shortest cycle available — rinse-only, no detergent, no dishes. Stay within earshot.
  - If the pump sounds normal and water drops, let it finish, then re-open the filter to confirm nothing recirculated.
  - If the hum returns or water doesn't drop, stop the cycle, kill the breaker, and submit the maintenance request.

Do not disassemble:
  - Side panels, toe kick, or anything requiring a screwdriver (scratches the cabinet, dents the panel, voids any simple service path)
  - The drain hose or its connection at the disposer/sink tailpiece
  - The pump, motor, control board, or door latch
  - Anything electrical while the breaker is on, including running another cycle before the filter check
  - Don't pour drain opener, bleach, vinegar, or boiling water into a sump that has standing water plus detergent residue and possibly aluminium components — risk isn't worth whatever it might clear

Submit a maintenance request (normal path) if:
  - The filter and sump check doesn't reveal a clear jam
  - The filter was already clean and properly seated when you opened it (rules out the easy fix; pump-side fault)
  - A test cycle after clearing still doesn't drain, or the hum returns
  - You just want a tech to look at it regardless — the hum-against-stall observation alone is service-relevant

Symptom description for the request (short, useful):
  "Dishwasher stopped mid-cycle with standing water above the filter. Pump hums on restart attempt; no restart yet done with breaker off. No floor leak, no supply-side moisture under sink, no burning odor, no breaker trip. Filter [state once you check it]."

Treat as more urgent (same-day, not 911) if:
  - Water begins actively leaking onto the floor or into the cabinet
  - A burning odor develops (breaker off, ventilate, then call)
  - The breaker trips when you restore power (leave breaker off, call)
  - Any sign of electrical distress — sparking, scorch marks, repeated breaker trips

One geography note from prior history: the Aug 2024 sink-backup event was a blockage in the common sink-and-dishwasher branch downstream of the appliance connections. A drain that won't go down can sit on the same branch and present differently. Worth mentioning in the maintenance request even if your filter check clears — the tech can decide whether to scope the branch.

I can draft the maintenance request message in whatever channel you usually use (email/Slack to the front desk) if you want — say the word.

Three passages that hold together as a sequence — and they read as if they were meant to be read in order.

The first reframes edges as a sequence of attention rather than a count of hard versus soft boundaries. The hierarchy comes from where attention lands and in what order, not from the total tally of crisp or feathered transitions. That fits the controlled-edge / softened-reflection work naturally: the painting isn't stronger because it has "the right number" of hard edges — it's stronger because attention was sequenced. In the rainy-doorway studies, attention went to the cool-wash continuity and then to the warm doorway edge; that ordering is what produced the hierarchy, not a count of crisp marks.

The second is sharp about the role of repetition. Timing studies earn their keep only until the variable is bounded — which means once the timing question is settled, more timing trials are not the next step. The 5 / 6 / 5.5-minute rainy-doorway trials were doing exactly that job: bounding the interruption window so it stops pulling attention. The 5.5-minute confirm-or-don't is the closing step of that ladder, not the opening of a new one.

The third is what comes after. Once a variable is bounded, the next experiment is composition — a different kind of question. The variable-bounding studies (the grid, the 35° angle, blot frequency, brush moisture) were mechanical; composition is the painting itself. It's the shift from "what is each piece doing" to "what is the piece doing."

Read together, the three passages imply that bounded studies aren't the practice — they're preparation for the practice. Once the timing ladder has done its job, attention belongs to composition. That probably also means the next useful study is one where timing, brush, paper, and pigment are held constant and the variable being tested is the painting's own arrangement.

What the three trials say together:

- 5 min — wash still too wet at the moment the rain mark was added, so the mark dispersed into a soft bloom rather than reading as a mark.
- 6 min — the wash has moved past the useful window; the rain mark reads crisp, but the integration with the surrounding cool wash and the warm doorway edge has thinned.
- 5.5 min — lands in the band where the cool wash + warm doorway relationship holds (both preserved). But within that same sheet the upper rain mark held while the lower one feathered — a within-sheet asymmetry, not a clean pass.

Reading: 5.5 min is close to the timing that satisfies the wash/doorway constraint, but timing alone is not yet sufficient to bound the rain-mark behavior. The asymmetry (upper holds, lower feathers) points away from timing as the primary cause of feathering and toward something more likely environmental — wetness gradient on the sheet, pre-wet unevenness, board tilt, or brush pressure. Timing is one variable; it is not yet the whole answer.

Compact next study — personal practice, no exhibition or demonstration commitment:

One more 5.5-min trial under the same conditions — 140 lb cold-press, blue + brown mix, same brush load, large cool wash, warm doorway edge, no third pass, 15-minute hard cap — with timing as the only intentional variable. Alongside it, record one short note:

  - where on the sheet the rain mark landed (upper / middle / lower)
  - whether the sheet was pre-wet or dry-started
  - board tilt during the wash
  - brush pressure and load on the rain mark
  - room and paper temperature / humidity, if easily noted

Decision rule after that single trial:

  - If the lower feathering reproduces, the cause is more likely environmental than temporal; the next move is to flatten the board, even the pre-wet, and re-test at the same 5.5 min. Timing still stands.
  - If the lower feathering does not reproduce, timing is plausibly sufficient on its own, and the natural next step becomes a brush-moisture ladder at a fixed 5.5 min — only then.

This pairs with the other passage you marked from the collection. The two together set up an arc: one about attention hardening into a ledger, the other about what the ledger can and can't do once it exists.

Discussion question, framed to preserve the tension: where does exposure end and repair begin? The passage says a record can expose neglect without repairing it, but doesn't say what would count as repair, or who decides. That leaves room for the group to disagree about whether repair means changing the conditions that produced the neglect, acknowledging the people named inside the record, or something the institution can't do from inside its own documentation at all.

Brief interpretive angle: the passage isn't anti-record. It names a specific move — pointing to the record's visibility as proof that the people inside it have already been answered — as the danger. The risk isn't documentation, it's documentation standing in for response. That distinction gives the group room to push either direction: no record can repair, or some records, under the right conditions, can.

A recorded problem is now visible — named, located, held as an object of attention. A response commits to an action, a direction, or a change. The two can substitute for each other in ways that feel productive but aren't: recording can perform the work of responding without producing any change in the situation, and responding can outrun recording, acting on a problem that was never clearly understood. The gap between them is where most missteps sit — logs no one reads, interventions that don't match what's actually going on.

Question: Where in your own work has the act of recording started to feel like the response — and what tipped you off?

1. What this recall means, conservatively

The fuel pump moves fuel from the tank to the engine at a controlled pressure. The impeller is the rotating part inside the pump. A deformed impeller can drop fuel pressure below what the engine needs; in a worse case, pressure can be lost while driving. The manufacturer has determined your specific vehicle (by VIN) is affected and has authorized a free repair — typically a fuel-pump or impeller replacement at a dealer.

What this recall is NOT, on the basis of what you've shown me:

  - It is not a "stop driving" order. The notice explicitly does not say that.
  - It is not an immediate safety emergency in the same sense as, e.g., a Takata airbag inflator order. Many fuel-pump recalls fall in "drive but monitor."
  - It is not a technical service bulletin (TSB). Recalls are mandatory manufacturer action; TSBs are advisory and not free.
  - It is not yet a completed repair. Until the dealer has done the work and you have the invoice, the matter is open.

2. Records to retain

Keep everything below together — a single paper folder, or one scanned PDF — and keep it for the life of the vehicle (pass it to a buyer at sale; do not discard after the repair).

  - The original notice letter. Note the date received (2025-09-25). Capture both sides if it is two-sided.
  - The recall campaign ID(s) and the NHTSA campaign number printed on the letter. If those are not on the first letter, the second letter or a VIN lookup will provide them.
  - Your VIN (17 characters). Confirm it matches the VIN on the notice.
  - A short running log with four columns: date, event, source/contact, outcome. Add a row for each dealer call, each dealer visit, the second-letter receipt, and the completed repair. One row per event, not per symptom.
  - The dealer repair invoice after the remedy is done. It should list: recall campaign ID, parts replaced, labor, "no charge," odometer reading, date.
  - Any dealer correspondence (emails, work-order printouts) about parts availability, scheduling, or temporary operating guidance.

Why this matters: the paper trail ties the recall to your specific VIN. It is the only way to later prove the repair was performed under recall rather than as paid maintenance, which is relevant for resale, for any related warranty dispute, and for your own peace of mind that the campaign is closed.

3. Symptoms that should end a trip or prompt urgent service

The notice lists four symptoms. Graded conservatively:

End the trip (pull off the road; do not continue):

  - Engine stall while moving that does not restart immediately on the first attempt.
  - Sudden loss of power on a highway or intersection that does not recover. Coast to a safe spot.

Schedule service promptly — within days, not weeks:

  - Hard starting that recurs across multiple drive cycles (cold or hot).
  - Rough running, misfire, or hesitation under acceleration.
  - Illuminated check-engine or fuel-related warning light that does not clear on the next normal start.
  - A single engine stall that restarts immediately and then runs normally.

Log and mention at next routine service:

  - A single brief hesitation episode that does not repeat.
  - Slightly longer cranking on one cold start with no other symptom.

If multiple symptoms cluster (e.g., rough running plus an illuminated light plus one stall), treat the cluster as "schedule promptly" even if no single symptom is severe — clustering suggests pressure is degrading, not a one-off.

Triage rule when in doubt: stop the vehicle in a safe place, wait 10–15 minutes, restart. If it restarts cleanly and the symptom does not repeat on the next drive, log it and schedule service. If it repeats or a second symptom appears, treat the situation as escalating and do not drive further than necessary.

This is symptom triage, not a diagnosis. Do not attempt to isolate the failure yourself; the remedy, when parts are available, is a dealer repair.

4. Verifying remedy availability without relying on unsolicited links

Three independent channels. Each works with only your VIN. None of them require clicking a link from an email, text, or social-media post.

a. Manufacturer recall lookup — best for "is the remedy available right now."

  - Open a browser and type the manufacturer's recall URL directly. The URL printed on the notice is fine; the brand's main site also has an Owners → Recalls page.
  - Enter your VIN.
  - The page returns: campaign ID, description, status (e.g., "remedy available," "parts not yet available," "completed").

b. NHTSA recalls database — best for an independent second check.

  - Open nhtsa.gov/recalls by typing the address into the browser. Do not follow a link.
  - Enter your VIN.
  - It returns every open recall on the vehicle, the campaign number, and the manufacturer's reported remedy status.

c. Dealer service department — best for scheduling.

  - Call the dealer service desk using the phone number on existing dealer correspondence, on the manufacturer's site, or on a previous repair invoice. Do not call a number from an unexpected email or text.
  - Give them the VIN; they will pull the recall status from the manufacturer system and tell you whether parts are in stock.
  - Ask for the recall reference number and write it in your log.

Avoiding unsolicited links, in practice:

  - When the second letter arrives, open it. If it contains a link, type the manufacturer URL yourself rather than tapping the link in the letter.
  - Ignore emails or texts about this recall that you did not expect. Phishing routinely piggybacks on real recalls.
  - If anyone calls you claiming to schedule the recall repair, ask for the recall campaign ID and your VIN, then independently verify by calling the dealer back at a number you already have.

A reasonable cadence: check (a) or (b) once a month until status reads "remedy available," then call (c) to schedule. After the repair is done, your log plus the invoice closes the matter; no further routine monitoring is needed unless a new symptom appears.

I do not have the recall campaign ID, the NHTSA campaign number, the manufacturer name, or your VIN in your record, so I cannot pull a current status for you. The three channels above close that gap using only the VIN — and the VIN, campaign ID, and NHTSA number should already be on the notice or the second letter. If you can share those, I can help you interpret the manufacturer's status language precisely, but I would not act on a recalled lookup result that you have not seen.

ONE-SKILLET BRUNCH HASH — TWO PEOPLE, ~30 MIN, ONE PAN

PREP (do all of this before the burner goes on, ~5 min)
- Dice 2 cups cooked potatoes into 1/2-inch pieces (smaller = faster crust)
- Slice 3 scallions, keep whites and greens in two piles
- Wash 2 big handfuls spinach
- Grate 3/4 cup sharp cheddar
- Beat 4 eggs in a bowl with a pinch of salt and pepper

TIMED SEQUENCE (12-inch nonstick or cast iron, medium burner)

  0:00  2 Tbsp olive oil + 1 Tbsp butter in the skillet, medium-high until butter foams
  0:30  potatoes in a single layer, press flat, light salt — don't stir yet
  3:00  flip/toss potatoes, add the scallion WHITES, drop heat to medium
  8:00  potatoes should be golden and crisp; push to one side, pile spinach into the empty side, cover 60 sec
  9:30  stir spinach into the potatoes, open a well in the center
 10:00  pour eggs into the well, fold gently from the edges ~90 sec until just barely wet
 11:30  scatter cheddar + scallion GREENS on top, kill heat, lid on 60 sec to melt
 12:30  off heat, plate straight from the skillet

TOTAL COOK TIME: about 13 minutes. The rest of the 30 is prep + plating.

CLEANUP (about 10 min, finishes before Sam heads out)
- Wipe the warm skillet with a paper towel, then one wash, one rinse
- Cutting board, knife, egg bowl, grater → dishwasher in one load
- Total dishes: 1 skillet, 1 board, 1 knife, 1 bowl, 2 plates, 2 forks

QUICK VARIATIONS
- Faster: warm the diced potatoes 60 sec in the microwave before they hit the pan (cuts crisp-time by ~3 min)
- Heartier: skip the in-pan scramble, fry 2 eggs sunny-side-up on top of the hash at minute 10
- Hold for Sam: cook the hash to minute 8, kill heat, cover; finish his portion in the pan 4 min when he's ready to eat

Setup before touching anything:

  • Flat, clean surface; soft lint-free cloth down first.
  • Wash and dry hands; nitrile or clean cotton gloves if you have them.
  • Diffuse light only. No direct sun on the sheet.
  • Stable room conditions (typical indoor RH ~45–55%). If the room is unusually dry/humid right now, pause and stabilize before opening.
  • Tools ready: bone folder or plastic microspatula, soft brush, clean microfiber. If replacing: a fresh archival corner mount (polyester/Mylar, adhesive on the outer tab only).

Open and lay out (face-down on the cloth, glazing up):

  1. Face the frame down on the cloth. Release the backer — turnbuckle-style clips, flexible points, or friction tabs; do not pry.
  2. Lift the backer straight off. Note orientation; if you took a quick phone photo of the back before opening, you have a recovery reference.
  3. Lift the mat package off the glazing. Set glazing aside where it can't fall or scratch.
  4. Keep the sheet cornered in the mat. Do not flip the mat; work from the back with the mat face-down and the sheet sandwiched between mat and your view of the mat's rear.

Assess the shifted corner (don't touch the sheet yet):

  • Is the corner mount still firmly seated on the mat, only displaced (rotated/translated), or has the adhesive let go entirely?
  • Is the sheet itself still trapped correctly inside the corner fold, or has it slipped partly out?
  • Any fiber lift, abrasion, tide line, or pigment disturbance anywhere on the sheet? Stop signs below.

Reseat (preferred when the mount is intact and the adhesive tab is still sticky):

  1. With the mat still face-down, slide the bone folder under the mount's adhesive tab only — not under the corner fold itself.
  2. Gently lift the tab from the mat; the corner should remain holding the sheet.
  3. Rotate/translate the mount back so the sheet sits square, fully inside all four corner folds, with no fold edge visible through the window opening and no point load on the sheet edge.
  4. Re-press the adhesive tab flat against the mat with the bone folder's tip. No PSA is on or near the sheet — the sheet is held mechanically by the fold; adhesive only contacts the mat.

Replace (when the existing mount is deformed, won't re-stick, or the fold no longer traps cleanly):

  1. Slide the old mount off the sheet from the back without pulling on the sheet edge.
  2. Fit a fresh conservation corner: slide the sheet corner into the fold so the fold wraps the corner on all four sides; verify the fold edges sit just inside the mat window opening and don't intrude on the image.
  3. Adhere only the outer tab to the mat. Trim the tab if it overhangs the mat board edge.

Close:

  1. Confirm sheet is flat, square, and free of any corner edge in the window. Raking-light check (tilt the mat and shine a light across it) — no shadow from a fold, no bump.
  2. Replace backer; re-engage fasteners evenly. Keep the painting face-up only at the end, briefly, to confirm framing.

Stop handling the sheet at home if any of these appear:

  • Moisture: tide line, cockle, ripple, waviness, condensation, dampness, or any change in flatness.
  • New marks: pigment lift, smudge, flake, offset, or transfer; foxing, spotting, mold, or biological growth.
  • Surface disturbance: fiber lift, abrasion, scuff, tear, or new edge damage — especially near the shifted corner.
  • Adhesive evidence: tackiness, gloss, staining, halo, or residue on the sheet, or any sign PSA reached the paper.
  • Material failure: mount adhesive has failed on more than one corner, or the corner fold no longer traps the sheet cleanly.
  • Environmental: room RH swings, water leak, smoke, cooking residue, or an unfamiliar odor during work.
  • Structural: sheet becomes brittle, soft, warped, or a piece detaches; mat boards delaminate or off-gas.
  • Unknowns: anything you can't immediately identify. Photograph under raking and diffuse light with a small ruler, then stop.

If any stop sign appears, leave the sheet cornered in the mat (or back in the frame if it's still flat), document with photos under both raking and diffuse light, and hand it to a paper conservator. Don't try to dry, press, blot, or clean the sheet at home.

One narrower note for this piece: since the matting finished on Dec 14, a single corner shifting ~1/8" this soon most often means the adhesive tab on the mat didn't fully bond (common with smoother mat board surfaces) or a small settling shift during the first weeks of display. Reseat is the right first move; replacement only if reseat doesn't hold cleanly.
