Five-minute setup, in this order:

1. Light placement (~1 min)
   - Use the painting corner with the window already diffused (sheer or curtain) so the light is indirect, not direct sun.
   - Keep all room lights OFF — any second source will throw the phone's auto-WB off and is the main reason the wash reads too blue and the warm edge too orange.
   - Angle the painting so the window sits roughly 30–45° off-axis from the painting surface (not straight-on, not grazing). Straight-on invites glare on the wash; grazing makes the cold-press tooth cast micro-shadows and warms unevenly.
   - If the sun is moving into the frame (south/west exposures), pull the sheer tighter or wait two minutes — direct sun shifts color temp fast.

2. Neutral reference (~30 sec)
   - Tape an 18% gray card (or a true neutral gray paper swatch) right next to the painting, in the same plane, receiving the same light. This is your WB anchor for both the camera lock and any later edit.

3. Camera alignment (~1 min)
   - Prop or hang the painting vertical against a neutral wall (white or mid-gray, no color cast from a colored wall or wood).
   - Hold the phone at the painting's vertical center, lens axis perpendicular to the surface — eyeball by checking that all four corners of the sheet sit equidistant from the frame edges.
   - Frame so the painting fills about 85% of the frame with a thin border, and the gray card sits in one corner of the frame.

4. Capture and minimal correction (~1–2 min)
   - In the phone camera app, tap-and-hold on the gray card to lock AE/AF and exposure there. That alone gives you a neutral exposure anchor.
   - If your phone has a Pro / manual mode or a third-party app (Halide, Lightroom Mobile, ProCam), set WB manually to roughly 5500–6000 K for indirect daylight. This single setting is what undoes the phone's "too-blue / too-orange" over-correction.
   - Shoot 2–3 frames.
   - In the phone editor, if it still leans blue, drop the blue channel a few points or warm WB by ~200–300 K; if the warm edge still reads hot, drop overall saturation 5–10% rather than re-coloring it. Do not crush contrast — watercolor sits in a narrow value range and lifts easily.

Net: one light, one neutral card, perpendicular camera, locked exposure on the card, manual WB if available, minimal nudges afterward. Private-inventory faithful, not exhibition-grade.

ONE-POT CHICKPEA-ORZO WITH KALE
3 portions (2 dinner + 1 lunch leftover)  |  ~25 min active  |  1 pot, 1 board, 1 knife

QUANTITIES
  Orzo .................. 1.5 cups dry
  Crushed tomatoes ...... 1 can (28 oz)
  Broth (chicken or veg)  4 cups
  Chickpeas ............. 1 can (15 oz), drained + rinsed
  Kale .................. 1 small bunch (~5 oz), stems off, leaves chopped
  Garlic ................ 4 cloves, minced
  Parmesan .............. 1/2 cup finely grated, plus more at the table
  Olive oil ............. 2 tbsp
  Salt, pepper, pinch of red pepper flakes if you have them

PREP 0:00-5:00 (parallel with pot heating)
  Put pot over medium heat with the olive oil. While it heats:
  mince garlic, chop kale, drain chickpeas, grate parm, measure orzo and broth.

COOK
  5:00   garlic in, stir 60 sec — fragrant, not brown
  6:00   add orzo, stir to coat, toast 90 sec
  7:30   crushed tomatoes + broth + 1 tsp salt + pepper + pepper flakes,
         stir, bring to a steady simmer
  8:30   medium-low, uncovered, stir every couple of min — orzo tender
         and liquid mostly absorbed but still loose/saucy (~8-9 min)
  17:00  stir in chickpeas and kale, 2-3 min until kale wilts
  20:00  off heat, stir in Parmesan, lid on, rest 2 min
  22:00  taste for salt, serve

SERVING AROUND SAM'S RETURN
  Holds fine off-heat, covered, 20-25 min. When Sam walks in, plate his
  portion, splash 1 tbsp water or broth over it, microwave 60-90 sec at
  70% — loosens the sauce back up.

LUNCH LEFTOVER
  Cool 10 min in a container, lid on, fridge. Reheat with 1-2 tbsp
  water or broth, covered, 60-90 sec at 70%. Orzo and kale both hold
  well; chickpeas don't go chalky.

CLEANUP (5-7 min)
  Pot soaks while you eat. One rinse of the board and knife, the pot
  gets hot soapy water. Nothing else.

The move: one thin burnt-sienna glaze dropped into the yellow-ochre band immediately around and behind the cup, easing into the existing shadow. Same palette, no new pigment, single variable. This is value separation, not more saturation — it deepens the local surround so the cup reads as the lightest element by contrast, and it stays inside the warm family so the cool ultramarine window still anchors the back.

Brush-and-water sequence:

1. Confirm the sheet is fully dry to the touch (no cool spot under a breath).
2. Mix burnt sienna at roughly half the strength of your shadow puddle — fully dissolved, the color of weak tea. Test on a scrap of the same cold-press if you have one; you want a wash that dries about one value step darker than the dry ochre band, not two.
3. Load a soft mop or #8 round; tap off so the brush is wet but not drippy — no shine on the belly of the brush.
4. Paper flat. One continuous pass: lay the glaze along the tabletop band right behind and beside the cup's base, letting it soften into the existing burnt-sienna shadow so the join disappears. Stop at the cup's contour; don't cross it. Don't go all the way across the band.
5. Walk away. Don't "even it out" with a second stroke — that's the move that overworks it.

Stop condition:

- One pass total. Judge only after it dries, at normal viewing distance (arm's length, room light, not under the lamp).
- Done if: the cup reads as the lightest local value with a clear step between it and the tabletop behind it, and the new tone melts into the existing shadow with no visible seam.
- STOP if: the glaze leaves a hard edge, muddies where it crosses the ochre, or the cup still reads equal-value after one pass. Do not glaze again to "deepen." At that point the choice is accept the result, lift gently with a barely-damp brush while still wet if you catch it soon, or crop the band — not rework.

This follows the same logic that's been working for you: change one variable, let it dry fully, read at distance. If this pass lands, you stop and live with it; one successful trial is not a permanent method, just a confirmed move for this painting.

Helio Start Capped Test Shapes — Decision Math
Prepared 2026-03-27 14:10 CT for Priya's review.
Organic-only posture through 3/31 stays. No approval, budget, pipeline, or forecast claim implied.

1. WHAT THE CAPS TELL US, AND WHAT THEY DON'T

What the caps ARE:
  - Hard exposure ceilings. The recommended shape caps downside at the earlier
    of $15,000 spent or 50 admitted workspaces. The fallback caps downside at
    the earlier of $8,000 or 25 admitted workspaces.
  - A stop rule. Whichever limit is reached first ends the test. The other
    limit becomes irrelevant at that point.
  - A pair of independent ceilings. Spend and admission count are not
    interchangeable; either can bind first.

What the caps are NOT:
  - Expected cost-per-admission. The $300 and $320 ratios are arithmetic
    results of dividing the two ceilings, not estimates of what a paid-source
    admission will cost.
  - A cost-per-admission ceiling. Under the recommended shape, realized
    cost-per-admission could land anywhere from roughly $0 (admissions
    effectively free; admission cap binds) up to $15,000 (only one admission
    before spend cap binds). Under the fallback, the range runs from roughly
    $0 to $8,000.
  - A forecastable acquisition cost. We have no paid-source conversion
    evidence, so we cannot anchor a point estimate or a credible interval.
  - A refund-adjusted or support-adjusted unit economics number. The caps are
    gross spend and gross admission count; refunds and support effort live in
    separate deferred windows.

What we CAN infer from the caps alone:
  - Maximum dollar loss on the recommended shape is $15,000; on the fallback,
    $8,000. Both are bounded regardless of conversion outcome.
  - Maximum admitted-workspace exposure is 50 or 25, which bounds downstream
    support, refund, and lifecycle surface area even if every admitted
    workspace later requires remediation.
  - The shape of the test is "stop at the first binding limit." This is a
    containment rule, not a learning rule — what we learn is whatever we have
    observed by the moment the binding limit fires.

What we CANNOT infer from the caps alone:
  - Whether the spend or the admission limit will bind first.
  - The realized cost-per-admission.
  - Whether paid-source traffic changes the admission-eligibility mix, the
    day-7 first-integration rate, the support profile, or the refund profile
    relative to organic.
  - Whether the result is repeatable, scalable, or forecastable.

2. RECOMMENDED (50 / $15K) VS FALLBACK (25 / $8K) — WHAT EACH SHAPE TEACHES AT ITS EXPOSURE

Recommended, six-week, 50-workspace / $15,000 cap:
  - At most $15,000 of paid spend can be committed.
  - At most 50 admitted workspaces can be created from paid traffic.
  - Day-7 first integration can be read on up to 50 paid-admitted workspaces.
    That is the largest sample the shape allows before the cap fires.
  - If realized cost-per-admission is below $300, the admission cap binds and
    we learn from 50 workspaces at less than $15K.
  - If realized cost-per-admission is above $300, the spend cap binds and we
    learn from fewer than 50 workspaces. The smaller the realized
    cost-per-admission, the more we learn; the larger it is, the less we learn
    on the same dollar ceiling.

Fallback, 25-workspace / $8,000 cap:
  - At most $8,000 of paid spend can be committed.
  - At most 25 admitted workspaces from paid traffic.
  - Day-7 first integration readable on up to 25 paid-admitted workspaces.
    Roughly half the operating-indicator sample of the recommended shape.
  - Lower exposure in dollar terms (about 53% of the recommended cap) and in
    admitted-workspace terms (50% of the recommended cap).
  - If realized cost-per-admission is below $320, the admission cap binds and
    we learn from 25 workspaces at less than $8K.
  - If realized cost-per-admission is above $320, the spend cap binds with
    fewer than 25 workspaces, and the per-workspace signal gets thinner.

Trade-off framing:
  - The recommended shape buys more operating-indicator sample and a wider
    spend ceiling at higher exposure on both axes.
  - The fallback buys a tighter exposure posture and a smaller commitment,
    at the cost of about half the day-7 first-integration sample.
  - Neither shape, on its own, produces refund-adjusted cash, paid-active
    status, or account-level support-effort windows at maturity. Those
    outcomes remain deferred past the cap.
  - Day-7 first integration is the only outcome either shape can fully observe
    within its own window; it remains a leading operating indicator, not a
    mature claim.

3. REMAINING UNKNOWNS

Unknowns about the underlying economics we are testing:
  - Paid-source conversion rate to admission. We have no prior. Without it,
    we cannot say which cap will bind first.
  - Paid-source day-7 first-integration rate. We have an organic baseline but
    no paid baseline, and paid intent may differ.
  - Paid-source admission-eligibility mix. Paid traffic may over-index on
    conditions the eligibility flow already excludes (admin access, supported
    billing, first-week-connectable integration), shifting the route-out
    ratio.
  - Paid-source support profile. Per-account support minutes under paid
    intent, especially relative to the existing organic guardrails.
  - Paid-source refund profile. Whether paid-admitted accounts differ in
    refund rate, and over what window.
  - Pacing. Whether spend accumulates faster or slower than admissions under
    the chosen channel mix.

Unknowns about the cap mechanics themselves:
  - Mid-experiment authority. Who decides whether to stop, continue, or
    pause at any partial reading before the binding limit fires.
  - Stop-loss beyond the cap. Whether there is a refund-rate or
    support-p90 trigger that should fire before either cap binds.
  - Re-evaluation cadence. How often the running spend-and-admission tally
    is reconciled against the cap, and by whom.
  - What is reported to whom at what cadence while the cap is still open.
  - Whether partial-read authority belongs to Riley, to Priya, to the budget
    owner, or to a named owner.
  - Channel mix. Which paid surfaces are in scope, and whether the channel
    itself can change the cost-per-admission distribution within the same
    dollar ceiling.
  - Attribution rules. How a paid-admitted workspace is defined and counted,
    and how the count is reconciled against any platform-reported spend.

Unknowns that survive even after the cap fires:
  - Mature paid-active status, refund-adjusted collected cash, and
    account-level support effort. None of these have complete windows inside
    either cap. Any mature commercial or scale decision remains deferred
    until those windows close, regardless of what the cap-bound observation
    shows.

4. DECISION QUESTIONS FOR PRIYA AND THE BUDGET OWNER

For Priya (decision posture):
  - Is the recommended ($15K / 50) shape the right exposure for a first paid

Ginger-soy chicken — scaled to 1.25 lb

Scaled marinade (whisk together first, before any chicken goes in):

  - Soy sauce:           3 tbsp + 1 tsp
                          (margin note honored — half soy / half water is fine if you want it less salty;
                           do not reduce the sweetener)
  - Honey (in place of brown sugar):   1 tbsp + 3/4 tsp
  - Rice vinegar:         about 2 tsp  (precise: 1 tsp + 7/8 tsp)
  - Grated ginger:        about 2 tsp  (precise: 1 tsp + 7/8 tsp)
  - Garlic, crushed:      2 cloves
  - Sesame oil:           3/4 tsp
  - Black pepper:         a few grinds

RESERVE BEFORE THE CHICKEN GOES IN — this is the part you asked me to flag clearly:

  Spoon 1 tbsp + 3/4 tsp of the mixed sauce into a SEPARATE small bowl right now,
  before any chicken touches the marinade. That bowl is your clean finishing glaze —
  it stays untouched by raw poultry. Cover and refrigerate it until the last few
  minutes of cooking. The remaining sauce in the main bowl is what the raw chicken
  will marinate in; that one gets discarded after cooking, never reused as a sauce.

Math note: scale factor is 5/8 (1.25 / 2.0). Honey is the only substitution; I kept the
sweetener at the full scaled amount because your margin note says not to reduce it.
Honey is roughly 1:1 with brown sugar by volume, so this works cleanly.

Prep sequence

Sunday night
  - Move the 1.25 lb frozen thighs from freezer to fridge to thaw overnight.
    (Backup if Monday timing is tight: sealed bag in cold water, change water every
    30 min, about 1–2 hr.)

Monday
  - About 2.5 hr before you want to eat: pull thighs from fridge, pat dry.
  - Whisk the marinade ingredients in a bowl or a zip bag big enough for the chicken.
  - >>> REMINDER: scoop 1 tbsp + 3/4 tsp of the mixed sauce into a separate small
      bowl NOW and put it in the fridge. This is the only sauce that will brush on
      at the end, and it must not come into contact with the raw chicken. <<<
  - Add the thighs to the remaining marinade. Toss to coat.
  - Marinate 2 hours, turning once or twice. Per your standing note, do NOT
    marinate overnight — the vinegar softens the texture too much.
  - About 25 min before serving: preheat oven to 400°F (or a skillet over medium
    heat if you'd rather pan-sear).
  - Cook thighs until done — roughly 18–22 min in the oven, or 6–8 min per side in
    a skillet — turning once. Internal temp 165°F in the thickest part.
  - During the LAST 2–3 minutes of cooking: brush the reserved clean sauce over
    the chicken to glaze.
  - Discard the used marinade. Do not serve it, do not reuse it.
  - Rest a couple of minutes, plate, serve.

THREE-VALUE PLAN
- Value 1 (lightest): warm light strip across the floor
- Value 2 (mid): cool interior shadow on wall/floor behind Kibo
- Value 3 (darkest): Kibo's body mass

Logic: Kibo sits one value darker than the shadow behind him, so value carries him even when hues are close. Where his silhouette crosses the warm light strip, dark-vs-light contrast does the separation work for you.

MIXES (all weak-tea unless noted)
- Warm light strip: yellow ochre + touch burnt sienna. Thin, a full value step lighter than the cool wash. No ultramarine.
- Cool interior shadow: ultramarine + a tiny touch of burnt sienna (the blue-brown mix). Mid value.
- Kibo's coat: ultramarine + burnt sienna, balanced or slightly burnt-sienna leaning. Darkest value. If the deepest mass wants to read warmer without going brown, add the warmth as a separate weak burnt-sienna glaze on dry paper, not by adding pigment to the dark mix.
- Connecting shadow under Kibo (only if needed): burnt sienna, weak, soft edge toward his belly, harder edge into the warm light.

PAINTING ORDER + STOP
1. Light pencil contour of Kibo's silhouette. No interior detail.
2. Warm light strip: yellow ochre + touch burnt sienna. Paint up to his contour, not across it. Dry fully.
3. Cool interior shadow: ultramarine + tiny burnt sienna, mid value. Paint up to his contour, leaving a 1–2 mm paper halo. Dry fully.
4. Kibo's body: ultramarine + burnt sienna, darkest value. Single wet-on-dry pass inside the contour. No scrubbing, no second coat, no glazing back into the mass. Dry fully.
5. Optional: thin burnt-sienna shadow under him, one pass, soft-to-hard edge as above.
6. STOP. Evaluate at normal viewing distance. If the coat reads as separated from the wall shadow and the warm strip frames him, you're done. No eyes, whiskers, fur lines, or texture.

If the coat flattens into the wall after drying: one weak burnt-sienna glaze over the dry coat (temperature fix, not value fix), then stop. Do not re-wet or add pigment to the dark mass — that's what flattens it.

Morning of the filling replacement (May 6, 8:30am Central):

MORNING CHECKLIST
- Eat a light normal breakfast (office confirmed no fasting needed since it's local anesthetic, not sedation)
- Take your usual medications with a small sip of water unless your dentist has told you otherwise
- Drink water, but go easy right before leaving so you're comfortable in the chair
- Brush and floss the area gently so the dentist has a clean field
- Bring photo ID, insurance card, and a form of payment if there's a copay
- Plan to arrive around 8:20am (ten minutes early as requested)
- No driver needed — local anesthetic doesn't impair driving; you can drive yourself home and return to normal activities

PRACTICAL PRECAUTIONS WHILE NUMB (typically 2–4 hours)
- Do NOT eat until the numbness fully wears off — the main risk is biting your cheek, tongue, or lip without realizing it
- Avoid hot drinks while numb; you can't judge temperature accurately and can burn the soft tissue
- Sip cool water if your mouth feels dry
- Be careful talking and smiling — it's easy to catch a numb lip on a cup or teeth
- Chew on the OPPOSITE side once eating resumes
- If your bite feels "off" or the new filling feels high when you close your teeth, call the office — a quick adjustment prevents jaw soreness and protects the restoration

EASY FOODS FOR THE FIRST FEW HOURS
- Yogurt or kefir
- Applesauce
- Smoothies (spooned, not through a straw — straws are fine here since this isn't an extraction, just skip if you find the suction uncomfortable)
- Mashed potatoes, lukewarm
- Scrambled or soft-boiled eggs
- Lukewarm (not hot) soup — broth, pureed vegetable, chicken and rice
- Oatmeal or cream of wheat, cooled to warm
- Cottage cheese, ricotta
- Pasta or rice cooked very soft
- Soft fruit: banana, ripe pear, canned peaches
- Skip: very hot foods, hard/crunchy things (chips, nuts, raw carrots), sticky candy, and chewing gum until the filling is settled

ORDINARY POST-FILLING SENSITIVITY (normal, usually settles in 1–2 weeks)
- Brief twinge to cold or air that fades within a second or two
- Mild tenderness or soreness at the injection site or in the jaw from keeping it open
- Slight pressure or awareness when biting firmly on the new filling for the first day or two
- Mild gum tenderness around the tooth

CALL THE DENTIST ABOUT
- Severe, throbbing, or steadily worsening pain that doesn't respond to OTC pain relief
- Pain that wakes you at night or pain that starts spontaneously (not just triggered by cold/bite)
- Swelling of the gums, face, or jaw, or a feeling of pressure/abscess
- Fever or feeling generally unwell
- The filling feeling noticeably high or your bite feeling uneven (simple fix, but worth calling promptly)
- Numbness that hasn't resolved after 4–5 hours, or persistent tingling
- The tooth feeling loose, or the filling feeling rough, cracked, or like it's come loose
- An allergic-type reaction: rash, itching, hives, or difficulty breathing (this one is urgent — call 911 or go to ER if breathing is affected)

Pan-seared gnocchi with blistered tomatoes, spinach, and parmesan — one skillet, ~25 min, no oven.

Approximate amounts (2 servings):
- Gnocchi: about 14–16 oz of the 17.6 oz package (save the rest, or use it all for heartier appetites)
- Olive oil: ~3 tbsp, plus a little more if needed
- Cherry tomatoes: the whole pint, halved
- Garlic: 3–4 cloves, thinly sliced or minced
- Baby spinach: all 5 oz
- Parmesan: ~1/2 cup finely grated, plus extra for serving
- Salt, black pepper, optional pinch of red pepper flakes

Sequence (one large skillet):

0:00  Set a large skillet over medium-high. Add 3 tbsp olive oil and let it heat while you halve the tomatoes.
0:05  Add gnocchi to the hot oil in a single layer. Don't stir for 3–4 min — let them get a golden crust.
0:09  Flip the gnocchi. Reduce heat to medium.
0:12  While the second side crisps, slice the garlic and grate the parmesan.
0:15  Push gnocchi to one side. Add garlic and tomatoes to the cleared space with a pinch of salt, pepper, and red pepper flakes if using. Let tomatoes blistered and burst, ~3 min, stirring just that side.
0:20  Add the spinach on top of the tomatoes. Stir gently until wilted, ~1–2 min.
0:22  Off heat. Fold everything together, scatter parmesan over the top, and toss once more so it melts into a light sauce.
0:25  Taste for salt, plate, finish with a drizzle of olive oil and more parm.

Minimal-cleanup notes:
- One skillet, one cutting board, one knife, a grater, and a spatula is all you need.
- Halve tomatoes directly into the skillet once it's hot if you want to skip the cutting board.
- If the gnocchi looks dry while crisping, add a small splash of oil rather than moving them.

If Sam is eating later, hold his portion off the heat a couple minutes before adding the parmesan and spinach, leave both components loose, and reheat with a splash of water in a covered pan over low heat — keeps the gnocchi from going gummy.

THREE-VALUE PLAN (eyeball these first; faint pencil marks only)

Light  -  paper white, reserved for the window reflection on the bottle
Mid    -  cool interior shadow; ultramarine + a tiny burnt-sienna touch (~8:1), one value step lighter than the bottle
Dark   -  bottle body; ultramarine + burnt sienna ~1:1, deep chromatic dark, NOT black

Reserve yellow ochre unmixed. Use it only as an optional thin warm glaze at the bottle's base or as a separator, never inside the three-value structure.

MIXING ORDER (separate wells, no cross-contamination)

1. Cool surround: ultramarine + tiny burnt sienna. Test swatch first. Should read as a grayed cool, not chalky.
2. Bottle dark: ultramarine + burnt sienna ~1:1. Test swatch. If it goes to mud on the paper, shift toward more ultramarine until it stays chromatic.
3. Pure ultramarine reserved only if you need to deepen a pass.
4. Yellow ochre stays clean in its own well until step 5 (and only if used).

45-MINUTE SEQUENCE

0:00-0:05  Setup. Two clean water jars, three wells, scrap paper. Swatch both mixes. Faintly mark the highlight outline on the support so you can paint right up to it without touching it.

0:05-0:15  Cool surround wash. Pre-wet the shadow area with clean water (NOT over the highlight, NOT inside the bottle silhouette). Drop the cool mix in. End each stroke a hair short of the highlight so the highlight edge stays dry and crisp. Step away and let it dry fully - do not "fix" anything while it's wet.

0:15-0:25  Surround dries. Use this time to mix and re-test the bottle dark on scrap. Brushes rinsed, jar water changed.

0:25-0:40  Bottle body. One confident shape, silhouette as a single pass. Hard edges against the now-dry surround - the value jump does the edge work for you; do not chase the edge with a second stroke. Leave the highlight as paper. If a cast shadow under the bottle needs to soften into the surround, soften it now with a barely-damp clean brush, ONE touch, while the bottle's lower edge is still damp. If you missed the timing window, leave it hard.

0:40-0:45  Stop, stand back at arm's length. Three values resolving? Highlight still paper-white? Edges where you wanted them? If yes and only if yes, you may add one optional thin yellow-ochre glaze on a small warm reflection at the bottle's base - skip otherwise.

EDGE STRATEGY

Hard edges:  bottle silhouette against the cool surround. Earned by value contrast, not by redrawing the line. Anywhere you want a crisp read between bottle and surround, make sure that edge is dry before the adjacent wash arrives.
Soft edges:  only two places - the bottle's reflected light fading into the surround, and the cast shadow dissipating at its outer edge. Both via one barely-damp clean-brush touch on a still-damp neighbor wash. If the timing window is gone, leave the edge hard and walk away.

HIGHLIGHT PRESERVATION

The muddiness you keep seeing is almost certainly from re-touching the highlight or glazing over it. Treat it as untouchable paper:

- Mask with a small dot of masking fluid if you want insurance; let it fully dry before any wash goes near it.
- Otherwise, keep the highlight bone dry and paint up to it. Stop the stroke a hair short of the highlight outline.
- Never glaze the highlight area. Never lift from it. Never "clean it up" after the surround dries - the more you touch it, the muddier it gets.

STOP CONDITION - stop if ANY of these is true

- 45 minutes elapsed
- highlight shows any pigment creep, halo, or muddiness
- three values are not reading distinctly at arm's length
- paper shows bloom, cauliflowers, scrubbing, or lifted fiber
- you find yourself reaching for a second pass on bottle or surround

What this is:

The new opening resists the "overcome hardship" frame while still producing paragraph-length, essay-usable writing in five minutes from a high-school senior. The new feedback rubric gives partners a concrete thing to point at and trains the room to give specific notes rather than verdicts.

That frame fits inside the existing 10 minutes without a reallocation.

35-MINUTE WORKSHOP BLOCK — Scene + Opening (revised)

What this is: a single 35-minute segment where students draft one concrete scene from a self-chosen experience, exchange tight peer feedback, and rewrite an opening paragraph.

What this is not: a personal-narrative unit, a therapy space, or a graded task. Sharing aloud at any point is optional. If a student opts out by switching path, framing at distance, or keeping the source private, do not follow up. The writing is the writing.

FRAME — 2 min
  - Tell students: today you draft one scene, exchange feedback, and rewrite an opening.
  - Two paths to choose from: an ordinary experience or a difficult one. Pick whichever you have material for.
  - Opt-out from personal disclosure. If "difficult" feels too close, you can:
      (a) choose ordinary instead,
      (b) write it as someone else's story you witnessed or know about,
      (c) write in third person, or from an animal or object's view,
      (d) keep the source private and only share the writing.
  - Feedback will always be about the writing, never about the life behind it.

DRAFT — 10 min
  - Pick one moment. Not a whole day, not the moral — one scene.
  - Five anchors on the board or a half-sheet handout:
      1. A specific place with one sensory detail (sound, light, smell, texture, temperature).
      2. A time anchor inside the day.
      3. Two people, or one person and one object, doing something.
      4. One line of dialogue or one piece of overheard speech.
      5. One small physical action that shows feeling (hands, posture, breath, gaze).
  - If you finish early, push for one more sensory detail. Do not start a second scene.

PAIRED FEEDBACK — 8 min, 4 min each direction
  - Reader writes one short sentence under each of three criteria:
      1. PLACE — Can I see the spot? What's still missing?
      2. MOMENT — Did the scene stay inside the moment, or did it summarize? Point to the line where it drifts.
      3. TELLING DETAIL — What's the smallest physical thing that carries feeling? Could it be one shade more specific?
  - No general praise. No advice about the life. No second read.

OPENING REWRITE — 10 min
  - Pull the strongest line or image from your draft.
  - Rewrite the opening paragraph so that line lands in the first or second sentence.
  - Hard constraint: the new opening must be under 80 words.
  - Working from your own draft, not starting over.

WRAP — 5 min
  - Optional: read the new opening aloud. You can pass.
  - Optional: copy the one feedback note you found most useful onto the top of your draft for next time.
  - Quiet exit: if you'd rather not speak at all in the last five minutes, that is also the opt-out path.

TIME CHECK: 2 + 10 + 8 + 10 + 5 = 35 minutes.

NOTE ON FIDELITY: This redesign keeps the original 35-minute length, keeps one scene as the unit of work, keeps peer feedback, and keeps an opening rewrite. It changes three things: the choice between an ordinary or difficult experience, a narrower three-criterion feedback frame (place / moment / telling detail), and an explicit four-route opt-out from personal disclosure stated up front rather than assumed.

Materials (all clean, archival, reusable):
  - 2 sheets of glassine (slightly larger than the painting), or smooth uncoated scrap paper as substitute
  - Flat, clean work surface
  - Even distributed weight — 3 or 4 clean flat books totaling ~5-10 lb, or foam board + a couple of bricks
  - A sealable plastic container or large clean trash bag that can be loosely closed
  - A small glass or ceramic dish (water source)

Before starting: photograph the buckle in normal room light so you have a "before" reference.

Sequence (one step at a time; do not skip ahead):

Step 1 — Weight only (start here; usually enough for a mild edge buckle)
  1. Place one glassine on the work surface.
  2. Lay the painting painted-side UP on it, fully supported (no overhang).
  3. Lay the second glassine over the painted surface.
  4. Center the weights evenly — no single point load on the buckle.
  5. Leave 24 hours at normal room humidity (45-55%). Check; if flat, leave another 24-48 hr to set, then store. If still buckled, remove weight and go to Step 2.

Step 2 — Ambient humidity relaxation in a sealed space (only if Step 1 didn't resolve it)
  1. Set the painting on its glassine base, painted side UP, into the container. No weight yet.
  2. Place the dish of room-temperature water in the container, well away from the painting — not touching it.
  3. Close or loosely seal the container. Do NOT add heat, do NOT seal airtight, do NOT exceed 45 minutes total.
  4. After 20-30 minutes, remove the painting promptly.
  5. Reassemble as in Step 1 (bottom glassine, painting face up, top glassine, even weight) and leave 24-48 hours, then check.

Step 3 — Back-only very light moisture (last-resort home step, only if 1 and 2 failed)
  1. Lay the painting painted-side DOWN on clean glassine (paint against glassine — confirm glassine is unprinted and clean).
  2. With a sponge rung out so no water drips, touch only the back of the buckled area for 2-3 seconds. Do not soak. Do not touch the painted face.
  3. Immediately flip back to painted-side UP on the glassine, top glassine on, weight as before.
  4. Leave 48 hours weighted, then check.

Stop conditions — take it to a professional paper conservator if any of these occur:
  - Buckle does not improve after two full Step-2 cycles (or one Step-3 cycle if you tried it).
  - Any new crease, wrinkle, tear, fiber lift, or surface disturbance appears during handling.
  - Pigment migrates, feathers, lifts, or visibly changes.
  - The buckle sits along a critical compositional edge where additional handling risk outweighs the benefit.
  - You simply don't want to handle it further — that is a valid reason. A 140-lb cold-press sheet with the paint surface intact is in good shape for a conservator to flatten cleanly.

Portfolio storage after flattening:
  - Interleave with clean buffered glassine or archival interleaving paper.
  - Store flat in the portfolio, not under compression beyond the portfolio's own closure.
  - Keep in stable, moderate humidity away from exterior walls and any direct light.

What this is not:
  - Not a substitute for conservation. If the painting is high-value or you want certainty, default to a conservator from the start.
  - Not a fix for lifted fibers, tears, flaking, or adhesive residue — those are different problems.
  - Not a guarantee of long-term flatness; archival storage conditions still matter.

Crispy smoked-paprika cabbage and chickpeas, warm-corn-tortilla tacos, lime-yogurt sauce. About 25 minutes. Two tacos tonight for you, the rest of the filling plus two tortillas and extra sauce set aside for Sam's lunch — the filling reheats well and actually tastes better on day two.

Plan (serves 1 dinner + 1 lunch portion)

Sauce first (5 min)
- In a small bowl stir together: about 1/3 cup Greek yogurt, juice of half the lime, half the sliced scallions (whites and greens), pinch of salt, a few grinds of pepper. Loosen with a teaspoon of water if thick. Refrigerate.

Filling (12–15 min)
- Shred the half cabbage into thin ribbons (about 3 packed cups). Mince 2 garlic cloves. Drain the chickpeas.
- Heat 1.5 tablespoons oil in a large skillet over medium-high until shimmering.
- Add the cabbage and a pinch of salt. Spread and let it sit 1–2 minutes to char, then stir. Repeat 2–3 times, total about 6–8 minutes, until wilted with browned edges.
- Push the cabbage to one side. Add another teaspoon of oil, the garlic, and the drained chickpeas to the empty side. Let the chickpeas warm and lightly blister 2–3 minutes, then stir everything together.
- Add about 1 teaspoon smoked paprika, toss to coat, cook 30 seconds. Off heat, squeeze in the remaining half-lime. Taste for salt and pepper.

Tortillas and plating
- Warm the tortillas one at a time directly over a gas flame or in a dry skillet, about 10–15 seconds per side. Keep warm in a clean towel.
- Build two tacos: tortilla, generous spoonful of filling, a few spoonfuls of sauce, a scatter of the remaining scallion greens. Eat immediately.

Sam's lunch portion
- Spoon the remaining filling into a container, tuck the two unused tortillas alongside (or wrap them in foil), pour the extra sauce into a small jar. Refrigerate.
- To reheat: warm the filling in a covered skillet with a splash of water over medium-low 4–5 minutes, or microwave covered 60–90 seconds. Warm the tortillas 20–30 seconds in a damp paper towel in the microwave, or briefly in a dry skillet. Assemble and sauce as above.

Notes
- Half the small cabbage and the full can of chickpeas give roughly 3 cups of filling — enough for two generously filled tacos plus a solid lunch portion.
- If you want extra char, finish the cabbage under the broiler for 60–90 seconds before adding the chickpeas.
- Stop conditions: if the garlic burns before the chickpeas warm, lower the heat and start that step over — burnt garlic ruins the batch.

Chickpea-and-cabbage skillet tacos (2 servings, ~20 min, one skillet)

Ingredients (only these two):
  - 1 can (15 oz) chickpeas, drained and rinsed
  - 1 small head of cabbage (gives both the shells and the filling)

Approximate amounts:
  - 4-6 large outer cabbage leaves for the wraps
  - About 2 cups of shredded inner cabbage for the filling
  - Reserve about 1/3 cup of chickpeas whole; mash the rest for texture

Sequence:
  0:00  Pull off 4-6 large outer leaves; tear the rest into rough shreds
        (~2 cups). Drain and rinse the chickpeas.
  0:05  Warm a large skillet over medium heat. Add the shredded cabbage
        dry with a tablespoon of water; cover and wilt 3-4 min.
  0:09  Add the chickpeas. Press about two-thirds with a fork or potato
        masher right in the pan. Cook 4-5 min, stirring now and then,
        until the chickpeas are hot and pick up a few brown spots.
  0:14  Stack the whole leaves in the skillet (or in the same covered
        pan with a splash of water), 30-60 seconds until pliable.
        Move to a plate.
  0:16  Pile the chickpea-cabbage filling into each leaf; fold like
        tacos. Eat over the plate or standing.

Minimal cleanup:
  - One skillet (does both the filling and the leaf-softening)
  - One colander or small strainer
  - One fork for mashing
  - One cutting board and one knife for the shredding
  - Skip extra bowls — the can becomes the chickpea measuring cup

75-MINUTE LIMITED-PALETTE SEQUENCE — KIBO ON RUG, COOL WINDOW × WARM FLOOR REFLECTION

Palette: ultramarine, burnt sienna, yellow ochre (your standing three). Paper: whatever you set out for the Sunday block; stop the moment it blooms or lifts.

Three-value plan
  Light   paper white, reserved. Brightest window patch on rug; thin sliver inside the warm reflected edge along Kibo's back/belly.
  Mid     Kibo's body mass. Two sub-steps — mid-warm (lit/reflected side), mid-cool (window-shadow side). The shape lives in the gap between these two mids, not in a separate "dark shape."
  Dark    inside of the curl, deep folds, the cast shadow directly under him, eye/nose/ear interior. Used sparingly.

Mixing order
  1. Cool window gray     ultramarine + a touch of burnt sienna. Test for temperature first, darkness second. This sets the rug's cool half.
  2. Warm reflected gray  burnt sienna + a tiny ultramarine + a touch of yellow ochre. Desaturated on purpose — warmth comes from value contrast with the cool wash, not from extra orange. Keep it a full value step lighter than the cool wash and noticeably thinner on the brush.
  3. Body mid             ultramarine + burnt sienna, roughly equal. Pull two strengths on the same palette well: one for the lit side (warm mid), one for the shadow side (cool mid, lean ultramarine).
  4. Deepest dark         the same U+BS mix concentrated, with a hint of yellow ochre if it goes chalky-purple. Reserve for the curl interior and face dots only.

Painting order (with rough time budget)
  0-10   Set out three value swatches side by side on scrap. Confirm the warm swatch sits a clean step lighter than the cool one at arm's length. If it doesn't, adjust before you touch the painting.
  10-25  Cool window wash on the rug and across the window-shadow side of Kibo. Leave crisp paper white in the brightest rug patch. Let the wash lap onto Kibo's cool side — that's how the form reads as one cat, not a cutout.
  25-38  Warm reflected edge. Thin, full step lighter than the cool wash, applied along Kibo's back and belly where the floor bounce would land. If the brush drags or beads, stop and reload thinner — do not push more pigment into it. Reserve a thin paper-white sliver inside this band.
  38-55  Mid-value body pass over Kibo. One connected shape. Preserve a slightly cooler, slightly darker note on the shadow side so the lit/reflected side reads as the warmer mid without adding saturation. Let dry fully.
  55-65  Deepest darks — inside of the curl, folds, cast shadow under the body. Keep the silhouette broken in two or three places (lost edges) so the dark coat doesn't read as one stamped value.
  65-72  Face: minimum. Wait until everything beneath is dry. One small concentrated touch per eye. One for the nose. One for the ear interior that faces you. No whiskers. No fur lines. If a face feature needs a second touch, stop and reassess instead of layering.
  72-75  Arm's-length check, then stop.

Edge strategy
  Hard   Kibo's back silhouette where it crosses the cool rug shadow. One clean pass; do not soften.
  Soft   Warm reflected edge — lay the thin warm mix, then immediately pull a clean damp brush perpendicular to the edge for a centimeter or two. No scrubbing. If it beads, you've overloaded; lift off, dry, and try thinner on the next pass.
  Lost   Along the underside where the body curls into its own cast shadow. Let the dark mix bleed a short distance into the rug shadow.
  Found   The cheek/jowl and the leading paw edge — let these stay defined so the face has somewhere to land.

Face-detail priorities
  1. Eye placement and value — done together with one touch. If the eye position is wrong, fix the position before touching it again.
  2. Nose — single touch, slightly cooler than the surrounding fur.
  3. Ear interior that faces the viewer — single small touch.
  Nothing else belongs in the face for this study. No whisker lines, no mouth line unless a shadow already implies it.

Stop conditions (any one is final)
  - Reserved highlight takes on any color.
  - At arm's length the three values collapse to two, or Kibo's body reads as one flat dark shape.
  - The warm reflected edge needs a second pass to "look warm" — that means it was laid too thin or too cool; either is fixable only by re-wetting, which you won't do. Stop and note the parameter.
  - A face feature needs a second touch.
  - Paper blooms, lifts, or the edge buckles.
  - 75 minutes, whichever comes first.

What this sequence is not
  Not a finished painting, not a signature candidate, not a value study you commit to. It is one Sunday-block read of Kibo in mixed light with three values and one limited palette, and it stops the moment any of the above fires.

Conservative sequence for the front-right tire, treating this as "probably weather + maybe a slow leak" until the recheck data says otherwise.

WHAT THIS IS NOT
- Not a clearance to keep driving as normal before the recheck.
- Not a diagnosis. The 6 psi drop on one corner is plausibly weather (≈1 psi per 10°F; one corner dropping 6 while the other three held 34–35 is more than a uniform cold-soak would produce, so a small leak is not ruled out).

STEP 1 — PRE-INFLATION INSPECTION (before you add air)
Do this while the tire is still cold and low.
- Tread: run a fingernail or a small screwdriver tip across each tread groove and across the contact patch. Feeling a hard metal tip = embedded screw/nail. Check the center tread and both shoulders.
- Sidewall and rim area: look for a blister, bulge, crack, wet streak, or scuff. Run a finger around the inside of the rim lip if visible.
- Valve stem: look for wetness or crusty white/teal residue (slow leak signature). Push the valve core gently with the cap off — it should feel springy, not sticky.
- Smell/listen at the tire for any faint hiss. Soapy water in a spray bottle on the bead, valve, and any suspect spot will reveal a leak as growing bubbles.

If you find a screw/nail, a wet valve, or anything bulging:
- Do not pull the screw out.
- Inflate only enough to reach the tire shop (≈30–35 psi is fine for a slow drive).
- Go to a tire shop same day. See the shop-directly list below.

STEP 2 — INFLATE TO SPEC, COLD
- Target: 35 psi exactly, matching the door placard. Do not "over-inflate to compensate" — pressure rises ~3–5 psi once you drive, and you want the cold reading to land at 35, not above.
- Add air in short bursts and recheck. Tire inflators with gauges are often off by 1–2 psi; trust a separate calibrated gauge.
- Inflate the other three only if they read below 34 psi — otherwise leave them.
- Record: time, FR reading before inflation, FR reading after, ambient temp if your gauge has one.

STEP 3 — SAME-DAY RECHECK (after some driving, then back to cold)
- Drive normally for a few miles (your usual errands are fine).
- Let the tire sit cold: 2–3 hours parked, or overnight. "Cold" means not driven for that long.
- Recheck FR cold.
- Also recheck the other three for comparison.

STEP 4 — NEXT-MORNING COLD RECHECK (the decisive one)
- Before driving, first thing. Compare FR cold reading to 35.

INTERPRETING THE DATA
- FR holds at 33–35 psi both rechecks, other three unchanged, no visible damage → weather-driven, monitor weekly through any cold snaps.
- FR drops 2–3 psi between rechecks with no visible leak source → borderline; recheck again next morning. If the second drop is similar, schedule a tire shop before Oct 21.
- FR drops ≥3 psi in 24 hours sitting still, OR drops again after you re-inflate, OR the TPMS light returns → slow leak confirmed. Tire shop, not weather.

DRIVING LIMITS UNTIL CLEARED
- Speed: stay ≤55 mph. No highway.

What "$49 preferred-pharmacy copay after the deductible" means in plain language

"Copay" is the fixed dollar amount Mom pays at the pharmacy counter for a prescription. "After the deductible" means that $49 only starts applying once Mom's year-to-date out-of-pocket spending on covered drugs for 2027 reaches $615. Until that happens, Mom pays the full allowed (negotiated) price of the Ventolin inhaler, not $49.

"Preferred pharmacy" means River Park (or any other preferred in-network pharmacy) — at a standard in-network pharmacy or out of network the copay is different and the deductible can work differently, but for the question Mom asked, "preferred pharmacy" is the $49 setting.

Before the $615 deductible is met (year-to-date covered-drug spending under $615)
  Lisinopril 10 mg (tier 1): $0
  Atorvastatin 20 mg (tier 1): $0
  Ventolin HFA 90 mcg: full allowed price, NOT $49

After the $615 deductible is met (year-to-date covered-drug spending at or above $615)
  Lisinopril 10 mg (tier 1): $0
  Atorvastatin 20 mg (tier 1): $0
  Ventolin HFA 90 mcg: $49 per fill at a preferred pharmacy

A simple before/after example

Suppose Mom refills Ventolin once (say the allowed price at River Park is roughly $72 per inhaler) and that's her only non-generic fill of the year.

  Before deductible is met: Mom pays $72 at the counter for that Ventolin fill, not $49. If she never hits $615 in covered-drug spending that year, every Ventolin fill costs $72, and the $49 figure on the ANOC never actually applies.
  After deductible is met: Mom pays $49 for that Ventolin fill instead of $72. Each later fill that year is also $49 until the year resets.

If Mom reaches the deductible through something else during the year (a one-time antibiotic, a short course of another covered drug, etc.), the first Ventolin fills cost full allowed price and the later ones cost $49. If she never reaches it, every Ventolin fill that year costs full allowed price.

The one precise question to confirm how the deductible applies

"In the 2027 benefits chart, which tier(s) does the $615 annual deductible apply to — only tiers 3–5, or does it apply to all covered drugs including the tier 1 generics?"

That single answer tells you three things at once: whether Mom's $0 generic copays are $0 from day one or only after the deductible, whether those generic fills can ever help her reach $615, and whether Ventolin is realistically going to land at the $49 copay or stay at full allowed price for most fills in a typical year.

Where to find the answer: the ANOC benefits chart usually has a "Deductible" row that lists which tiers it applies to (often phrased as "Applies to tiers 3, 4, 5" or similar), and the formulary tier table usually has a "deductible applies / does not apply" column for each tier. Member Services on the back of the plan ID card can also answer it directly.

This is just a wording explanation — no enrollment or coverage recommendation, and nothing changes about Mom's current 2026 plan.

Still life: one pear, white bowl, folded blue dish towel, in the window light. Each of you on your own board, palette, brushes, paper, water container. Palette choices stay independent — pick whatever you want; no need to match.

The exercise is 90 minutes (1:30–3:00). The remaining hour is cleanup and unhurried wrap.

1:30–1:40 — Settle (10 min)
    Arrange the still life together. Agree on viewpoint.
    Each set up your station.
    Optional quick swatch to settle pigment and brush.

1:40–2:05 — Three-value study (25 min)
    Small paper, big brush. Three values only. No color matching, no edges, no detail.
      Light: paper white, used directly
      Mid:    one mid-tone wash covering the bulk of each shape
      Dark:   the deepest accent — bowl shadow under the rim, deepest
              towel fold, pear stem cavity, cast-shadow line

    One pass per value. No layering for depth. Stay loose.
    Goal is to lock WHERE the values fall, not to finish anything.
    Stop at 2:05 even if it's rough.

2:05–2:20 — Midpoint pause (15 min)
    Put brushes down. Place the two studies side by side.

    Compare decisions, not corrections. Each describes what they did and
    why; the other listens and notices.

    Prompts (use any):
      - Where did you put the darkest dark? Same place on both?
      - How did you handle the bowl/towel boundary?
      - What did the pear's stem area ask you to do?
      - Was there a value you almost added but didn't?

    Out of bounds: "you should have," "I would have," "next time try,"
    "the problem is." Description and noticing only.

    Refill water if needed. Stand up, stretch.

2:20–2:55 — Develop into a painting (35 min)
    Move to fresh paper (or keep pushing the study if you want). Your
    own palette, your own choices.

    Loose sequence that usually works:
      - Thin overall wash to lay the value structure
      - Local color and form, still mostly wet
      - A few dark accents, mostly dry brush, hard edges where light hits
      - Leave the highlight alone. If it gets muddy, lift or leave it;
        don't repaint.

    Stop on any one:
      - 2:55 arrives
      - A highlight won't lift cleanly
      - A bloom runs into a value you wanted clean
      - You find yourself fussing

2:55–3:00 — Wind down (5 min)
    One last mark only if it earns its place, otherwise stop.
    Stand back. Look at both paintings.
    One sentence each about what surprised you, if you want. Or just look.

3:00 — Exercise ends. Cleanup begins.
    You have a full hour. No rush.
      - Rinse brushes before pigment dries
      - Wipe palette with a damp soft rag (don't scrub a cracked tray)
      - Dump and rinse water containers
      - Return still life to the kitchen
      - Move wet paintings to dry flat
      - Whatever else you usually do

CONSERVATIVE 3-COPY BACKUP + VERIFICATION SEQUENCE
Date: 2026-10-29. Source of truth: laptop scan folder + scanner card (combined). Targets: 26 photographs × {front, back} = 52 image files.

PRINCIPLES (held throughout)
- Scanner card stays untouched until BOTH copies verify.
- Filenames and front/back pairings preserved exactly as scanned. No renames.
- No image-internal metadata edits. Only filesystem copies and one new text manifest file.
- Verification = sha256sum byte-equality. Implicitly covers pixel dims, bit depth, and embedded scan timestamps.
- 14 undigitized photographs are out of scope for this sequence; they stay in archival sleeves.

PHASE 0 — Reconcile source onto laptop (read-only on card)
0a. Mount scanner card.
0b. Copy any files still only on card into the laptop scan folder using byte-copy: rsync -avh /mnt/card/DCIM/ /laptop/scan_folder/   (or cp -p). Do not delete from card.
0c. Confirm laptop scan folder has 52 image files, paired by filename (e.g. P001_front.tif / P001_back.tif). Do not proceed if count is off.

PHASE 1 — Generate source manifest (laptop, non-destructive)
1a. cd /laptop/scan_folder/
1b. sha256sum * > MANIFEST_2026-10-29.txt   (use the actual extensions present; one line per image)
1c. Confirm the manifest has 52 image lines + the line for MANIFEST_2026-10-29.txt itself (53 lines). One file added; zero image files modified.

PHASE 2 — Copy to encrypted external SSD
2a. Mount the encrypted SSD's decrypted volume.
2b. Create destination folder, e.g. /mnt/ssd/family_photos_2026-10-29/
2c. rsync -avh /laptop/scan_folder/ /mnt/ssd/family_photos_2026-10-29/    (single trailing slashes — copy contents, not folder)
2d. Confirm the MANIFEST file is also in the SSD folder.

PHASE 3 — Verify SSD copy (must pass before continuing)
3a. cd /mnt/ssd/family_photos_2026-10-29/
3b. sha256sum -c MANIFEST_2026-10-29.txt
3c. Every line must report OK. Any FAILED line → STOP. Do not continue, do not clear card. Investigate (re-run rsync, check disconnects, check free space).

PHASE 4 — Copy to private cloud folder
4a. Initiate sync of the SSD folder (already verified) into the private cloud folder. Sync from the SSD, not the laptop, so cloud = verified byte-identity.
4b. Wait for sync to fully complete. Confirm the cloud folder includes MANIFEST_2026-10-29.txt.

PHASE 5 — Verify cloud copy (must pass before continuing)
5a. Pull the cloud folder contents back to a laptop temp area, e.g. ~/verify_cloud_2026-10-29/. (If your cloud tool has a server-side hash subcommand, you may use that instead — e.g. rclone hashsum sha256, or provider-side integrity check.)
5b. cd ~/verify_cloud_2026-10-29/
5c. sha256sum -c MANIFEST_2026-10-29.txt
5d. Every line must report OK. Any FAILED → STOP. Do not clear card.

PHASE 6 — Spot-check + clear card (only after Phase 3 AND Phase 5 both pass)
6a. Open 3 random front/back pairs on the laptop; confirm correct pairing by filename and that the image renders correctly.
6b. Optional: file P001_front.tif   (or exiftool -G1 -s P001_front.tif) to confirm pixel dimensions and bit depth match the known reference for that file.
6c. Confirm file counts: laptop 52, SSD 52, cloud 52 (plus one MANIFEST in each).
6d. Only now: format the scanner card, or securely delete its DCIM contents.

STATE AFTER ALL SIX PHASES
- Copy 1 (primary): laptop scan folder.
- Copy 2 (local offline): encrypted external SSD.
- Copy 3 (offsite): private cloud folder.
- MANIFEST_2026-10-29.txt co-located with images in all three locations — enables re-verification on any future date with a single sha256sum -c.
- Scanner card cleared and ready for the next batch (when the 14 remaining photographs are eventually scanned; that batch will get its own dated manifest, not appended to this one).

WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO
- Does not modify any image metadata (EXIF, IPTC, ICC, embedded timestamps).
- Does not rename any files or alter front/back pairings.
- Does not clear the scanner card until verification of both backup copies passes.
- Does not address, scan, or alter the 14 undigitized photographs in archival sleeves.
- Does not write to any document, inventory, or inventory comment — the manifest is a standalone text file in the scan folder and its copies.

Two-part answer: placement, then a short check sequence that catches lamp bias before it lands in a wash.

PLACEMENT (one-time)

1. Lamp on the side opposite your painting hand, head raised above your normal sight line when you look down at the paper. Tilt it down at roughly 30 degrees from vertical so the brightest reflection on a wet wash lands off the paper edge, not back at your eyes. If the bulb is in your peripheral vision, it is too low.

2. Foam board on the side of the paper opposite the lamp, leaning slightly forward. Its job is fill: bouncing light back into the shadow side so dark passages do not read inky under lamp light. Aim matters more than distance; angle it at the painting, not at you.

3. If the LED has a sharp specular hotspot on wet paper, soften it. A folded paper towel clipped over the bulb, or a small piece of card as a barn door, spreads the reflection. A bare LED on a wet sheet makes a white smear that moves when you move - that is glare, not a highlight.

CHECK SEQUENCE (about a minute, before you start)

A. Specular check. Brush clean water across a scrap of the same paper. Tilt your head a few degrees left and right. The lamp reflection should slide off the paper or land in a corner you are not painting on. If it sits dead-center on your working area, reposition before you begin.

B. Value check. Tape a 3-value gray strip (or paint light / mid / dark on a scrap and let it dry). With daylight faded and only the lamp on, the relationships should still read. If your dark looks pure black and your light looks pure white, your iris has stopped down - turn the lamp down one notch. You want the midtone to sit clearly in the middle.

C. White-point check. Hold a scrap of the paper next to anything you have a daylight memory of - a swatch on a card, a wall you painted by window light. They do not have to match, but the lamp should not look yellow or blue-white. If it does, your eye will adapt in roughly 10 minutes and you will misjudge warm/cool mixes for the rest of the block.

DURING THE BLOCK

- Every 20 to 30 minutes, glance at the window or step into remaining daylight for five seconds. When you come back to the lamp, any shift you notice across the WHOLE painting is the lamp's bias, not a painting error. A shift in one passage only is real.

- Do not lock in a warm/cool decision until you have either checked under daylight or photographed the area under both lights. A phone snap near a window is enough.

- If a passage looks wrong under the lamp, leave it alone for the session. Wet watercolor under a single light source is unreliable for color judgment. Wait for daylight or for the wash to dry fully - dried passages read more accurately than wet ones, especially for value.

DISTINGUISHING LAMP FROM PAINTING PROBLEM

- Whole-painting shift = the lamp.
- Localized shift = the painting.
- Reverses when you step to daylight = the lamp.
- Still wrong in daylight = the painting.
- Wet reads different from dry = mostly the wet; do not "fix" wet.

STOP CONDITIONS

- Lamp reflection sits in your working area and will not slide off with head tilt - reposition before the next wash.
- Squinting flattens the whole painting to one value - lamp is too bright or too close; dim or move it back.
- You cannot tell whether a passage is wrong or the lamp is wrong - that is a signal to stop making mix decisions, not to commit one.

That covers the four constraints: lamp out of sight (above sight line, opposite painting hand), no glare on wet washes (off-center specular plus optional diffusion), readable values (midrange check plus foam-board fill), and lamp effect separable from a painting problem (daylight cross-check, wet versus dry, whole-painting versus local).

A note on scope first: I don't know which specific in-network provider, which online retailer, or which vision-plan terms apply to you. The patterns below are generic; the plan documents and retailer policies override anything here.

IN-NETWORK

Adjustment access — highest
In-person fitting, nose-pad and temple adjustments, minor repairs; usually included for the life of the Rx at the issuing office. Walk-in or short-notice.

Remake terms — strongest
30–90 days is standard for Rx or fabrication errors; some plans extend 6–12 months for adaptation issues (especially progressives). The office handles the remake paperwork; you don't ship anything.

Reimbursement work — lowest
Direct billing to the vision plan; you pay only the patient portion at point of sale. CPT/HCPCS codes, provider tax ID, and the doctor's signature are already on file.

December 31 timing — cleanest
Place and complete the order before 12/31/26 to use the 2026 benefit. Most shops fabricate and dispense single-vision or lined multifocal lenses in 5–10 business days; progressives can run 7–14. As of 11/12, that's roughly 7 weeks — comfortable.

ONLINE

Adjustment access — lowest
Self-adjust, or visit a local optician (some charge a small fee, some won't touch frames they didn't sell). Warby Parker retail locations adjust WP frames free in many markets; most online-only retailers have no physical adjustment network.

Remake terms — thinner and slower
Common policy is 30 days from delivery for Rx errors; adaptation remakes vary by retailer and often require the doctor to re-verify the Rx. You ship frames back, the lab remakes, you wait. Total remake turnaround is often 2–3 weeks door-to-door.

Reimbursement work — highest
Out-of-pocket at checkout, then file a claim with itemized invoice and the lab's Rx details. Many plans require CPT/HCPCS codes, the lab's tax ID, and a separate "paid at point of sale" verification. First-submission denials are common when a code or signature is missing — expect back-and-forth.

December 31 timing — tightest
To use the 2026 benefit, the order usually needs to be placed (and per some plans, shipped or delivered) before 12/31. If you file a claim after-the-fact, the purchase date on the receipt is what counts — but check the plan's filing deadline, typically 90–180 days post-purchase. Order now to be safe.

WAITING

Adjustment access — N/A on a new Rx. Current glasses are working for distance; mild end-of-day screen blur is the only reported symptom.

Remake terms — N/A. No remake exposure if no order is placed.

Reimbursement work — N/A until 2027.
The risk: if the 2026 frame or lens allowance is use-it-or-lose-it, waiting forfeits it. Most vision plans are use-it-or-lose-it on a calendar-year basis; some plans roll over or stack, but that's the exception. If the frame allowance is on a 24-month cycle and you used it in 2025, 2026 may not have had a frame allowance to forfeit in the first place.

December 31 timing — the 2026 benefit is either used, forfeited, or simply not available depending on plan structure. 2027 benefit resets 1/1/27 on the new cycle. The 11/5/26 Rx is valid for whatever period state law and the plan allow — commonly 1–2 years from exam; verify with the plan.

WHAT THE $7 GAP CHANGES

With price no longer the deciding factor:
- Service safety net: in-person fitting, adjustment, and remake handling vs. self-service with shipping back-and-forth.
- Paperwork: direct billing vs. claim filing.
- Timing: a 2026 benefit use vs. letting it lapse and starting the 2027 cycle clean.

VERIFY BEFORE ACTING

(a) Whether the 2026 vision benefit is use-it-or-lose-it and what's left in the 2026 allowance (frames, lenses, contacts, exam).
(b) Whether the online retailer you're considering files insurance directly — some do, which moves them closer to the in-network experience.
(c) Whether the in-network option is the prescribing doctor's office or a separate in-network optical — both work, but selection, frames inventory, and remake handling differ.
(d) The plan's filing deadline if you go out-of-network and claim back.
(e) Whether the 11/5/26 Rx is still valid for the in-network office to fill, or whether it needs a re-check before they can order.

NON-MEDICAL NOTE

Whether to update the prescription at all is between you and the prescribing doctor. I'm working from your summary of the 11/5/26 exam, not the chart. The dimensions above cover how to fill a prescription you've already decided to fill, not whether to fill it.

HANDS-ON MONTHLY AUDIT — DESIGN INPUT FOR DECEMBER 4 PROPOSAL
Status: proposal-stage design input only. Nothing below changes current authority, current escalation behavior, or current closure practice. No role change is implied.

FRAME
The audit is Riley's reserved channel for directly testing the evidence system, not a parallel re-closure of what Owen already certified. The strongest designs concentrate on the boundary Owen is NOT authorized to close — exceptions and disputed cases — rather than on lanes he has already declared complete, and avoid creating a gate that reads as approval. Preservation of escalation triggers and of causal/revenue/forecast/board-readiness/final-claim authority is a hard constraint on the design.

OPTION-BY-OPTION COMPARISON

Option 1 — Rotating deep recheck of one evidence lane after closure
- Direct evidence-system contact: HIGH. Pulls records, walks freshness, suppression reconstruction, governed-field state, hold/recheck history, audit trail, cross-view agreement.
- Duplicates Owen's source-completeness work: PARTIAL. Owen has already declared the lane complete. Re-walking the same lane risks re-litigating what he certified, especially on completeness; semantic depth differs from completeness depth, but the boundary is not always cleanly separated.
- Owner-role ambiguity: MEDIUM. If a discrepancy surfaces, does the audit reopen closure, write a corrected version, or simply flag? Requires an explicit "audit findings are an escalation signal, not a re-closure action" rule to prevent drift.
- Second approval queue risk: MEDIUM-HIGH. The natural reading of "deep recheck after closure" is "Riley verifies before publication." That becomes a gate unless the proposal frames it as observation.

Option 2 — Targeted sample drawn from that month's exceptions
- Direct evidence-system contact: HIGH. Pulls hold records, reasons, dispositions, fresh-check evidence, source-age alerts, escalation decisions, customer-correction trail, hold-age distribution.
- Duplicates Owen's source-completeness work: LOW. Exceptions are by definition the cases Owen is required to escalate, not close. Sampling them tests the escalation boundary, which is exactly where Owen's discretion ends.
- Owner-role ambiguity: LOW. Clear ownership: Owen owns closure; exceptions that should have escalated but did not are the audit's natural finding. No silent re-closure by Riley.
- Second approval queue risk: LOW. Exceptions are not in any closure queue. The audit cannot delay routine closure because routine closure is not what is being sampled.

Option 3 — Small cross-lane trace of governed fields and claim treatment
- Direct evidence-system contact: HIGH. Cross-cuts lane boundaries, governed-field meaning, claim-treatment language, board/exec wording.
- Duplicates Owen's source-completeness work: HIGH on the governed-field side (Owen's "no cross-surface discrepancy" check already covers cross-lane governed-field agreement); overlaps with Riley's own retained lane on claim treatment, executive language, and board readiness.
- Owner-role ambiguity: HIGH. The trace sits exactly on the boundary between Owen's closure authority and Riley's claim authority. Without tight scoping it pulls both lanes into one review.
- Second approval queue risk: HIGH. Cross-lane checks that touch claim treatment will read as a pre-publication review unless explicitly out of scope.

RECOMMENDATION (carry into the proposal)
Primary monthly audit: OPTION 2 (exceptions sample).
Option 2 directly tests the highest-risk boundary in the system (the Owen→Riley escalation boundary), with the lowest duplication of Owen's closure work, the lowest owner-role ambiguity, and the lowest queue risk. It produces findings that map cleanly onto the existing escalation triggers rather than creating a new category.

Complement to consider at December 4 (not in the primary monthly audit): OPTION 1 as a quarterly deep recheck rotating across the four lanes, with each lane receiving one deep recheck per quarter. Framed explicitly as observation, not reopening, and with findings routed to the existing escalation triggers. This would give Riley hands-on contact with each lane four times per year, separate from the monthly cadence.

EXCLUDE OPTION 3 from the monthly hands-on audit. Cross-lane governed-field and claim-treatment traces remain Riley's standing authority work, performed on trigger (disputed claim, board-readiness question, new exception type, disputed semantics, executive-language decision). They are not a fixed-cadence monthly item and would otherwise pull the audit into Owen's closure lane and into a pre-publication gate.

WHY THIS DESIGN HOLDS
- Tests the right boundary. The escalation boundary is where routine work either holds or fails. Sampling exceptions tests it directly.
- Preserves Owen's lane. He is not re-audited on what he already closed correctly.
- Preserves Riley's lane. Causal, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, and final-claim decisions stay with Riley by design, exercised when the work requires it, not on the monthly cadence.
- Avoids the queue. Exceptions are not queued for closure; the quarterly deep recheck is observation, not gate; cross-lane traces happen on trigger.
- Bounded monthly cost. An exception sample is finite and predictable; the cost is roughly the size of the month's exception set, not the size of the system.
- Maps findings to existing triggers rather than creating a new escalation channel.

WHAT THIS IS NOT (explicit limits)
- Not a second approval queue. Audit findings are escalation signals. A finding does not pause a lane, block closure of unrelated work, or gate publication.
- Not a re-closure action. Riley does not rewrite Owen's closure or correct a closed lane in place. Findings are recorded as append-only audit entries with named operators, exact dates, and field-level provenance; corrections route through the existing triggers.
- Not a venue for causal, revenue, forecast, board-readiness, or final-claim decisions. Those remain Riley's retained authority, exercised when the work requires it.
- Not a change to existing escalation triggers. Missing fields, disputed semantics, cross-surface discrepancies, customer corrections, incident stops, and executive-language decisions escalate to Riley today and continue to escalate regardless of the audit.

The problem is the reflector at close range acting as a second point source instead of fill. The fix is to find a position where it bounces ambient-level light onto the dark side — one primary terminator is the goal.

Setup sequence (about 10 minutes, do not start painting):

1. Park the reflector first. Start with the foam board 20–24 inches from the cup, angled so its face is roughly parallel to the cup's dark side, not aimed at it. It is a bounce surface, not a second lamp.

2. Set the lamp height. With the reflector parked far, raise or lower the task lamp in 2–3 inch steps until the cup's primary terminator reads as one clean soft edge — form shadow on the body, one cast shadow on the supporting surface, no secondary edge.

3. Bring the reflector closer in small steps. Move it in 2–3 inch increments toward the cup, pausing 10–15 seconds at each step to look at the reflected (dark) side. It should read as a smooth value gradient.

   Stop moving closer at the first sign of a second edge on the cup body. Pull the reflector back 2–3 inches past that point. That is your safe distance.

4. If the second edge still appears at 20+ inches, the lamp beam is too narrow or the foam board too bright for the room. Pick one fix, not both:
   - Tilt the reflector so it bounces toward the wall or ceiling corner above the cup, not at the cup directly. The cup still receives fill, but the reflector no longer acts as a point source on it.
   - Swap to a larger matte-white surface (a second foam board, or mat board) so the bounce covers a wider angle and the terminator softens.

5. Lock the position. Mark the lamp arm height and the reflector foot position with low-tack tape on the table so you return to the same setup next session.

Neutral-value check without wet-wash glare:

- Make a 5-step value scale on scrap paper using the same palette (white / light-mid / mid / dark-mid / near-black). Let it dry.
- Hold the dry scale next to the cup under the locked setup. Compare each cup region — lit side, terminator, reflected side, cast shadow — to the scale. This is what you read into the painting.
- Check the painting on a DRY area only (a test swatch or corner) under the same lamp. Wet wash reads 1–2 values darker than it will dry, so do not compare wet wash directly to the cup.
- Cross-check the lamp itself: turn it off and view the scale plus a dry test swatch under the room's neutral daylight. Values should agree within one step. If they don't, the lamp has a color cast — note it, do not compensate in the painting.

Stop conditions (the one you asked for):

- Stop adjusting once the cup shows one form shadow and one cast shadow. The reflected side should grade from terminator into shadow as a smooth step, not an edge.
- Do not add a second connecting shadow in the painting to match the second edge you saw earlier. That edge was a lighting artifact, not part of the still life. The painting stays on the actual cup.
- Do not move the reflector closer than the locked position to "soften more" — that recreates the second edge.
- If no reflector position gives one clean terminator (very small workspace, very narrow beam), do the value check with the lamp off under window light, paint under the lamp, and stop hunting the lighting further this session.

What this is not: it is not a directive to add or remove anything from the painting. The painting is unchanged. The setup change is for the next pass, and only after the current wash dries.

- Dice small = fast, even penetration to 165°F internal without long danger-zone dwell. Verify with instant-read in a chicken piece (should read ≥165°F). Stuffing hits 165°F at the same time since it's dispersed and thin.
- Order matters: densest/most-mass first (sweet potato), then protein (chicken, must reach 165°F), then quick-crisp starch (stuffing — burns fast), then already-cooked veg last (just warming). Putting stuffing in too early = burnt before chicken is safe; putting green beans in too early = mush.

- Chicken doesn't dry because: dice is chunky not shredded, sweet potato releases moisture, oil coats, total pan time on the protein is only ~4 min.

Comparison of three cadence choices for the hands-on evidence audit, across the four lenses Priya named. Decision input for the December 4 draft. No role change approved or proposed.

OPTION A — Monthly rotating one-lane
Each month, audit one of the four lanes (Helio Start reporting, Expansion Assist selection, lifecycle preflight, CS auto-nudge operations). Rotate so each lane is re-touched roughly once every four months (~3x per lane per year). This is the cadence implicit in the November 25 proposal's "concrete monthly hands-on audit."

  Direct system contact: HIGH. ~12 touchpoints per year. Riley stays close to ledger, governed fields, holds, suppression reconstruction, freshness outcomes, and claim treatment as actually run.

  Duplicate work: HIGH. Owen closes routine source-completeness across the four lanes (Sept 24 authority: when all required fields are present, definitions unchanged, named owners certified, no cross-surface discrepancy). A monthly rotation means Riley re-walks a lane within weeks of Owen's closure — same records, same governed fields, same holds. That re-walk is most of the audit work and it repeats.

  Owner-role ambiguity: MODERATE–HIGH. Owen's closure is supposed to be definitive for routine. If Riley touches the same lane every 1–2 months, the boundary between audit and second closure check blurs. The risk is not intent; it is that downstream readers and the team start treating Riley's monthly audit as a quality gate before any consumer-facing use of the lane.

  Second-approval-queue risk: HIGH. Monthly frequency is short enough that "did Riley sign off?" can embed in the operating rhythm even if Riley never claims that role. Same failure mode Priya has consistently rejected — the June 9 CS auto-nudge admission review and the declined fifth-consumer connection both turned on this concern.

OPTION B — Quarterly rotating one-lane
Each quarter, audit one lane; full rotation through four lanes per year; each lane audited once per year.

  Direct system contact: MODERATE. ~4 touchpoints per year; each lane once per year. Riley still touches the ledger directly, but the gaps are long. By Q4, the lane audited in Q1 may have drifted substantially from current state.

  Duplicate work: MODERATE. Same shape as A (re-walk of Owen's recent closure), lower frequency. Each instance duplicates work Owen closed ~90 days earlier.

  Owner-role ambiguity: MODERATE. Same dynamic as A — Owen closes, Riley re-walks — but the longer interval makes the audit role easier to distinguish from closure. Quarterly is rarely mistaken for real-time approval.

  Second-approval-queue risk: MODERATE. Same shape as A, lower frequency. Unlikely to embed in any monthly release rhythm, but predictable enough that informal sign-off expectations can grow over time.

OPTION C — Exception-triggered only
No fixed cadence. Audit fires only when an exception event occurs: customer correction, semantic dispute, rollback, disputed ownership, suppressed fail-open risk, contested claim treatment, or other event Riley would otherwise engage on ad hoc.

  Direct system contact: VARIABLE / LOW scheduled. In a quiet quarter, possibly zero touchpoints. In a heavy-exception quarter, possibly several deep engagements. Contact happens on highest-stakes events, not the routine baseline.

  Duplicate work: LOW. Most exception triggers are not Owen's routine closure — they are edge cases where something has already broken or is being disputed. The audit work is the response, not a re-walk of Owen's clean closure.

  Owner-role ambiguity: LOW. Owen owns routine closure; Riley owns exception review. Lanes don't overlap on the same records at the same time. Cleanest authority split of the three.

  Second-approval-queue risk: LOW. Reactive, not a gate on normal operations. Does not sit in front of any release.

Synthesis
The four lenses pull in different directions. On direct system contact, A is highest and C is lowest. On duplicate work, owner-role ambiguity, and second-approval-queue risk, A is highest and C is lowest. B is between on every lens.

If the explicit goal is to preserve Riley's scheduled hands-on fluency with the evidence system as it actually runs, A is closest to that goal but costs the most on the three concerns Priya has been most consistent about. C is cleanest on those concerns but under-delivers on scheduled contact. B is the middle; whether it's the right middle depends on how much scheduled contact Priya is actually trying to protect versus how much queue risk she is willing to accept.
