Setup
- Existing inventory: 3 full sheets of 22×30 paper already on hand
- Each full sheet cuts into 4 quarter-sheets (your prior practice)
- Option A: add 1 sheet at $8
- Option B: add a 5-pack at $32
- Window: Jan–Apr 2027 (4 months)

Per-sheet unit cost (raw)
- Option A: $8 / 1 = $8.00 per full sheet
- Option B: $32 / 5 = $6.40 per full sheet
- The 5-pack is $1.60 cheaper per sheet, or 20%. So far the 5-pack "wins" on price.

Inventory including your existing 3 sheets
- Option A: 3 + 1 = 4 full sheets → 16 quarter-sheets
- Option B: 3 + 5 = 8 full sheets → 32 quarter-sheets
- Option B gives 16 more quarter-sheets than Option A, but you have to spend $24 more to get them.

How long each lasts through Jan–Apr
Realistic usage in your practice (75-minute limited-palette studies, bounded stop conditions) is closer to 1–2 quarter-sheets per month, so 4–8 quarter-sheets across the four months. At that rate:

| Usage in Jan–Apr | Option A (16 qtrs on hand) | Option B (32 qtrs on hand) |
|---|---|---|
| 4 quarter-sheets (1/month) | used 4, leftover 12 | used 4, leftover 28 |
| 6 quarter-sheets (1.5/month) | used 6, leftover 10 | used 6, leftover 26 |
| 8 quarter-sheets (2/month) | used 8, leftover 8 | used 8, leftover 24 |

Either option easily covers Jan–Apr. Option A leaves roughly 8–12 quarter-sheets for May onward; Option B leaves 24–28 sitting in a flat-file.

Effective cost per quarter-sheet actually used in the window
- 6 quarter-sheets used across Jan–Apr:
  - Option A: $8 / 6 = $1.33 per used quarter
  - Option B: $32 / 6 = $5.33 per used quarter
- 8 quarter-sheets used:
  - Option A: $8 / 8 = $1.00 per used quarter
  - Option B: $32 / 8 = $4.00 per used quarter

The 5-pack's $1.60/sheet discount only matters if you actually consume those 5 new sheets within the window. You won't. The lower unit cost is real on paper but gets paid for in inventory you don't use, plus the storage burden of keeping 8 full sheets flat and dry instead of 4.

Recommendation
Buy the 1 sheet at $8. Your existing 3 sheets already push total inventory well past Jan–Apr at any realistic study pace, so the 5-pack's per-sheet advantage is converted into leftover stock rather than into savings. Option A is the lower-waste fit for the four-month window: smaller spend, comparable coverage, less idle paper, and you keep the 5-pack available later if a stretch of more frequent studies actually materializes.

60-MINUTE SEQUENCE — SILVER RIBBON ON BROWN KRAFT

SUBJECT READ
Silver reads as a mid-dark cool-neutral mass with reserved paper-white
highlights, not as a light value. The kraft reads warm and matte and
should stay quieter than the ribbon. Most overwork comes from painting
every reflection as a separate light value. Instead, the ribbon is
mostly one cool-neutral gray with reserved highlights and hard fold
creases. Reflections live in the highlights and creases, not in
mid-value paint.

PALETTE AND MIXING ORDER (restrained)
Pick one cool-leaning neutral mix you trust — the discipline is the
order, not the specific pigments.
  1. Water in the well first, pigment second.
  2. A trace of the cool pigment (e.g. ultramarine) into a lot of
     water — pale tint only.
  3. A trace of the neutralizing earth (e.g. burnt umber) into the
     same well until the chroma dies. Test on scrap.
  4. Adjust by adding more earth to deepen, more water to lighten.
     Never add fresh cool pigment into a deep puddle — that is how
     "silver" turns to mud.
  5. Reserve a second, smaller well of a thin warm earth (raw sienna
     or burnt umber) only for the kraft, if it needs a touch.
No opaque white. The brightest spots are paper white.

TIMED SEQUENCE

0:00–0:05  Setup
  Two water jars, a clean highlight brush kept apart from the mixing
  brush, scrap paper for value tests, a tissue for blotting.

0:05–0:12  Value map on scrap, not on the painting
  Reduce the still life to three values:
    Light  = reserved paper (speculars on fold crests)
    Mid    = cool-neutral gray — the bulk of the ribbon faces
    Dark   = deep folds, contact shadow, crease lines
  Mark 4–6 HARD edges (fold creases where value jumps abruptly) and
  2–3 LOST edges (where the ribbon's cool blends into the kraft's
  warmth, or where two folds share a value and the crease should
  disappear). Decide which tiny highlights are worth reserving —
  fewer is better.

0:12–0:15  Reserve highlights
  Confirm specular dots are clean paper. If anything is smudged,
  lift now with clean water and blot once. Do not plan to paint
  around them later.

0:15–0:32  First pass — the cool-neutral mass
  Paint ribbon faces in continuous strokes, working wet-into-wet
  within a single fold but letting adjacent folds meet at a hard
  edge. Do not blend across creases — the abrupt value shift is the
  read. Stay inside the ribbon outline; do not touch the kraft yet.

0:32–0:45  Hard edges (while still damp)
  Drop a slightly stronger mix into the marked crease lines. One
  touch, no second pass. Leave the lost edges untouched — they
  should already be fading from the first pass. If a lost edge has
  dried too crisp, soften with a barely damp clean brush, then stop.

0:45–0:52  Optional kraft touch (only if needed)
  A single thin warm-earth pass in the kraft's deeper folds or
  directly under the ribbon's contact shadow. If the kraft already
  reads warm and matte from the paper itself, skip this step
  entirely. The kraft is the ground, not a subject.

0:52–0:58  Highlight check at normal viewing distance
  Reserved highlights still bright? Any chroma contamination = stop.
  Value map still three values? Any collapse = stop.
  Kraft still warm and matte? Any graying = stop.

0:58–0:60  Stop.

STOP CONDITIONS (fire BEFORE the painting is overworked, not after)
- A reserved highlight picks up chroma and will not lift clean
- Two adjacent folds merge into a single value and lose the crease
- You reach for a third touch on any area
- The kraft starts to look painted rather than matte
- A lost edge is repainted and becomes a visible seam
- 60 minutes, regardless of state

WHAT THIS IS NOT
- Not a finished painting. It is a 60-minute study.
- Not a reflection-by-reflection rendering.
- Not a multi-pass study. One pass on the ribbon, possibly one on
  the kraft, then stop.

HSA payroll-election arithmetic for 2027 (employee-only HDHP, 24 pay periods)

Per-paycheck | Annual employee | Employer ($225 × 4, eligibility-contingent) | Combined annual
$75          | $1,800          | $900                                          | $2,700
$100         | $2,400          | $900                                          | $3,300
$125         | $3,000          | $900                                          | $3,900

All employer deposits count toward the same statutory HSA annual cap as the employee amount — they are not "extra." If any $225 quarterly deposit is missed because eligibility lapses at that deposit time, the $900 ceiling also drops to whatever was actually deposited that year.

Statutory 2027 limit is not stated on the screen, and I do not have an authoritative 2027 IRS figure I can give you. The 2026 self-only HDHP cap was $4,400 (catch-up $1,000 if age 55+ at year end). The 2027 number is published by the IRS, typically via a Revenue Procedure in the spring preceding the year; the limit for self-only HDHP coverage has historically risen modestly each year. Treat any number you see as illustrative until verified.

For reference only, framed against the 2026 self-only cap of $4,400:
  - $75 + $900 employer = $2,700 → ~$1,700 of cap headroom
  - $100 + $900 employer = $3,300 → ~$1,100 of cap headroom
  - $125 + $900 employer = $3,900 → ~$500 of cap headroom
Any of the three preset options sits under the 2026 cap, but the screen offers no confirmation that 2027 will be at or above $4,400. Do not elect based on a presumed cap.

What remains before you submit (separate from the medical-plan network checks already closed for the HDHP):
  - Verify the published 2027 self-only HDHP HSA limit (IRS Rev. Proc. for 2027, IRS Pub. 969, HSA custodian notice, or Helio benefits portal once they post it).
  - Confirm remaining personal HSA-eligibility tests: enrolled in qualifying HDHP (done for 2027 election), not covered by a general-purpose FSA or non-HDHP plan (incl. spouse's plan that pays medical), not enrolled in Medicare, not claimed as a dependent on someone else's return.
  - Confirm catch-up eligibility if you are 55+ at year end — adds a separate $1,000-class contribution on top of the self-only limit.

Election mechanics (general, confirm against Helio's plan document):
  - HSA contributions through a Section 125 cafeteria plan can usually be changed prospectively at any time during the plan year — they are not locked like an FSA election. Direct contributions outside payroll can also be made up to the unextended tax filing deadline the following April.
  - Reversibility is therefore high; submitting an initial amount is not an irrevocable decision. Submitting too low is easier to fix than submitting over the cap.

Recommendation:

Hoppin' John-style black-eyed peas and collard greens over rice

A Southern New Year's tradition that happens to fit exactly what you have on hand. Easy lunch for two, ~25 minutes active.

Quantities:
  2 cans (15 oz) black-eyed peas, drained and rinsed
  1 bunch collard greens, stemmed and chopped into 1-inch ribbons
  3 cups cooked rice
  3-4 garlic cloves, minced
  1 lemon — half juiced (~1 Tbsp), other half in wedges
  3/4 cup vegetable broth, divided
  3 Tbsp olive oil, divided
  Salt, black pepper, smoked paprika

Sequence:
  1.  0:00  Prep collards (fold each leaf, slice out the thick stem, stack and cut into 1-inch ribbons). Drain and rinse peas. Mince garlic.
  2.  0:05  Large skillet over medium heat, 2 Tbsp olive oil. Add garlic, stir 30 seconds — don't brown.
  3.  0:06  Add collards with a pinch of salt, in two handfuls if needed. Toss until wilted, 3-4 minutes.
  4.  0:10  Push greens to one side. Add peas, 1/2 cup broth, 1 tsp smoked paprika. Simmer 5 minutes to meld.
  5.  0:15  Stir greens and peas together. Add more broth if dry. Season with salt and pepper to taste.
  6.  0:18  Off heat. Squeeze half a lemon over the pan (~1 Tbsp) and stir. Reserve the rest for serving.
  7.  0:20  Reheat rice — microwave covered with a splash of water (2-3 min), or warm in a separate pan with 1 Tbsp olive oil and a splash of water (3-4 min).
  8.  0:23  Plate: rice on the bottom, peas and greens over the top. Drizzle with olive oil, serve with a lemon wedge.

What this is / is not:
  This is: a quick week-of-New-Year's lunch using only what you listed.
  This is not: a classic Hoppin' John (no pork, no onion), but the principle is the same. Collards here are sautéed, not long-braised, so they keep a bit of bite.

Optional if you happen to have one around: a fried or soft-boiled egg on top is excellent — not in your ingredients, so just noting it.

Note: if Sam's lunch slides later than yours, the peas and greens reheat well with a splash of broth over low heat, so you can hold them 30-60 minutes without harm.

ONE-POT WHITE BEAN & PASTA SOUP  (lunch for 2 + 1 leftover)

Approximate amounts (serves 3):
  - 2 tbsp olive oil
  - 1 small onion, diced (~1 cup)
  - 1 medium carrot, diced (~1/2 cup)
  - 3 garlic cloves, minced
  - 1 tsp dried oregano
  - 1/2 tsp dried thyme
  - 1/4 tsp red pepper flakes (optional)
  - 2 cans (15 oz) white beans, drained (cannellini or great northern)
  - 1 can (14 oz) diced tomatoes, with juice
  - 5 cups chicken or vegetable broth
  - 1 parmesan rind (optional)
  - 4 oz small pasta (ditalini, small shells, or orzo)
  - 3 cups baby spinach or chopped kale
  - Salt and black pepper
  - Juice of 1/2 lemon
  - Grated parmesan for serving

Timing (about 30 min):
  0:00   Heat oil in a large pot over medium. Add onion and carrot; cook 5 min, stirring occasionally.
  5:00   Add garlic, oregano, thyme, and red pepper; stir 30 sec.
  6:00   Add beans, tomatoes (with juice), broth, and parmesan rind. Bring to a simmer, scraping any bits off the bottom.
 10:00   Add pasta. Simmer 9-10 min, stirring 2-3 times so it doesn't stick.
 20:00   Stir in greens; simmer 2-3 min until wilted.
 23:00   Remove rind. Stir in lemon juice. Season with salt and pepper.
 25:00   Plate two bowls; ladle the remaining third into the leftover container first.

Cleanup:  one pot, one cutting board, one knife, one wooden spoon, one ladle. Rinse the beans in their cans before opening the tomatoes (saves a colander and a bowl).

Cooling the leftover safely:
  1. Ladle the hot soup into a shallow container no more than 3 inches deep. If your container is deeper, split between two.
  2. Set the container in an ice-water bath (a larger bowl with ice and cold water) and stir gently for 5-10 min until the soup stops steaming and feels cool to the touch.
  3. Loosely cover (lid tilted or vented) - do not seal airtight while still warm; condensation will pool on top.
  4. Move to the fridge once cool to the touch (40 F or below). Aim to reach 70 F within 2 hours and 40 F within the next 4 hours; the ice bath handles the first stage.
  5. Eat within 3-4 days. Reheat on the stovetop over medium-low with a splash of broth or water, or microwave covered at 50 percent power, stirring once.

Easy swaps if you're short an item:  carrots optional; greens can be omitted (add lemon at the end for brightness instead); pasta can be a handful of broken spaghetti; skip the rind and finish with extra parmesan.

What this is not:  not a freezer plan, not a 5-day prep, not a one-pot where you can walk away (pasta needs an occasional stir).

Cold-and-granule plan for Kibo (31°F, deicing visible, no current symptom):

Pre-walk
- Keep the walk short and necessary-only. 31°F itself is not a paw-freeze threshold for a healthy dog, so no booties or balm are required on that basis alone — the concern is granule contact.
- If you can, route toward grass/curb edges where granule residue tends to be thinner, but don't add distance to do it.

During the walk
- Leash close; let him sniff/pace rather than dawdle on visibly treated patches.

Post-walk (in order)
1. Visual check of all four paws before touching — pads, between each toe, around the nail beds, and the dewclaws. Note any redness, cracking, swelling between pads, or stuck granules.
2. Wipe each paw with a damp paper towel or unscented paw wipe to lift granules off the surface. Wipe direction: pad → between toes → fur edge, so you don't grind residue into the skin.
3. Lukewarm (not hot) water rinse — quick dip or gentle pour over each paw to dissolve any residue the wipe left. Plain water is fine; saline is fine if you already have it.
4. Dry thoroughly between toes and on pads. Moisture left on cold paws can chill skin and soften pads, which makes the next walk worse.
5. Quick second look for stuck material, bleeding, or a pad crack you didn't see wet.

If he licks at one paw more than the others once inside, redirect and re-check that paw.

Vet-call thresholds
- Same-day call: persistent favoring or non-weight-bearing on a paw; repeated licking of one spot that doesn't stop after wiping/drying; visible pad crack, bleeding, or blister; swelling or discharge between pads; a granule or piece of ice still embedded after rinsing.
- Watch overnight: mild pinkness between pads, brief licking that stops, slight coolness to the touch — recheck in the morning and call if not back to baseline.
- No action needed: brief sniff-lick of all four paws, normal weight-bearing, pads look intact and dry.

What this is not: this does not change Kibo's existing trazodone instruction (storm/fireworks only), and it does not introduce a new medication, balm, or booty protocol on the strength of one cold morning. If granules are a recurring concern this winter, that's a separate conversation about routine paw protection.

A small, fresh black-coffee spill with no milk or sugar is one of the more reversible stains on cotton — the bigger risk right now is the dye in the jacket, since you haven't confirmed colorfastness, not the coffee itself. Order of operations matters because once it goes through a dryer (which the label already forbids) or sits hot-set, you lose reversibility.

Conservative sequence, in order:

1. Blot, do not rub. Press a clean dry cloth or plain paper towel against the spot and lift. Replace and repeat until no more coffee transfers. Rubbing grinds the tannin deeper into the cotton fibers and can spread the ring.

2. Colorfastness check first, on hidden fabric. Before any water or soap hits the stained area, wet a cotton swab with plain cold water and touch it to an inside seam, inside cuff facing, or hem allowance. Press a white paper towel against it for 30 seconds. If any dye transfers, stop and either hand-wash the cuff very gently in cold water without detergent (water only, lowest agitation), or take it to a cleaner. Do not proceed to machine wash if dye is bleeding — the whole jacket could streak.

3. If the colorfastness check is clean, rinse from the back. Hold the cuff under a cold running tap with the stained side facing down so the water pushes the coffee out of the fabric instead of through it. 30–60 seconds is usually enough for a small fresh spill.

4. Pre-treat, gently. A small amount of plain liquid laundry detergent (non-bleach, per label) worked into the spot with your fingertip, then let it sit 5 minutes. A dilute white-vinegar rinse (1 part vinegar to ~4 parts cold water) is also reasonable on cotton for tannin, but only after the colorfastness check has passed — vinegar can pull dye too.

5. Wash per label, or hand-wash the cuff. Either machine-wash the whole jacket on cold, or, if you want to limit exposure, hand-wash just the cuff in a basin of cold water with a small amount of mild detergent. Cold only — warm or hot can set a tannin stain even without milk.

6. Inspect while still damp, before any drying. This is the step most people skip. If the stain is gone or only faintly visible, air-dry flat or on a hanger away from direct sun. If it's still visible, repeat steps 3–5 and recheck — do not let it air-dry with the stain present if you can avoid it, because oxidation can darken a faint tannin ring over time even without heat.

7. Air dry only. The label already says no tumble dry, which protects both the cotton and, right now, your ability to retreat the stain if step 6 didn't fully clear it. Heat is what locks tannin in.

Stop conditions:
- Any dye transfer during the colorfastness check.
- Visible color shift on the stained area after pre-treatment.
- Stain still present after two full cycles (rinse → pre-treat → wash → inspect). At that point, further home effort risks damaging the fabric or dye, and a professional cleaner is the conservative next step rather than a stronger agent.

What this is not: a guarantee the stain will fully come out, advice to use anything stronger than mild detergent (the label forbids bleach; I'd also avoid oxygen bleach or stain-remover pens until colorfastness is confirmed), or a substitute for a cleaner if the spot persists after two careful attempts. Tannin on untested-dye cotton is a small but real risk pair.

Known inputs in scope: fresh spill, black coffee only (no milk, no sugar); cuff of a washable cotton jacket; care label says machine wash cold, do not bleach, do not tumble dry; colorfastness not yet tested.

Stain type: tannin only. Tannin stains are set by heat and by alkali. So the whole sequence is built around cold water, gentle contact, no heat at any step, and a check for residue before the jacket is allowed to dry.

Pre-checks before touching the stain
  Confirm the cuff is the same fabric as the body (cuffs are sometimes ribbed knit with a different fiber content).
  Pick a hidden test spot: inside fold of the cuff, inside seam allowance, or inside hem.
  Have ready: clean white cloths or white paper towels (white so transfer is visible), plain cold tap water, mild liquid laundry detergent.

Step 1. Spot-test for colorfastness. Do this first, every time.
  Dampen a white cloth or cotton swab with cold water.
  Press (do not rub) it against the hidden spot for 10 to 15 seconds.
  Lift, inspect the cloth and the fabric, wait 1 to 2 minutes, inspect again.
  Any dye on the cloth, any visible change at the test spot, or any uncertainty is a stop signal. Pause wet treatment and either accept the risk and proceed with extra caution or take the jacket to a professional cleaner first. Untested dye plus wet work can ruin the garment in a way that is not reversible. Do not skip this step.

Step 2. Blot, do not rub. This is the bulk of the work for a fresh spill.
  Lay the jacket with the stained cuff face-down on a clean white cloth, so coffee wicks into the cloth instead of deeper into the fabric.
  Replace the cloth underneath as it picks up coffee.
  With a second clean white cloth on top of the cuff, press straight down and hold for several seconds; lift; move to a clean area; repeat.
  Work from the outside edge of the stained area inward, so the leading edge never touches clean fabric.
  Stop and assess when little or no coffee transfers. Do not rub, scrub, twist, or wring. Friction spreads the stain and pushes it into the fibers, which is the main way to spread it.

Step 3. Cold water rinse, from the back.
  Hold the cuff under a gentle stream of cold tap water on the BACK side of the fabric (the inside of the cuff facing the stream).
  Back-flushing pushes the stain out of the fibers the same way it went in, instead of driving it through to the face.
  Let the water run clear.
  No warm water, no hot water. Heat at this stage can begin to set the tannin.
  If the stain is gone or barely visible after the rinse, you can often skip pre-treatment and go to the wash.

Step 4. Mild pre-treatment only if residue remains.
  If the stain is still visible, put a small drop of mild liquid detergent directly on the residual mark and press-and-lift with a fingertip for 30 to 60 seconds. No scrubbing.
  Or submerge only the cuff in a basin of cold water with a small amount of detergent for 15 to 30 minutes. Re-check every 10 minutes and stop as soon as the stain releases.
  Do not use bleach (label forbids it), oxygen bleach, vinegar, baking soda, hydrogen peroxide, or any stronger stain product. The label forbids bleach; the others risk color loss on untested dye, and several of them can set tannin if combined with any heat.

Step 5. Machine wash, per the care label.
  Wash cold. Use your usual detergent. No bleach.
  Wash the jacket alone or with similar colors. Keep the load simple so you can read variables on the cuff afterward.

Step 6. Check the stain before drying. This is the second main rule.
  Take the jacket out of the washer while still wet and inspect the cuff in good light.
  Wet fabric hides residue. A faint tan or yellow ring that is invisible wet will reappear when the fabric dries, and once it has been through a dryer it becomes permanent.
  If the stain is gone, proceed to air dry.
  If the stain is still visible, do not dry. Repeat steps 2 through 4 on the still-damp cuff, then re-wash. Do not run more than two or three cycles; each cycle adds friction and dye risk.
  If the stain persists after two cycles, stop. Further home treatment is unlikely to help and can damage the fabric.

Step 7. Air dry, per the care label.
  No tumble dryer. No radiator, hair dryer, iron, or clothesline in direct hot sun. Any of these can set residual tannin.
  Hang or lay flat at room temperature, in shade if possible, with airflow. Confirm the cuff is fully dry before storing or wearing.

Stop conditions, in one place
  Color transfers during the spot test: pause, reassess, consider a professional cleaner.
  Stain spreads despite working from the outside in: stop wet work, let dry, reassess.
  Fabric shows dye loss, pilling, weakening, or any change from the test spot: stop.
  Stain remains after two careful wash cycles: stop and consider a professional cleaner.
  Any moment of uncertainty: stop. The jacket is more valuable than the time saved.

What this is not
  Not a guarantee. A fresh black-coffee spill on cotton with cold-water treatment has a reasonable chance of full removal; that is the most this sequence supports, not a promise.
  Not professional cleaning advice. If the spot test fails, if the stain dried before treatment, or if residue remains after two cycles, a professional cleaner is the conservative next step.

Sheet-pan chickpea, sweet-potato & broccoli with couscous + lemon-tahini
(serves 2 dinners + 1 lunch portion; active ~12 min across ~30 min total)

Prep at the counter (5 min, seated if helpful):
- Cube 1 medium sweet potato into ~3/4" pieces
- Cut 1 head broccoli into bite-size florets
- Drain 1 can chickpeas; pat dry with a clean towel
- Smash 1 garlic clove; mince 1 more
- Put 2/3 cup water in a small pot; set on a back burner
- Oven to 425°F; line a rimmed sheet pan with parchment

Pan load (2 min):
- On the pan, toss sweet potato + chickpeas with 2 tbsp olive oil, the smashed garlic clove, 1 tsp smoked paprika, 1/2 tsp salt, several grinds pepper
- Spread in a single layer (sweet potato cut-side down where you can)
- Roast 12 min

Mid-roast (1 min):
- Pull the pan; add broccoli florets; drizzle 1 tbsp olive oil + pinch salt; toss with what's already on the pan
- Roast 13 more min (25 min total)

While it finishes (start ~10 min before done):
- Bring the 2/3 cup water to a boil with a pinch of salt
- Pour over 1/2 cup dry couscous in a heatproof bowl
- Cover with a plate; rest 5 min; fluff with a fork

Sauce (2 min, in a small jar):
- 3 tbsp tahini + juice of 1/2 lemon + 1 minced garlic clove + 3-4 tbsp warm water + pinch salt
- Shake until pourable (add water 1 tsp at a time if it seizes)

Plate: couscous, veg + chickpeas on top, drizzle sauce.

Safe cooling for the lunch portion
- Within 30 min of cooking, lift the lunch portion out of the hot pile into its own shallow bowl (don't let it cool in a deep mound)
- Cool to room temp — total time at room temp must stay under 2 hours
- Move to a shallow airtight container (shallow = faster, safer cooling in the fridge)
- Refrigerate promptly; eat within 3-4 days
- Reheat covered with a splash of water, ~90 sec in the microwave, then stir; or eat cold over greens

Ankle-friendly choices built in
- Parchment = no pan scrubbing
- One oven trip, one pan, one roast
- Couscous is pour-boil-cover-rest — no stirring, no babysitting
- Sauce in a jar — no whisk
- Slide the hot pan in/out on a folded towel rather than lifting it loaded

Keep the mug mostly white until the end, and put the cool shadow down before the warm reflection.

The cool shadow is the form-defining pass. In your past studies — the cool window wash against the warm interior edge, the dark bottle against the cool interior shadow — the cool wash goes on first because it's the structural dark and gives the white object its volume. The warm reflection from the orange is a smaller, secondary influence. Treat it as the accent, not the structure.

Why not warm first:
  - Your standing rule is to let the first pass dry fully before touching the warm edge. If the warm reflection goes down first, you can't establish the cool cleanly on top of it without either muddying the boundary or lifting the warm.
  - Orange and blue-gray meeting in a wet edge go neutral gray and kill both readings. This is the same failure mode as the reflected window highlight on the bottle that went muddy when the surrounding neutral was adjusted. Don't set up the meeting in advance.
  - A white ceramic mug should not become a gray object. The mug body stays paper-white; only the shadow zones receive pigment.

Sequence for the 75 minutes:
  1. Light pencil map, nothing heavier.
  2. Cool blue-gray shadow pass — form shadow on the mug and the cast shadow on the surface. Transparent; a half-value step lighter than you think you need, because whites in shadow still read as white.
  3. Let it dry fully. Paper that feels cool, not glossy.
  4. Warm reflection pass — ultramarine plus a small amount of burnt sienna mixed toward orange, but desaturated and a full value step lighter than the cool shadow, not the same value. Apply only on the mug side facing the orange. Thin, not opaque.
  5. Mug body stays paper-white. No midtone wash over the whole form.
  6. Stop at 75 minutes or earlier.

Stop conditions specific to this setup:
  - The warm reflection starts reading as a second shadow edge on the mug. This is what happened when the reflector was moved close to the white cup in your earlier study — it flattened the reflected side and created a competing edge. If the warm edge starts defining a form of its own, stop.
  - The cool shadow and warm reflection meet at a wet edge and the boundary goes neutral gray. Let it dry and accept the separation; do not chase it in-session.
  - The mug starts to look like a gray object rather than a white object in shadow. Step back, compare to the still life, and resist filling in.

One change this session: the order — cool first, warm last, mug body kept as paper-white between them.

Premise check (matches the clinician's rule):
  - Strengthening block today: clean — no symptom.
  - Walking since the 1/8 reassessment: no focal ankle pain.
  - The ride counts as a clean trial only if both the session itself AND the following day stay symptom-free.

Setup (do these before clipping in or stepping on):
  - Posture: upright, hands light on the bars. No aggressive forward lean — that loads the ankle through the forefoot.
  - Saddle height: knee slightly bent at the bottom of the pedal stroke. Neither cramped nor locked out.
  - Foot position: flat on the pedal, or slight heel drop. No cleats that lock the foot/ankle in place.
  - Footwear: ordinary shoes. Not the running shoes being load-tested for anything else.
  - Resistance: lowest practical setting (or near-lowest). Easy enough that the legs drive the flywheel, not the other way around.
  - Cadence: roughly 60–70 rpm — easy conversational walking effort, not spin-class speed.

Structure (17 minutes total — sits cleanly inside the 15–20 window):
  - Minutes 0–3  Warmup — very easy spin, minimal resistance. If any focal ankle sensation shows up here, end the session and reassess.
  - Minutes 3–15  Main — easy effort, low resistance, ~60–70 rpm. Should feel sustainable indefinitely. No surges, no out-of-saddle climbing, no cadence bumps.
  - Minutes 15–17  Cooldown — easier still, resistance drops toward zero, then stop.
  - Upper-bound option: 3 + 15 + 2 = 20 min if you want to land on the high end. Do not exceed 20.

Stop conditions — end the session immediately if any of these appear:
  - Focal ankle pain (especially inside-right ankle, where the recurrent ache has lived).
  - Increasing pain during the ride.
  - Pain at rest while still pedaling.
  - Gait change or limp on dismount.
  - New mechanical sensation — click, catch, give-way.
  - Swelling, bruising, or instability during or right after.
  - Lightheadedness, chest pain, or anything cardio-respiratory.

Same-day check (later that day, before bed):
  - Ordinary walking at normal distance — any focal ankle sensation?
  - One flight of stairs down — any focal sensation?
  - This is the "session-day" half of the rule.

Following-day check (next morning):
  - First ordinary walk — any focal ankle sensation?
  - First stair descent — any focal sensation?
  - This is the "following-day" half of the rule.

Decision logic:
  - Session clean + same-day clean + following-morning clean = one clean stationary-bike trial. No progression implied. Next time is the same 17 (or 20) minutes, same low resistance, same easy cadence.
  - Session clean + same-day has focal sensation = do not ride again this week; note for clinical discussion if it persists.
  - Any focal sensation on the following morning = do not repeat the ride; treat as recurrent focal pain signal; clinical follow-up before another bike session.

What this ride is NOT:
  - Not running clearance.
  - Not the 30-minute brisk-walk test.
  - Not one of the future run-walk sessions (4:1 × 20 min format).
  - Not a third weekly session of any kind.

  - Not a load test for the ankle beyond the current session-plus-following-day rule.

Recommendation: block the apple as one simple shape first, then carve the bag around it.

Why this beats starting with the folds:

- The folds will keep competing as long as they are the active shape. Once the apple is committed as a flat silhouette, the folds become supporting context and naturally read as a wrapper instead of a second drawing.
- A hard apple edge gives the bag somewhere to stop. Right now every fold has to find its own boundary, which is what is making them read independently.
- A negative-space-only approach is the right call when the bag is the subject and the apple is a small accent. Here the apple is doing real compositional mass, so it needs an actual value commitment, not just a reserved hole.

Suggested order for the 75 minutes:

1. Light pencil outline of both. Schematic only: placement, the apple's full silhouette, the bag's main mass and a few major fold anchors. No fold detail yet.
2. Block the apple as one flat shape: a single mid-value wash in its local red, full silhouette, hard edge all the way around. No modeling, no highlight, no stem. Treat it as a stamp.
3. Let the apple dry fully. Paper should feel cool, not glossy.
4. Paint the bag against the apple's edge. Two or three values only: paper light, a warm brown mid, and a darker fold accent. Vary edges deliberately: hard where a fold comes forward or meets the apple, soft or lost where it recedes into shadow or tucks behind the apple.
5. Stop before the highlight, the stem, the cast shadow on the bag, or any second pass on the apple. Those belong to a later session if the read still works.

Stop conditions for this block — pick up another day if any of these fire:

- The apple silhouette softens or picks up adjacent bag color
- A fold edge crosses the apple boundary and reads as a line through the fruit
- The bag's value range starts matching the apple's, so they compete on equal terms again
- 75 minutes reached

What this is not:

- Not a finished-painting plan, just a sequencing choice for this block
- Not a recipe for the whole piece; stem, highlight, cast shadow stay out of scope today
- Not a judgment that the bag should be less developed, only that the apple should be committed first so the folds stop competing

If you actually want to reverse the priority and treat the bag as the primary subject with the apple as a small accent, the negative-space approach makes more sense in that case — but from how you described it, the apple is the figure and deserves the first block.

A backrun is a pigment deposit from reactivated moisture. Your clean window edge is the load-bearing constraint, so every step below works from the bloom outward into the surrounding wash and never toward the window.

0. Pre-check (don't skip)
   - Sheet bone-dry everywhere (press a clean tissue to a corner; if it picks up dampness, wait).
   - Window edge traced with your eye. The window itself is never touched at any point.
   - Ready: a round brush slightly smaller than the bloom footprint, a second clean damp brush for lifting, tissue, and your wash color mixed at the original dilution.

1. Lift pass (one)
   - Load the brush with clean water, then offload on tissue until it is damp, not wet.
   - Touch the bloom only. Hold 10–15 seconds. Do not stroke.
   - Blot straight down with tissue, or pull up with a barely-damp clean brush. No scrubbing.
   - Dry fully. Inspect (hair dryer on low is fine for a fast read; no overheating).

2. Decision gate — stop lifting, switch to glazing if any of these is true:
   - the bloom has spread, developed a cauliflower edge, or sent a tendril toward the window
   - the surrounding wash has feathered or lifted at its inner edge
   - the paper surface looks fuzzy, flocked, or nap-raising (abrasion starting)
   - you've completed two lift passes and the bloom is still clearly there

   Otherwise proceed to step 3.

3. Lift pass two (optional)
   - Same procedure, same brush footprint, same offload discipline.
   - Stop the moment the bloom sits within roughly half a value step of the surrounding wash. Do not chase full invisibility — that is where overwork starts.

4. Decision gate
   - Within ~half a value of the wash → dry fully (10+ minutes, or low dryer plus 2 minutes rest). You can stop and accept, or do one thin glaze to harmonize.
   - Still prominent after two lifts → stop lifting entirely, go to step 5. Further scrubbing will cost the sheet more than it returns.

5. Glaze (only if needed)
   - Mix the surrounding wash at original dilution. Test on scrap if available.
   - Load the brush, then offload heavily — you want a damp glaze, not a wet one.
   - Single pass covering the bloom and feathering slightly into the wash. Stay at least one brush-width clear of the window edge.
   - Dry fully. Inspect. One additional pass is the cap.

Hard stops — any one ends the procedure:
   - moisture or pigment migrates toward the window edge — blot immediately, let dry, do not touch this sheet again for at least an hour
   - paper surface abrades, pills, or raises a nap
   - three total interventions (lifts plus glazes combined) and the result is not where you want it
   - the bloom remains but you've hit a defined plateau — leaving it costs the sheet less than continuing

One framing note: a single soft backrun sitting just inside a window in a small study often reads as a tonal note rather than a flaw. If after step 1 the bloom is reduced to a soft mark, that is a legitimate stopping point. The stop condition exists precisely so you can stop there without feeling like you quit early.

1. Stop. Don't open the split further, don't feed from it, and don't decant kibble into another container to "save" it.

2. Quarantine.
   - Leave the kibble inside the damaged bag.

   - Store it apart from your existing Kibo food — different shelf, ideally a different spot.

What the finding likely is

Two holes in wool plus one dry empty casing, no live insect, no cotton damage is most consistent with clothes moth (casemaking or webbing species) larval feeding. Cotton is largely untouched because larvae prefer keratin (wool, silk, fur, feathers). One casing means at least one larva completed pupation; that is a real finding, not "just an old bug." Scope is not yet established.

Isolation — do this first

  1. Bag the throw sealed (heavy plastic, zip-seal or contractor bag). Fold gently; do not shake.
  2. Move Kibo out of the room before the next steps. The throw itself is not a hazard to him, but cleaning stirs particles and you do not want him on the light sheet or near the vacuum exhaust.
  3. Lay a light-colored sheet on a table and unfold the throw over it, section by section, in good light. Look for: live larvae (cream, ≤1 cm), more casings, webbing in folds, fine gritty frass, adult moths (pale, ~6–8 mm, weak flutter).
  4. Photograph each finding before handling further. Date and item noted.
  5. Inspect adjacent storage: closet shelves, under furniture, other wool/silk/fur/feather items. Anything stored undisturbed for weeks near the throw is the priority zone.
  6. Bag any other suspect item separately. Do not mix with clean items.

Wool-appropriate treatment for the throw, in preference order

  - Freezing: sealed bag, 0°F (-18°C) for at least 72 hours. Kills all life stages. Pet-safe.
  - Dry cleaning: standard solvents kill all stages. Tell the cleaner you suspect moth activity so the load is isolated.
  - Hot wash + high-heat dryer only if the care label permits; many wools do not.
  - Skip: home laundering alone (eggs/casings can survive), mothballs (pet toxic), any spray, bomb, or fogger.

Storage area — no pesticides

  - Vacuum slowly along baseboards, shelf seams, and under nearby furniture. Vibration pulls larvae out of crevices.
  - Immediately seal and remove the vacuum bag, or empty the canister into a sealed bag, outside.
  - Wipe hard surfaces with a damp cloth and dilute dish soap, or dilute white vinegar. Dry fully.
  - Do not return wool/silk items to the area until the monitoring window closes.

Monitoring — run for 6 weeks (one full life cycle)

  - Pheromone wing traps for webbing clothes moth, one per storage zone. Place high and behind items where Kibo cannot reach. Catch indicates active adult males, not severity.
  - Weekly visual check of remaining wool/silk/fur items: new holes, casings, frass, adults.
  - Note any flying adults near stored clothes. Casemaking moths tend to scuttle; webbing moths flutter weakly.
  - Keep a brief log (date, item, what you saw). A log helps if you escalate.

Call a professional if any of these appear

  - Live larvae or adults on more than one item.
  - Webbing on walls, ceiling, or closet interiors (signals a larger population).
  - Pheromone traps catching more than a few moths per week consistently across 2–3 weeks.
  - New damage appearing on additional wool or silk items despite cleaning.
  - You cannot identify a likely source zone, or items sit in long-undisturbed storage you cannot fully access.
  - Anything that makes you unsure. One inspection is cheaper than waiting.

What this is not

Not yet a confirmed "infestation" — one casing is a single developmental event, not a scope claim. Treat it as possible, prepare as if small, and escalate on the triggers above. Do not assume the rest of the closet is fine without checking; do not assume the throw is ruined without treatment.

Pre-flight check (do this before any tool contact):
- Confirm the gap edge by running a clean, dry fingertip slowly along all four edges. The unglued gap will feel like a 2–3 mm smooth indent; the glued edges feel slightly raised or tacky. Note which edge it is and its full length. Do not assume "top" — different manufacturers place the gap on different edges.
- Reconfirm dryness with the back of a hand held just above the painted surface for ~5 seconds, then a fingertip touch in a margin area. Paper should feel room-temperature (not cool) and not tacky. If it feels cool or sticky anywhere, stop and wait. A damp sheet will tear on removal.

Stabilize the block:
- Work on a clean, flat, rigid surface (table or cutting mat).
- Place a sheet of clean glass or a heavy flat book on top of the block, but offset it so the gap edge protrudes by roughly 1 cm (just enough to insert the tool). The weight keeps the lower sheets from lifting with the top sheet.
- If the block tends to slide, set it on a damp towel or non-slip mat. Don't grip the block with your free hand during the cut — that pressure can buckle the top sheet.

Tool choice:
- A flat, thin, blunt plastic palette knife (about 3–4 cm wide, edges slightly rounded) is the standard choice. It is rigid enough to slide between sheets but blunt enough not to shear fibers.
- Acceptable substitutes: a flexible plastic ruler edge, an old credit card, or a bone folder with the corner blunted. Avoid sharp metal palette knives, X-Acto blades, or anything serrated. The tool separates by sliding, not by cutting — sharpness is not what you need.
- Wipe the tool clean and dry before starting. Any moisture or dried paint on the edge can transfer to the next sheet or grab fibers.

Direction of travel — this is the critical point:
- The tool moves PARALLEL to the paper surface, sliding in the plane between sheet 1 and sheet 2. It does NOT angle down into the stack.
- Insert the tool into the gap at a very shallow angle (almost flat, maybe 5–10° up from horizontal), tip pointing along the gap edge.
- Slide along the bound edge in one direction at a time. If the gap is on the top short edge, slide from one corner of that edge toward the other, then withdraw.
- Work in short increments (3–5 cm), withdraw slightly, then re-insert and advance further. Do not try to traverse the whole edge in one continuous stroke on the first pass.
- The tool should always feel like it is sliding between two sheets of paper. You should feel mild adhesive resistance, but never a "bite."

Stop immediately and reassess if any of these occur:
- The tool catches, snags, or starts to drag rather than slide. (Cause is usually the tool tipping downward — back it out parallel to the sheets, not upward.)
- You feel the tool pressing into a sheet below the top one. (This means the angle has gone wrong. Withdraw, re-flatten, reinsert at the gap.)
- You see paper fibers lifting on either the painting or the underlying sheet.
- The top sheet starts to buckle, ripple, or lift in the middle (not just at the gap edge).
- Adhesive accumulates on the tool in a way that gums the tip. (Wipe clean, then resume only if you can re-insert without dragging residue across the next sheet.)
- The second sheet begins to ride up with the top one. (Stop — your weight/stabilization is insufficient, or the adhesive is bonding multiple sheets.)
- You hear any tearing sound, however faint.

How to recover from a stop:
- Withdraw the tool slowly, keeping it parallel to the paper. Do not jerk it up or sideways.
- Set the tool aside. Let any disturbed adhesive settle for 2–3 minutes.
- Inspect the gap edge under raking light for lifted fibers or torn adhesive.
- Resume only after identifying the cause (usually angle or pressure) and correcting it. If the same stop condition repeats on the next increment, abandon the removal — a sheet that resists removal is not worth damaging.

Releasing the other three edges (most blocks glue all four):
- Once the gap edge is fully released, do not lift the sheet yet. Gently flex the top sheet upward from the freed edge, just enough to break the adhesive on the next edge. The adhesive should let go with mild resistance — if it doesn't, stop and re-evaluate rather than pulling harder.
- Repeat for the remaining two edges, working around the sheet. The corners are the most likely spots to catch; if a corner resists, work the two adjacent edges a little further before retrying the corner.

Final lift:
- Once all edges are free, lift the sheet straight up off the block. Do not slide it sideways — sliding can catch the leading edge on remaining adhesive or the next sheet's lip.
- Set it painted-side up on a clean sheet of glass or a smooth board.

What this is not:
- Not a recommendation for any specific block brand or adhesive type — these vary, and if yours turns out to be heavily glued or aged, the safer outcome is to leave the painting in the block and trim around it later.
- Not advice for blocks with no gap (some cheap blocks glue all four edges with no entry point). Those require a different technique and higher risk; consider a conservator or leaving the work attached.
- Not a license to force the sheet off if resistance appears. The stop conditions above are absolute, not advisory.

REAR TIRE — DIAGNOSTIC INFLATION + INSPECTION (NOT ROAD-READY)

Framing: You asked for a conservative stationary inflation, a short-interval recheck schedule, a visible-damage sequence, and clear conditions for leaving the bike unridden for shop inspection rather than treating inflation alone as proof of road-readiness. That is exactly what is below. The protocol does not authorize riding — ankle rehab is the separate gate.

WHAT THIS PROTOCOL IS NOT
  - Not a riding authorization.
  - Not a substitute for shop inspection.
  - Not proof the tube, tire, or rim is sound if pressure holds short-term.
  - Not a verdict on the cause of the 38 psi reading (slow leak vs. cold-temperature loss vs. bead not fully seated). The 16 psi gap vs. the front tire (54 psi), assuming similar storage, points to a rear-specific issue rather than uniform ambient loss — but that is a pointer, not a conclusion.

INFLATION SEQUENCE (STATIONARY, STAGED)

  Run the visible-damage inspection first. You do not want to pressurize a tire you are about to find is damaged.

  1. Note starting state: 38 psi, [time], [ambient temp], valve position (e.g., 6 o'clock). Recheck the gauge at the same valve position every time for comparable readings.
  2. Confirm valve type (Schrader vs Presta) and that the pump head seats cleanly. A poor seal at the head will read as a leak that is not the tire's fault.
  3. Inflate in stages, pausing to listen at the valve and watch the gauge for drift between strokes:
     - to 30 psi — pause 30 sec, hand near valve, listen for hiss
     - to 40 psi — pause 30 sec
     - to 50 psi (marked minimum) — pause 30 sec
     - to ~55 psi — small buffer above the marked minimum, still conservative. Do NOT exceed the marked maximum on the sidewall (which you have not stated; read it before pushing higher).
  4. Disconnect the pump. Hold a fingertip or wet lip near the valve stem for ~10 seconds. Any air movement = leak at the valve/core.
  5. Record the final pressure, time, and ambient temp. The tire is now at diagnostic pressure, not riding pressure. Riding pressure is a shop-set number.

PRESSURE RECHECK SCHEDULE (SHORT-INTERVAL)

  Recheck at the same gauge, same valve position, with the tire cold (not just after pumping or after rolling the bike across the room):

  - T+15 min post-inflation: Fast leak screen. Drop >1–2 psi = problem.
  - T+2 hours: Thermal equilibration + moderate leak screen. Indoor warming from an outdoor-cold reading typically adds ~1 psi per 10°F. Note the temp delta so you know what is equilibration and what is drift.
  - T+12 hours / next morning (cold): True cold-soak baseline. This is the comparison point for all later checks.
  - T+24 hours: Slow-leak screen. Drop >2 psi vs. the T+12 reading = leak.
  - Optional T+72 hours: Very-slow-leak confirmation. Not required, but useful before relying on the tire for a commute.

  Log each reading with pressure, time, ambient temp, and valve position. Calendar reminders at T+15 min, T+2 hr, T+12 hr, T+24 hr are reasonable if you want the schedule to actually fire.

VISIBLE-DAMAGE INSPECTION SEQUENCE

  Can be run at 38 psi — no need to pressurize first. Order is outside-in.

  1. Tread, full circumference: Sweep a finger across slowly. Feel for embedded glass, wire, thorn, staple. Look for cuts that reach the casing (visible casing threads or cord = no-go for reuse). Do NOT pull embedded objects you find — that is a shop call.
  2. Sidewalls, both sides, full circumference: Look for cuts, cracking, scuffing through to casing, and any bulge — even a subtle 5 mm raised area. A bulge means broken internal casing fabric; the tire is not reuseable regardless of pressure.
  3. Bead, both sides, full circumference: Tire should sit evenly in the rim well. No tube visible between bead and rim (pinch). Bead hook uniformly engaged on the rim flange all the way around. Uneven seating is a slow-leak path even when pressure holds.
  4. Valve: Core straight and seated, not tilted. Locknut (if any) snug, not over-tight. No hiss when the pump is removed. Stem base not bulging or weeping.
  5. Rim: No cracks at spoke holes, no dents, no flat spots. Spin the wheel and watch for lateral wobble (out of true) or vertical hop. Rim tape intact, covering every spoke hole, no tears or displacement.
  6. Spokes: None broken or visibly loose. Pluck each — tone should be consistent across the wheel. Skipped or dull spokes = wheel needs truing before the bike carries a rider.

  Front tire at 54 psi needs no inflation action now, but include it in any shop drop-off if the rear shows a confirmed issue, since road debris tends to be selective by wheel.

SHOP INSPECTION — LEAVE THE BIKE UNRIDDEN IF ANY OF THESE APPLY

  Escalate to the shop (do not treat inflation success as road-readiness) if ANY of the following is true at any point in the protocol:

  Pressure-side:
    - Pressure cannot be raised to 50 psi (gross leak, blockage, valve failure).
    - Audible hiss during inflation or at rest.
    - Wet-lip or finger test shows air movement at the valve.
    - Drop >2 psi between any 24-hour interval (e.g., T+12 → T+24).
    - Drop >5 psi in any single shorter interval (e.g., T+15 min, T+2 hr).
    - Pressure holds 24 hours but you want certainty before relying on the bike for a commute — default to shop. A hold is evidence, not a verdict.

  Damage-side:
    - Any sidewall bulge, even subtle.
    - Any cut reaching the casing (threads/cord visible).
    - Any crack, abrasion-through, or exposed casing.
    - Bead will not seat evenly, or tube is visible between bead and rim.
    - Valve stem crooked, leaking at the base, or core will not hold.
    - Spoke broken, nipple loose, or wheel out of true.
    - Rim crack, dent, or damaged/missing rim tape.
    - Embedded object found that you cannot remove with certainty — leave it in place and let the shop decide.

  Uncertainty-side:
    - Any finding you cannot classify with confidence — do not guess.
    - Tire age unknown (no readable date code on the sidewall) AND any slow-leak signal.
    - Front tire also showing unexpected behavior — suggests a systematic issue, not an isolated rear problem.

WHY INFLATION-ALONE IS NOT ROAD-READINESS

  A 24-hour pressure hold demonstrates the tire can hold static pressure at rest. It does NOT demonstrate:
    - The tube is sound long-term (a slow leak can take days to manifest).
    - The casing is structurally intact (a broken casing can look fine when static and fail under load).
    - The bead will hold under cornering and braking loads.
    - The rim is structurally sound (spoke-hole cracks, dents).
    - The wheel is true and evenly tensioned.
    - The tire is appropriate for your load, route, and speed.

  Shop inspection converts "holds pressure" into a road-readiness verdict. Until that verdict exists, the bike stays parked — independent of ankle rehab status, which is a separate and earlier gate.

NEXT CONCRETE STEPS (NARROW)

  1. Inspection first (tire still at 38 psi, no inflation yet).
  2. If inspection is clean, run the staged inflation to ~55 psi.
  3. T+15 min and T+2 hr recheck tonight.
  4. T+12 hr and T+24 hr recheck tomorrow / day after.
  5. Decide at T+24 hr whether to (a) book a shop inspection with current evidence, or (b) extend to T+72 hr if the hold is clean and you want one more data point before booking.
  6. Do not change riding plans based on pressure holding alone. The shop verdict is the gate.

ROSEMARY — INDOOR ACCLIMATION (FEB 7, 2027)

What this is: a stabilization sequence based on what you observed today. Not a diagnosis of cause. Not a recommendation to fertilize or repot.

Observed baseline (yours, not changing):
- Several dry brown tips
- Slightly drooping newer growth
- Pot drains freely, no standing water, top inch of soil dry
- No webbing, sticky residue, or visible insects
- Near a bright window, away from the heating vent

Together these are consistent with normal acclimation stress from outdoor → indoor (light drop, humidity drop, microclimate change). Brown tips plus drooping newer growth is a common and usually reversible pattern if conditions are held steady.

WATERING (next 1-2 weeks):

1. Today: water thoroughly until water exits the drainage holes. Room-temperature water. Let the pot drain completely. Empty any saucer/catch tray within ~15 minutes — the pot must not sit in runoff.

2. Between waterings: check the top 1 inch of soil with a finger. Water again only when the top inch is dry AND the pot feels noticeably lighter than just after watering. Do not water on a calendar schedule.

3. Avoid small frequent splashes. Rosemary prefers a deep soak followed by a partial dry-down.

4. Same water source each time is fine; tap is normal in Austin. If a white crust appears on the soil surface later, that is mineral buildup and we can revisit.

LIGHT:

- Rosemary wants 6+ hours of direct sun. Indoors in February this is hard to deliver.
- Window direction check: south-facing is best (Northern Hemisphere), east/west acceptable, north-facing usually insufficient. If you don't already know which, the sun's midday position on the sill tells you.
- Quick test at midday: is direct sun actually on the leaves for at least 4-5 hours? "Bright" can mean strong ambient light without direct rays.
- If direct sun is under ~4 hours: a full-spectrum LED grow light 6-8 inches above the plant, on a 12-14 hour timer, is the conservative fix. One ~$20-30 bulb is enough.

DRAINAGE:

- Already confirmed: pot drains, no standing water. Do not change pots unless one of the triggers below appears.
- At each watering: confirm water exits the bottom within seconds and clear the saucer promptly.

ACCLIMATION (next 1-2 weeks):

- Expect some continued stress: a little more browning or minor leaf drop during the transition is normal.
- Temperature: stable 60-70°F if possible. Avoid cold drafts and any direct heat source.
- Humidity: indoor winter air in Austin is often 20-30%; rosemary prefers 40-50%. Conservative boost: pebble tray with water under the pot (pot on pebbles, water below the pebble tops — the pot must not sit in water).
- Do not fertilize. Stressed roots plus fertilizer = burn risk.
- Do not repot. The move indoors is enough root disturbance for now.

MONITORING:

- Daily: finger-check soil moisture; visual scan for any new symptom.
- Every few days: rotate the pot a quarter turn so growth stays even.
- Weekly: take one photo from the same angle. Compare against today.
- Track three things only: new growth appearing, brown tips holding vs. spreading, drooping resolving vs. continuing.

SIGNS THAT JUSTIFY CONSULTING A LOCAL PLANT PROFESSIONAL:

Escalation triggers, not diagnoses. Contact a nursery with horticulture staff (not a big-box floor associate) only if any of these appear:

- Sudden or rapid leaf drop (multiple stems losing leaves within a day or two)
- Stems becoming soft, mushy, black, or collapsed at the soil line
- Foul smell from the soil
- White, yellow, or fuzzy growth on the soil surface
- Visible insects, webbing, or sticky residue appearing on the plant or nearby surfaces
- Continued drooping after 2 weeks of consistent watering and adequate light
- Roots emerging from drainage holes (this is the one trigger that opens the repotting door)
- Any symptom that is spreading rapidly rather than holding steady

Bring a current photo plus a short note: when moved indoors, what you've changed, what you've observed.

WHAT THIS PLAN IS NOT:

- Not a diagnosis of cause
- Not a recommendation to fertilize
- Not a recommendation to repot
- Not a pest or disease assessment
- Not a recovery claim — this is a stabilization path; the observed outcome will tell us

If after 2 weeks the brown tips have stopped spreading, the drooping has resolved, and new growth looks normal, the plant has acclimated and you can return to ordinary rosemary care. If anything in the escalation list appears, escalate.

For the unaltered preservation master, every setting that mutates pixel values before the file is written has to be off. That includes the three you already saw enabled — Auto enhance, Dust removal, Color restore — and the related defaults that usually travel with them: auto-tone / auto-exposure, auto white-balance, sharpening / unsharp mask, noise reduction / despeckle, backlight or shading correction, deskew, and auto-crop. Those are the same class of operation that dropped the faint pencil writing off P037's back in August 2024, so none of them belong on the master pass. Keep color-profile embedding on — it's metadata describing the captured values, not a change to the pixels — and set resolution and bit depth explicitly (e.g., 600 DPI, 48-bit color); those are capture parameters, not corrections.

For output controls, use the two-track structure as designed. "Save original capture" stays on and is your master. It must only ever receive a scan run with all of the above corrections disabled, so the bytes written match what the sensor saw plus the embedded profile and the resolution / bit-depth parameters — nothing else. "Create adjusted copy" stays off during the preservation session itself: any dust removal, color restore, tone curve, sharpening, rotation, or crop lives on a derivative, never on the master. When a derivative is later wanted, generate it from the master in a separate step (a non-destructive editor, or a fresh export to a different filename), save it with a distinct suffix like `_access`, and never overwrite, replace, or "save back to" the master.

That's the rule that keeps any optional later adjustment a derivative rather than a change to the original capture: corrections are off when the master is written, and any later adjustment is confined to a separately named copy made from — not back into — the master. The master stays verifiable by checksum and timestamp regardless of what later happens to the derivative.

SHORT-TERM DRIVING BOUNDARY (UNTIL THE DRIVER BLADE IS REPLACED)

What is OK:
- Dry conditions. Drive normally. Do NOT run the driver wiper on dry glass — the split rubber can drag grit across the windshield and shorten the new blade's life too.
- Light drizzle in full daylight, only if the streak does not cross the center of your primary sight line at any point in the sweep.

What is not OK:
- Any sustained rain that needs the driver blade. The passenger blade alone cannot clear the driver-side glass.
- Night rain at any intensity — the smear turns oncoming headlight glare into a flash.
- Heavy rain, pooling water, storms, sleet, wet snow.
- Any rain combined with low sun, tunnel lighting, or oncoming glare.

Practical containment:
- Treat the driver blade as out of service until the new one is on.
- If unexpected rain starts before you have the new blade, pull over and wait it out rather than relying on a half-clearing driver side.

WHEN YOU SHOULD NOT DRIVE IN RAIN

- Any rain at night.
- Any rain heavy enough to require continuous wiping across the driver side.
- Any rain where the smear overlaps your primary sight line.
- After fitting the new blade, also do not drive in rain until the post-fit verification below is clean.

REPLACEMENT SEQUENCE

1. Confirm fit before buying.
   - Driver-side length: read it off the existing blade or the owner's manual. Driver and passenger are usually different lengths — do not swap them.
   - Attachment type: most modern cars use a J-hook (also called hook or side-hook). Others use a side pin, pinch tab, top lock, or push button. Look at the fitting where the blade meets the arm, or photograph it and match against the new blade's packaging diagram.

2. Lift the driver arm.
   - Raise the arm away from the glass until it stays up on its own.
   - Lay a folded towel on the windshield under the arm. If the arm snaps back without a blade on it, it can crack the glass. This is the single most common wiper-related windshield injury — do not skip it.

3. Remove the old blade.
   - Most J-hook blades: depress the small release tab under the connector, then slide the blade downward (away from the arm) until the hook clears.
   - If no visible tab: rotate the blade parallel to the arm and slide it off the hook.
   - If unsure, follow the printed instruction sheet that comes with the new blade — they almost always include a vehicle-specific diagram.

4. Inspect the arm before installing the new blade.
   - Confirm the hook is not bent, cracked, or worn.
   - Confirm the spring tension: the arm should hold the blade firmly against the glass. A weak arm will streak even with a new blade.

5. Fit the new blade.
   - Slide the new connector into the hook from below until the locking tab clicks.
   - Tug gently to confirm it is fully seated.
   - Make sure the blade sits centered along the arm, not angled.

6. Return the arm.
   - Lower it back onto the windshield slowly by hand. Do not let it snap down.

7. Leave the passenger blade in place — you said it is intact.

POST-FIT VERIFICATION (BEFORE DRIVING IN ANY RAIN)

Do all of these. None is optional.

- Seating: visually confirm the blade lies flat against the glass, with no lift at the ends and no curl along the length.
- Click test: tug the blade toward you; it should not slip off the hook.
- Washer-fluid test: with the engine running, spray washer fluid across the entire sweep.
  - No streaking, no chattering, no skipping.
  - Both up and down strokes clear evenly.
  - No "hopping" anywhere in the arc.
  - The rubber edge should leave a uniform, almost dry film — not beads, not a smear.
- Edge check: dry the blade edge and run a clean finger along it. You should feel a single clean wiping lip with no nicks, lifted sections, or hard edges. If the new blade itself has a defect, exchange it before driving.
- Listen: any tick, slap, or skipping sound means the blade is mis-seated or the arm is weak.
- Park position: confirm the blade returns to the bottom of the windshield, not higher up the glass.

Post-fit, do not assume:
- One daylight spray test is not a guarantee. Do one more check at low speed in actual light rain before relying on it in heavier conditions.
- A streak that reappears in real rain is a fitting or arm issue, not a bad blade.

If the new blade still streaks:
- Re-seat the connector first — most streaking after a swap is mis-seating.
- Clean the windshield with isopropyl alcohol or a dedicated glass cleaner; any remaining film looks exactly like a blade defect.
- If still streaking after both, the arm spring is likely weak. That is a separate fix.

WHAT THIS IS NOT

- Not a windshield diagnosis. You said the glass has no chip or crack, so I am treating the glass as sound.
- Not a passenger-side blade recommendation. You said it is intact.
- Not a washer-fluid or washer-pump diagnosis. If the spray above is uneven, that is a separate issue.
- Not a specific blade-length or brand recommendation. Confirm against your vehicle's existing blade or owner's manual.

Tuscan-style white beans and kale, with lemon-rosemary toast. One pot, ~25 min, dinner tonight + one lunch portion for Sam.

Setup before you start
- Half onion, diced (≈1/2 cup)
- 2–3 garlic cloves, minced
- 1/2 tsp dried rosemary
- 1 tbsp olive oil
- 2 cans white beans, drained and rinsed (≈3 cups)
- 14-oz can diced tomatoes (use as-is, with juice)
- 2 cups vegetable broth
- Small bunch kale, stems stripped out, leaves torn (≈3 packed cups)
- Half lemon
- 4 slices sturdy bread, salt, pepper

Timed sequence (one pot, medium heat throughout)

0:00  Pot on medium. Oil, then onion and rosemary. Stir occasionally.

3:00  Add garlic. Stir 30–60 sec until fragrant — do not let it brown.

4:00  Add the can of diced tomatoes (juice and all). Stir, scraping up any onion fond.

5:00  Add both cans of beans and the 2 cups broth. Bring to a gentle simmer. Lightly mash a few beans against the side of the pot with the back of a spoon — this thickens the stew without cream.

10:00 While the simmer is on, toast the bread. Toaster or dry skillet, 2–3 min total; you want sturdy, not rock-hard. Set 2 slices aside for tonight, keep 2 for Sam's lunch so they don't go soggy in the container.

12:00 Add the kale. Push it under the liquid; it looks like too much but it collapses fast. Return to a gentle simmer.

18:00 Taste. Salt and pepper. Simmer 4–5 min more so the stew reduces slightly and the kale is fully tender, not just wilted.

22:00 Off heat. Zest the half lemon straight in, then squeeze in 1–2 tbsp juice. Stir. The acid brightens the whole pot.

Plate
- Shallow bowl, slice of toast on the bottom, ladle stew over and around it; second slice on the side. A small drizzle of olive oil on top is nice if you have it.

Sam's lunch (1 portion + 2 toast slices)
- Ladle the remaining stew into a SHALLOW container — not the deep cooking pot. Shallow = faster, safer cooling.
- Pack the 2 toast slices separately so they stay firm.
- Fridge once it has stopped steaming, ideally within ~30 min; eat within 3 days.

Safe-cooling notes
- Do not seal the hot pot and drop it straight in the fridge — trapped steam warms the fridge and slows cooling of everything in it.
- Shallow container, lid set on but slightly vented, into the fridge; aim to cross 70°F within ~30 min on the counter first if you have time.
- Next day: reheat gently with a splash of broth or water (beans drink the liquid overnight), stir often, heat until steaming throughout (≈165°F).

Cleanup
- One pot, one spoon, one cutting board, one knife. If you toast in a skillet, that's the only extra pan. Soak the pot while you eat — dried beans come off easily after a 10-min soak.

The first mistake is structural, not value or texture: you rendered the bow, shaft, and teeth as three separately-modeled masses, each with its own internal light logic, instead of as one brass form resting on the same cloth in the same light. That is why the eye is reading three small icons rather than one key.

The corrective move, before any highlight or cloth texture, is to lay down **one continuous cast shadow running beneath and to one side of the whole key — bow, shaft, and teeth together — in a single light direction.** That single shadow mass is what physically anchors all three parts to the same ground and turns three shapes into one object. Without it, even correct highlights and clean tooth notches will reinforce the three-symbol reading rather than fix it.

Two things belong to the same fix, not as separate steps:

- **One light direction, applied consistently across all three parts.** If the bow's highlight is upper-left, the shaft and teeth highlights are upper-left too, and the cast shadow is lower-right (or whichever way you commit to). Don't let the bow and teeth have different implied light.
- **One brass value family across all three parts.** If the bow is sitting at a mid brass and the teeth are noticeably darker for no optical reason, the eye reads them as different objects in the same picture.

Order for the rest of the block:

1. Lift or soften any cast-shadow fragments already painted under the individual parts so they can be re-laid as one shape.
2. Paint one unified cast shadow across the key's full footprint in one direction.
3. Only then add highlights — they will now reinforce one object instead of three.
4. Cloth texture last, after the key reads as one.

Stop condition worth naming now: if after the unified shadow the bow still visually floats from the shaft, the problem has shifted from shadow to **contour** — there's likely a hard color or value break where bow meets shaft rather than a continuous brass tone carried across the join. That is a different fix (carry the brass tone across the join, soften the seam) and is worth distinguishing from the shadow work so you don't try to solve a contour problem by repainting shadows.

One thing this diagnosis is not: it is not a call to repaint the tooth notches, the bow's inner cutout, or the brass hue. Those are downstream of the read-as-one-object problem and won't fix it on their own.

Semantic problem

`connector_authentication` and `external_authority` are not the same fact. One records that the connector transport completed successfully — token exchange, refresh state, the OAuth handshake. The other records that the verified external-system authority is current and `yes`, i.e. an available owner (or available owner-equivalent) can actually perform the required owner-level permission or network-allowlist action inside the target system. A workspace can have an authenticated connector and still lack the authority the connector needs; it can also hold verified authority while the connector itself is unauthenticated, stale, or pending. Collapsing them into one `setup_ready` boolean would force four real states into one label, and the two states that fail closed (authority unresolved, connector unauthenticated) would be indistinguishable from each other and from the true ready state. The proposed mapping — "yes means setup prompts may proceed" — is exactly the loss of meaning that the governed-field design was built to prevent. A yes on the merged field would describe a connector-authenticated record that looks ready while owner-level permission or network-allowlist action is still unresolved.

Operational problem

The two fields have different source owners, different freshness rules, different fail-closed behaviors, and different escalation paths. Merging them:

  hides which source is stale, conflicting, or missing when only one is,
  collapses distinct owner lanes into a single implicit owner,
  prevents the visible field-specific hold that the rest of the system relies on,
  lets a `yes` drive customer-facing prompts and lifecycle decisions on a foundation that cannot certify what the yes actually certifies,
  removes the semantic disagreement a shadow replay would need to detect.

Any reuse of a merged `setup_ready` as a routing or prompt trigger would re-introduce the exact suppressed-suppression / fail-open risk the existing design rules out.

CTA — reject.

RISKY IMPLICATIONS OF THE PROPOSED COPY

1.  Categorical upgrade claim.  "You're ready to upgrade" and "outgrown your current plan" convert a behavior-based eligibility signal (integration depth + recent active admin activity + a usage-ceiling crossing within the prior 14 days) into a categorical statement that the account IS ready and HAS outgrown.  Eligibility is a precondition for exposure, not a determination of customer need.  The language makes a logical leap the observed signals do not support.

2.  Plan / entitlement drift.  "Outgrown your current plan" and "next tier" frame Helio's plan as the entitlement unit.  That is the sales-oriented, plan-fit language previously rejected for the controlled beta.

3.  CTA collapses the help-or-options path.  "Upgrade now" is a single commercial-direction button.  The standing Expansion Assist design is a neutral help-or-options path that preserves three legitimate outcomes (help, options, no change).  A single upgrade CTA forecloses the help branch (customer may just want to understand what triggered the message or configure existing setup) and removes the no-change branch from view.

4.  Loses the "no plan change initiated" anchor.  Prior required wording explicitly stated that no plan change had been initiated; the proposed copy implies the opposite — that the customer is already on an upgrade path.

5.  Eligibility window not anchored.  Behavior-based eligibility is window-bound (usage ceiling crossed within the prior 14 days, recent active admin, sustained integration depth).  The body reads as a generic "recent usage" claim, which overstates the strength and freshness of the signal.

6.  Causal / forecast leakage.  Phrasing the prompt as a state of being "ready to upgrade" implies that action is warranted and likely.  Expansion Assist is descriptive and must remain non-causal and must not produce pipeline, revenue, or forecast treatment.  Sales-flavored exposure copy contaminates the descriptive evidence base.

7.  Handoff contamination.  CS-first handoff suppression is already enforced upstream for active CS adoption / renewal work, so by construction an exposed account has none.  But a categorical upgrade prompt can cause downstream handlers to default to commercial routes when the customer was actually asking for help, eroding the help-or-options design.

9.  Brand / trust risk in a beta.  A categorical sales frame in a controlled beta erodes the neutrality of the experiment and risks customer backlash that would not be attributable to Expansion Assist but would still harm the program's standing.

10. Subject / signal conflation.  The copy does not name signup age (good), but it conflates signals with verdict.  A tightened version should anchor to the actual signals observed (recent usage threshold, active integrations, recent admin activity) rather than to a plan-fit conclusion.

  - Tofu: pressed → fried dry → held UNCOVERED on a rack (covering traps steam → soggy) → re-seared at service
  - Vegetables: high heat, fast, no salt (salt draws water out → mush), no lid (lid steams them), sauce applied only at the moment of eating so the cornstarch slurry coats instead of pools
  - Sauce split and held in jars, not poured over and forgotten

TIMING
  - Press + prep: 7 min
  - Cook: 12 min
  - Total active: ~20 min
  - Sam's refresh: 3 min

LIMITS
  - Assumes Sam arrives within ~2 hours. Past that, refrigerate the tofu and veg; refresh in a dry hot pan (tofu may lose a touch of crispness, the re-sear recovers most of it). Never refrigerate sauced veg — the cornstarch slurry breaks and turns gluey.
  - If Sam arrives in <30 min, time the cook so you finish ~5 min before he walks in and skip the hold entirely.
  - The cornstarch slurry assumes you're using soy sauce with normal salt content; if you ever swap to low-sodium soy, the slurry is still the right amount.

Sequence for the buckle situation. First wash is already dry and even, so the first-pass-dry rule is satisfied — proceed with the next pass under these controls.

A. SUPPORT + ROTATE
  - Sheet stays glued in the block. Do not press on the buckle, do not flip, do not detach.
  - If the cardboard BACK feels dry, mist it lightly with clean water (a couple of fine sprays from ~30 cm). Skip if it still holds dampness from the first wash. This nudges the sheet to relax toward the back without ever touching the painted surface.
  - Tilt the block 1–3° so the pot's light edge is UPHILL. Gravity now carries any wash AWAY from the light edge instead of toward it.
  - If the buckle lies between wall and pot, orient so the buckle becomes the LOW terminus of the wash — the bead can pool there harmlessly, well short of the light edge.

B. WATER LOAD
  - Brush holds a small bead, not a drip. One firm blot on a clean scrap edge before each pass (standing blot rule).
  - Lay the wash in 2–3 short strips rather than one broad continuous stroke, so each segment finishes before the buckle can act on it.
  - Keep pigment load modest — you can deepen value later on a dry sheet; you cannot undo a flooded buckle.

C. PRESERVE THE LIGHT EDGE
  - Paint inward 5–8 mm from the pot's light edge — the edge itself stays paper-white.
  - Hold a scrap-paper shield (NOT taped) along the light edge as you approach it; fresh strip each pass. No adhesive touches the painting sheet.
  - If a second cool pass is needed close to the edge, pre-wet a 5–8 mm band along the pot side with clean water, then paint FROM the dry side toward the wet band — the wet band acts as a stop and prevents creep onto the edge.

D. STOP CONDITIONS — any one of these fires, halt immediately
  - Bead collects in the buckle → lay a clean damp brush flat on the pool, lift straight up. Brush catch only. Once or twice; do not chase, do not press, do not scrub.
  - Wash creeps past the 5–8 mm margin toward the light edge → stop the stroke, let it feather where it lies. Do not chase it back.
  - Backrun forming, value collapsing, highlight taking color, or paper starting to fuzz → stop. Let the sheet dry fully. Reassess on a dry sheet only — no glazing, lifting, or second touch while wet.
  - Pooling keeps recurring in the same spot after two brush catches → stop the session, not just the stroke.

E. AFTER
  - Leave the block in its working tilt until the sheet is fully dry (cool to the touch, no gloss). Do not carry, flip, or detach mid-painting.
  - Sheet removal is a separate procedure performed only on a fully dry sheet, per the standing rule.

What this is not: it is not a flattening step, not a stretch-and-press, and not a rescue of the buckle itself. The buckle stays; the controls keep it from governing your wash.
