PREPARE
- Cut ~24" of single thread (not doubled — doubled shows through). Knot the tail end.

PRESS
- Iron the leg flat first to settle the fabric.
- Refold the hem along the original crease line and press firmly along the fold to re-set it. Let it cool before pinning (folds set on cooling).
- Press the folded-under allowance flat. Do not stretch or shift the hem line while pressing.

PIN
- Pin only the opened 1" span, perpendicular to the fold, every ~1/2". Pin heads out so they come out easily as you stitch.
- Leave the intact hem on both sides of the opening undisturbed.

HAND-STITCH (slip stitch / blind hem)
- Start ~1/4" inside the intact hem on one side of the opening. Anchor with 2 tiny backstitches inside the fold only (not through to the right side).
- Travel through the fold ~1/4", then catch 1–2 threads of the right-side fabric right at the fold crease. Needle enters and exits within the fold — only a thread or two of the outer layer is picked up.
- Pull thread taut, not tight. Repeat: 1/4" travel through fold, single-thread catch, 1/4" travel.
- Spacing 1/4–3/8" between catches is durable and nearly invisible. End ~1/4" past the opening, inside intact hem.

KNOT
- Take a small backstitch into the fold, pass the needle through that loop twice, pull snug.
- Trim thread close to the fold, not flush with the right-side fabric.

CHECK
- Right-side out, hold to light: only pin-pricks, no loops or bars.
- Run a finger along the hem: smooth, no visible stitches, no pucker.
- Tug the hem allowance away from the leg: stitches hold, no gap.
- Flex the hem with thumbs to simulate knee bend: no snap or shift.
- Press again from the right side through a press cloth to set the line flat.

STOP / RETHREAD IF
- A stitch shows on the right side → your catch was too deep; redo that pick-up (1–2 threads only).
- Fabric puckers → tension too tight; loosen subsequent stitches.
- Fold drifts from the original hem line → stop, re-press, re-pin before continuing.
- Thread breaks → backstitch at the break point inside the fold, then resume.

What this is, and what it is not:
- It is: a fingernail-sized hydrophobic spot on an otherwise sound sheet. Most likely a localized contaminant — fingerprint oil, waxy residue, or a trace of something that transferred during handling. The surrounding wash is going down normally, which means the sheet's sizing is intact except at the spot.
- It is not: a whole-sheet sizing failure, a fiber-lift situation, or a reason to discard the sheet. The paper is intact, the spot is local, and you stopped before doing anything irreversible.

Working principle for the whole sequence: dry, observe, test off-sheet, then decide. No abrasion. No opaque disguise. No rewetting of the spot.

Step 1 — Let everything dry as-is, untouched
- Do not touch the beaded spot with brush, finger, tissue, or anything absorbent.
- Do not add water or pigment to or near it.
- Do not extend the wall wash toward it.
- Do not blot, wick, lift, or scrub.
- Reasoning: a dry contaminant stays put; a wet one migrates. Pigment drying on top of the spot is easier to read than a half-wet one.
- Stop and advance when the wall wash meets your standing "fully dry" rule — paper feels cool, not glossy, no damp cold. At that point the spot is also dry.

Step 2 — Inspect the dried spot without abrasion
- Visual at normal viewing distance: note size, shape, edge quality, and whether the dried pigment there is lighter (bead = pigment sat on top), darker (pigment pooled at the bead's edge as it dried), or absent.
- Raking light: tilt the sheet under a window or lamp so light grazes across. Look for a raised sheen (residue film), a slight depression (sizing loss with fibers intact), or fiber disturbance.
- Magnification if you have a 10x loupe, same checklist at higher resolution.
- Do not touch. Do not breathe on it. Do not tape-lift.
- Stop condition: if inspection tempts you to press, rub, or "test" by touch, defer. The whole point of this step is to characterize the spot without altering it.

Step 3 — Run the same wash on scrap before touching the painting again
- Take a corner of the same paper, ideally the same batch or pad.
- Apply the same pigment, same dilution, same pre-wet method you used for the wall wash.
- If the scrap beads, the wash itself was off and the spot is incidental. If the scrap lays flat, your wash technique is fine and the spot on the painting is genuinely local.
- Reasoning: a one-minute scrap test separates "wash problem" from "spot problem" before you commit to any integration plan. It also gives you a control sample for what the wash looks like on clean paper at the same dilution.
- Stop condition: if the scrap test shows a wash problem, abandon the integration question for this session. The fix is the wash, not the spot, and you don't want to keep adjusting one variable while the other is unknown.

Step 4 — Pick one integration path; do not combine
  Since the spot is away from the focal object, option (a) is the most likely workable path. The other two remain available if (a) doesn't suit the composition.

  a. Paint around the spot (most conservative)
     Treat the spot as a fingernail of paper white. Continue the wall wash on either side, leaving a small halo of unpainted paper around the spot — wider than the spot itself, not touching its edge. Pigment creep toward the halo is fine; pigment reaching the spot is not, because it will bead or backrun unpredictably.
     Reads as: a small light interruption in an otherwise even wash. Reads as texture, not damage.

  b. Accept the spot's own dried character
     Leave the beaded pigment in place. Do not rewet, blend, or glaze over it on a later pass. Glaze over a hydrophobic patch will bead the same way the wash did. Limit future glazing to areas where the wash lays flat.
     Reads as: a slightly mottled or speckled patch within the wash. Reads as paper character.

  c. Stop the painting and budget for the sheet
     If the spot sits where compositional flow needs continuity, do not work around it. Let the sheet fully dry, set it aside, and accept it as a study. The sheet is preserved; the spot is recorded.
     Reads as: a held-back sheet with no further risk.

  Forbidden across all three: gouache, white or opaque paint, masking fluid, scrubbing, rewetting and blotting, sizing fluid, solvents of any kind. None of these "fix" the spot — they only disguise it or move damage around.

Step 5 — Stop conditions that end the session, regardless of which path you picked
- Paper surface lifting anywhere on the sheet — at the spot, around the wash, or in the margin. One raised fiber under raking light is the line.
- A buckle developing or worsening. If it does, mist the BACK only, never the front, and let the sheet relax flat under its own weight.
- Backruns in the surrounding wash traveling toward the spot.
- New beading or wetness rejection appearing in places that previously took the wash cleanly — a sign the contaminant is migrating.
- The integration choice starting to feel like work — if you are about to scrub, glaze over the spot, or "fix" it, you have left the conservative path. Stop, dry the sheet, reassess next session.

What to note for next session, no action now:
- Where the spot sits on the sheet (inches from a corner, or compass direction).
- What the wash was doing when it beaded: pigment, dilution, pre-wet method, brush.
- What the spot looked like dry: raking-light description in one sentence.
- What the scrap test showed.
- Which integration path (a, b, or c) you took, and why.

Why this sequence is bounded:
- No abrasion at any point — only dry, passive inspection.
- No opaque disguise — no paint, no fluid, no solvent applied to the spot.
- No silent rewriting of the plan — if the scrap test contradicts your read of the spot, the plan changes.
- Every step is reversible — the spot is either unchanged (steps 1–2) or the decision is made off-sheet (step 3) before any change happens on the painting (step 4).
- The stop conditions are named before you start, so "the paper starts to lift" is a hard boundary, not a judgment call mid-brush.

Approximate amounts (two generous plates, with a little leftover):

- Couscous: 1 cup dry + 1 cup water or broth + pinch of salt + 1 tbsp olive oil. Off-heat, cover, rest 5 min, fluff.
- Chickpeas: the whole can, drained and rinsed (~1.5 cups).
- Fennel: most of the small bulb. Halve lengthwise, cut out the core, then slice thinly across (3–5 mm). Keep a few of the feathery fronds for garnish.
- Cherry tomatoes: about 1.5 cups, halved. A few left whole looks nice.
- Garlic: 3 cloves, thinly sliced.
- Lemon: 1 whole. Juice of half goes into the dish, the other half gets cut into wedges for serving.
- Feta: ~3 oz, crumbled (about 1/3 cup).
- Olive oil: 3–4 tbsp total.
- Dried herbs: 1 tsp oregano or thyme. Fennel likes both.
- Salt, pepper.

The fennel is the part that goes wrong most often, so the technique matters.

Slice it thin, not matchstick-thin. Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low. Add the fennel with a small pinch of salt and toss to coat. Cover and cook 5–6 minutes — the steam from its own moisture is what softens it without forcing it to high heat. Don't rush this step; the cover is doing the work.

Uncover, raise heat to medium, add another tbsp of oil. Let the fennel sit undisturbed for about a minute so the edges pick up a little color, then stir. Add the sliced garlic and the dried herbs; cook 30–60 seconds until fragrant — don't let the garlic brown. Add the cherry tomatoes and a generous pinch of salt. Cook 3–4 minutes, pressing a few tomatoes with the back of a spoon so they burst and make a light sauce. Add the chickpeas and warm through for 2 minutes, just until they're coated and hot. Kill the heat.

Feta and lemon both go in off the burner, and for slightly different reasons.

Feta: if it goes into a hot pan, it melts into greasy clumps and you lose the briny-creamy bite. You want it warmed through by residual heat, not cooked. Crumble it on top of the plated dish, or fold it in after the pan has been off the heat for a minute.

Lemon: heat flattens citrus and can turn it bitter. Squeeze in the juice of half a lemon at the end, taste, then add more. The bright acidity needs to land on the finished dish, not the cooking dish.

Plating: couscous in shallow bowls, fennel-chickpea-tomato mixture on top, feta crumbled over, a few fennel fronds scattered, a small drizzle of olive oil, and a lemon wedge on the side. Black pepper at the table.

Total active time is about 25 minutes, most of it hands-off while the fennel steams. Holds well on low heat if one of you runs later — just add the lemon and feta to each plate as you serve.

Short conservative sequence for one pulled loop on the front of a washable knit, yarn intact, blunt tapestry needle on hand.

1.  Set up on a flat, well-lit surface, right side up.
    -    Reconfirm the situation: yarn continuous, no break, no hole, one loop protruding.
    -    Identify the vertical column the loop sits in.
    -    Note the stitches immediately above and below — they will look slightly tighter than the rest. That is where the loop's slack came from.

2.  Smooth the fabric with flat palms only.
    -    Stroke gently outward from the loop in all four directions.
    -    Do not pull. This is just to see the baseline tension before you touch the loop.

3.  Engage the loop from the front with the blunt needle.
    -    Slip just the tip of the needle through the center of the loop.
    -    Do not pass through the fabric body. The blunt tip protects the yarn plies.

4.  Pass the loop through to the wrong side.
    -    Push the needle (with the loop carried on it) through the smallest path to the inside — through the base of the same stitch or the nearest adjacent stitch opening.
    -    Stop as soon as the front surface lies flat. Do not pull a yarn tail, do not snug it. The goal is to relocate the loop, not tighten it.

5.  Redistribute the tension while the garment lies flat.
    -    Front side: with flat thumbs, lightly stroke up and down the affected column, several passes. Tiny nudges, no pulling.
    -    Inside (turn the garment or feel through): ease the loop into a relaxed curve along the column. If it wants to sit as a small U or S, let it.
    -    The slack should spread across many stitches, returning the column to the same gauge as its neighbors.

6.  Rest.
    -    Leave the sweater flat and undisturbed for 10–15 minutes so the yarn memory relaxes and any minor unevenness settles.

7.  Inspect before washing.
    -    Front: loop gone, no pucker, column matches its neighbors, no new distortion.
    -    Back: a small relaxed yarn curve sits along the column, not a tight line.
    -    Light horizontal stretch test on the affected column: it should rebound evenly with no new loop forming.
    -    If anything looks off, do not wash. Either repeat step 5 gently or set the garment aside.

8.  Wash only after the area lies flat and even.
    -    Inside-out, cold, gentle cycle or hand wash, lay flat to dry.

Stop conditions:
    -    If the loop resists moving to the back, leave it rather than force it — forcing can break the yarn.
    -    If a ply looks disturbed during redistribution, stop and reassess before washing.
    -    If redistribution creates a pucker or a new tight spot, ease back the opposite direction rather than compensating by pulling elsewhere.

Brothy tomato, lentil, pasta for two — using the parmesan rind if you have one is the move here, since you didn't list broth. The starchy pasta water plus a rind simmering in the pot gives you a silky, savory base without needing stock.

Approximate amounts (two generous bowls with leftovers for one):
  Olive oil: 3 tbsp, plus a small drizzle to finish
  Garlic: 3-4 cloves, sliced thin (not minced — sliced goes sweet, minced goes harsh in broth)
  Cherry tomatoes: the whole pint, halved or lightly smashed
  Dried herbs: 1 tsp (oregano/thyme/basil — whatever you have)
  Salt: about 1 tsp for the broth, then adjust at the end
  Pasta: 6 oz of the 8 oz (save the rest for another night; 8 oz will drink all your broth)
  Lentils: the whole can
  Pasta water: reserve a big mug before draining
  Spinach: 3-4 handfuls
  Lemon: half to start, more to taste
  Parmesan: a small wedge for shaving on top; if you have a rind, throw it in the broth

Rinse the lentils. Canned lentil liquid is starchy and inconsistently salted across brands, and it will muddy a brothy bowl. Drain, rinse under cool water, drain again. You lose a little flavor but you gain a clean, tomato-forward broth and control over the seasoning.

Method, roughly:
  1. Salt a large pot of water and bring it to a boil for the pasta.
  2. In a wide pot or braiser, warm the 3 tbsp olive oil over medium-low. Add the sliced garlic and a pinch of salt; cook gently until just turning gold at the edges. Don't brown — browned garlic turns a bright tomato broth bitter.
  3. Add the tomatoes and herbs. Raise heat to medium. Press a few with a spoon and cook 5-7 minutes until they soften and release their juice — you want a chunky, juicy base, not a smooth sauce.
  4. Add about 5 cups of water and the parmesan rind (if you have one). Season with the teaspoon of salt. Simmer 5-10 minutes to let the rind give up its umami.
  5. Cook the pasta in the salted water until just shy of al dente. Scoop out a big mug of pasta water, then drain.
  6. Add pasta and rinsed lentils to the broth. Simmer 2-3 minutes together so the pasta finishes and drinks some broth flavor. Loosen with splashes of the reserved pasta water if it tightens up — you want it to look like a shallow lake, not a stew.
  7. Fish out the rind. Kill the heat.

How to keep the bowl bright:

  Spinach: stir it in AFTER you turn off the heat. The residual broth wilts it in about 30 seconds, leaves it vivid green and just tender. If you simmer it, it goes gray, slimy, and loses that fresh note you bought it for.

  Lemon: squeeze it in off heat, right at the end, to taste. Start with half a lemon — citrus volatiles cook off fast, so lemon simmered into broth turns flat and almost metallic. Off-heat, it lifts everything: tomato, lentil, the oily sheen. Add more if it still tastes heavy.

  Parmesan: use a Microplane, not a box grater. You want fluffy, snow-like parm that melts into the broth instead of clumpy shreds that sit on top. Shave it over each bowl — a light snow, not a blanket. A heavy hand is the fastest way to make a brothy supper feel like a casserole. Finish each bowl with a small drizzle of good olive oil and a crack of pepper.

Skip the parmesan rind if you don't have one — the dish still works, just slightly less savory depth. If you do have one, it is doing more work here than any broth would.

Stop working the wet area now, and let it dry.

"Correcting it makes the surface stiff" is the paper already telling you the surface fibers have been disturbed. A small lift on a damp wash that has already been worked tends to do one of two things: lift pigment without removing the disturbance (so you get a paler stiff spot), or lift the fibers themselves and make the surface fuzzier than the surrounding wash. Either outcome is worse than a dried bloom for keeping the onion reading as papery and alive. The standing rule still holds: stop further lifting, don't scrub, don't re-wet the spot.

Once the wash dries fully, re-evaluate from normal viewing distance in the same light. A bloom where two pale onion skins overlap often reads as a natural soft transition once dry — it can actually be optically correct, because onion skins do shift tonally where they meet. The "problem" may have been a wet-stage reaction to a feature that belongs in the finished painting.

If the dried bloom still reads wrong, then yes — granulating pigment around it, not over it. Two ways that keep the surface alive:

  1. Lay a thin granulating mix (a touch of French ultramarine, or raw/burnt sienna into a cool blue-gray) into a wet edge just *outside* the bloom, letting it settle inward by a millimeter or two. Granulation settles into the paper tooth and creates adjacent texture without you touching the already-disturbed fibers. The bloom becomes the negative shape the granulation defines, which keeps the onion form-revealing rather than texture-revealing.

  2. Or, when the area is bone-dry, use a controlled drybrush of the same pigment mix *next to* the bloom to sharpen the boundary you want. This is a deliberate edge, not a fix of the bloom itself.

Either way, never re-wet the stiff spot. If you eventually need a value shift there, glaze with a thin cool mix on a barely damp (not wet) brush once the area is fully dry, and only on the edges that still read too soft.

One meta-note for the next onion study, not today's: where two pale shapes overlap on damp paper, blooms at the overlap are almost inevitable. Painting the overlap zone slightly drier than the surrounding wash, or leaving a thin dry gap between shapes so the second shape lands on dry paper, usually prevents it without changing the look. Worth a controlled test next block — but for today's piece, the recovery path is dry, then granulate around, not wet lift.

    Hold one glass under warm running tap water and gently wipe the filmed area with a soft cloth or your thumb.
      -  Film lifts / washes away  ->  residue or hard-water deposit; the dishwasher is a plausible cause. Continue to steps 2-4.
      -  Film does NOT lift, or feels rough/pitted and stays put under running water  ->  likely permanent etching. STOP on the appliance side here. Etching is glass chemistry (typically soft water + alkaline detergent + heat over time), not a dishwasher fault. No cleaner, cycle change, or filter work will remove it. The only remedies are lowering detergent dose, lowering water temperature or final-rinse heat, or replacing the affected glasses. Do not start treating the dishwasher.

2.  Detergent check (verify state only, do not change yet)
    -  Confirm the dispenser cup actually opened last cycle (no undissolved tablet sitting in a closed cup, no clump blocking the spring latch).
    -  Confirm dose matches your water hardness and load size. Over-dosing is the most common cause of cloudy film that won't rinse clean; if you have soft water, you're probably using too much.
    -  Do not switch brands or add detergent until steps 3 and 4 are done.

3.  Rinse-aid check
    -  Open the rinse-aid dispenser. If the in-door indicator window reads empty, fill to the marked line with standard automatic-dishwasher rinse aid.
    -  If your model has an adjustment dial, leave it at the factory default (usually 2-3). Don't turn it up as a first move.
    -  If you deliberately don't use rinse aid, skip this step and just note the current state.

4.  Removable filter only
    -  Pull only the user-removable filter per your model's manual (usually a coarse flat screen at the bottom of the tub, twist-out).
    -  Rinse it under warm tap water. Use a soft brush (an old toothbrush is fine) on the filter mesh only.
    -  No soap, no abrasive pads, no scrubbing the tub, door, or spray arms.
    -  Re-seat the filter and confirm the quarter-turn lock is fully engaged before the next run. A filter that didn't fully lock on prior cycles can also leave film because recirculated wash water gets dirtier.

Stop conditions (do not cross):
    -  No abrasive cleansers or scrub pads on the glasses, tub, door, or filter.
    -  No vinegar or citric-acid "cleaning cycle" yet. Re-run a normal cycle first and check the same two glasses.
    -  Do not treat cloudiness that survived Step 1 as a dishwasher defect.

Next cycle, check the same two glasses:
    -  Clear or noticeably less filmed  ->  residue/rinse-aid related; the dishwasher is functioning.
    -  Identical to before  ->  the glasses are etched; the dishwasher is not at fault.

Also not changing: the dishwasher filled, washed, drained, and dried normally with no leak, cabinet moisture, electrical odor, smoke, unusual heat, or error indicator. None of those symptoms are present, so this is a film/chemistry question only, not a service-call question.

Read of what you have: the ferrule-to-handle joint has lost its grip, but the bristle bundle, ferrule body, and crimp edge still look intact. That means the fault is at the handle end of the ferrule, not the bristle end, and the bristles are not yet contaminated by wicking. Most likely cause: the internal glue bond has failed or the wood handle has shrunk slightly inside a seamless/crimped ferrule. Either way, water reaching the gap is the main long-term risk — it can swell the handle, corrode the ferrule interior, or wick into the bristle bundle.

  Dry inspection (1–2 minutes, no water)

    1. Visual at the joint. Hold the brush at eye level under good light. Look for: a visible dark line or step at the ferrule-handle seam; glue residue, dust, or dried pigment in the gap; any distortion, crack, or uneven crimp at the ferrule edge; rust specks anywhere on the ferrule.
    2. Light rotational check. Pinch the ferrule between thumb and forefinger and the handle between the other hand. Rotate the ferrule gently around the handle. Note: smooth free-spinning = internal bond gone; gritty/notchy = debris inside; firm resistance with no movement = bond still partly intact.
    3. Light tap test. Hold the brush horizontal, bristle away from you. Tap the butt end of the handle once, gently, against the heel of your other hand. Listen and feel: a faint single click at the seam = loose joint; a hollow rattle or double-tap = the handle has separated inside the ferrule (retire — internal separation cannot be fixed without adhesive).
    4. Bristle-side check. Look at the ferrule-to-bristle junction. Confirm bristles still sit flush, no shine or moisture line on the inside of the ferrule, no pigment creeping up under the crimp.
    5. Pull test, very gentle. Hold the bristles end with one hand and the handle with the other. Apply a slow, steady, light pull along the axis — no yanking. Any telescoping movement of the handle out of the ferrule means the bond is effectively gone.

  Low-stress wet test (only if all of the above are clean)

    Use scrap paper only — not the painting sheet. Pre-wet only the bristle tip, no deeper than the ferrule, by dipping and then pinching off excess on a scrap edge. Make three or four short strokes on scrap. Then hold the brush bristle-up for 30 seconds and watch the ferrule-handle seam for any moisture wicking up to it. Blot, dry, and inspect the seam again.

  Retirement conditions — retire the brush if any one of these is true

    - Any bristle shedding during the dry inspection or the wet test.
    - Any moisture reaches the ferrule-handle seam during the wet test.
    - The tap test produces a hollow rattle or double-click.
    - The handle telescopes at all under the gentle pull test.
    - The rotational check shows smooth free-spinning with no resistance.
    - Visible rust, pitting, swelling, distortion, or pigment creep at the crimp edge.
    - Any visible movement, splay, or shift in the bristle bundle during use.
    - The seam gap visibly widens, the handle slides further, or you notice it under normal handling again later.

    Per your standing rule, no adhesive at the bristle end and none proposed for the handle end either — a ferrule-handle repair without a proper ferrule press and the right gap-filling adhesive tends to fail and can let solvent or adhesive wick into the bristles. If it retires, it retires; do not patch.

  If everything above is clean, it can sit as a backup under these limits

    - Used only for low-stakes passages — washes, large soft areas, or pigment pickup — never for fine detail where hand feel matters.
    - Bristle-dip only, never soak. No bristle-down rest in water; use a brush rest or lay it flat.
    - Dry bristle-side up between uses; reshape while damp, not wet.
    - Re-inspect with the dry checklist above before each use. The first sign of widening seam, bristle shift, or any retirement trigger means it stops being a backup.
    - Storage: cool, dry, horizontal or hanging bristle-down is fine; avoid humidity swings, which will only widen an already-loose joint.

    This is a judgment, not a clearance. The brush is on probation the moment the ferrule shifts at all, and the probation ends the first time any trigger above appears.

The cast shadow on the linen.

Before any reflection work, check whether the cast shadow is actually telling you the spoon's turn: how high the bowl sits off the cloth, which way it's tilted, and whether it's convex-up or convex-down. If the shadow reads as a flat dark blob directly under a flat shape, the spoon will look pasted on no matter how carefully you paint the highlights — the reflections will just decorate the lie. A correct cast shadow should shift in softness and density (harder and darker right under the rim/contact edge, softer and lighter as it stretches away) and its shape should describe the bowl's angle, not just its footprint.

Once the cast shadow is doing that job, the next check is the value break across the bowl — the terminator where the lit curve turns into shadow inside the concavity. That break is what makes reflections sit *on* a three-dimensional form rather than *on* a sticker. If the terminator is in the wrong place, too soft, or missing, reflections will keep flattening the turn even after the shadow is fixed.

In short: shadow first (anchor + tilt), then terminator (concavity + value structure), then reflections.

Edge test first, then gentle roll-lift only if clean. Stop on any fiber pickup or surface change.

1. Edge test (lowest risk). On the outermost 1–2 mm of the patch, touch a clean, dry, slightly tacky rubber pickup (or a clean fingertip — dry, no lotion) to the fluid. Roll once, don't drag. Inspect both the fluid fragment and the paper. If the rubber/finger comes away with any paper fiber, fuzz, or pigment, stop. Do not continue on the patch.

2. Work the patch only if the edge test was clean. Anchor the sheet flat (block taped to cardboard back, as established). Starting from the edge nearest the open paper, lift the fluid with the same rolling motion — peel, don't scrub. Move inward in small increments. Keep the angle shallow and the pressure light; let the rubber do the work.

3. Tiny residue. If a faint film remains in the paper tooth, leave it. Don't chase it with an eraser, kneaded rubber, brush, water, or solvent — all of those abrade cold-press or disturb the wash.

Stop conditions (any one ends the attempt):
- Fiber, fuzz, or pigment on the rubber or finger
- Surface tooth visibly disrupted, pilling, or thinning
- Fluid resists and starts to drag instead of releasing
- Any edge of the surrounding wash lifting or feathering

If the edge test fails, the fluid can stay indefinitely on a dry sheet — it's not time-sensitive. Reassess later or leave it.

Kibo's profile matches the July 2024 tick event: one small attached tick, no systemic signs, normal behavior. That one resolved with a clean removal, a small 4 mm pink bump at day ~5, and a dry scab at day ~10 — no vet call. The same conservative path applies here, with explicit thresholds so you know when to escalate.

Supplies
  - Fine-tipped tweezers (you have them)
  - Clean sealable container — small vial, jar, or zip bag
  - Rubbing alcohol (isopropyl) OR a slightly damp cotton ball
  - Mild antiseptic wipe (chlorhexidine 0.05% or povidone-iodine diluted to weak tea color)
  - Phone camera, ideally with a coin or ruler for scale
  - Optional: nitrile/latex glove, paper towel

Pre-removal evidence — photograph it IN PLACE first
  - Take one photo of the tick on Kibo's shoulder with a coin or ruler next to it for scale. This captures engorgement state, approximate species (Lone Star female has a single white dot; American dog tick has whitish marbled scutum; blacklegged/deer tick is small and dark), and body condition.
  - Note the time found, the walk location if relevant, and which shoulder. You don't need to identify the species before removal — removal timing matters more.
  - This is not a substitute for vet ID; it's a record in case symptoms develop later.

Removal — fine-tipped tweezers, mouthparts at the skin
  1. Glove up if you have one. Tick fluids carry pathogens that affect humans too (especially Lone Star and American dog ticks). Direct skin contact is avoidable.
  2. Part the fur so you can see the skin at the bite point. Do not stretch the skin taut.
  3. Grasp the tick with the tweezer tips as close to the skin as you can — at the mouthparts, not the body. Squeezing the body can push gut contents into the bite and increase pathogen transmission.
  4. Pull straight up with steady, even pressure. The pull often takes 30-60 seconds of constant force. That is normal — do not jerk or increase force abruptly.
  5. Do not twist, "unscrew," or wiggle. Twisting is the most common cause of retained mouthparts.
  6. After the tick releases, inspect the bite. A small dark dot may remain (mouthpart fragment). Do not dig for it. Mark the spot mentally; most fragments work themselves out over a few days.

Do NOT use
  - Petroleum jelly, nail polish, essential oils, soap, heat (match/lighter), or freezing in place. These can cause the tick to regurgitate into the bite or delay removal, both of which raise transmission risk.

Specimen / photo preservation
  - Photo option (often sufficient): photograph the removed tick on a white paper towel with the same coin/ruler, dorsal view (top) and if possible ventral view (gently flip with tweezers — do not crush). Save with date.
  - Specimen option (preferred if you want a backup for species ID): drop the tick into a small vial with rubbing alcohol, OR into a zip bag with a barely damp cotton ball. Label with date, dog, body location. Store in the freezer. Keep at least 30 days; discard when no symptoms have emerged.
  - Pathogen testing of the tick itself is generally not a useful clinical decision (false reassurance, false alarm). Your vet's patient is Kibo, not the tick. The specimen is for ID, not diagnosis.
  - This is not authorization to mail the tick to a lab or to base treatment on tick-test results.

Site cleaning
  - Wipe the area once with the diluted antiseptic. Do not scrub, soak, or pour alcohol directly on the skin (stings, can inflame the bite).
  - Do not apply antibiotic ointment preemptively. Small puncture wounds close faster dry.
  - Do not bandage routinely. If Kibo is licking persistently, a brief cover is reasonable — at the shoulder, a small sock pinned to a harness strap or a snug shirt leg works better than tape. Take it off for air after an hour or two. An e-collar is the most reliable option if licking continues.

Expected local course (this is normal, no call needed)
  - A few-millimeter raised bump, pink or skin-colored, sometimes with a dry scab center. The 2024 site followed this pattern at day 5 and was dry and clean by day 10.
  - Brief, mild attention to the area for 1-3 days is common.

Local signs that warrant a vet call (today or tomorrow — not necessarily urgent)
  - Expanding redness beyond ~5 mm, especially with a target or bull's-eye appearance (raised ring, clearer center)
  - Spreading redness without a target shape
  - Increasing swelling, warmth, or tenderness
  - Drainage, pus, or crusting that worsens past day 3
  - A lump at the site that grows past ~1 cm or persists past 2 weeks
  - Visible mouthpart fragments that remain red, swollen, or draining past 48-72 hours

Systemic signs — watch for ~30 days (most tick-borne illness shows 2-14 days; some longer)
  Call the vet (routine, next available appointment):
  - Lethargy, dullness, less interest in walks or play
  - Appetite drop; skipping more than one meal
  - Fever signs: panting at rest, warm ears/paws, shivering
  - Limping, joint stiffness, shifting-leg lameness, reluctance to rise
  - Vomiting or diarrhea (single mild episode can be watched; repeated or bloody is not)
  - Unusual bruising or pinpoint red dots on gums or belly skin
  - Any unexplained behavior change

Same-day vet or urgent care
  - Hindlimb weakness or wobbly gait that progresses (tick paralysis is rare but real; more often with engorged females; reversible with prompt removal only if caught early)
  - Difficulty breathing
  - Collapse or unresponsiveness
  - Repeated vomiting, bloody stool, or severe lethargy
  - Sudden facial swelling, hives, or pawing at the face (allergic reaction, separate from disease transmission)

Regional note (informational, not a claim about this tick)
  - In central/east Texas and the south-central US, Lone Star ticks are common and aggressive. Females carry a single white dot. They can transmit ehrlichiosis, tularemia, and STARI; they are also associated with alpha-gal syndrome in humans. In dogs, alpha-gal–type reactions are less documented but worth mentioning to the vet if Kibo develops unusual GI or skin symptoms after red meat in the coming weeks.
  - No tick-borne vaccine exists for dogs. Kibo's tick-preventive status is not in your file — if he is not currently on one, that's a next-visit conversation, not a tonight decision.

What this is NOT
  - Not a Lyme test. Do not request bloodwork tonight; testing is symptom-driven, geography-driven, and species-driven, and a negative right now would not be informative.
  - Not antibiotic prophylaxis in itself. A single doxycycline dose after a high-risk Ixodes bite is a vet decision (and only in Lyme-endemic areas with confirmed >36-hour attachment); it is not a home call.
  - Not authorization for any new medication, supplement, or diet change tonight.
  - Not a guarantee that no disease was transmitted — most tick bites do not transmit, but none can be ruled out by removal alone. The 30-day watch is the operative window.

Closing
  - Removal tonight is the right call. Transmission risk for most pathogens rises with attachment time, but the 24-48-hour rule is approximate and species-specific — earlier removal is simply better than later.
  - Save the pre-removal photo, the post-removal photo, and the freezer specimen. After 30 days of normal behavior, normal appetite, and a clean healing site, you can discard the specimen and close the watch.
  - No vet visit is needed tonight unless any of the urgent-systemic signs above appear.

What this most likely is
- Local inflammatory/fibrous reaction to tick saliva or residual mouthpart material.
- Common after tick removal. Can take several weeks to flatten. Not infected unless local signs change.

Why this is not, on its own, Lyme / anaplasma / ehrlichia / RMSF
- Those illnesses present systemically — shifting-leg lameness, fever, lethargy, inappetence, joint swelling — typically weeks to months later, not as a localized 4 mm bump at day 8.

- Routine post-bite bumps are not diagnostic of tick-borne disease; that requires a 4Dx snap test (or equivalent), which only your vet can run.

- Leave it alone. No scrubbing, picking, squeezing, or topical ointments.
- No preventive antibiotics — not indicated by what's described.

- New or visibly expanding redness around it.

- Bump grows noticeably, softens, or becomes fluctuant.
- A target / bull's-eye appearance develops.
- New bumps appear elsewhere.

- Shifting-leg lameness or reluctance to bear weight on a leg.
- Lethargy or reduced interest in walks / play beyond his normal.
- Appetite drop lasting more than a meal.
- Feverish behavior (warm ears, panting at rest, seeking cool surfaces).
- Vomiting, diarrhea, or any unexplained bleeding or bruising.

Urgent / ER if
- Sudden breathing trouble.
- Collapse, pale gums, or any sign of acute distress.
- Rapidly spreading swelling of the face or muzzle (rare anaphylaxis-type reaction).

Compact, preservation-safe phone workflow — private portfolio record

Setup (about 5 minutes)
- Light: indirect natural light from a north-facing window, or shaded daylight from another window. Direct sun off. Room lights off if they would cast a color cast.
- Surface: clean, flat table covered with a neutral mid-gray background (mat board, gray paper, or an 18% gray card) larger than the painting.
- Painting: place flat, image up. If the sheet curls, set clean smooth weights (ceramic tile, a smooth glass weight) on the gray mat at the corners only — never on the paper. Handle by the edges or with clean dry hands.
- Phone: rear camera, flash off, lens wiped. Lock exposure (AE-L) and focus (AF-L) once the painting is in place. Set white balance to Daylight or Cloudy.

Parallel camera placement
- Position the phone directly above the painting so the lens axis is perpendicular to the paper plane. Use a small tripod, clamp mount, or a balanced stack of books. No tilt.
- Frame the full sheet with a small border (about 1–2 cm) of gray mat visible around all four edges. Do not crop the paper's edges.

Glare checks
- Take one test frame. Inspect for hot spots, sheen, or banding, especially in light passages or any slightly glossy area. Cotton paper's tooth can catch light at certain angles.
- If glare appears: shift the painting a few centimeters, adjust the window shade, or rotate the camera 2–5° in plane (still parallel). Repeat until clean.
- Optional: clip-on circular polarizing filter on the phone lens; rotate until reflections drop without dimming the colors.

Color-neutral reference
- Place an 18% gray card or small color checker in the same plane as the painting, lit by the same light. Capture one reference frame with the card beside (not on) the painting.
- Use this frame to set white balance and exposure in post. Keep it with the portfolio record.

Full-sheet image
- Lock AE/AF and white balance from the gray card or from the painting.
- Capture one full sheet. Verify on screen: pinch to zoom on a corner and on the center to confirm focus and exposure.

Detail frames (three to four)
- For each detail: move the phone — not the painting — so the chosen area fills roughly 70–80% of the frame. Keep the same lens distance and angle. Re-lock AE/AF. Capture.
- Choose details that record edge quality, value transitions, color mixing, or brushwork you want preserved in the portfolio.

After capture
- Verify each frame on screen: focus, exposure, color neutrality against the gray card, no shadows from your hand or the phone.
- Handle the painting by edges only.
- Return it to its sleeve or folder. Do not apply tape, adhesive, glass, mounting corners, or any surface treatment to the paper.

What this is not
- Not a reproduction for exhibition, sale, or print.
- Not a substitute for a calibrated ICC-profile capture — the color checker frame is reference, not full profiling.
- Not a multi-light or copy-stand setup; one window source is enough for a private record.

Not shippable. The method section violates four standing rules and reads like a checklist of how not to write one. Specifics, then a redraft.

1. "Run for seven days. Check the primary conversion result each day."

   Seven days is a calendar window, not a sample size. Daily reads mean repeated significance tests on accumulating data; the false-positive rate inflates well above the nominal 5%. The day-7 read is the first read, not confirmation.

2. "If treatment reaches p<0.05 on any daily read, stop and roll out."

   This is the first-significance-without-stabilization pattern we've explicitly rejected. The Growth checklist work is the canonical case: first cohort +0.7 pp / p=.04 (n=1,184), stabilization cohort +0.2 pp / p=.31 (n=1,262). A first hit alone is not authorization to ship.

3. "Effect-size reporting is optional."

   Effect size travels with the hypothesis stack and is visible before any ship discussion. Making it optional is the mechanism that hid the +0.7 to +0.2 pp shrinkage in the checklist case.

4. "No separate stabilization cohort is planned."

   The stabilization cohort is what turns an early read into something actionable. Removing it eliminates the only check between a noisy first hit and a rollout.

The method section is also missing four items that belong in any ship-ready writeup:

  - Cohort definition (eligibility, exclusion, exposure)
  - Hypothesis stack with primary metric and expected effect-size magnitude
  - Sample-size or power basis for the stabilization cohort
  - Pre-registered decision rule distinguishing first-significance, stabilization-confirmation, and observation-not-shippable

Suggested redraft of the method section:

  "Run the experiment for a pre-registered window against a pre-specified cohort, primary conversion metric, and minimum detectable effect. Report the day-7 read as a first read only: cohort, n, observed effect size with point estimate and CI, p-value, and a check of whether effect-size direction and magnitude match the hypothesis stack. Do not ship on first significance. After the first read, run a pre-specified stabilization cohort of adequate size and power to confirm the effect. A ship recommendation requires the stabilization cohort to replicate direction and magnitude, with effect size reported in both reads. If the first read is significant but the stabilization cohort does not replicate, the result is exploratory and does not support rollout."

Recommended next step: send Growth the redraft plus a short note that first-significance-without-stabilization is not a conservatism preference, it is the specific failure mode the checklist work surfaced. Ask them to come back with cohort, hypothesis stack, stabilization-cohort design, and a pre-registered decision rule before the test launches, not after.

Methodological conflicts in the Growth team's draft method section:

1. Predeclared metric and powered window — not stated. The draft sets a 7-day runtime and a daily primary-conversion check, but does not predeclare the primary metric, the minimum detectable effect, the required sample size per arm, or the analysis window required to reach it. Runtime is calendar-based, not power-based.

2. Effect size with the hypothesis stack — marked optional. Without a predeclared decision-relevant effect size, a significant p-value cannot be distinguished from a result large enough to act on.

3. Ship on first significance — the draft rolls out on the first daily read at p<0.05. This treats first significance as a ship signal rather than as a flag for stabilization-cohort confirmation.

4. Stabilization cohort — none planned. No held-out or replication cohort, no observation beyond the test window, no confirmation step before rollout.

5. Peeking structure compounds the above. Daily primary-result checks on a 7-day calendar window with a stop-and-roll-out rule at p<0.05 inflate the false-positive rate and bias the observed effect size upward — exactly the conditions under which first significance is least trustworthy.

These are method issues only. The product hypothesis is not being addressed here.

"Remove the stop-and-roll-out rule on the first daily read at p<0.05. First significance is a directional flag, not a ship decision. Interim significance should route to the stabilization cohort, not to production."

WINDOW-SHADOW STUDY — THUMBNAIL SEQUENCE
Palette: ultramarine, burnt sienna, yellow ochre. No additions. Working method is value separation, not added orange.

1. VALUE SEPARATION TEST (thumbnail)
   - Paint three swatches on scrap: cool mid, warm wood tint, cool dark.
   - Rule: the warm wood tint must dry a FULL VALUE STEP LIGHTER than the cool mid. Do not compensate with more pigment or extra orange.
   - Cool mid = ultramarine diluted to a clean middle value.
   - Warm tint = yellow ochre + a touch of burnt sienna, kept thin and clearly lighter than the cool mid.
   - Re-check at the five-minute mark: warm loses chroma as it dries; if the dried warm edge still sits clearly below the cool mid in value, separation holds.

2. RESERVING THE WARM EDGES
   - Cool wash goes down first. Dry. Then the warm pass.
   - Two ways to reserve — pick one and stay with it:
     a) Leave the wood edge paper-white; lay the thin warm glaze next to it after the cool wash dries.
     b) Lay a thin warm tint first, then reserve a paper-white highlight inside it for last.
   - Either way: warm pass is noticeably thinner than the cool wash — pigment load is the warmth lever, not saturation.
   - Do not mask. Use clean water and a clean brush to keep the narrow wood edge crisp if a hard transition is planned.

3. MIXING THE COOL DARKS
   - Base is ultramarine, dominant.
   - Add burnt sienna in small increments to neutralize toward a deep cool neutral — test on scrap, stop the moment the mix tips brown or warm.
   - Yellow ochre stays out of the cool dark unless a slight green-cool is wanted; never use it to "warm" the dark passage.
   - Verify on scrap: the dried cool dark should read cooler than the cool mid by one to two value steps, not as a different hue.

4. EDGE HIERARCHY CHECK (before committing final dark passages)
   - Three tiers, in this order of attention:
     - Hardest edge: focal transition — usually where the cool shadow meets the warm wood. Protect it; do not let it bleed soft.
     - Soft / lost edges: peripheral shadow fading to paper. Leave them soft; do not crisp them later.
     - Reserved paper: the brightest wood highlight. Untouched until last, if at all.
   - Rake-eye test on the thumbnail: does the warm edge still read after the cool wash is dry? If yes, proceed. If it has been absorbed or muddied, widen the value step before going larger.

STOP CONDITION
- Stop before any second pass on the warm edge. One thin glaze only.
- Stop before reworking a hard edge wet-on-wet. If crispness is lost, dry and re-establish with a clean brush; do not chase it.
- Stop before darkening the cool dark beyond a clean two-step drop from the cool mid. Going further flattens the value map and erases the wood-edge separation.

NOT THIS — not a finished painting, not a study of reflected-light temperature, not a value-ladder beyond three zones. The thumbnail's only job is to confirm the warm edge survives drying against the cool wash, so the final dark passages can be committed without second-guessing.

DRY-FLATTENING — 9×12 watercolor, curl along two edges, paint intact

Preconditions (verify before starting):
- Paint film fully dry (cool, not glossy), no flaking, lifting, tackiness, or pigment-transfer risk.
- Hands clean and dry. Work area clean, rigid, level, out of direct sun and exterior-wall heat. Stable room (≈65–72°F, normal indoor humidity).

Materials:
- Rigid flat base: clean glass, smooth melamine shelf, or acid-free foam board.
- Interleaving: one sheet of archival glassine or acid-free tissue, cut slightly larger than the painting.
- Cover board: second rigid flat board (foam board or mat board), clean and dry.
- Light distributed weight: a few clean flat books or a smooth weight, ~5–10 lb total over the 9×12 area (under ~1 psi). No point loads.

Sequence:
1. Place the painting FACE UP on the rigid base. Painted side up.
2. Lay the glassine/tissue interleaving over the entire painted face.
3. Set the cover board on top of the interleaving — flat, no overhang that could lever the sheet.
4. Add the light distributed weight across the cover board, not on the sheet's edges directly.
5. Leave undisturbed 24–48 hours.
6. Lift cover board and interleaving. Inspect: is the curl reduced? Paint intact? Any new cockle, tide line, pigment transfer, or surface change?
7. If curl is reduced and paint is clean and dry: optional second 24–48 hour cycle to settle further. If curl persists after two cycles, treat as essentially flat-set.

Stop signals — remove weight and interleaving, lift sheet gently by opposite corners, do not re-stack:
- Pigment transfer onto the interleaving.
- Tide line, bloom, moisture mark, or color shift anywhere on the sheet.
- Surface lifting, scuff, abrasion, or fiber pick on the paint film.
- New cockling, limpness, or waviness in the sheet body (interleaving trapped humidity — rule out any nearby humidity source before retrying).
- Tackiness or visible softening of the paint film.

When to leave the sheet alone:
- A faint residual edge curl with paint fully intact and no further reduction after two cycles is preferable to continued manipulation. Final flatness, if needed, comes from matting with a window mat — not more weight.
- Any stop signal: stop. Do not resume until the cause is identified and addressed.

What this is NOT:
- Not a wash, stretch, or rehumidification. No water contacts the sheet.
- Not a heat or steam relax. No iron, hair dryer, heater, kettle, or bathroom steam.
- Not a face-down press. Weight always sits on the cover board over interleaving — never directly on the painted face, never on the back while the face is unprotected.
- Not a substitute for a paper conservator if the curl persists alongside any risk sign, or if the sheet has value beyond practice.

What the estimate itself shows:

  - Preventive examination and cleaning: $0.00 patient responsibility — covered as a standard preventive benefit.
  - Fluoride treatment: $38.00 patient responsibility — listed as a separate line with a non-zero patient share.

The $0 vs. $38 split is itself informative. Insurers price fluoride as a separate service; it is not bundled into a routine cleaning. Listing it on the estimate with a positive patient share means the plan is treating it as a non-covered (or not-preventive) service in this case, not as part of the $0 preventive package.

What this typically means for adult fluoride at a routine cleaning:

  - Most dental plans cover topical fluoride for children up to a stated age (often 14 or 18) and exclude it for adults.
  - Adult fluoride at a routine visit is, in the great majority of cases, presented as an optional or elective add-on. The dental office may recommend it based on risk factors (caries history, dry mouth, recession, sensitivity, recent restorations), but the patient declines or accepts.
  - A $38 patient share is consistent with a typical non-covered adult topical-fluoride fee, not with a covered preventive service the plan is paying in full.

So the estimate, read on its face, is consistent with an elective add-on rather than a required part of the visit.

What the estimate does not establish:

  - Whether the dentist's clinical recommendation for you specifically is "should have," "must have," or "optional." That is a clinical call tied to the exam findings, caries risk, and any active conditions — not something the estimate, the plan's default rules, or I can settle.
  - Whether your specific plan has any exception (e.g., adult fluoride covered only with a documented caries-risk diagnosis, or a plan rider) that would lower or zero the $38. Estimator systems only apply the plan's default rules; they do not adjudicate medical-necessity overrides.
  - Whether the office requires informed consent or a signed decline if you choose not to have it.

Why the request fails the method:

1. Primary was predeclared. The whole point of declaring the primary metric and minimum effect before launch is that the team cannot shop the primary after exposure. Three days of data is still exposure. Editing the primary now is the failure mode the new method was built to prevent — same shape as Growth's earlier draft that called for stopping on first daily p<0.05.

2. "Either primary" inflates the test. Promoting a secondary to co-primary and shipping on whichever one crosses is roughly 1 − (0.95)² ≈ 9.75% per-decision false-positive rate rather than the 5% the method protects. It's a different test, not a more flexible one. Calling it "co-primary" doesn't restore the protection; only a single predeclared primary does.

3. 3 of 21 days is not the powered read. 3/21 ≈ 14% of the window. A favorable secondary pattern over three days is consistent with noise in either direction. Powered inference lives at the end of the 21-day window (close ≈ August 3).

What stays:

- Declared primary metric and minimum effect remain in force.
- The 21-day run continues unchanged. No mid-flight design edits.
- Secondary completion stays secondary. It can be reported alongside, used for context, and as a hypothesis-generator for a future test. It is not a ship gate under this method.
- At close, evaluate the predeclared primary against the predeclared minimum effect using the predeclared decision rule. That is the only result that decides ship/no-ship.

If completion is genuinely the more interesting measure, the correct next step after a null primary is a new, separately scoped, predeclared test with completion declared as the primary before launch — not a retroactive reclassification of the live run.

Pre-flight framing: this is a checksum-mismatch incident, not a date-provenance finding. Byte-level divergence tells you the local working copy is no longer the master; it tells you nothing about when P027 was taken. The catalog date stays "April 1994 Portland garden outing, exact day unresolved" regardless of what you find.

PHASE 0 — FREEZE BOTH COPIES
  Goal: no verification step can mutate either file.
  Do:
    - Stop any process holding either file open (viewers, sync clients, indexers, AV).
    - Do not open either file in any tool that writes metadata on read.
  Don't:
    - Copy, rename, "fix," or re-save either file yet.
  Prevents: a verification tool silently rewriting EXIF/XMP/IPTC and then being mistaken for evidence.

PHASE 1 — READ-ONLY CHECKSUMS + METADATA
  Goal: confirm the mismatch and capture current byte identity.
  Do:
    - sha256sum on the cloud master; sha256sum on the local working copy.
    - Compare each to the stored cloud checksum.
    - In a dated incident note, record for each file:
        filename (confirm unchanged on both sides per your frame)
        freshly-computed sha256
        bytes
        mtime, ctime, atime (informational only)
        any separable metadata-block hash if present
  Don't:
    - Treat larger size, newer mtime, or more recent access time as authoritative.
      Timestamps are observable, not evidentiary.
  Expected outcome: cloud fresh-hash matches the stored cloud checksum; local fresh-hash does not. If cloud fresh-hash also fails to match, the incident pivots upstream and Phase 4 needs to widen.

PHASE 2 — QUARANTINE THE LOCAL COPY WITHOUT MODIFYING IT
  Goal: get the divergent bytes off the master name without touching them.
  Do:
    - mv the local file to a non-master incident-evidence name encoding date + mismatch, e.g.
      P027_local_working_mismatch_2027-07-24.tiff
    - sha256sum the renamed file; confirm hash unchanged from Phase 1.
    - Leave the working-copy path empty until Phase 5.
  Don't:
    - Copy-then-delete (can touch mtime; loses original on-disk identity).
    - Use any name containing "master" or "verified" for the quarantined file.
    - Put it back under the master name even temporarily.

PHASE 3 — CAUSE INVESTIGATION (READ-ONLY)
  Goal: explain why the local copy drifted, without using that explanation to assert anything about the date.
  Likely candidates, rough order:
    - viewer/editor wrote metadata on save (most common; small byte delta, metadata block grows)
    - partial save, crash recovery, or sync conflict resolved in place
    - a re-encoding copy path (cloud-to-local through a tool that touched color profile or thumbnail)
    - AV or backup touching atime/ctime only — rules itself out if hashes differ
  Do:
    - diff the local metadata block against the cloud's, if separable, without modifying either
    - check viewer/sync/backup logs that touched the working-copy path
  This is a file-identity investigation, not a date investigation. P027's catalog date is unchanged regardless of the cause.

PHASE 4 — EVIDENCE THAT ESTABLISHES THE PRESERVATION MASTER
  Goal: name the test that lets you call one copy master without defaulting to either.
  Evidence that DOES establish the cloud master:
    (a) Strongest. A contemporaneous checksum log from the original preservation
        scan whose recorded value matches the cloud file's freshly-computed
        sha256. If it matches, the cloud copy is the master; the local copy is
        the divergent working file. Run this first.
    (b) Provenance showing the cloud upload predates any plausible local
        modification event, combined with the local file having no equivalent
        provenance of its own.
    (c) An independent third copy (external drive / offline medium from the
        original scan session) whose freshly-computed sha256 matches the cloud
        copy. Independent corroboration.
  Evidence that does NOT establish master, even if it feels persuasive:
    - newer mtime on the local file (mtimes can be touched)
    - larger size on the local file (consistent with a metadata write, not with authority)
    - visual inspection (subjective; doesn't establish byte identity)
    - opening "successfully" on another machine (proves readability, not identity)

Method-only judgment on the Growth team's three-part question.

On retaining the fully backfilled interval in the original denominator:

Retain. Three conditions are met: (a) assignment logs remained complete, so exposure status is not gap-affected; (b) the delay was symmetric across both arms, so the contrast is unbiased even if individual event timing within the interval is off; (c) the declared primary metric has no missing events after backfill, so the metric definition and denominator are unchanged. The 45-minute window is a transport/latency incident in the ingestion pipeline, not a coverage or assignment incident. As long as backfill is verifiably complete and delayed events are restored with their original session timestamps (not synthetic batch times), the interval stays in the original denominator. The power cost is a property of the run, not a reason to drop observations.

On documenting the delay as reliability evidence:

Yes, required. The incident belongs in the audit trace as reliability evidence: incident window, both-arm scope, root cause, backfill completion timestamp, verification that no primary-metric events are missing post-backfill, and the method decision to retain. This is what lets a later reader distinguish "no incidents" from "no recorded incidents." The documentation is bounded -- it does not authorize a metric change, a denominator change, a reweighting, or a language upgrade. It is evidence, not license.

On the condition that would justify different treatment:

Different treatment (excluding the interval, restricting the denominator, or reweighting) is warranted only if at least one of the following is true post-backfill:

  - Backfill is incomplete or unverifiable for any primary-metric event in the window.
  - Backfill completeness differs by arm, in which case the contrast is biased and the interval cannot be retained symmetrically.
  - The metric definition was implicitly altered by backfill (events reclassified, session windows redefined, event-time replaced with ingestion-time).
  - The delay created a selection mechanism (sessions that would have produced the primary event during the window churned, were filtered, or were assigned a different identity before backfill, so the backfilled set is not the would-be observed set).
  - The primary metric depends on a downstream analytic step that requires strict real-time event ordering the delay broke (e.g., a sequential eligibility guardrail).

Any one of those converts "transport delay with successful backfill" into "coverage failure with partial recovery," at which point exclusion is no longer a post hoc cut but a method-consistent treatment aligned with how prior instrumentation breaks have been handled.

What this is not:

  - Not a ship recommendation. The read at the predeclared powered window remains the read.
  - Not authorization for a favorable post hoc cut (excluding only the arm with unfavorable direction, or only sessions where the primary metric moved against the hypothesis).
  - Not a basis for changing the declared primary metric, the minimum effect, the powered window, or the stabilization cohort.
  - Not a basis for re-classifying the run as "cleaner than expected."

Method decision: retain + document. Run continues under its existing bounds.

ADJACENT DARK GLAZES, DRY SHEET — COMPACT SEQUENCE

Bead control (off-sheet calibration, before either passage)
  - Load brush; tap once on palette rim to settle the bead. Tilt: bead holds, no drip.
  - Test stroke on scrap or palette towel: continuous advancing front, no flood, no skip.
  - Reload drier if bead floods; reload wetter if it skips. Do not adjust on the study sheet.
  - One confident pass per passage. Do not return to fix an edge.

Moisture check 1 — sheet readiness (before passage 1)
  - Back of hand 1 inch above sheet: no cool spot, no sheen, room-temp and matte.
  - If any sheen or coolness, wait. Do not start.

Passage 1
  - Lay from dry starting edge to the stop line. Brush stops; clean soft edge forms at the stop line.
  - Lift. Do not return. Do not tilt to chase. Leave undisturbed — no fan, no tilt.

Drying order (passage 1 must finish drying before passage 2 begins)
  - Passage 1 dries fully first.
  - Passage 2 begins only after the drying gate passes; its wet edge stops before reaching passage 1.
  - Both passages then dry undisturbed together.

Moisture check 2 — drying gate (before passage 2)
  - Surface matte AND back of hand 1 inch above passage 1 reads the same as the surrounding dry sheet — paper cool, not glossy (same definition as the prior edge-dry study).
  - If any sheen or coolness remains, wait. "Looks dry" is not the test.

Moisture check 3 — bead recalibration (before passage 2)
  - Brush charge drifts during the wait. Recalibrate on the test strip before approaching passage 1.

Passage 2
  - Start at the far edge; advance wet edge toward passage 1.
  - As the bead closes to within ~3–5 mm of the dried passage-1 edge, slow and watch: bead should sit as a thin advancing line, not climb or wick toward passage 1.
  - End passage 2 with a clean wet edge that stops 1–2 mm short of passage 1. Do not let the two wet edges touch.

Stop signals (stop, do not chase)
  - Bead climbs or wicks toward passage 1 → bead is too wet; reload drier, do not paint on.
  - Pigment pools at the approach line → stop, lift, let that edge dry, do not push through.
  - Passage 1 still cool or glossy at the drying gate → sheet was not truly dry; restart with a drier sheet, not a wetter brush.

What this is not
  - Not a wet-on-wet or glaze-over-wet technique. Sheet stays dry throughout; underlayer must be fully dry.
  - Not a scrub, lift, or scratchback. No reworking, no return.
  - Not a fixable mistake. One bead, one pass per passage; distinct by dry margin between the two.

What carries forward from prior studies
  - Dry definition: paper cool, not glossy, back-of-hand confirms.
  - Bead rule: settle off-sheet, one confident pass, no return.
  - New constraint specific to adjacent glazes: do not let wet edges touch — leave a dry margin between them.

FRAMING

Our reading this week keeps returning to two distinctions that are easy to conflate. The first is between labor that goes unseen and a failure that is treated as personal — the difference between a household, an institution, or a family record absorbing the work, and a single person being held to account for what the structure around them actually produced. The second is between being formally recognized for that work and the redistribution of responsibility that would make recognition unnecessary. Recognition names a person; redistribution changes who is asked to do what. The book gives us chances to sit with both, and tonight I'd like us to stay inside the gap between them rather than close it.

QUESTION 1 — Invisible labor vs. individual failure

Where in the book does a character absorb responsibility for an outcome that the surrounding structure actually produced? What changes in that scene if we hold the structure accountable and read the character's response as something other than personal failing — habit, loyalty, exhaustion, or the absence of any other name for what is happening to them?

QUESTION 2 — Formal recognition vs. fair redistribution of responsibility

The book offers at least one moment where a character's contribution is acknowledged — named, credited, apologized to, or made visible. After that acknowledgment, does the underlying division of labor shift, or does recognition land on top of an unchanged arrangement? What does the text seem to think recognition is actually for — repair, or something closer to absolution that lets the original distribution stay in place?

QUESTION 3 — Whose ledger counts

A third tension runs quietly alongside the other two: who is permitted to keep the accounts. Which characters in the book get to define what counts as contribution, and which are entered into a record they did not author? What does it cost a character — in the story's terms, not ours — to be defined by someone else's ledger rather than their own description of the work?

Compact glaze sequence — transparent cool over a dry shadow mass

Pre-checks
- First wash must be bone dry: back-of-hand cool, no gloss, no tack. Any sheen → wait.
- Sheet flat, not cockled.

1. Test swatch first
   - Same paper (scratch sheet or margin), same cool pigment, same water ratio, same brush.
   - One confident pass on dry paper; let dry fully.
   - Confirm: value lifts about a half step, edge feathers clean, no tide line.
   - Adjust load here, not on the study.

2. Glaze mix
   - Same cool pigment family as the shadow. Goal is deeper cool, not warmer cool.
   - No orange. No complement. Thin the mix so the glaze darkens by value, not hue.
   - Brush: damp, not beaded. Pigment holds in the tip without drip.

3. Planned stopping edge
   - Stop the glaze 1.5–2 mm short of the warm wood edge. That margin is the buffer — do not paint into it.
   - End the pass inside a damp area of the shadow, not at a hard paper boundary, so the trailing edge feathers as it dries back.
   - The dry margin is what prevents the tide line: pigment settles inward from the edge instead of piling on it.

4. One pass only
   - Single confident stroke path across the shadow mass.
   - No return strokes, no tilting, no chasing, no scrubbing, no wet-edge contact with the warm edge.
   - If a bead climbs or pools at the stopping edge, touch it once with a thirsty brush tip — do not work it.

5. Full dry before evaluation
   - Cool to the back of the hand, no gloss anywhere on the sheet.
   - Then read the value gap. Stop. No third pass, no softening pass, no signature, no frame this session.

Value-separation check after dry
- Warm wood edge should still read a full value step lighter than the glazed shadow.
- If the gap closed, the glaze was too heavy or drifted warm — note it for next sheet; do not fix on this one.

Stop signals (any one → halt)
- Bead climbing the stroke
- Pooling at the stopping edge
- Residual coolness or gloss on the first wash or the glaze
- Tide line forming as the glaze dries
- Any urge to retouch the warm edge from the glaze side

This is a glaze, not a re-paint. One controlled change per session; evaluate after the second pass dries.

SEQUENCE — Lost and Found Edge on a Dry Ceramic / Shadow Boundary

1. Confirm full dry. Cool to touch, no gloss on either side. If either is even slightly cool or dewy, wait.

2. Mark the lost/found boundary. Light pencil tick or a dry-brush dot where the edge behavior changes. Decide before loading.

3. Small value test. Same paper, same pigment, dried beside the painting. Aim one step darker than the dry shadow mass — wet reads darker than dry, so judge at dry.

4. Recalibrate off-sheet. Bead climbing = too wet, no flow = too dry. Both are stop signals.

5. LOST section — extend the shadow into the ceramic without scrubbing it:
   a. With a clean damp brush (water only), wet a 2–3 mm band INSIDE the shadow mass, stopping exactly at the ceramic. Do not cross the edge.
   b. Load the brush with the test-confirmed shadow mix.
   c. One confident pass into the wet band. Let capillary carry the last half-millimeter onto the ceramic. No return stroke, no tilt chase, no second pass.
   d. If the edge lifts, beads climb, or orange bleeds: stop, dry fully, reassess.

6. FOUND section — keep the ceramic crisp:
   a. Do not wet near this segment.
   b. Hold the brush back 1–2 mm from the ceramic so the existing dry shadow stops short.
   c. If the dry shadow already meets the edge, leave it alone — the crispness comes from not disturbing it.

7. Stop signals: bead climbing onto ceramic, glossy pooling, edge lift, orange bleed, return-stroke tide marks. Any one → stop, dry fully, reassess.

8. Full dry before judging. Cool, no gloss. The lost edge will deepen and the found edge will read crisper once adjacent value sets. If the lost edge sharpens on drying (it often does), repeat 5a–5d with a slightly wetter brush on the shadow side only — never on the ceramic.

Why the constraints hold:
  - No lifting: rewetting stays on the shadow side; the ceramic is touched only by the last half-millimeter of capillary carry, not by the brush.
  - No scrubbing: one pass per segment, no return strokes.
  - No orange boost: cool pigment rides a narrow wet bridge over a dry ceramic layer; the cool volume is small and the orange underneath stays in place.

Centered symmetry with nearly equal margins reads as arranged — the eye registers the pattern before the subject, which is what "decorative" means here. Offsetting the window left and letting the right mass sit heavier and unbroken breaks the symmetry and shifts the composition from deliberate to observed. Quiet is what asymmetric balance produces when neither mass is decorated.

What protects the quiet in #2:

  - The right shape has to stay a single dark field. If you modulate it into a gradient, add internal detail, or texture it, it stops being quiet and starts being a thing — competing with the window instead of holding the composition.
  - The boundary between the two masses is the entire tension. A single clean vertical (or a slightly angled cut) keeps the value separation sharp; a softened or wandering edge reintroduces decoration because the eye starts reading along it.
  - Two clear value masses is restraint. Three or more becomes visual storytelling; two is stillness.

One thing to check on the sheet itself: how each shape resolves at its boundaries. If both masses terminate cleanly rather than trailing into each other, the composition holds. If one trails into the other, the quiet breaks.

The visible speckle is yellow ochre's heavy particles dropping into the cold-press tooth before the wash can carry them off. Three independent knobs quiet this — thinner pigment ratio, a water-heavy brush load, and a steeper board angle so the wash flows across the tooth instead of sitting and settling. None of them require scrubbing, lifting, or pushing the mix stronger.

  Test swatch (same paper stock, same brush)

  1. Mix fresh at roughly 1 part yellow ochre to 8–10 parts water — visibly
     thinner than tea, closer to pale cider. Pre-hydrate 60–90 seconds so the
     particles are fully suspended before loading.
  2. Pre-wet the brush fully, blot once on a clean towel, then load so the
     belly is water-heavy, not pigment-heavy. The brush should drip, not bead.
  3. Hold the board at roughly 30–35° (steeper than flat, well short of
     vertical). One continuous pass top-to-bottom on a 2×3" scrap.
  4. No return strokes. Lay flat to dry, no heat.

  If the dry swatch still shows ochre caught in the tooth, the mix is still
  too heavy — drop to 1:12 and retest before touching the passage.

  Apply to the passage

  1. Same ratio that tested clean, same brush, same 30–35° angle.
  2. One continuous pass top-to-bottom in a single confident stroke; load
     the brush fully enough to finish the passage without a mid-stroke reload.
  3. Hold the angle until the sheen just dulls, then lay the board flat.
     No tilt-back, no return stroke, no second pass.
  4. Leave undisturbed until fully dry. The cold-press tooth keeps the
     quiet, transparent value on its own; any added water or pigment pushes
     it back toward orange.

  Stop signals

  - Bead climbing or pooling mid-pass — mix still too heavy or brush
    under-loaded. Stop, remix thinner, retest on scrap.
  - Sheen gone before the stroke finishes — reload came too late. Stop,
    remix, restart on fresh scrap.
  - Visible ochre drop on drying — ratio was right but angle was too
    flat; add one more degree of tilt on the next test.

  What this is not: a lift, a scrub, or a re-wash. If the dry passage still
  reads too cool or too pale after this sequence, the next move is a
  second fully dry pass at the same ratio on top — not a rework of the
  first wash.

Short answer: the bounded recommendation is to leave it. It's in a pale margin, off the focal edge, fully dry, and undamaged — and a faint construction line is almost always less visible than the paper-tooth disturbance a careful erase will leave behind, especially on cold-press. Once erased, you can't undo that, and the disturbance can telegraph through a later wash or a mat.

If you decide the line still bothers you after living with it on the dry sheet, the fail-safe sequence is:

1. Soft kneaded eraser only. No vinyl, plastic, or gum eraser — they're too aggressive on watercolor paper and will crush the tooth.
2. Pinch a fresh clean corner. A kneaded eraser picks up graphite, paper fibers, and any surface pigment residue; a used face redeposits all of it.
3. Test first on an expendable margin of the same sheet, or on a scrap from the same pad if one is available. Stop if the surface pills, fluffs, or shows a visible "polished" patch.
4. Dab, don't rub. Touch, lift, rotate to a clean face, touch again. No strokes, no pressure, no direction.
5. Stop signal: any visible change in paper texture, any hint of pigment lift, or any spreading of the graphite (which means the eraser face is dirty or the pressure is too high). Stop immediately.
6. No moisture, ever. Water, a damp brush, or breath on the spot will migrate graphite into the surrounding pale wash and into the paper's tooth in a way you cannot recover.
7. Reassess on the dry sheet under raking light after 10–15 minutes. Paper-tooth disturbance reads more clearly after the surface has settled.

What this is not: it isn't permission to chase the line with multiple passes, escalate to a firmer eraser, or address a second line while you're at it. One line, one fresh eraser face, one dab, one reassessment — then either it's gone or it's staying.

Compact, conservative sequence:

1. Visual gate (decide first, don't touch yet).
   - View at normal reading distance under the light you'll exhibit under.
   - Is the line actually pulling the eye away from the subject? If no, stop. Leave it. A line you only notice under a loupe is not a distraction.
   - If yes (or "yes, and it's in a focal area"), proceed to step 2.

2. Low-pressure test only.
   - Test off the artwork first: a clean, damp (not wet) brush tip, then a clean dry brush, then a barely-damp rubber pickup — one pass each, no scrubbing.
   - On the painting, work from the edge of the line nearest open paper (away from any wash), shallow angle, light pressure, one rolling pass. No return strokes. No rewetting over the line itself.
   - Re-judge only after that single pass has fully dried.

3. Stop signals (any one = stop, do not escalate).
   - Cold-press surface resists — tooth visibly disrupted, fiber lifting, pilling, or a pale halo where pigment was anchored into the texture.
   - Edge softens instead of cleaning (you're dissolving, not lifting).
   - Surrounding wash begins to lift or feather.

If any stop signal trips, leave the line. A faint ruled line ages more gracefully than a scrubbed patch on cold-press.

One pass, fully dry, then judge. Not before.
